events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1809, the first stone was laid for the Gloucester and Cheltenham Tramroad, which was the first 'guided bus' passenger wagonway in England. This development marked an important step in the evolution of public transportation.
events.name: First stone laid of Gloucester and Cheltenham Tramroad

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1809, British diplomat Benjamin Bathurst mysteriously disappeared in Perleberg, near Berlin. His disappearance, which may have involved foul play, sparked considerable intrigue and speculation in diplomatic circles.
events.name: Benjamin Bathurst mysteriously disappears

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1809, American physician Ephraim McDowell performed the first successful ovariotomy, removing a 22-pound tumor from a patient. This groundbreaking surgery marked a significant advancement in medical practice and women's health.

image.caption: Portrait of Ephraim McDowell.
image.credit: P. H. Davenport — http://ihm.nlm.nih.gov/images/B29869
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the surgeon associated with the ovariotomy; the portrait’s date is unknown, though it was published before 1900. It is not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ephraim McDowell performs first ovariotomy

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1809, a British invasion force departed from Vlissingen, Netherlands, as part of the ongoing military campaigns during the Napoleonic Wars. This operation was aimed at disrupting French control in Europe.
events.name: British invasion force leaves Vlissingen

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1809, the city of Boston, Massachusetts, enacted a ban on wearing masks at balls, reflecting societal concerns about anonymity and potential misconduct during social gatherings. This regulation was part of broader efforts to maintain public order.
events.name: Wearing masks at balls forbidden in Boston

events.enhanced_description: In 1810, Major-General Lachlan Macquarie was officially appointed as the Governor of New South Wales. His tenure was marked by significant reforms and developments in the colony, shaping its future.
events.name: Major-General Lachlan Macquarie becomes Governor of New South Wales

events.enhanced_description: In 1810, Napoleon Bonaparte dissolved the Kingdom of Holland, which had been ruled by his brother Louis, and annexed it into the French Empire. This action was part of Napoleon's broader strategy to consolidate power in Europe.
events.name: Napoleon dissolves the Kingdom of Holland

events.enhanced_description: In 1810, Russia acquired Sukhumi through a treaty with the Abkhazian dukes, declaring a protectorate over the entire region of Abkhazia. This acquisition was part of Russia's expansionist policies in the Caucasus.
events.name: Russia acquires Sukhumi

events.enhanced_description: In October 1810, King George III of the United Kingdom was deemed permanently insane, leading to the establishment of the Regency. This marked a significant shift in British governance as his son, George, Prince of Wales, took on the role of Prince Regent.
figures: George III of the United Kingdom
events.name: King George III deemed permanently insane

events.enhanced_description: In 1810, Amadou Lobbo initiated a jihad in present-day Mali, aiming to establish a purer form of Islam and to combat local traditions that he viewed as corrupt. This movement significantly influenced the religious landscape of the region.
events.name: Amadou Lobbo initiates jihad

events.enhanced_description: In 1810, notorious pirates Ching Shih and Cheung Po Tsai surrendered their fleet to the Chinese government, marking a significant moment in the fight against piracy in the South China Sea. Their surrender led to the integration of former pirates into the imperial navy.
events.name: Ching Shih and Cheung Po Tsai surrender

events.enhanced_description: In 1810, a significant quantity of 4,500 chests of opium was sold in China, reflecting the growing trade in opium that would have profound social and economic impacts on Chinese society in the years to come.
events.name: Opium sold in China

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1810, Australian seal hunter Frederick Hasselborough discovered Campbell Island, a remote subantarctic island known for its unique wildlife and harsh weather conditions. This discovery contributed to the knowledge of the region's geography and ecology.
events.name: Discovery of Campbell Island

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1810, the marriage between Napoleon Bonaparte and Joséphine de Beauharnais was annulled, primarily due to Joséphine's inability to produce an heir. This event marked a significant turning point in Napoleon's personal life and political ambitions.
events.name: Annulment of Napoleon and Joséphine's Marriage

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1810, after a series of military successes, Napoleonic troops, commanded by General Horace Sebastiani, entered Málaga, solidifying French control over southern Spain during the Peninsular War. This event was part of the broader conflict against Spanish resistance.
events.name: Napoleonic Troops Enter Málaga

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1810, Napoleon Bonaparte issued a decree declaring Rome the second capital of the French Empire, reflecting his ambitions to expand French influence in Italy. This decision was part of his broader strategy to consolidate power in Europe.
events.name: Napoleon Declares Rome as Second Capital

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1810, Tyrolean rebel leader Andreas Hofer was executed in Innsbruck after leading a resistance against French and Bavarian forces during the Napoleonic Wars. His execution became a symbol of the struggle for Tyrolean independence.
events.name: Execution of Andreas Hofer

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1810, Napoleon Bonaparte married Marie-Louise of Austria by proxy in Vienna, a strategic alliance aimed at strengthening ties with Austria. This marriage was significant for consolidating Napoleon's power and securing an heir.
events.name: Napoleon Marries Marie-Louise by Proxy

events.enhanced_description: In April 1810, King Kaumualii of Kauai received assurances regarding the continued independence of the Kingdom of Hawaii, amidst the growing influence of foreign powers in the Pacific. This event was significant for the sovereignty of Hawaii during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Kaumualii Receives Assurance of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1810, Napoleon Bonaparte married Marie-Louise of Austria in person in Paris, solidifying their political alliance. This marriage was crucial for Napoleon's dynastic ambitions and his relationship with the Habsburgs.
events.name: Napoleon Marries Marie-Louise in Person

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1810, the people of Caracas removed Vicente Emparán, the Governor of the Captaincy General of Venezuela, and established a Supreme Junta, marking Venezuela's first step towards independence from Spanish rule. This event was pivotal in the South American independence movements.

image.caption: Martín Tovar y Tovar’s painting depicting the Battle of Carabobo.
image.credit: Martín Tovar y Tovar — Capitolio Nacional de Venezuela.
image.date_qualification: The depicted battle is dated 1821; the painting’s image date is recorded as between 1821 and 1887. Neither date is the 1810 event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Venezuela Achieves Home Rule

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1810, Ludwig van Beethoven composed his famous piano piece, Für Elise, which has since become one of the most recognized and beloved pieces in classical music. The piece exemplifies Beethoven's unique style and emotional depth.

image.caption: First page of the first edition of Beethoven’s Für Elise, reproduced in Ludwig Nohl’s publication.
image.credit: Ludwig van Beethoven/Ludwig Nohl — Ludwig Nohl: Neue Briefe Beethovens, Stuttgart 1867, S. 28
image.date_qualification: Dated 1810/1867 in the supplied metadata; the image description identifies the 1867 publication. The dates do not establish a photograph or manuscript made on 27 April 1810.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Beethoven Composes Für Elise

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1810, Macon's Bill Number 2 was enacted in the United States, aiming to motivate Britain and France to cease the seizure of American vessels during the ongoing Napoleonic Wars. This legislation reflected the growing tensions between the U.S. and European powers.
events.name: Macon's Bill Number 2 Becomes Law

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1810, Lord Byron famously swam across the Hellespont, a feat that symbolized his romantic ideals and connection to classical literature. This event became a celebrated moment in Byron's life, reflecting his adventurous spirit and poetic legacy.
events.name: Lord Byron Swims Across the Hellespont

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1810, Rev. Henry Duncan opened the world's first commercial savings bank in Ruthwell, Scotland. This innovative institution aimed to encourage savings among the working class and laid the groundwork for modern banking practices.
events.name: First Commercial Savings Bank Opens

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1810, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe published his influential work Zur Farbenlehre (Theory of Colours), which presented his theories on color perception and aesthetics. This work challenged Newtonian views and contributed to the fields of art and science.
events.name: Goethe Publishes Theory of Colours

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1810, the May Revolution took place in Buenos Aires, where armed citizens expelled Viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros and established the Primera Junta, marking a significant step towards Argentine independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: May Revolution in Buenos Aires

events.enhanced_description: In June 1810, Nicolas Appert published L'art de conserver pendant plusieurs années toutes les substances animales ou végétales, detailing the first modern methods of food preservation using airtight containers. This work laid the foundation for the canning industry.
events.name: Nicolas Appert Publishes Food Preservation Techniques

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1810, Argentina's new junta published the country's first newspaper, the Gazeta de Buenos-Ayres, edited by Mariano Moreno. This publication played a crucial role in disseminating revolutionary ideas and information during the independence movement.
events.name: First Newspaper Published in Argentina

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1810, John Jacob Astor formed the Pacific Fur Company, aiming to establish a fur trading network in the Pacific Northwest of North America. This venture marked a significant development in the American fur trade and westward expansion.
events.name: Formation of the Pacific Fur Company

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1810, Napoleon dissolved the Kingdom of Holland, which had been ruled by his brother Louis Bonaparte, and annexed it into the French Empire. This action reflected Napoleon's consolidation of power and control over Europe.
events.name: Dissolution of the Kingdom of Holland

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1810, Frederick Hasselborough discovered Macquarie Island, another subantarctic island known for its unique biodiversity and geological features. This discovery added to the understanding of the region's ecological significance.

image.caption: NASA Earth Observatory satellite image of Macquarie Island.
image.credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Wanmei Liang, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey — https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/151568/a-waypoint-in-the-southern-ocean
image.date_qualification: Satellite image of the island, not a depiction of its 1810 discovery. Image date: 2022-02-08.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Discovery of Macquarie Island

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1810, a junta of seven patriots, led by José Acevedo y Gómez, assembled in Bogotá to declare independence from the Spanish Empire, marking a significant moment in Colombia's struggle for freedom.

image.caption: Flag of the United Provinces of New Granada.
image.credit: Racso — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image metadata gives 2008-01-20; this is not the depicted flag’s date. The flag description identifies it with 1811 and 1814, after the 1810 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Patria Boba in Bogotá

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1810, Paraguay governor Bernardo de Velasco and the Cabildo of Asunción declared their loyalty to Ferdinand VII of Spain, severing ties with Buenos Aires. This declaration reflected the complex political dynamics in the region during the independence movements.
events.name: Paraguay Declares Loyalty to Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1810, royalist troops slaughtered 200 citizens in the Royal barracks and surrounding streets of Quito, Ecuador, during a violent crackdown on independence movements. This tragic event highlighted the brutal repression faced by those seeking freedom from Spanish rule.
events.name: Massacre in Quito

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1810, the city of Santa Cruz de Mompox in modern-day Colombia declared its independence from the Spanish Empire, joining the wave of revolutionary movements sweeping across Latin America during this period.
events.name: Santa Cruz de Mompox Declares Independence

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1810, during the Battle of Grand Port, French forces defeated a Royal Navy frigate squadron attempting to blockade a harbor on Isle de France (modern-day Mauritius). This victory was significant for French naval power in the Indian Ocean during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Battle of Grand Port

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1810, Jean Baptiste Bernadotte, a Marshal of France, was elected Crown Prince of Sweden by the Swedish Riksdag of the Estates. This unexpected choice marked a significant shift in Swedish royal lineage and influenced the country's future alliances and politics.
events.name: Jean Baptiste Bernadotte elected Crown Prince of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1810, the ship Tonquin departed from New York Harbor carrying 33 employees of John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company. After a challenging six-month voyage around South America, the ship reached the mouth of the Columbia River, where Astor's men established the fur-trading settlement of Astoria.

locations.name: New York Harbor, New York, United States

events.name: The Tonquin sets sail

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1810, Miguel Hidalgo, a Catholic priest in Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato, issued the Grito de Dolores, calling for the revolt that would ignite the Mexican War of Independence. This pivotal moment marked the beginning of a struggle for independence from Spanish colonial rule.
events.name: Grito de Dolores

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1810, Chile established its First National Junta, marking a crucial step towards independence from Spanish rule. This assembly laid the groundwork for Chile's eventual declaration of independence and the formation of a national government.
events.name: Chile forms its First National Junta

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1810, Argentine leader Manuel Belgrano began preparations for an invasion of the Provincia del Paraguay. This military action was part of the broader struggle for independence in South America against Spanish colonial forces.
events.name: Manuel Belgrano prepares invasion of Paraguay

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1810, the Republic of West Florida declared its independence from Spain. This brief republic was established by American settlers and lasted only a few months before being annexed by the United States.
events.name: Republic of West Florida declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1810, the Riksdag of the Estates in Sweden adopted a new Act of Succession, officially making Jean Baptiste Bernadotte the heir to the Swedish throne. This decision solidified Bernadotte's position and influenced the future of the Swedish monarchy.
events.name: Act of Succession adopted in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1810, the first Oktoberfest was held in Munich, Bavaria, celebrating the marriage of Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria to Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen. This festival has since evolved into a major cultural event, attracting millions of visitors each year.
events.name: First Oktoberfest

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1810, the United States formally annexed the Republic of West Florida, which had declared independence from Spain just weeks earlier. This annexation was part of the U.S. expansionist policies in the early 19th century.
events.name: United States annexes Republic of West Florida

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1810, a peace treaty in Haiti confirmed the division of the country between the northern State of Haiti, ruled by Henri Christophe, and the southern Republic, led by Alexandre Pétion. This division reflected the ongoing struggles for power and governance following the Haitian Revolution.
events.name: Peace treaty in Haiti confirms division

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1810, Sweden declared war on the United Kingdom, marking the beginning of the Anglo-Swedish War (1810–12). This conflict was part of the broader Napoleonic Wars and reflected Sweden's shifting alliances during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Anglo-Swedish War declared

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1810, British forces successfully invaded Isle de France (now Mauritius), forcing the French garrison to surrender. This event was part of the British campaign to control key territories during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Invasion of Isle de France

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1810, Manuel Belgrano crossed the Paraná River into the Itapúa Department, initiating his military campaign against Spanish forces in Paraguay. This action was part of the broader struggle for independence in South America.
events.name: Manuel Belgrano crosses the Paraná River

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1810, the British ship of the line HMS Minotaur was wrecked on Texel in the West Frisian Islands, resulting in the loss of approximately 500 lives. This tragic incident highlighted the dangers faced by naval vessels during this period.
events.name: HMS Minotaur wrecked

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1810, the chartered British East Indiaman Elizabeth was wrecked off the coast of Dunkirk, resulting in the loss of more than 360 lives, many of whom were lascar seamen. This disaster underscored the perilous nature of maritime trade during this era.
events.name: East Indiaman Elizabeth wrecked

events.enhanced_description: In September 1811, Nathan of Breslov led the first annual Rosh Hashana kibbutz (pilgrimage) of Breslov Hasidim to the grave of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov in Uman, Ukraine. This event has become a significant tradition in the Hasidic community.
events.name: Rosh Hashana kibbutz of Breslov Hasidim

events.enhanced_description: In January 1811, explorer David Thompson reached the mouth of the Columbia River, where he encountered Fort Astoria, a trading post being constructed by the Pacific Fur Company. This moment marked a significant point in the exploration and settlement of the Pacific Northwest.
events.name: David Thompson reaches the mouth of the Columbia River, finding Fort Astoria under construction

events.enhanced_description: In 1811, the Red River Colony was founded in what is now Manitoba, Canada. This settlement became a significant site for the fur trade and played a crucial role in the development of Western Canada.

image.caption: Engraving of the Protestant Church and Mission School in the Red River Colony.
image.credit: C. Heath — https://www.flickr.com/photos/lac-bac/31142651300/in/album-72157677492475586/
image.date_qualification: Depicts a site within the Red River Colony, not the colony’s 1811 founding event. Image date is given as between 1820 and 1840.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Red River Colony is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1811, French chemist Bernard Courtois discovered iodine while extracting sodium from seaweed. This discovery would later have significant implications in medicine and chemistry.
events.name: Iodine discovered by Bernard Courtois

events.enhanced_description: In 1811, Jane Austen published her first novel, Sense and Sensibility, which received critical acclaim and established her as a prominent author in English literature. The novel explores themes of love, social class, and the role of women in society.
events.name: Publication of Sense and Sensibility by Jane Austen

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1811, Charles Deslondes led an unsuccessful slave revolt in St. Charles and St. James Parishes, Louisiana. This uprising was one of the largest slave revolts in U.S. history and highlighted the growing tensions surrounding slavery in the southern states.

locations.name: St. Charles Parish, Louisiana, United States
St. James Parish, Louisiana, United States

events.name: Charles Deslondes leads slave revolt

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1811, during the Mexican War of Independence, a heavily outnumbered Spanish force of 6,000 troops achieved a decisive victory against nearly 100,000 Mexican revolutionaries at the Battle of Calderón Bridge. This battle underscored the challenges faced by the independence movement.
events.name: Battle of Calderón Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1811, the Casas Revolt began in San Antonio, Spanish Texas, as a response to the oppressive colonial rule. This revolt was part of the broader context of independence movements in the Americas.
events.name: Casas Revolt begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1811, George, Prince of Wales, became Prince Regent due to the perceived insanity of his father, King George III of the United Kingdom. This marked the beginning of the Regency era, during which the Prince Regent exercised royal powers.
figures: George III of the United Kingdom
events.name: British Regency established

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Gebora, fought on February 19, 1811, was a significant engagement during the Peninsular War where French forces under Marshal Édouard Mortier decisively defeated a larger Spanish army near Badajoz. This battle showcased the tactical prowess of the French despite being outnumbered.
events.name: Battle of the Gebora

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1811, the Citadel Massacre occurred in Cairo, where Muhammad Ali, the Ottoman governor of Egypt, ordered the execution of the last Mamluk leaders, effectively ending their power in Egypt. This brutal act was part of his efforts to consolidate power and modernize the state.
events.name: Citadel Massacre in Cairo

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Barrosa, fought on March 5, 1811, was a crucial engagement during the Peninsular War where an Anglo-Portuguese-Spanish force successfully repelled a French attack aimed at lifting the Siege of Cádiz. This battle highlighted the resilience of the allied forces against the French.
events.name: Battle of Barrosa

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Lissa, occurring on March 13, 1811, saw the British fleet achieve a significant victory over the French navy. This battle was part of the broader naval engagements during the Napoleonic Wars, demonstrating British naval superiority.
events.name: Battle of Lissa

events.enhanced_description: Presented on March 22, 1811, the Commissioners' Plan for Manhattan laid out a grid plan for the development of New York City, establishing the street layout that still largely defines the city today. This plan was a pivotal moment in urban planning history.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The Commissioners' Plan for Manhattan

events.enhanced_description: The Great Comet of 1811 was discovered on March 25, 1811, by French astronomer Honoré Flaugergues. It became one of the most observed comets of the 19th century, noted for its spectacular tail and brightness.
events.name: Discovery of the Great Comet of 1811

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Anholt, fought on March 27, 1811, was a naval engagement where the British Navy defeated Danish forces. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Napoleonic Wars.

image.caption: War monument in Anholt By.
image.credit: Peter Grosen — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of a monument commemorating the battle, not a contemporary depiction of the fighting. Original image date: 2017-07-01 11:39:36.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Anholt

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1811, Henri Christophe was proclaimed King Henri I, establishing the Kingdom of Haiti in the northern part of the island. This marked a significant moment in Haitian history following its independence from France.
events.name: Henri Christophe proclaimed King Henri I

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1811, revolutionary riots erupted in Buenos Aires as tensions escalated against Spanish colonial rule. These riots were part of the broader movement towards independence in South America.
events.name: Revolutionary riots in Buenos Aires

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1811, Paraguay declared its independence from the Spanish Empire, a significant step in the broader independence movements across Latin America. This declaration was officially recognized on May 15.
events.name: Paraguay declares independence

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Albuera, fought on May 16, 1811, was a significant engagement during the Peninsular War where Spanish, Portuguese, and British forces united to defeat the French army. This battle was crucial in maintaining the allied presence in the Iberian Peninsula.

image.caption: Thomas Sutherland and William Heath’s retrospective illustration of Marshal Beresford disarming a Polish officer at La Albuera.
image.credit: Thomas Sutherland y William Heath. — David Brass Rare Books
image.date_qualification: The image date is 1815, not the battle date of 16 May 1811.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Albuera

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Las Piedras, fought on May 18, 1811, marked the first significant victory for the independentists of Uruguay against Spanish colonial forces. This battle was a pivotal moment in Uruguay's struggle for independence.
events.name: Battle of Las Piedras

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1811, a volcanic eruption in the Azores briefly created Sabrina Island. This geological event was part of the ongoing volcanic activity in the region.
events.name: Volcanic eruption creates Sabrina Island

events.enhanced_description: The Klågerup riots erupted on June 15, 1811, in Sweden, reflecting social unrest and dissatisfaction with local governance. These riots were part of a broader wave of civil disturbances in Europe during this period.
events.name: Klågerup riots

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1811, the Carlton House Fête was held at the Prince Regent's residence in London to celebrate the establishment of the Regency era. This lavish event showcased the opulence of the British monarchy and the cultural life of the time.
events.name: Carlton House Fête

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1811, Venezuela declared its independence from the Spanish Empire, marking a significant step in the Latin American independence movements. This declaration was part of a broader struggle for freedom across the continent.
events.name: Venezuela declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1811, the Great Podil fire broke out in Kyiv, causing extensive damage to the historic Podil district. This catastrophic event highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban centers to fire hazards during this period.
events.name: Great Podil fire

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1811, British explorer David Thompson posted a notice at the confluence of the Columbia and Snake Rivers, claiming the area for the United Kingdom. This act was part of the broader exploration and territorial claims in North America.

locations.name: Columbia River and Snake River, Washington, United States

events.name: David Thompson claims territory

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1811, the Russian Empire removed Anton II, the Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia, from his office, replacing him with a Russian-appointed bishop. This event marked a significant moment in the Russian influence over the Georgian Orthodox Church.
events.name: Removal of Anton II

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1811, Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro published his memoir detailing the molecular content of gases, laying the groundwork for modern chemistry and the concept of the mole. This work was pivotal in advancing the understanding of gas laws.
events.name: Amedeo Avogadro publishes memoir

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1811, devastating forest fires broke out in the Tyrol region of Switzerland, reportedly destroying 64 villages and hamlets. This disaster had significant ecological and social impacts on the region.
events.name: Forest fires in Tyrol

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1811, priest and military leader Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla was executed by the Spanish government in New Spain, marking a pivotal moment in the Mexican War of Independence. His execution galvanized further resistance against colonial rule.
events.name: Execution of Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1811, the Jungfrau, the third highest summit in the Bernese Alps, was first ascended. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the history of mountaineering.
events.name: First ascent of Jungfrau

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1811, inventor John Stevens launched the Juliana, marking the beginning of the first steam-powered ferry service between New York City and Hoboken, New Jersey. This innovation played a crucial role in the development of steam transportation in the United States.
events.name: John Stevens' boat, the Juliana, begins operation as the first steam-powered ferry service

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1811, silver deposits were discovered at Agua Amarga in Chile, which would become instrumental in financing the Chilean War of Independence. This discovery significantly impacted the economic landscape of the region during a time of political upheaval.
events.name: Discovery of silver deposits at Agua Amarga, Chile

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1811, José Gervasio Artigas, a key figure in the early independence movement of Uruguay, led 16,000 orientales into exile from the Banda Oriental. This event marked a significant moment in the struggle for independence in the region.
events.name: José Gervasio Artigas and 16,000 orientales leave the Banda Oriental del Uruguay, to go into exile

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1811, the Argentine Government officially declared freedom of expression for the press, a pivotal moment in the development of democratic principles in Argentina. This declaration laid the groundwork for a more open and free society.
events.name: The Argentine Government declares freedom of expression for the press

events.enhanced_description: The Luddite uprisings began on November 4, 1811, in northern England and the Midlands, where workers protested against industrial machinery by destroying weaving machines. This movement highlighted the tensions between labor and industrialization during the early 19th century.
events.name: Luddite uprisings begin in northern England and the Midlands

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1811, American troops led by Governor William Henry Harrison engaged in the Battle of Tippecanoe against Native American forces led by Tenskwatawa, known as The Prophet. This battle was a significant conflict in the struggle between American expansion and Native American resistance.
events.name: Battle of Tippecanoe

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1811, José Miguel Carrera was sworn in as President of the executive Junta of the government of Chile. His leadership was pivotal in the early stages of Chile's struggle for independence from Spanish rule.

image.caption: Posthumous portrait of Chilean General José Miguel Carrera, painted by Miguel Venegas Cifuentes.
image.credit: Miguel Venegas Cifuentes (1907-1979) — http://www.jmcarrera.cl/im%C3%A1genes
image.date_qualification: Posthumous portrait dated 1950; not contemporary with the 1811 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: José Miguel Carrera sworn in as President of the executive Junta of Chile

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1811, Reverend Samuel Marsden sent the first commercial shipment of wool from New South Wales to England. This event marked the beginning of Australia's wool industry, which would become a cornerstone of its economy.
events.name: Reverend Samuel Marsden sends the first commercial shipment of wool from New South Wales to England

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1811, the New Madrid earthquake struck the Mississippi Valley near New Madrid, Missouri, causing significant geological changes, including a temporary reversal of the river's course. This earthquake was one of the most powerful in U.S. history.

image.caption: Map of earthquake measurements in the New Madrid seismic zone.
image.credit: Sara Boore and Susan Mayfield — USGS
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1996; not contemporary with the 1811 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The New Madrid earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1811, the first Constitution of the Republic of Venezuela came into effect following its declaration of independence from Spain. This constitution established the legal framework for the new republic and was a significant step in its nation-building process.
events.name: The first Constitution of the Republic of Venezuela goes into effect

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1811, a devastating fire broke out at the Richmond Theatre in Virginia, resulting in the deaths of 72 individuals, including Governor George William Smith and Abraham B. Venable, the president of the First National Bank of Virginia. This tragedy highlighted the need for improved fire safety measures in public venues.
events.name: The Richmond Theatre fire

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1812, the Allgemeines bürgerliches Gesetzbuch, or the Austrian civil code, came into effect in the Austrian Empire. This legal code was a significant reform in civil law, influencing legal systems in many countries.
events.name: Allgemeines bürgerliches Gesetzbuch enters into force

events.enhanced_description: During the Argentine War of Independence, Manuel Belgrano raised the flag he designed in Rosario, marking a significant moment in Argentina's struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Manuel Belgrano raises the Flag of Argentina

events.enhanced_description: In his inaugural speech as a member of the British House of Lords, Lord Byron defended the Luddite movement, which protested against the industrialization that threatened traditional livelihoods.
events.name: Lord Byron's first address in the House of Lords

events.enhanced_description: The Boston Gazette published a political cartoon that introduced the term 'Gerrymander,' highlighting the manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favor Elbridge Gerry's political party.
events.name: Boston Gazette coins the term Gerrymander

events.enhanced_description: The Caracas earthquake struck the capital of Venezuela, causing widespread destruction and loss of life, significantly impacting the city and its inhabitants.

image.caption: Tito Salas’s oil painting “Terremoto de 1812,” depicting the Caracas earthquake.
image.credit: Tito Salas — https://venezuelaenretrospectiva.wordpress.com/2016/03/27/el-terremoto-de-venezuela-de-1812/
image.date_qualification: Painted in 1929, 117 years after the 1812 earthquake; this is not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Caracas earthquake destroys Caracas

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1812, the Bishop James Madison Society was founded at the College of William & Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia. This society aimed to promote scholarly pursuits and foster a sense of community among students.
events.name: Founding of the Bishop James Madison Society

events.enhanced_description: In 1812, the Woodford Reserve Bourbon whiskey distillery, established in 1780 along Glenn's Creek in Woodford County, Kentucky, passed into the control of Oscar Pepper. This distillery would later become renowned for its premium bourbon.
events.name: Oscar Pepper takes control of Woodford Reserve

events.enhanced_description: In 1812, Ranikot Fort in Sindh was reconstructed, preserving its historical significance as a military fortification. This fort is often referred to as the 'Great Wall of Sindh' and is one of the largest forts in the world.
events.name: Reconstruction of Ranikot Fort

events.enhanced_description: Around 1812, the Battle of Shela took place, where the people of Lamu Island achieved victory against forces from other parts of the Kenyan coast. This battle was significant in the context of local power dynamics and coastal trade.
events.name: Battle of Shela

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1812, during the Peninsular War, the Anglo-Portuguese Army, led by the Duke of Wellington, stormed the French-held fortress of Ciudad Rodrigo. This victory was a crucial step in the campaign against French forces in Spain.
events.name: Siege of Ciudad Rodrigo during the Peninsular War

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1812, the last of a series of significant earthquakes struck New Madrid, Missouri, with an estimated moment magnitude of over 8. This earthquake was part of a sequence that dramatically altered the landscape of the region.
events.name: Last New Madrid earthquake strikes Missouri

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1812, Napoleon Bonaparte authorized the usage of Mesures usuelles, which laid the groundwork for the metric system. This decision had a lasting impact on measurement standards in France and beyond.
events.name: Napoleon authorizes the usage of Mesures usuelles

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1812, the first Chilean newspaper, Aurora de Chile, was published, focusing on political philosophy and supporting the new national government. This publication played a crucial role in shaping public opinion during Chile's fight for independence.
events.name: First Chilean newspaper Aurora de Chile published

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1812, Prussia and France signed the Treaty of Paris, establishing a military alliance. This treaty was part of the shifting alliances during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Prussia and France sign the Treaty of Paris

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1812, during the Argentine War of Independence, Manuel Belgrano raised the Flag of Argentina for the first time in the city of Rosario. This act symbolized the emergence of national identity and the struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Manuel Belgrano raises the Flag of Argentina for the first time

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1812, Prussia and Austria signed the Treaty of Paris, further solidifying their alliance during the Napoleonic Wars. This treaty was significant in the context of European power dynamics at the time.
events.name: Prussia and Austria sign the Treaty of Paris

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1812, Luddites attacked the wool-processing factory of Frank Vickerman in West Yorkshire, protesting against the mechanization of labor. This incident was part of the broader Luddite movement, which sought to resist the changes brought by the Industrial Revolution.
events.name: Luddites attack wool-processing factory in West Yorkshire

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1812, during the Peninsular War, the Anglo-Portuguese Army, under the Duke of Wellington, besieged the fortress of Badajoz in Spain, ultimately forcing the surrender of the French garrison. This victory was crucial for the Allied forces in their campaign against Napoleon.
events.name: Siege of Badajoz during the Peninsular War

events.enhanced_description: The Cortes of Cádiz convened during the Peninsular War, resulting in the promulgation of the first modern Spanish constitution, known as La Pepa, which established principles of sovereignty and individual rights.
events.name: The Cortes of Cádiz creates the first modern Spanish constitution

events.enhanced_description: In response to ongoing tensions with Britain, President James Madison enacted a 90-day embargo on trade with the United Kingdom, aiming to protect American interests and assert national sovereignty.
events.name: James Madison enacts a 90-day embargo on trade with the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: Tsar Alexander I of Russia signed an edict moving the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland from Turku to Helsinki, a decision that would shape the future administrative and cultural landscape of Finland.
events.name: Capital of Finland moved from Turku to Helsinki

events.enhanced_description: Louisiana was officially admitted to the Union as the 18th state, marking a significant expansion of the United States and reflecting the growing influence of the southern states.
events.name: Louisiana is admitted as the 18th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: John Bellingham assassinated British Prime Minister Spencer Perceval in the lobby of the House of Commons, marking the first assassination of a British Prime Minister in history.
events.name: John Bellingham assassinates British Prime Minister Spencer Perceval

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Bucharest was signed by Russian field marshal Mikhail Kutuzov, concluding the Russo-Turkish War and resulting in the annexation of Bessarabia to Imperial Russia.
events.name: Treaty of Bucharest signed

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic explosion at the Felling colliery near Jarrow resulted in the deaths of 96 miners, highlighting the dangers of coal mining during the Industrial Revolution.

image.caption: The John Pit at Felling Colliery, Gateshead.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Gateshead Council public archives at iSee Gateshead
image.date_qualification: Photographed on 2006-06-13; depicts the site, not the 1812 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Felling mine disaster

events.enhanced_description: President James Madison formally requested the U.S. Congress to declare war on the United Kingdom, marking the beginning of the War of 1812, driven by issues such as trade restrictions and impressment of American sailors.
events.name: James Madison asks Congress to declare war on the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: After Louisiana was admitted as a state, the remaining territory was renamed the Missouri Territory, reflecting the ongoing expansion and organization of U.S. territories.
events.name: Missouri Territory renamed following Louisiana's admission

events.enhanced_description: New York State officially chartered the City Bank of New York, which would later become Citibank, marking a significant development in American banking history.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: City Bank of New York chartered

events.enhanced_description: The War of 1812 officially began when the United States declared war on the United Kingdom, driven by maritime disputes and national sovereignty issues.

image.caption: Montage of five artworks depicting events and figures associated with the War of 1812.
image.credit: Clockwise, from top: George Munger, John David Kelly, Anton Otto Fischer, William Emmons, Edward Percy Moran — See images below.
image.date_qualification: The montage combines images dated 1814, 1896, unknown, 1833, and 1910; most are retrospective depictions, while the Capitol damage image shows aftermath. The montage itself has no supported display date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: War of 1812 begins with US declaration

events.enhanced_description: France declared war on Russia, escalating tensions that would lead to the invasion of Russia by Napoleon's forces later that year.

image.caption: Albrecht Adam’s artwork depicts the IV Corps of the Grande Armée during the Russian campaign.
image.credit: Albrecht Adam — http://napoleon1812.wordpress.com/2012/07/page/2/
image.date_qualification: Retrospective artwork depicting the 1812 campaign; the supplied image date identifies it only as a 19th-century work, with no supported display date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: France declares war on Russia

events.enhanced_description: Napoleon's Grande Armée crossed the Neman River, marking the beginning of the disastrous invasion of Russia, which would ultimately lead to significant losses for the French forces.
events.name: Napoleon's Grande Armée invades Russia

events.enhanced_description: During the War of 1812, American forces launched an invasion into Canada at Windsor, Ontario, as part of their military strategy against British-held territories.
events.name: Americans invade Canada at Windsor

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Klyastitsy, Russian forces under Kulnev achieved a tactical victory against the French, although Kulnev himself was mortally wounded in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Klyastitsy

events.enhanced_description: The renowned composer Ludwig van Beethoven met the celebrated poet Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in Teplice, marking a significant cultural encounter between two of the greatest figures of their respective fields.

locations.name: Teplice, Ústí nad Labem, Czech Republic

events.name: Beethoven and Goethe meet in Teplice

events.enhanced_description: During the Peninsular War, British forces led by the Duke of Wellington achieved a decisive victory over French troops at the Battle of Salamanca, significantly impacting the course of the war.
events.name: Battle of Salamanca

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic ambush, Tecumseh's Indian forces attacked a group of 200 American soldiers at Brownstone Creek, forcing them to retreat and showcasing the resistance against American expansion.
events.name: Tecumseh's Indian force ambushes Americans at Brownstone Creek

events.enhanced_description: Following the victory at the Battle of Salamanca, the combined English and Portuguese army under the command of the Duke of Wellington entered Madrid, marking a pivotal moment in the Peninsular War.
events.name: Wellington enters Madrid after Battle of Salamanca

events.enhanced_description: During the War of 1812, the Battle of Fort Dearborn saw Potawatomi warriors overrun the United States fort in Illinois Territory, resulting in significant casualties and demonstrating Native American resistance.
events.name: Battle of Fort Dearborn

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1812, the USS Constitution, commanded by Captain Isaac Hull, engaged and defeated the British frigate HMS Guerriere off the coast of Nova Scotia. This victory not only boosted American morale but also earned the Constitution the nickname 'Old Ironsides' due to its resilience against British cannon fire.

locations.name: Off the coast of Nova Scotia

events.name: USS Constitution defeats HMS Guerriere

events.enhanced_description: The Jujuy exodus on August 23, 1812, was a massive evacuation of people from Jujuy Province, Argentina, during the Argentine War of Independence. This strategic withdrawal was crucial for the patriot forces as they regrouped to continue their fight against Spanish colonial rule.
events.name: Jujuy exodus

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Borodino, fought on September 7, 1812, was one of the bloodiest battles of the Napoleonic Wars, resulting in a tactical victory for Napoleon's forces. The battle saw at least 70,000 casualties, with significant losses on both sides, and marked a pivotal moment in the French invasion of Russia.
events.name: Battle of Borodino

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1812, as Napoleon's troops entered Moscow, the city was set ablaze by its inhabitants under the orders of Governor Fyodor Rostopchin. This act of destruction aimed to deny the French army resources and shelter, resulting in significant losses for both sides during the ensuing chaos.
events.name: Fire of Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1812, American naval forces under Lieutenant Jesse Duncan Elliott captured two British warships, HMS Detroit and HMS Caledonia, during the War of 1812. This victory was crucial in establishing American naval dominance on the Great Lakes.
events.name: Capture of HMS Detroit and HMS Caledonia

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1812, the capital of Pennsylvania was permanently moved from Lancaster to Harrisburg. This decision was made to better serve the growing population and improve accessibility for state governance.
events.name: Capital Move to Harrisburg

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1812, during the War of 1812, American forces under General Stephen Van Rensselaer attempted to invade Canada at the Battle of Queenston Heights but were repulsed by British and Native American troops led by Sir Isaac Brock, who was killed in the battle. This defeat marked a significant setback for the American campaign in Canada.
events.name: Battle of Queenston Heights

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1812, the Second Battle of Polotsk saw Russian forces attack and defeat a Franco-Bavarian contingent. This engagement was part of the broader conflict during the Napoleonic Wars and highlighted the resilience of Russian troops against the invading forces.

image.caption: Photograph of the Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Polatsk, Belarus.
image.credit: Alex Zelenko — Photo made by EugeneZelenko 's brother, Alex Zelenko.
image.date_qualification: Modern photograph of a site in Polatsk, not an image of the 1812 battle; the depicted-date metadata is 2006-07-17.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Second Battle of Polotsk

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1812, Napoleon Bonaparte began his retreat from Moscow, marking a critical turning point in the Napoleonic Wars. The retreat was fraught with hardship, leading to devastating losses for the Grande Armée due to harsh winter conditions and continuous Russian attacks.
events.name: Napoleon's Retreat from Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1812, General Claude François de Malet attempted an unsuccessful coup to overthrow Napoleon's regime in Paris. The coup highlighted the growing discontent and instability within France as the consequences of the failed invasion of Russia began to take their toll.
events.name: Malet Coup of 1812

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Maloyaroslavets, fought on October 24, 1812, was an inconclusive engagement between Napoleon's forces and Russian troops. The outcome led Napoleon to decide to retreat along the same route he had advanced, which would result in catastrophic losses for his army.
events.name: Battle of Maloyaroslavets

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1812, during Napoleon's retreat from Russia, the Battle of Vyazma occurred, where the rearguard of the French army was defeated. This battle exemplified the dire situation of Napoleon's forces as they faced relentless Russian attacks during their withdrawal.

image.caption: Map of French and Russian army positions during the Battle of Vyazma, created by Edward Foord.
image.credit: Edward Foord — Napoleon's Russian Campaign of 1812
image.date_qualification: The depicted date is November 3, 1812; the image itself is dated 1908-01-01 in the supplied metadata.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Vyazma

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1812, James Madison was re-elected as President of the United States, defeating DeWitt Clinton. This election took place during the ongoing War of 1812, reflecting the political climate and public sentiment regarding the conflict.

image.caption: Electoral college map for the 1812 United States presidential election.
image.credit: Cg-realms (current) AndyHogan14 (original) — This image was adapted from ElectoralCollege1804.svg , itself adapted from Map of territorial growth 1775.svg and ElectoralCollege1964.svg (both based off Blank US Map.svg ) using data from ElectoralCollege1812-Large.png , the original version uploaded by AndyHogan14 , United States 1812-06-1812-12.png and the National Atlas of the United States
image.date_qualification: Map representing the 1812 election; the supplied image date is 2008-12-31 and is not the date of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 1812 United States Presidential Election

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1812, the Tory Party, led by Robert Jenkinson, 2nd Earl of Liverpool, emerged victorious in the United Kingdom general election. This election was significant as it occurred during the Napoleonic Wars, influencing British policy and military strategy.
events.name: 1812 United Kingdom General Election

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1812, the Battle of Krasnoi took place, where Napoleon's retreating army faced a series of defeats against Russian forces. This battle further weakened the French army as they struggled to escape the advancing Russian troops during the harsh winter.
events.name: Battle of Krasnoi

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1812, a significant earthquake with a magnitude between 6.9 and 7.5 struck San Juan Capistrano, California, causing extensive damage and resulting in the deaths of 40 parishioners at Mission San Juan Capistrano. This event highlighted the seismic activity in the region.
events.name: San Juan Capistrano Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1812, the remnants of Napoleon's Grande Armée were expelled from Russia, marking the end of the disastrous French invasion. This event significantly altered the course of the Napoleonic Wars and led to a shift in the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: End of the French Invasion of Russia

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1812, the first Spanish Christmas Lottery was drawn in Cádiz, a tradition that continues to this day. This lottery has become a significant cultural event in Spain, known for its large prizes and festive atmosphere.
events.name: First Spanish Christmas Lottery

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1812, the first volume of Grimms' Fairy Tales was published in Germany by brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm. This collection of folk tales has had a lasting impact on literature and culture, influencing countless adaptations and interpretations worldwide.
events.name: Publication of Grimms' Fairy Tales

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1812, the USS Constitution, under Captain Isaac Hull, defeated the British frigate HMS Java off the coast of Brazil. This victory further solidified the reputation of the USS Constitution as a formidable naval vessel during the War of 1812.
events.name: USS Constitution defeats HMS Java

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1812, the Convention of Tauroggen was signed, marking an agreement between Russian and Prussian forces during the Napoleonic Wars. This agreement facilitated the cooperation of these forces against Napoleon's army, significantly impacting the course of the conflict.

image.caption: Signatures of Generals Yorck and Diebitsch on the Convention of Tauroggen.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies the signatures on the convention dated 30 December 1812; the saved image date is 1812.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Convention of Tauroggen

events.enhanced_description: The second siege of Fort Meigs during the War of 1812 was an unsuccessful attempt by British forces to capture the fort, which was strategically important for controlling the Great Lakes region. The failure of this siege demonstrated the resilience of American forces and contributed to the eventual American victory in the war.
events.name: Second Siege of Fort Meigs

events.enhanced_description: In 1813, American missionaries Adoniram Judson and his wife, Ann Hasseltine Judson, arrived in Burma, marking the beginning of significant missionary work in the region. Their efforts laid the groundwork for the spread of Christianity in Burma and had lasting impacts on the local culture and society.
events.name: Arrival of Missionaries in Burma

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of San Marcial was a crucial engagement during the Peninsular War, where the Spanish Army of Galicia, led by Manuel Freire de Andrade, successfully repelled the last major offensive by French Marshal Soult against the allied forces. This victory was significant in maintaining Spanish resistance against French occupation.
events.name: Battle of San Marcial

events.enhanced_description: After a prolonged siege, allied troops in the Peninsular War rampaged through San Sebastián, ransacking and burning down much of the town. This event highlighted the brutal realities of war and the impact of military campaigns on civilian populations.
events.name: Sacking of San Sebastián

events.enhanced_description: Mathieu Orfila's publication of Traité des poisons is considered a foundational work in the field of toxicology. This groundbreaking text established the principles of forensic toxicology and set the stage for future developments in the discipline.
events.name: Publication of Traité des poisons

events.enhanced_description: Charles Waterton began transforming his estate at Walton Hall into what is recognized as the world's first nature reserve. His pioneering efforts in conservation laid the groundwork for modern environmentalism and wildlife preservation.
events.name: Creation of the world's first nature reserve

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father, Wossen Seged, Sahle Selassie arrived at the capital Qundi and was appointed Meridazmach of Shewa. This position marked the beginning of his rise to prominence in Ethiopian politics.
events.name: Sahle Selassie becomes Meridazmach of Shewa

events.enhanced_description: The Supreme Council for the Northern Jurisdiction of the United States of America was founded, establishing a significant governing body within the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. This organization has played a crucial role in the development and dissemination of Masonic principles.
events.name: Founding of the Supreme Council for the Northern Jurisdiction

events.enhanced_description: George E. Clymer is credited with the invention of the Columbian press, a significant advancement in printing technology that revolutionized newspaper production. This innovation facilitated the widespread dissemination of information and contributed to the growth of the press.

image.caption: A Columbian printing press in Thiruvananthapuram, India.
image.credit: Shajinss — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 19 September 2026 according to Exif data; it does not depict the c.1813 invention event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Invention of the Columbian press

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1813, Denmark declared a state bankruptcy due to the financial strains of the Napoleonic Wars and the loss of trade. This event marked a significant turning point in Danish economic history, leading to reforms and changes in governance.
events.name: The Danish state bankruptcy of 1813 occurs

events.enhanced_description: Fought on January 18, 1813, the Battle of Frenchtown was a significant conflict during the War of 1812, where American forces faced a combined British and Native American alliance. The battle resulted in a decisive victory for the British, impacting American morale and strategy in the region.

image.caption: Tim Kurtz’s painting depicts the Battle of the River Raisin.
image.credit: Tim Kurtz — https://npshistory.com/publications/rira/ (National Park Service History Electronic Library & Archive)

events.name: Battle of Frenchtown

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1813, the Philharmonic Society was founded in London, which later became known as the Royal Philharmonic Society. This organization played a pivotal role in promoting classical music and supporting composers and musicians in the UK.

image.caption: Street view of Great Marlborough Street in Soho, London.
image.credit: Paul The Archivist — Soho: Great Marlborough Street
image.date_qualification: A 2016 photograph of Great Marlborough Street, the society’s present address; it is not a depiction of the society’s 1813 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of the Philharmonic Society

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1813, Jane Austen's beloved novel 'Pride and Prejudice' was published anonymously in London. The novel has since become one of the most cherished works in English literature, known for its wit and commentary on social class.

image.caption: Character and family relationship map for Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice; a contextual diagram of the novel, not an image of its 1813 publication.
image.credit: Cmglee — Own work
image.date_qualification: No depicted date supplied; this diagram is not contemporaneous evidence of the novel’s publication.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Publication of Pride and Prejudice

events.enhanced_description: The Assembly of the Year XIII was inaugurated on January 31, 1813, in Buenos Aires, marking a significant step in the Argentine War of Independence. This assembly aimed to establish a government independent of Spanish rule.
events.name: Inauguration of the Assembly of the Year XIII

events.enhanced_description: In February 1813, General William Henry Harrison attempted to send an expedition across Lake Erie to burn British vessels at Fort Malden. However, the expedition was thwarted by insufficient ice conditions, forcing a retreat.
events.name: Harrison's Expedition to Fort Malden

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1813, during the Argentine War of Independence, José de San Martín led his Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers to a symbolic victory against Spanish royalist forces at the Battle of San Lorenzo. This battle was crucial in boosting the morale of the independence movement.
events.name: Battle of San Lorenzo

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1813, the French frigate Aréthuse engaged in battle with the British ship HMS Amelia near the Îles de Los on the Guinea Coast. Both ships retired from the engagement without a decisive victory.

image.caption: Louis-Philippe Crépin’s retrospective illustration of Aréthuse and HMS Amelia in action near the Îles de Los.
image.credit: Louis-Philippe Crépin — https://www.meisterdrucke.uk/fine-art-prints/Louis-Philippe-Crepin/81485/Battle-Between-the-French-Frigate-%27Arethuse%27-and-the-English-Frigate-%27Amelia%27-in-View-of-the-Islands-of-Loz%2C-7th-February-1813.html
image.date_qualification: The image date supplied is 1815-01-01, not the date of the 1813 action; present it as a retrospective illustration, not a contemporary photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Action of 7 February 1813

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1813, Prussia abolished the canton system, which had been a military conscription system. This reform was part of broader changes in response to the pressures of the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Abolishment of the Canton System in Prussia

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1813, construction began on Fort Meigs in Ohio under the command of General William Henry Harrison. This fortification was crucial for American forces during the War of 1812, serving as a defensive stronghold against British attacks.
events.name: Construction of Fort Meigs

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1813, the French garrison evacuated Berlin, allowing Russian troops to enter the city without resistance. This event marked a significant shift in the Napoleonic Wars, as it indicated the weakening of French control in Europe.
events.name: Evacuation of Berlin by French Garrison

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1813, Prussia declared war on France and introduced the Iron Cross military award, which was backdated to March 10. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the Napoleonic Wars, as it united various German states against Napoleon.
events.name: Prussia declares war on France

events.enhanced_description: The Malta plague epidemic began spreading from Egypt on March 28, 1813, leading to significant health crises in the region. This epidemic highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban populations to infectious diseases during this period.
events.name: Malta Plague Epidemic

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1813, during the Mexican War of Independence, the Republican Army of the North achieved a victory against the Spanish Royalist Army at the Battle of Rosillo Creek in modern-day Bexar County, Texas. This battle was part of the broader struggle for independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Battle of Rosillo Creek

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1813, Fort Meigs was besieged by British allied forces under General Henry Proctor and Native American leader Tecumseh. This siege was part of the larger conflict of the War of 1812, highlighting the strategic importance of the fort.
events.name: Siege of Fort Meigs

events.enhanced_description: In 1813, explorers Gregory Blaxland, William Lawson, and William Wentworth successfully crossed the Blue Mountains, a significant geographical barrier in New South Wales. Their journey opened up new lands for settlement and exploration, paving the way for further expansion into the Australian interior.

locations.name: Blue Mountains, New South Wales, Australia

events.name: Crossing of the Blue Mountains

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Bautzen, fought in April 1945, marked the last significant German panzer offensive during World War II. Despite initial successes, the German forces were ultimately unable to hold the city against the advancing Soviet troops.
events.name: Battle of Bautzen

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1813, American forces captured Fort George in Canada during the War of 1812. This victory was significant for the United States as it allowed them to gain a foothold in British-held territory.
events.name: Capture of Fort George

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1813, the British Royal Navy frigate HMS Shannon captured the American frigate USS Chesapeake in Boston Harbor. This event was a significant naval engagement during the War of 1812, showcasing British naval superiority.

image.caption: Chesapeake Mill in Wickham, built using timbers from USS Chesapeake.
image.credit: Richard Thomas — From geograph.org.uk ; transferred by User:Magnus Manske using geograph_org2commons .
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2006-05-29; depicts a later site, not the 1813 capture.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Capture of USS Chesapeake

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Stoney Creek was a significant engagement during the War of 1812, where British forces under John Vincent successfully defeated a much larger American contingent. This victory helped to bolster British morale and secure their position in Upper Canada.
events.name: Battle of Stoney Creek

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Tarragona, which began on June 11, 1813, was a significant military engagement during the Peninsular War. The siege highlighted the fierce resistance of Spanish defenders against French forces, reflecting the broader struggle for independence in Spain.
events.name: Siege of Tarragona

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Vitoria was a decisive conflict in the Peninsular War, where a coalition of British, Spanish, and Portuguese forces under the Duke of Wellington defeated the French army led by Joseph Bonaparte. This victory marked a turning point in the war, leading to the expulsion of French forces from Spain.
events.name: Battle of Vitoria

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on July 5, 1813, British forces launched a series of raids on Fort Schlosser and other locations along the Niagara River. These raids were part of the broader conflict of the War of 1812 and aimed to disrupt American supply lines and military operations.

locations.name: Fort Schlosser, New York, United States

events.name: British Raids on Fort Schlosser

events.enhanced_description: The Carabinieri, Italy's national military police force, was established by King Victor Emmanuel I in 1813 as a police force for the Kingdom of Sardinia. This organization has since evolved into a key component of Italy's law enforcement and military structure.
events.name: Founding of the Carabinieri

events.enhanced_description: In July 1813, Sir Thomas Maitland was appointed as the first Governor of Malta, overseeing the transition of the island from a British protectorate to a de facto colony. His administration significantly influenced Malta's governance and development during this period.
events.name: Appointment of Sir Thomas Maitland as Governor of Malta

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1813, Austria declared war on France, marking a significant escalation in the Napoleonic Wars. This declaration was part of a broader coalition effort to counter Napoleon's expansion across Europe.
events.name: Austria Declares War on France

events.enhanced_description: Gervasio Antonio de Posadas joined Argentina's second triumvirate on August 19, 1813, a governing body that played a crucial role in the early years of the Argentine War of Independence. His involvement was pivotal in shaping the political landscape of the region during this tumultuous period.

locations.historical_name: United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata
locations.name: Buenos Aires, Argentina

events.name: Gervasio Antonio de Posadas Joins Argentina's Second Triumvirate

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Großbeeren on August 23, 1813, saw the combined forces of Prussia and Sweden defeat Napoleon's army. This battle was part of the War of the Sixth Coalition and marked a significant setback for Napoleon's campaign in Germany.

image.caption: Carl Röchling’s painting depicts the Battle of Großbeeren, with the village church in the background.
image.credit: Carl Röchling — ( Original text: aus dem Buch: "Die deutschen Befreiungskriege. Deutschlands Geschichte von 1806-1815" von Hermann Müller-Bohn, Band 2, Berlin 1907/08, S. 580/81. ) Original uploader was Ulrich Waack at de.wikipedia
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting of the 1813 battle; the saved image date is 1907-08, and the display date is qualified as 1907.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Großbeeren

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Katzbach, fought on August 26, 1813, resulted in a decisive defeat for Napoleon's forces against the coalition of Prussia and Russia. This battle was pivotal in weakening Napoleon's grip on Central Europe during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Battle of Katzbach

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dresden, fought on August 27, 1813, was a significant victory for Napoleon against the coalition forces. This battle showcased Napoleon's tactical prowess and temporarily halted the advance of his enemies in the region.
events.name: Battle of Dresden

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Kulm, fought on August 29, 1813, saw the defeat and capture of French Marshal Vandamme by coalition forces from Russia, Prussia, and Austria. This battle was part of the broader conflict of the Napoleonic Wars and marked a significant victory for the coalition.
events.name: First Battle of Kulm

events.enhanced_description: The Fort Mims massacre on August 30, 1813, was a tragic event during the Creek War, where a force of Red Sticks, a faction of the Creek Nation, attacked the fort and killed hundreds of settlers. This event escalated the conflict between Native Americans and American settlers.
events.name: Fort Mims Massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dennewitz, fought on September 6, 1813, was another defeat for Napoleon's forces against the coalition of Prussia and Russia. This battle further weakened Napoleon's position in Germany and contributed to the eventual downfall of his empire.
events.name: Battle of Dennewitz

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Lake Erie, fought on September 10, 1813, was a pivotal naval engagement during the War of 1812, where Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry led American forces to victory over the British. This victory secured American control of Lake Erie and was crucial for subsequent military operations in the region.
events.name: Battle of Lake Erie

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Kulm, fought on September 17, 1813, saw the Allied Coalition achieve a significant victory over Napoleon's forces, forcing him to retreat. This battle was part of the broader campaign against Napoleon during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
events.name: Second Battle of Kulm

events.enhanced_description: The Philomathean Society, founded at the University of Pennsylvania, is recognized as the oldest continuously existing literary society in the United States. It has played a significant role in promoting literary and intellectual pursuits among its members since its inception.
events.name: The Philomathean Society of the University of Pennsylvania is founded

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of the Thames during the War of 1812, American forces led by General William Henry Harrison defeated the British and their Native American allies. The battle resulted in the death of the prominent Native leader Tecumseh, significantly impacting Native American resistance in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Thames

events.enhanced_description: In a significant ceremony in Caracas, the municipality bestowed upon Simón Bolívar the title of El Libertador, recognizing his pivotal role in the liberation of several South American countries from Spanish rule. This title has since become synonymous with Bolívar's legacy as a champion of independence.
events.name: Simón Bolívar is given the title of El Libertador

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Leipzig, also known as the Battle of Nations, marked a decisive defeat for Napoleon Bonaparte against the forces of the Sixth Coalition. With over 600,000 troops engaged, the battle resulted in significant casualties and led to the defection of several German states from Napoleon's control.
events.name: Battle of Leipzig

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Gulistan was signed between Persia and Russia, concluding the Russo-Persian War. As a result of the treaty, Persia ceded significant territories, including modern-day Georgia and parts of Azerbaijan, to Russia, reshaping the geopolitical landscape of the region.
events.name: Treaty of Gulistan

events.enhanced_description: During the War of 1812, the Battle of the Chateauguay saw Canadian forces under Charles de Salaberry successfully repel an American invasion. This victory was crucial in maintaining British control over Canada and bolstered Canadian morale.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the Battle of Chateauguay, by E. H. de Holmfield.
image.credit: E. H. de Holmfield — https://www.historynet.com/the-battle-that-saved-canada-how-the-u-s-failed-to-invade-montreal-in-the-war-of-1812/the-battle-of-the-cha%CC%82teauguay/
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1896, decades after the 1813 battle; it is a retrospective illustration, not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of the Chateauguay

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Crysler's Farm was a significant engagement during the War of 1812, where a British-Canadian force, despite being outnumbered, successfully repelled an American attack. This battle effectively halted American attempts to capture Montreal.
events.name: Battle of Crysler's Farm

events.enhanced_description: In the aftermath of the Napoleonic Wars, an independent government was restored in the Netherlands, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of Europe. This restoration laid the groundwork for the modern Dutch state.
events.name: Restoration of independent government in the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1813, Prince William of Orange returned to the Netherlands at Scheveningen beach, marking the beginning of the restoration of the Dutch monarchy. This event was pivotal in the establishment of a constitutional monarchy in the Netherlands following years of foreign rule.
events.name: Landing of the Prince
