events.enhanced_description: Ludwig van Beethoven premiered his Symphony No. 7 and Wellington's Victory in Vienna, conducting a benefit concert for soldiers wounded in the Battle of Hanau. The symphony is celebrated for its rhythmic vitality and has become one of Beethoven's most popular works.
events.name: Premiere of Beethoven's Symphony No. 7

events.enhanced_description: In a retaliatory act during the War of 1812, British soldiers burned the city of Buffalo, New York. This event was part of a broader campaign of destruction aimed at undermining American morale and military capability.
events.name: Burning of Buffalo

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Prussian Army, under the command of Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, crossed the Rhine River, marking a significant strategic maneuver during the War of the Sixth Coalition against Napoleon. This action was pivotal in the coalition's efforts to push back French forces.
events.name: Royal Prussian Army crosses the Rhine

events.enhanced_description: During the War of the Sixth Coalition, the Siege of Antwerp saw Allied forces besiege the French-held city of Antwerp. This siege was part of the larger campaign to reclaim territories from French control and was characterized by intense military engagements.
events.name: Siege of Antwerp

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Calebee Creek was a significant conflict during the War of 1812, where U.S. forces under John Floyd defeated the Red Stick Creek Indians in Alabama. This battle was part of the broader struggle between American settlers and Native American tribes during the war.
events.name: Battle of Calebee Creek

events.enhanced_description: In February 1814, George Hamilton-Gordon, 4th Earl of Aberdeen, represented Britain at the Congress of Châtillon, which aimed to negotiate peace terms to end the ongoing conflict in Europe. The congress was a pivotal moment in the diplomatic efforts to resolve the War of the Sixth Coalition.

image.caption: Portrait of Armand Caulaincourt, French general and diplomat.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Portrait of a French representative at the Congress of Châtillon; the image date is unknown.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Congress of Chatillon

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, Lord Byron's semi-autobiographical poem 'The Corsair' was published by John Murray in London, selling 10,000 copies on its release day. This work solidified Byron's reputation as a leading figure in the Romantic literary movement.
events.name: Publication of The Corsair

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of La Rothière was a significant engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where the Allied army led by von Blücher defeated Napoleon's forces. This battle was pivotal in the series of confrontations that ultimately led to Napoleon's abdication.
events.name: Battle of La Rothière

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, Norway declared its independence from Denmark, effectively ending the Kalmar Union, which had united the two kingdoms since the late 14th century. This proclamation was a significant step towards establishing Norway as a sovereign nation, leading to the drafting of a constitution later that year.

image.caption: Photograph of Eidsvoll House, where the Constitution of Norway was adopted and signed.
image.credit: Kjetil Bjørnsrud — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated June 2004; it depicts the site, not the 1814 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Norway's independence is proclaimed, marking the ultimate end of the Kalmar Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, during the War of the Sixth Coalition, Napoleon's forces achieved a decisive victory against the Russian and Prussian troops led by Osten-Sacken and Yorck at the Battle of Montmirail. This battle was part of the Six Days' Campaign, showcasing Napoleon's tactical prowess despite the challenging circumstances of the war.

image.caption: Memorial to the February 1814 fighting at Marchais-en-Brie, France.
image.credit: François GOGLINS — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2012-12-21; this is a later memorial, not an image of the 1814 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Montmirail

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, a devastating fire broke out at the Custom House in London, causing significant damage to the structure and disrupting trade operations. This incident highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban infrastructure during this period.
events.name: A fire destroys the Custom House in the City of London

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, the Battle of Château-Thierry saw Napoleon's forces defeat the combined Russian and Prussian armies led by Yorck and Osten-Sacken. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the War of the Sixth Coalition, demonstrating Napoleon's ability to rally his troops against overwhelming odds.

image.caption: Jean-Antoine-Siméon Fort’s retrospective depiction of the Battle of Château-Thierry.
image.credit: Jean-Antoine-Siméon Fort — https://collections.chateauversailles.fr/#0769cf7c-4876-4690-ac57-617011ddd01b
image.date_qualification: Depicts the 12 February 1814 battle; the artwork is dated between 1842 and 1843.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Château-Thierry (1814)

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, during the Venezuelan War of Independence, Republican forces achieved a significant victory over Spanish Royalists at the Battle of La Victoria. This battle was crucial in the fight for independence, bolstering the morale of the revolutionary forces.
events.name: Venezuelan War of Independence – Battle of La Victoria

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, the Battle of Bar-sur-Aube resulted in a victory for the Allied forces led by Prince Schwarzenberg against the French under General MacDonald. This battle was part of the broader War of the Sixth Coalition, contributing to the eventual defeat of Napoleon.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Bar-sur-Aube

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1814, the Battle of Orthez saw the Allied forces, commanded by the Duke of Wellington, defeat the French army led by Soult. This battle was a critical moment in the Peninsular War, further weakening Napoleon's position in Europe.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Orthez

events.enhanced_description: In January 1814, the Battle of Laubressel saw Austrian forces under Prince Karl Schwarzenberg defeat the French army led by MacDonald. This engagement was part of the broader campaign against Napoleon during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
events.name: Battle of Laubressel

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Talca occurred in 1814 during the Chilean War of Independence, where Spanish royalists defeated Chilean rebel forces. This battle was part of the ongoing struggle for Chilean independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: First Battle of Talca

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Chaumont was signed in 1814 by four Allied powers, solidifying their alliance against France during the Napoleonic Wars. This treaty was crucial in coordinating military efforts against Napoleon and ultimately led to his downfall.
events.name: Treaty of Chaumont

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, the American naval schooner USS Enterprise returned to Wilmington, North Carolina, after participating in the War of 1812 against the United Kingdom in the Caribbean. This event highlighted the naval engagements of the United States during the war.
events.name: USS Enterprise Returns

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Limonest occurred in early 1814, where Austrian and Hessian forces defeated the French Army of the Rhône. This battle was part of the larger campaign during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
events.name: Battle of Limonest

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, the Battle of Membrillar took place during the Chilean War of Independence, where Chilean rebels achieved a significant victory over Spanish royalists. This battle was part of the ongoing struggle for Chilean independence.
events.name: Battle of Membrillar

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Fère-Champenoise took place in 1814, where the Allied army led by Prince Karl Schwarzenberg defeated the French forces under Marmont and Mortier. This battle was a significant engagement in the final stages of the Napoleonic Wars.

image.caption: Alexander Ivanovich Dmitriev-Mamonov’s retrospective painting, *The Battle of Fère-Champenoise (1814)*.
image.credit: Alexander Ivanovich Dmitriev-Mamonov (1787-1836) — https://runivers.ru/gal/gallery-all.php?SECTION_ID=7590&ELEMENT_ID=600986
image.date_qualification: Created before 1836; not a contemporary photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Fère-Champenoise

events.enhanced_description: De Nederlandsche Bank was established in 1814 as the central bank of the Netherlands. Its creation marked a significant development in the financial infrastructure of the country, aimed at stabilizing the economy post-Napoleonic Wars.

image.caption: Portrait of Willem Ferdinand Mogge Muilman, president of De Nederlandsche Bank.
image.credit: Thomas Lawrence — https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/collectie/SK-A-728
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the bank president; the supplied image date is 1800, before his presidency from 1835 to 1844 and before the bank’s establishment in 1814.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Establishment of De Nederlandsche Bank

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Courtrai occurred in 1814, where French forces defeated Saxon and Prussian troops. This battle was part of the broader conflict during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
events.name: Battle of Courtrai

events.enhanced_description: On April 18/19, 1814, Genoa surrendered to the British Royal Navy, marking a significant naval victory during the Napoleonic Wars. This event underscored the British naval dominance in the Mediterranean during this period.
events.name: Surrender of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Lircay was a significant agreement signed in 1814 between the Royalists and Patriots during the Chilean War of Independence, marking a temporary cessation of hostilities and an effort to unify the factions against Spanish colonial rule.
events.name: Treaty of Lircay signed between Royalists and Patriots during the Chilean War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, Ferdinand VII of Spain abolished the liberal Constitution of 1812, which had been enacted during the Peninsular War, effectively restoring absolute monarchy and reversing the constitutional reforms that had aimed to modernize Spain.
events.name: Ferdinand VII of Spain abolishes the Spanish Constitution of 1812, returning the country to absolute monarchy

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Antwerp in 1814 concluded with the capitulation of French forces, marking a pivotal moment in the War of the Sixth Coalition as Allied forces advanced against Napoleon's empire.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Siege of Antwerp ends in a French capitulation

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Mainz concluded in 1814 with the withdrawal of French troops from the fortress, symbolizing the weakening grip of Napoleon's forces in the face of the advancing Coalition armies.

image.caption: Auguste Raffet’s drawing depicts soldiers suffering from typhus in a hospital courtyard.
image.credit: Zeitgenössische Zeichnung, Zeichner Auguste Raffet — https://www.swr.de/swraktuell/rheinland-pfalz/mainz/Knochenfunde-bei-Bauarbeiten-Massengrab-in-Mainz-gefunden,skelette-gefunden-100.html
image.date_qualification: A 19th-century drawing associated with the typhus epidemic during the siege; it is a retrospective illustration, not a contemporary event photograph. Its original date is recorded as “19 th century date QS:P,+1850-00-00T00:00:00Z/7”; no supported display date is available.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Siege of Mainz ends as the French leave the fortress

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, the occupation of Monaco transitioned from French to Austrian control following the Napoleonic Wars, reflecting the shifting political landscape in Europe during this period.
events.name: The occupation of Monaco changes from French to Austrian hands

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Buceo during the Argentine War of Independence resulted in a decisive victory for the Patriots, leading to the destruction of five Spanish ships and the capture of two, significantly weakening Spanish naval power in the region.
events.name: Argentine War of Independence – Battle of Buceo ends in the burning of five Spanish ships and capture of two

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, as the French garrison withdrew, Barcelona was restored to Bourbon rule under Ferdinand VII, marking a significant shift in the control of the city during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Barcelona is restored to Spanish Bourbon rule as the French garrison leaves the city

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Carabobo in 1814 was a pivotal engagement in the Venezuelan War of Independence, where Republican forces led by Simón Bolívar achieved a decisive victory against Spanish Royalists, significantly advancing the cause of independence in Venezuela.
events.name: Venezuelan War of Independence – Battle of Carabobo: Republican victory under Simón Bolívar over Spanish Royalists

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, George Stephenson successfully tested his first locomotive, named Blücher, in England, marking a significant advancement in railway technology and paving the way for the future of steam locomotion.
events.name: George Stephenson tests his first locomotive Blücher

events.enhanced_description: Hadži-Prodan's rebellion, which began in 1814, was a significant uprising against Ottoman rule in Serbia. Led by Hadži-Prodan, the rebellion aimed to achieve greater autonomy for the Serbian people and was part of the larger Serbian Revolution.
events.name: Hadži-Prodan's rebellion against the Ottoman Empire begins

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Vienna officially opened in Vienna, Austria, in 1814, bringing together the major European powers to negotiate the reorganization of Europe following the Napoleonic Wars. The congress aimed to restore stability and balance of power in Europe, lasting until June 9, 1815.
events.name: The Congress of Vienna formally opens in Austria

events.enhanced_description: In 1814, Eli Terry's wooden pillar-and-scroll clock became the first complex machine to be mass-produced using interchangeable parts in Plymouth, Connecticut. This innovation marked a significant advancement in manufacturing processes and set the stage for the Industrial Revolution in America.
events.name: The world's first complex machine mass-produced from interchangeable parts, Eli Terry's wooden pillar-and-scroll clock, comes off the production line in Plymouth, Connecticut

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Cattaro was a crucial event during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where a French garrison surrendered to British forces after ten days of intense bombardment. This surrender marked a significant strategic gain for the British in the Adriatic region.
events.name: Siege of Cattaro

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Puruarán during the Mexican War of Independence, Spanish Royalists defeated Mexican rebels, marking a significant setback for the independence movement. This battle highlighted the ongoing struggle for control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Puruarán

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Hoogstraten saw Prussian forces under Friedrich Wilhelm Freiherr von Bülow achieve a decisive victory over the French. This battle was part of the broader conflict during the War of the Sixth Coalition, contributing to the eventual defeat of Napoleon.
events.name: Battle of Hoogstraten

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Kiel, signed in January 1814, marked a significant shift in Northern European politics as Frederick VI of Denmark ceded the Kingdom of Norway to Sweden in a personal union, in exchange for West Pomerania. This treaty effectively ended the centuries-long union between Denmark and Norway.
events.name: Treaty of Kiel

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Ragusa was a military engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where a French garrison surrendered to British and Austrian forces. This event underscored the weakening position of French forces in the region as the coalition advanced.
events.name: Siege of Ragusa

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Brienne was a significant engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where Napoleon's forces achieved a decisive victory against the Prussian army led by von Blücher. This battle was part of Napoleon's campaign to defend France against the advancing coalition forces.
events.name: Battle of Brienne

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1814, Gervasio Antonio de Posadas was appointed as the Supreme Director of the United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata, a position that granted him significant power during a tumultuous period in Argentine history. His leadership was marked by efforts to consolidate authority and navigate the challenges of independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Gervasio Antonio de Posadas becomes Supreme Director of Argentina

events.enhanced_description: The eruption of Mount Mayon in February 1814 was one of the deadliest volcanic eruptions in Philippine history, resulting in the deaths of over 1,200 people and the destruction of the Cagsawa Church. This event had a profound impact on the local population and the surrounding environment.
events.name: Eruption of Mount Mayon

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Lesmont was a military engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where French forces under General Joseph Lagrange defeated the Allied troops. This battle was part of Napoleon's efforts to maintain control over France amidst the coalition's advances.

image.caption: Historical illustration depicting French troops of Lagrange’s division repelling cavalry near the bridge at Lesmont.
image.credit: Théodore Jung — Jean Tranié et Juan-Carlos Carmigniani, « Napoléon : 1814 - La campagne de France », Pygmalion/Gérard Watelet, 1989, 315 pages.
image.date_qualification: A 19th-century retrospective illustration of the 1814 battle, not a contemporary photograph; original image date is recorded as “19 th century.”
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Lesmont

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Mincio River was a confrontation during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where French and Italian troops under Viceroy Eugène de Beauharnais engaged an Austrian army. The battle ended in a stalemate, reflecting the intense military struggles of the time.
events.name: Battle of the Mincio River

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Champaubert marked a significant victory for Napoleon during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where he effectively destroyed a small Russian corps led by General Zakhar Dmitrievich Olsufiev. This battle opened the Six Days' Campaign, showcasing Napoleon's tactical prowess.
events.name: Battle of Champaubert

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1814, Norway proclaimed its independence, marking the ultimate end of the Kalmar Union, which had united Denmark and Norway since the late 14th century. This declaration set the stage for Norway's subsequent union with Sweden.
events.name: Proclamation of Norway's Independence

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1814, a devastating fire destroyed the Custom House in London, a significant building for trade and commerce. The incident highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban infrastructure in the early 19th century.

locations.name: Custom House, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Fire at the Custom House

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Vauchamps was the last major action of the Six Days' Campaign, where Napoleon's forces achieved a significant victory against the Prussian army led by von Blücher. This battle demonstrated Napoleon's tactical skill and resilience in the face of overwhelming odds.
events.name: Battle of Vauchamps

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Garris was a confrontation during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where an Allied army led by the Duke of Wellington defeated French forces under General Jean Isidore Harispe. This battle was part of the broader campaign to defeat Napoleon and restore stability in Europe.
events.name: Battle of Garris

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Mormant was a significant engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where Napoleon's forces effectively destroyed a Russian division. This victory was part of Napoleon's efforts to regain control over the battlefield as the coalition forces advanced.
events.name: Battle of Mormant

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Montereau was a decisive engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where Napoleon's forces achieved victory against Austrian troops. This battle was part of Napoleon's campaign to defend France and showcased his military strategy.
events.name: Battle of Montereau

events.enhanced_description: The Great Stock Exchange Fraud was exposed in London on February 21, 1814, revealing significant corruption and manipulation within the financial markets. This scandal had far-reaching implications for the integrity of financial institutions and public trust.
events.name: The Great Stock Exchange Fraud

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Bar-sur-Aube was a significant conflict during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where an Allied army led by Prince Schwarzenberg achieved victory against the French forces under Jacques MacDonald. This battle was part of the coalition's campaign to defeat Napoleon.
events.name: Battle of Bar-sur-Aube

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Gué-à-Tresmes was a military engagement during the War of the Sixth Coalition, where two French corps led by Auguste Marmont and Édouard Mortier defeated Prusso-Russian forces. This battle highlighted the ongoing struggle between French and coalition forces.
events.name: Battle of Gué-à-Tresmes

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1814, the Battle of Saint-Julien resulted in a victory for the Austrian Army of the South against the French Army of the Rhône. This engagement was part of the ongoing War of the Sixth Coalition, showcasing the effectiveness of the Allied forces against Napoleon's troops.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Saint-Julien

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1814, the Battle of Laubressel saw Prince Schwarzenberg's forces defeat the French under General MacDonald. This battle was part of the War of the Sixth Coalition, further diminishing Napoleon's control over France.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Laubressel

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1814, during the War of 1812, an American raiding party achieved a victory against British regulars, militia, and Indian fighters at the Battle of Longwoods. This battle was part of the broader conflict between the United States and British forces in North America.
events.name: War of 1812 – Battle of Longwoods

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1814, the Battle of Craonne was fought between Napoleon's forces and the combined Prussian and Russian armies led by von Blücher and Vorontsov. Although Napoleon emerged victorious, the battle resulted in heavy French casualties, highlighting the toll of the ongoing conflict.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Craonne

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1814, a night attack by British forces under Sir Thomas Graham on the French fortress of Bergen op Zoom ended in failure. This event underscored the challenges faced by the British in their attempts to penetrate French defenses during the War of the Sixth Coalition.

locations.name: Bergen op Zoom, North Brabant, Netherlands

events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Bergen op Zoom

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1814, the Treaty of Chaumont was signed by four Allied powers, solidifying their alliance against France. This treaty marked a significant moment in the War of the Sixth Coalition, as it aimed to coordinate military efforts against Napoleon.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Treaty of Chaumont

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1814, the Battle of Laon resulted in a decisive defeat for Napoleon at the hands of von Blücher's forces. This battle was a critical turning point in the War of the Sixth Coalition, further eroding Napoleon's power in Europe.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Laon

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1814, during the Argentine War of Independence, the United Provinces of South America achieved a significant victory over Spanish royalists at the Battle of Martín García. This battle was crucial in the struggle for independence in South America.

locations.name: Martín García Island, Buenos Aires, Argentina

events.name: Argentine War of Independence – Battle of Martín García

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1814, the Battle of Mâcon saw the Austrian Army of the South defeat the French Army of the Rhône. This battle was part of the War of the Sixth Coalition, contributing to the decline of Napoleon's military dominance.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Mâcon

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1814, Louis Antoine, Duke of Angoulême, entered Bordeaux, marking the restoration of the House of Bourbon following the abdication of Napoleon. This event symbolized a significant shift in French politics and the end of the Napoleonic era.
events.name: Louis Antoine, Duke of Angoulême enters Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1814, the Battle of Reims saw Napoleon's forces defeat a combined Russo-Prussian corps. This battle was part of the War of the Sixth Coalition and demonstrated Napoleon's continued military capabilities despite his declining power.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Reims

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1814, during the Chilean War of Independence, Chilean rebels achieved a significant victory over Spanish royalists at the Battle of El Quilo. This battle was part of the broader struggle for independence in South America.
events.name: Chilean War of Independence – Battle of El Quilo

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1814, the Battle of Limonest resulted in a victory for Austrian and Hessian forces against the French Army of the Rhône. This battle was part of the War of the Sixth Coalition, contributing to the weakening of Napoleon's military position.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Limonest

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1814, the Battle of Arcis-sur-Aube saw an Allied army defeat Napoleon's forces. This battle was significant in the context of the War of the Sixth Coalition, further diminishing Napoleon's control over France.

image.caption: 19th-century engraving after a painting by Jean-Adolphe Beaucé, depicting Napoleon at the bridge of Arcis-sur-Aube.
image.credit: Jean-Adolphe Beaucé — http://www.culture.gouv.fr/public/mistral/joconde_fr?ACTION=CHERCHER&FIELD_98=REPR&VALUE_98=%20cavalerie&DOM=All&REL_SPECIFIC=1
image.date_qualification: Dated before 1875; retrospective depiction, not an image made during the 1814 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Arcis-sur-Aube

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1814, the Battle of Fère-Champenoise resulted in a decisive victory for the Allied army led by Schwarzenberg against the French under Marmont and Mortier. This battle was a crucial moment in the War of the Sixth Coalition, contributing to the eventual downfall of Napoleon.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Fère-Champenoise

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1814, the Battle of Saint-Dizier saw Napoleon's forces defeat the Russians under von Wintzingerode. This battle was part of the War of the Sixth Coalition and demonstrated Napoleon's resilience in the face of overwhelming odds.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Saint-Dizier

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1814, the Battle of Jobourg saw a British squadron defeat and capture two French frigates. This naval engagement was part of the broader conflict of the War of the Sixth Coalition, highlighting the ongoing maritime struggles between Britain and France.
events.name: War of the Sixth Coalition – Battle of Jobourg

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1814, during the War of 1812, United States forces under General Andrew Jackson defeated the Creek Indians at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. This victory was pivotal in the conflict, leading to the eventual Treaty of Fort Jackson and significant territorial gains for the United States.
events.name: War of 1812 – Battle of Horseshoe Bend

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1814, during the War of 1812, the British Royal Navy decisively defeated the USS Essex and its sister ship off the coast of Valparaíso, Chile. This battle showcased the naval superiority of the British forces and marked a significant moment in the naval engagements of the war.
events.name: Battle of Valparaíso

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1814, the First Battle of Cancha Rayada took place during the Chilean War of Independence, where Spanish royalists defeated Chilean rebel forces. This battle was a critical setback for the Chilean independence movement, leading to further conflicts in the region.
events.name: First Battle of Cancha Rayada

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Paris began on March 30, 1814, as part of the War of the Sixth Coalition. Coalition forces, comprising various European nations, aimed to capture the French capital, leading to significant military engagements that would ultimately result in the fall of Napoleon.
events.name: Battle of Paris

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1814, Coalition troops occupied Paris, marking a pivotal moment in the War of the Sixth Coalition. This occupation led to the abdication of Napoleon Bonaparte and the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy in France.
events.name: Occupation of Paris

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1814, Louis XVIII was invited to occupy the restored French throne following the abdication of Napoleon Bonaparte. This event marked the beginning of the Bourbon Restoration in France, a significant shift in the country's political landscape.
events.name: Bourbon Restoration

events.enhanced_description: In 721, the Battle of Toulouse took place after Muslim forces under Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani besieged the city for three months. The siege ended in defeat for the Umayyad forces at the hands of Eudes, the duke of Aquitaine, halting the expansion of Umayyad control in Gaul.
events.name: Battle of Toulouse

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1814, during the Napoleonic Wars, the Battle of Bayonne took place, where Allied forces defeated a French sortie from the city. This battle was part of the larger campaign against Napoleon's forces in southwestern France.
events.name: Battle of Bayonne

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1814, the Convention of Mantua was signed, returning the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy to provisional Austrian rule. This agreement was part of the broader reorganization of Europe following the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Convention of Mantua

events.enhanced_description: The Ligurian Republic was revived in 1814 following the fall of Napoleon, marking a brief period of independence for the region before it was absorbed into the Kingdom of Sardinia. This revival was part of the broader political changes in Europe after the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: The Ligurian Republic is revived

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1814, Louis XVIII declared his support for representative government while simultaneously asserting his claim to unlimited monarchical sovereignty. This declaration was significant as it set the tone for the constitutional monarchy that would follow in France.
events.name: Declaration of Saint-Ouen

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1814, Louis XVIII, formerly the Duke of Provence, returned to Paris after the abdication of Napoleon. His return marked the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy in France after years of revolutionary and Napoleonic turmoil.

image.caption: Portrait of Louis XVIII, King of France.
image.credit: Robert Lefèvre — https://www.magnoliabox.com/products/portrait-of-louis-xviii-42-59304985
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is the 19th century (recorded as 1850); it is not the date of the depicted return.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Duke of Provence returns to Paris

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1814, Ferdinand VII of Spain abolished the liberal Constitution of 1812, which had established a constitutional monarchy. This act marked the return to absolute monarchy and the repression of liberal movements in Spain.
events.name: Ferdinand VII abolishes the Spanish Constitution of 1812

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1814, British forces attacked Fort Ontario at Oswego, New York, during the War of 1812. The battle was part of a series of British offensives aimed at gaining control over key locations in the northeastern United States.
events.name: Battle of Fort Oswego

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1814, American forces conducted a raid on Port Dover, Ontario, destroying property and disrupting British supply lines during the War of 1812. This raid exemplified the ongoing conflict between the United States and British forces in North America.
events.name: American Raid on Port Dover

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1814, William Brown, an Irish-born rebel leader, initiated a blockade of Montevideo, the colonial capital of the Rio de la Plata, as part of the struggle for independence from Spanish rule. This blockade was crucial in the fight for independence in South America.
events.name: Blockade of Montevideo

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1814, the Constitution of Norway was signed at Eidsvoll, establishing Norway as a constitutional monarchy and electing Christian Frederik as its king. This event marked a significant step towards Norwegian independence from Denmark.
events.name: Constitution of Norway is signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1814, the Constitution of Norway was signed at Eidsvoll, establishing Norway as a constitutional monarchy and electing Danish Crown Prince Christian Frederik as its king, a significant step towards Norwegian independence.

image.caption: Handwritten original of the Norwegian Constitution of 4 November 1814, preserved in the Storting Archive.
image.credit: Grunnlovsgivende forsamling — Stortingsarkivet, nr. 3 i Stortingets Indre arkiv, http://www.wergelandogstortinget.no/grunnloven.html
image.date_qualification: The described document is dated 4 November 1814; the supplied image date, 2012-03-06, is not the date depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Constitution of Norway is signed and the Danish Crown Prince Christian Frederik is elected King of Norway, by the Norwegian Constituent Assembly

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1814, the Duke of Wellington arrived in Madrid from Paris in an effort to prevent civil war between supporters of Ferdinand VII and the liberal opposition. His presence was significant in stabilizing the political situation in post-Napoleonic Spain.
events.name: Duke of Wellington arrives in Madrid

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1814, the Siege of Hamburg concluded with a French capitulation, marking a significant defeat for Napoleon's forces during the War of the Sixth Coalition. This event contributed to the eventual downfall of the French Empire.
events.name: Siege of Hamburg ends

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1814, Barcelona was restored to Spanish Bourbon rule as the French garrison withdrew from the city. This event was part of the broader restoration of the Bourbon monarchy in Spain following the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Barcelona restored to Spanish Bourbon rule

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1814, U.S. forces captured British marines and sailors during the Battle of Big Sandy Creek, a minor engagement in the War of 1812. This victory contributed to the ongoing conflict between the United States and British forces.

locations.name: Big Sandy Creek, New York, United States

events.name: Battle of Big Sandy Creek

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1814, the First Treaty of Paris was signed, restoring France's borders to their 1792 extent and marking the end of the Napoleonic Wars. Napoleon was exiled to Elba on the same day, significantly altering the political landscape of Europe.
events.name: First Treaty of Paris

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1814, Louis XVIII issued the Charter of 1814, a written constitution that established a constitutional monarchy while retaining royal supremacy. This charter would govern France until the return of Napoleon in 1815.
events.name: Charter of 1814

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1814, Tsar Alexander I of Russia and King Frederick William III of Prussia sailed from Boulogne-Sur-Mer to Dover as guests of George, Prince of Wales. This visit symbolized the unity of the Allied powers following the defeat of Napoleon.
events.name: Allied sovereigns' visit to England

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1814, Lord Byron wrote the poem 'She Walks in Beauty,' which is celebrated for its exploration of beauty and love. This work is one of Byron's most famous and showcases his romantic style.
events.name: She Walks in Beauty written

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1814, the leaders exchanged ratifications of the Peace Treaty that ended the war with France in London. This event marked a significant step towards restoring peace in Europe after years of conflict.
events.name: Ratifications of the Peace Treaty exchanged

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1814, Gaspar de Vigodet, the last colonial administrator of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, surrendered Montevideo to independence fighters led by General Carlos María de Alvear. This event was pivotal in the struggle for independence in South America.
events.name: Surrender of Montevideo

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1814, the Eight Articles of London were signed, uniting the Low Countries under William I of the Netherlands. This agreement was part of the larger restructuring of Europe following the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Eight Articles of London signed

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1814, the USS Wasp sank the HMS Reindeer during the War of 1812, showcasing the naval engagements between the United States and British forces. This battle highlighted the ongoing maritime conflict in the Atlantic.

locations.name: Atlantic Ocean, near the United States

events.name: Sinking of HMS Reindeer

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1814, during the War of 1812, American forces under Major General Jacob Brown successfully captured Fort Erie from the British, marking a significant strategic victory in the conflict.
events.name: War of 1812 – Capture of Fort Erie by the Americans under Major General Jacob Brown

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Chippawa, fought on July 5, 1814, was a significant engagement in the War of 1812 where American forces led by Major General Jacob Brown defeated British General Phineas Riall, bolstering American morale and military reputation.
events.name: War of 1812 – Battle of Chippawa: American Major General Jacob Brown defeats British General Phineas Riall at Chippawa, Ontario

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1814, Walter Scott's novel 'Waverley' was published anonymously in Edinburgh, marking a significant moment in literary history as it is considered one of the first historical novels in English, selling out within two days.
events.name: Walter Scott's Waverley published anonymously by Archibald Constable in Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1814, the Carabinieri, Italy's national military police force, was established by Victor Emmanuel, serving as the police force of the Kingdom of Sardinia and laying the groundwork for modern Italian law enforcement.
events.name: The Carabinieri established by Victor Emmanuel as the police force of the Kingdom of Sardinia

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops and their Native American allies besieged and captured the frontier settlement of Prairie du Chien, demonstrating the ongoing conflict in the region.
events.name: War of 1812 – Siege of Prairie du Chien: British troops and Native Americans besiege and capture the frontier settlement

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1814, during the War of 1812, the Battle of Rock Island Rapids occurred when British-allied Native American tribes ambushed and defeated an American expedition, highlighting the complexities of alliances in the conflict.
events.name: War of 1812 – Battle of Rock Island Rapids: British-allied tribes ambush and defeat an American expedition in Illinois

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1814, the Treaty of Greenville was signed between the U.S. government and various Native American tribes, establishing peace and delineating territorial boundaries following the War of 1812.
events.name: War of 1812 – The Treaty of Greenville is signed between the U.S. government and Native American tribes

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1814, George Stephenson successfully tested his first locomotive, named Blücher, in Wylam, England, marking a significant advancement in railway technology and the beginning of the locomotive era.
events.name: George Stephenson tests his first locomotive Blücher successfully in England

events.enhanced_description: The Swedish–Norwegian War began on July 26, 1814, with a Swedish attack, marking the start of hostilities between Sweden and Norway over territorial disputes following the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: The Swedish–Norwegian War (1814) begins with a Swedish attack

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1814, the revived Ligurian Republic was dissolved, ending its brief existence following the Napoleonic Wars and re-establishing the region under different political control.
events.name: The revived Ligurian Republic is dissolved

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1814, during the Swedish–Norwegian War, the invasion of Hvaler concluded with a Swedish victory, further solidifying Sweden's military position in the conflict.
events.name: Swedish–Norwegian War: The invasion of Hvaler ends in a Swedish victory

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1814, a devastating fire swept through Tirschenreuth, Bavaria, destroying the town and 907 buildings, leading to significant loss and prompting reconstruction efforts in the aftermath.
events.name: The Great fire of Tirschenreuth in Bavaria destroys the town and 907 buildings

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1814, the Grand Jubilee was celebrated in Britain, marking the hundredth anniversary of the Hanoverian Succession, featuring grand festivities and public celebrations across the nation.
events.name: The Grand Jubilee of 1814 is held in Britain, celebrating the hundredth anniversary of the Hanoverian Succession

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1814, the Battle of Lier concluded with a Norwegian victory, marking a significant moment in the Swedish–Norwegian War and bolstering Norwegian morale.
events.name: Swedish–Norwegian War: Battle of Lier ends in a Norwegian victory

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1814, during the War of 1812, the Battle of Mackinac Island resulted in a British victory, thwarting an American invasion and maintaining British control over the strategic location.
events.name: War of 1812 – Battle of Mackinac Island results in a British victory over an American invasion

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1814, the Battle of Matrand concluded with a Norwegian victory, further establishing Norway's resistance during the Swedish–Norwegian War.
events.name: Swedish–Norwegian War: the Battle of Matrand ends in a Norwegian victory

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1814, Pope Pius VII issued the papal bull Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum, which reestablished the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) globally, affirming their existence in Russia and allowing them to resume their educational and missionary activities.
events.name: Pope Pius VII decrees the bull Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1814, the Treaty of Fort Jackson was signed, effectively ending the Creek War. The treaty resulted in significant territorial concessions from the Creek Nation to the United States, marking a pivotal moment in the expansion of U.S. territory in the Southeast.
events.name: Treaty of Fort Jackson

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1814, William Potter was executed, marking the last hanging under the Black Act, which had criminalized over 200 offenses. The case drew attention as the judge petitioned for a reprieve, highlighting the growing opposition to capital punishment.
events.name: Last hanging under the Black Act

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1814, the Anglo-Dutch Treaty was signed in London, restoring most of the Dutch Empire's territories that had been seized by the British since 1803, while retaining strategic locations like the Cape of Good Hope.
events.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1814, the Battle of Kjölberg Bridge concluded with a Swedish victory during the Swedish–Norwegian War, solidifying Sweden's territorial claims against Norway.
events.name: Battle of Kjölberg Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1814, British troops occupied Washington, D.C., after defeating American forces at the Battle of Bladensburg, leading to the burning of significant buildings, including the Capitol and the Presidential Mansion.
events.name: Burning of Washington

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1814, the Battle of Las Tres Acequias resulted in a decisive victory for Chilean forces led by José Miguel Carrera during the Chilean War of Independence, strengthening their fight against Spanish colonial rule.
events.name: Battle of Las Tres Acequias

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1814, the Battle of Caulk's Field saw American militia successfully repel a British landing attempt, contributing to the defense of Maryland during the War of 1812.
events.name: Battle of Caulk's Field

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1814, engagements on Lake Huron resulted in a British victory during the War of 1812, showcasing the naval power of the British forces against American attempts to control the Great Lakes.
events.name: Engagements on Lake Huron

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Fayal, fought on September 27, 1814, was a naval engagement during the War of 1812 where American forces achieved a significant victory over the British. This battle was part of the broader conflict between the United States and Great Britain, showcasing American naval capabilities.
events.name: War of 1812 – Battle of Fayal ends in an American victory over the British

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1814, the London Beer Flood occurred when a large vat of porter at Meux's Brewery burst, unleashing a torrent of beer that destroyed nearby buildings and tragically resulted in the deaths of eight people. This unusual disaster highlighted the risks associated with large-scale brewing operations in urban areas.
events.name: London Beer Flood: A large vat full of porter owned by Meux's Brewery of London bursts, demolishing buildings and killing 8 people

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Cook's Mills, fought on October 19, 1814, was a significant engagement in the War of 1812 where U.S. forces, led by General Winfield Scott, defeated British troops in Upper Canada. This battle was part of the larger campaign to secure American interests in the region.
events.name: War of 1812: Battle of Cook's Mills

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Nepalese War began on November 1, 1814, when Francis Rawdon-Hastings, the Governor-General of India, declared war on the Kingdom of Nepal. This conflict arose from territorial disputes and the expansionist policies of the British East India Company.
events.name: Francis Rawdon-Hastings, the Governor-General of India declares war on Kingdom of Nepal and Anglo-Nepalese War begins

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1814, King Charles XIII of Sweden was proclaimed King of Norway, taking the title Charles II. This event marked the union of Sweden and Norway under a single monarch, which lasted until 1905.
events.name: King Charles XIII of Sweden becomes King of Norway, as Charles II

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1814, during the War of 1812, General Andrew Jackson led American forces to seize control of Pensacola, Florida, from the Spanish. This strategic move was aimed at preventing British forces from using the area as a base for operations against the United States.
events.name: War of 1812: Andrew Jackson seizes Pensacola, Florida

events.enhanced_description: The Hartford Convention, convened on December 15, 1814, was a gathering of New England Federalists who opposed the War of 1812. The convention aimed to address grievances regarding the war and the federal government's policies, ultimately leading to the decline of the Federalist Party.
events.name: War of 1812: The Hartford Convention is convened, by members of the American Federalist Party

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814, in Ghent, Belgium, formally ending the War of 1812 between the United States and Great Britain. The treaty restored pre-war boundaries and marked a significant moment in U.S. diplomatic history.
events.name: War of 1812: The Treaty of Ghent is signed, formally ending the war

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1814, Samuel Marsden, a missionary from the Church Missionary Society, delivered the first sermon in New Zealand at Oihi, likely in the Māori language. This event marked the beginning of formal Christian missionary activity in New Zealand.
events.name: Samuel Marsden of the Church Missionary Society preaches the first sermon in New Zealand, probably in the Māori language, at Oihi

events.enhanced_description: In 1815, the first commercial cheese factory was established in Switzerland, marking a significant development in the dairy industry. This factory set the stage for the mass production of cheese, which would become a staple in Swiss cuisine and economy.
events.name: The first commercial cheese factory is founded in Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: In 1815, President James Madison signed into law the congressional charter for Georgetown University, formally establishing it as the first Catholic university in the United States. This event marked a significant milestone in American higher education.
events.name: Georgetown University's congressional charter is signed into law

events.enhanced_description: In 1815, Thomas King was born in the Bay of Islands, becoming the first full-blooded European native born in New Zealand. His birth marked a significant moment in the history of European settlement in New Zealand.
events.name: Birth of Thomas King

events.enhanced_description: In 1815, the second wave of Amish immigration to North America began, as groups sought religious freedom and a new life in the New World. This migration played a crucial role in establishing Amish communities in the United States.
events.name: Second wave of Amish immigration

events.enhanced_description: In 1815, the use of the pillory in the United Kingdom was limited to punishment for perjury, marking a significant change in the penal system. This reflected broader trends towards reforming harsh punishments in British law.
events.name: Limitations on the use of the pillory in the UK

events.enhanced_description: In 1815, Wisden Cricketers' Almanack began retrospectively recognizing statistics for first-class cricket in England. This publication would become a crucial resource for cricket statistics and history.
events.name: Wisden Cricketers' Almanack recognition

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1815, the famous poet Lord Byron married Anna Isabella Milbanke in Seaham, County Durham, England. Their tumultuous marriage would later become a subject of public interest and speculation, ultimately leading to separation.

locations.name: Seaham, County Durham, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Lord Byron marries Anna Isabella Milbanke in Seaham, county of Durham, England

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1815, Austria, Britain, and Bourbon-restored France formed a secret defensive alliance against Prussia and Russia. This alliance was a strategic move during the post-Napoleonic period to maintain the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: Austria, Britain, and Bourbon-restored France form a secret defensive alliance treaty against Prussia and Russia

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1815, the Battle of New Orleans took place, where American forces under General Andrew Jackson decisively defeated British troops led by Sir Edward Pakenham. This battle, occurring after the Treaty of Ghent was signed, became a symbol of American nationalism and military prowess.
events.name: Battle of New Orleans: American forces led by Andrew Jackson defeat British forces led by Sir Edward Pakenham

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1815, British troops captured Fort Peter in St. Marys, Georgia, marking the only battle of the War of 1812 to take place in the state. This engagement was part of the British strategy to control the southern states during the conflict.
events.name: War of 1812: British troops capture Fort Peter in St. Marys, Georgia

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1815, the American frigate USS President, commanded by Commodore Stephen Decatur, was captured by a squadron of four British frigates. This event highlighted the ongoing naval conflicts during the War of 1812 and the challenges faced by the U.S. Navy.
events.name: War of 1812: Capture of USS President

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1815, the Groninger Studentencorps Vindicat atque Polit was founded in Groningen, Netherlands, becoming the first Dutch student association. This organization played a significant role in student life and culture in the Netherlands.
events.name: The first Dutch student association, the Groninger Studentencorps Vindicat atque Polit, is founded in the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1815, New Jersey granted the first American railroad charter to John Stevens, paving the way for the development of rail transport in the United States. This milestone marked the beginning of a new era in transportation and commerce.
events.name: New Jersey grants the first American railroad charter to John Stevens

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish reconquest of Spanish America began on February 17, 1815, as Spain sought to regain control over its former colonies that had declared independence. This effort was part of the broader context of colonial struggles in Latin America.
events.name: The Spanish reconquest of Spanish America begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1815, the War of 1812 officially ended with the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent in Washington, D.C. This treaty restored pre-war boundaries and marked a significant moment in U.S. history, solidifying national sovereignty.
events.name: The War of 1812 officially ends, following ratification of the Treaty of Ghent in Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte escaped from his exile on the island of Elba, returning to France and reigniting his rule. This event marked the beginning of the Hundred Days, a brief period of renewed power for Napoleon before his ultimate defeat at Waterloo.
events.name: Napoleonic Wars: Napoleon Bonaparte escapes from Elba

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte returned to France from his exile on the island of Elba, marking the beginning of his brief but impactful rule known as the Hundred Days. His return sparked a series of events that would lead to the final conflicts of the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Napoleonic Wars: Napoleon returns to France from his banishment on Elba

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1815, Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, the last king of Kandy, was deposed under the terms of the Kandyan Convention, leading to the annexation of Ceylon by the British Empire. This event marked the end of the Kandyan monarchy and the beginning of British colonial rule in Sri Lanka.
events.name: Sri Vikrama Rajasinha of Kandy is deposed under the Kandyan Convention

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1815, the Congress of Vienna, a diplomatic meeting of European powers, declared Napoleon Bonaparte an outlaw following his return from exile. This decision aimed to unify European nations against the threat posed by Napoleon's resurgence.
events.name: Participants at the Congress of Vienna declare Napoleon an outlaw following his escape from Elba

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1815, Joachim Murat, the King of Naples, declared war on Austria in a desperate attempt to retain his throne amidst the chaos following Napoleon's return. This declaration marked the beginning of the Neapolitan War.
events.name: Joachim Murat declares war on Austria, starting the Neapolitan War

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1815, William I was proclaimed King of the Netherlands, following the establishment of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after the Congress of Vienna. His reign marked the beginning of a new constitutional monarchy in the region.
events.name: William I becomes King of the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte made a triumphant entry into Paris after escaping from Elba, rallying support and beginning his Hundred Days rule. This event reignited the Napoleonic Wars and set the stage for his final confrontations with European powers.
events.name: Napoleon enters Paris, beginning his Hundred Days rule

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted catastrophically, resulting in the deaths of over 92,000 people and triggering a volcanic winter that led to the Year Without a Summer in 1816. The eruption had profound effects on global climate and agriculture.
events.name: Mount Tambora erupts, leading to global climatic effects

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1815, the eastern part of the former Garhwal Kingdom was merged with the Kumaon division under British administration. This administrative change was part of the broader consolidation of British control in India.
events.name: Eastern part of Garhwal Kingdom joined with Kumaon division

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1815, the Second Serbian Uprising began in Takovo against Ottoman rule, leading to Serbia's eventual recognition as a semi-independent state by the end of the year. This uprising was a significant step towards Serbian autonomy.

image.caption: Paja Jovanović’s oil painting *The Takovo Uprising*.
image.credit: Muzej rudničko-takovskog kraja u Gornjem Milanovcu
image.date_qualification: Painting dated 1894; the supplied 2006 date is an image metadata date, not the date depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Second Serbian Uprising against Ottoman rule

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1815, the Battle of Tolentino took place, where Austrian forces decisively defeated the Kingdom of Naples, effectively ending the Neapolitan War. The defeat forced King Joachim Murat to flee, leading to significant political changes in Italy.

image.caption: Map of the Battle of Tolentino by Friedrich Schirmer.
image.credit: Friedrich Schirmer, k. u. k. Oberlieutenant, zugetheilt dem Generalstabe, ü. c. im Infanterie-Regimente Philipp Herzog von Württemberg, Nr. 77 — [1] , ("Feldzug der Österreicher gegen König Joachim Murat im Jahre 1815", by Friedrich Schirmer)
image.date_qualification: The map is dated 1898, not contemporaneous with the 1815 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Tolentino: Austria defeats the Kingdom of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1815, the Arniston, an East Indiaman ship, was wrecked near Waenhuiskrans, South Africa, resulting in the loss of 372 of the 378 people on board. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during the era.

image.caption: Memorial in Arniston (Waenhuiskrans), Western Cape, commemorating those lost in the Arniston shipwreck.
image.credit: A3alb — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image was photographed on 2011-02-13, long after the 1815 shipwreck; it depicts a memorial, not the wreck itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Arniston shipwreck near Waenhuiskrans, South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1815, the Final Act of the Congress of Vienna was signed, establishing a new political order in Europe after the Napoleonic Wars. This agreement created the German Confederation and guaranteed the neutrality of Switzerland.
events.name: Final Act of the Congress of Vienna is signed

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1815, the Duchess of Richmond's ball was held in Brussels, which has since been dubbed 'the most famous ball in history.' This event was attended by many military leaders and was a significant social gathering just days before the Battle of Waterloo.
events.name: The Duchess of Richmond's ball is held in Brussels

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1815, the Battle of Ligny occurred, where Napoleon Bonaparte achieved a significant victory against a Prussian army led by Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher. This battle was one of the key engagements leading up to the decisive Battle of Waterloo.
events.name: Battle of Ligny: Napoleon defeats a Prussian army

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1815, the Battle of Waterloo took place, where the Allied forces, commanded by Arthur Wellesley and Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, decisively defeated Napoleon Bonaparte. This battle marked the end of the Napoleonic Wars and led to Napoleon's final exile.
events.name: Battle of Waterloo: Allied forces defeat Napoleon

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte abdicated for the second time, briefly allowing his son, Napoleon II, to rule for two weeks. This event marked the final collapse of Napoleon's rule in France.
events.name: Napoleon abdicates again; Napoleon II rules for two weeks

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1815, Wellington's advancing Allied Army captured Péronne, a strategic location on their march towards Paris. This maneuver was part of the broader campaign to restore stability in France after Napoleon's defeat.
events.name: Wellington's army takes Péronne on the way to Paris

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte boarded HMS Bellerophon off Rochefort and surrendered to Captain Frederick Lewis Maitland of the Royal Navy. This act marked the end of his rule and the beginning of his final exile.
events.name: Napoleon boards HMS Bellerophon and surrenders

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1815, representatives from the United Kingdom, Austria, Russia, and Prussia signed a convention in Paris declaring Napoleon Bonaparte a prisoner and entrusting his safe keeping to the British government. This agreement formalized his status following his surrender.
events.name: Convention signed declaring Napoleon a prisoner

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte was transferred to HMS Northumberland, beginning his forced exile to the remote island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean. This marked the end of his political career and the start of his final years in isolation.
events.name: Napoleon transferred to HMS Northumberland for exile

events.enhanced_description: The Great September Gale of 1815 was a significant hurricane that struck New England, marking the first such event in 180 years. It caused extensive damage and loss of life, impacting the region's communities and economy.
events.name: The Great September Gale of 1815

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1815, Austria, Prussia, and Russia signed the Holy Alliance, a pact aimed at upholding the conservative order in Europe following the Napoleonic Wars. This agreement sought to maintain the status quo and prevent the spread of revolutionary movements.
events.name: Holy Alliance

events.enhanced_description: In October 1815, Robert Adams, an American sailor and the first Westerner to visit Timbuktu, was discovered wandering the streets of London in a destitute state. His harrowing experiences as a Barbary captive were later published, shedding light on his extraordinary journey.
events.name: Robert Adams found in London

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1815, the Chassigny Martian meteorite fell in Chassigny, Haute-Marne, France. This meteorite is significant for being one of the few known samples from Mars, providing valuable insights into the planet's composition.
events.name: Chassigny Martian meteorite fall

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte began his exile on the remote island of Saint Helena in the Atlantic Ocean, following his defeat at the Battle of Waterloo. This marked the end of his political and military career, as he was kept under strict surveillance.
events.name: Napoleon's exile to Saint Helena

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1815, a devastating 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck northern China, resulting in the collapse of numerous houses and caves. The disaster claimed the lives of at least 13,000 people, highlighting the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: Northern China earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1815, Sir Humphry Davy announced his invention of the Davy lamp, a safety lamp for coal miners that significantly reduced the risk of explosions in mines. This invention marked a major advancement in mining safety.
events.name: Davy lamp announcement

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1815, the Ionian Islands were established as a British protectorate, marking a significant shift in the region's governance. This arrangement was part of the broader geopolitical changes following the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Ionian Islands become British protectorate

events.enhanced_description: The Napoleonic Wars officially came to an end on November 20, 1815, after 12 years of conflict. The British government restored the status quo in France, aiming to stabilize Europe after decades of turmoil initiated by the French Revolution.
events.name: End of the Napoleonic Wars

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1815, the Constitution of the Kingdom of Poland was signed, establishing Congress Poland as a constitutional monarchy in personal union with the Russian Empire. This was a significant outcome of the Congress of Vienna.
events.name: Constitution of the Kingdom of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1815, Marshal Michel Ney was executed in Paris, near the Jardin du Luxembourg, for treason against the Bourbon monarchy. Ney was one of Napoleon's most trusted generals and his execution marked a significant moment in post-Napoleonic France.
events.name: Execution of Marshal Ney

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1815, Jane Austen's novel 'Emma' was first published anonymously in London. This work would go on to become one of her most celebrated novels, exploring themes of love, social status, and personal growth.
events.name: Publication of Emma by Jane Austen

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1815, the Handel and Haydn Society, the oldest continuously performing arts organization in the United States, gave its first performance in Boston. This event marked the beginning of a rich tradition of classical music in America.
events.name: First performance of the Handel and Haydn Society

events.enhanced_description: In 1816, Sir Humphry Davy's innovative Davy lamp was first tested underground at Hebburn Colliery in northeast England. This safety lamp significantly improved miner safety by preventing explosions caused by flammable gases, marking a pivotal advancement in mining technology.
events.name: First Testing of Davy Lamp

events.enhanced_description: In 1816, composer Ludwig van Beethoven successfully won a custody battle for his nephew Karl, which had significant implications for his personal life and emotional well-being. This victory allowed Beethoven to play a more active role in Karl's upbringing amidst his struggles with deafness and financial difficulties.
events.name: Beethoven Custody Battle

events.enhanced_description: In April 1816, Banjul, the capital of The Gambia, was founded as a trading post named Bathurst. This establishment marked the beginning of significant European influence in the region, which would shape the future of Gambia's trade and colonial history.
events.name: Foundation of Banjul

events.enhanced_description: Following the Napoleonic Wars, the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon were resettled by French citizens. This marked a significant moment in the islands' history, as they became a French overseas territory and played a role in the fishing industry.
events.name: Resettlement of Saint Pierre and Miquelon

events.enhanced_description: René Laennec invented the stethoscope, revolutionizing the practice of medicine by allowing physicians to listen to the internal sounds of a patient's body. This invention greatly enhanced diagnostic capabilities and is still a fundamental tool in modern medicine.
events.name: Invention of the Stethoscope

events.enhanced_description: Robert Stirling patented his Stirling engine, known at the time as 'Stirling's air engine', which operates on the principle of cyclic compression and expansion of air. This invention laid the groundwork for future developments in heat engines and renewable energy technologies.

image.caption: Photograph of a Philips Stirling generator.
image.credit: Geni — Photo by user:geni
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of a Stirling engine, not a depiction of the 1816 patent event. Original image date: 2016-08; supported display date: 2016.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Patent of the Stirling Engine

events.enhanced_description: E. Remington and Sons was founded as a firearm manufacturing company, which later expanded into typewriters and other machinery. It became a significant player in American manufacturing and contributed to the industrial revolution in the United States.
events.name: Founding of E. Remington and Sons

events.enhanced_description: Mutuelle de L'assurance contre L'incendie, the predecessor of Axa, was founded in Rouen, France, marking the beginning of organized fire insurance in the country. This institution played a crucial role in the development of modern insurance practices.
events.name: Founding of Mutuelle de L'assurance contre L'incendie

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1816, Tsar Alexander I of Russia signed an order expelling the Jesuits from St. Petersburg and Moscow. This decision reflected the growing tensions between the Russian Orthodox Church and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Expulsion of Jesuits by Tsar Alexander I

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1816, a devastating fire nearly destroyed the city of St. John's, Newfoundland. This disaster had significant repercussions for the community, affecting its infrastructure and economy.
events.name: Fire in St. John's

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1816, Friedrich Karl Ludwig, Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Beck, died and was succeeded by his son Friedrich Wilhelm, who would later found the House of Glücksburg. This transition marked a significant moment in the region's noble lineage.

image.caption: Portrait of Friedrich Karl Ludwig, Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Beck, attributed to Johann Friedrich August Tischbein.
image.credit: Johann Friedrich August Tischbein — Государственная третьяковская галерея. Каталог живописи XVIII-начала XX века (до 1917 года)
image.date_qualification: The image date is supplied as “1800” with year-level precision; it is not a depiction of the 1816 death event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Friedrich Karl Ludwig

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1816, Gioachino Rossini's opera buffa 'The Barber of Seville' premiered at the Teatro Argentina in Rome. This opera would become one of the most popular and frequently performed works in the operatic repertoire.
events.name: Premiere of The Barber of Seville

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1816, the Gorkha War between the United Kingdom and Nepal concluded with the ratification of the Treaty of Sugauli. This treaty resulted in Nepal ceding about one-third of its territory to British Indian control.
events.name: End of the Gorkha War

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1816, U.S. Secretary of State James Monroe was nominated by a caucus of Democratic-Republican Party members of Congress to be the party's representative in the upcoming presidential election. This nomination was a significant step in his political career.
events.name: James Monroe's nomination

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1816, King Louis XVIII of France reorganized the Institut de France into four royal academies, including the revived Académie française and the Royal Academy of Sciences. This reorganization aimed to promote arts and sciences in post-Napoleonic France.
events.name: Reorganization of the Institut de France

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1816, the United States signed a treaty with the Cherokee Nation, acknowledging the return of lands in Alabama and Georgia that had been ceded under duress by the Creek Nation in 1814. However, General Andrew Jackson refused to honor this treaty, using the controversy to justify the forced removal of Native Americans from their ancestral lands in the southeastern United States.
events.name: Treaty with the Cherokee Nation

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1816, the Second Bank of the United States was chartered in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. This institution was established to stabilize the economy and provide a uniform currency, reflecting the growing need for a centralized banking system in the post-Revolutionary War United States.
events.name: Charter of the Second Bank of the United States

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1816, the African Methodist Episcopal Church was established in Philadelphia by Richard Allen and other African-American Methodists. This marked a significant moment in American religious history as it became the first denomination in the U.S. completely independent of white churches, addressing the spiritual needs of African Americans.
events.name: Establishment of the African Methodist Episcopal Church

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1816, King Louis XVIII established the Caisse des dépôts et consignations in France, a public investment body aimed at promoting economic development and managing public funds. This institution played a crucial role in the modernization of France's financial system.
events.name: Creation of the Caisse des dépôts et consignations

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1816, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg married Charlotte Augusta, the daughter of the Prince Regent, at Carlton House in London. This union was significant as it strengthened ties between the British royal family and European nobility.
events.name: Marriage of Leopold and Charlotte Augusta

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1816, the Chambre introuvable in France abolished divorce, reversing the liberal policies that had been enacted during the French Revolution. This decision reflected the conservative backlash against the changes brought about by the Revolution and aimed to reinforce traditional family structures.
events.name: Abolition of Divorce in France

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1816, the Governorate of Estonia, part of the Russian Empire, emancipated its peasants from serfdom. This reform was part of a broader movement across Europe to abolish feudal practices and improve the rights of the lower classes.
events.name: Emancipation of Peasants in Estonia

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1816, the Society for the Promotion of Permanent and Universal Peace was founded in London. This organization aimed to advocate for peace and disarmament during a time of political upheaval and conflict in Europe.
events.name: Foundation of the Society for the Promotion of Permanent and Universal Peace

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1816, the Battle of Seven Oaks occurred near Winnipeg, Canada, where the North West Company defeated the Hudson's Bay Company. This conflict was a significant event in the struggle for control of the fur trade in North America.
events.name: Battle of Seven Oaks

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1816, the French passenger ship Medusa ran aground off the coast of Senegal, resulting in the loss of 140 lives during a botched rescue operation that lasted weeks. This tragic event led to a scandal in the French government and inspired the famous painting 'The Raft of the Medusa' by Théodore Géricault.
events.name: Shipwreck of the Medusa
