events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1816, the United Provinces of South America, comprising modern-day Argentina, Uruguay, Bolivia, and parts of Brazil, declared independence from Spanish rule. This event was a crucial step in the broader Latin American independence movements against colonial powers.
events.name: Declaration of Independence of the United Provinces of South America

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1816, the Treaty of St. Louis was signed between the United States and the Council of Three Fires tribes in St. Louis, Missouri. This treaty aimed to establish peace and regulate land use between the U.S. government and Native American tribes.
events.name: Treaty of St. Louis

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1816, the United Kingdom formally annexed the Tristan da Cunha archipelago in the southern Atlantic Ocean, ruling it from the Cape Colony. This annexation was part of Britain's broader strategy to expand its influence in the South Atlantic.

locations.name: Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic Ocean

events.name: Annexation of Tristan da Cunha

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1816, an Anglo-Dutch fleet bombarded Algiers, compelling Omar Agha, the Dey of Algiers, to free Christian slaves. This military action was part of a broader campaign against piracy and slavery in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Bombardment of Algiers

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1816, Pope Pius VII sent a directive to Stanisław Bohusz Siestrzeńciewicz, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Mohilev, advising against the Russian Bible Society's plans to circulate Scriptures in Russian. The Pope expressed concerns that such actions could lead to more harm than good within the Church.
events.name: Papal Directive on Russian Bible Society

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1816, King Louis XVIII dissolved the Chambre introuvable, the legislature elected after the Second Bourbon Restoration. This action reflected the ongoing political tensions in post-revolutionary France as the monarchy sought to consolidate power.
events.name: Dissolution of the Chambre introuvable

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1816, the Penang Free School was founded by Rev. Sparke Hutchings on the island of Penang, Malaysia. This institution was significant as it became one of the earliest English schools in Southeast Asia, promoting education among the local population.
events.name: Foundation of Penang Free School

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1816, James Monroe won the presidential election against Rufus King, marking the beginning of the 'Era of Good Feelings' in American politics. Monroe's presidency would be characterized by a sense of national unity and the absence of partisan conflict.
events.name: 1816 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1816, the British troop transport Harpooner was wrecked at Cape Pine, Newfoundland, resulting in the loss of 208 of the 385 people on board. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during this period and raised concerns about naval safety.
events.name: Wreck of the Harpooner

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1816, the University of Warsaw was established, marking a significant development in Polish education and culture. This institution would become a center for academic excellence and intellectual thought in Poland.
events.name: Establishment of the University of Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: The American Colonization Society was established to promote the emigration of free African Americans to Africa, particularly to Liberia. This organization was controversial as it reflected the complexities of race relations in early 19th-century America, advocating for a solution to the perceived 'problem' of free blacks in the United States.

image.caption: Emblem of the American Colonization Society.
image.credit: Felipe Fidelis Tobias — Own work File:American Colonization Society member certificate (color, Rev. S. R. Ely).jpg
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2023-10-07; it is not the date of the historical event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of the American Colonization Society

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1816, Indiana was admitted as the 19th state of the United States. This event marked a significant step in the westward expansion of the United States and the growth of its political landscape.
events.name: Indiana Admitted as a State

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1816, the thrones of Sicily and Naples were merged into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies under King Ferdinand I. This unification was a significant political development in southern Italy, shaping the region's governance for years to come.
figures: Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies
events.name: Merger of the Kingdoms of Sicily and Naples

events.enhanced_description: Otto von Kotzebue, a Russian explorer, discovered New Year Island while sailing through the Sandwich Islands. This discovery added to the European knowledge of the Pacific Islands during the age of exploration.
events.name: Discovery of New Year Island

events.enhanced_description: The U.S. Congress passed a law to split the Mississippi Territory, creating the Alabama Territory after Mississippi drafted a constitution. This legislative action was significant in the westward expansion and organization of new states.
events.name: U.S. Congress Passes Law to Split Mississippi Territory

events.enhanced_description: In 1817, tradesman Jeffery Sedwards founded the Skibbereen Abstinence Society in Skibbereen, County Cork, Ireland. This organization is recognized as the first dedicated to promoting teetotalism in Europe, advocating for complete abstinence from alcohol.
events.name: Establishment of the Skibbereen Abstinence Society

events.enhanced_description: The first cholera pandemic originated in Bengal, India, in 1817, reaching Calcutta by September. This outbreak marked the beginning of a global health crisis that would have devastating effects.
events.name: First cholera pandemic

events.enhanced_description: In 1817, a typhus epidemic struck Edinburgh and Glasgow, Scotland, leading to significant health crises in both cities. This outbreak highlighted the public health challenges of the time.

locations.name: Edinburgh and Glasgow, Scotland, United Kingdom

events.name: Typhus epidemic in Edinburgh and Glasgow

events.enhanced_description: General José de San Martín led an army of 5,423 soldiers across the Andes from Argentina to liberate Chile and Peru from Spanish colonial rule. This military maneuver was pivotal in the South American wars of independence.
events.name: Crossing of the Andes by José de San Martín

events.enhanced_description: Hindu College was founded in Kolkata by Ram Mohan Roy and David Hare, aiming to provide education in English and Western subjects. This institution played a significant role in the Bengal Renaissance and the modernization of education in India.
events.name: Founding of Hindu College

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Chacabuco was a decisive victory for Argentine and Chilean forces led by José de San Martín against Spanish royalist troops. This battle marked a turning point in the struggle for independence in South America.
events.name: Battle of Chacabuco

events.enhanced_description: On his last day in office, President James Madison vetoed John C. Calhoun's Bonus Bill, deeming it unconstitutional despite its passage through Congress. This action underscored the ongoing debates over federal power and states' rights in the early United States.
events.name: James Madison's Veto of the Bonus Bill

events.enhanced_description: James Monroe was inaugurated as the fifth President of the United States, succeeding James Madison. His presidency would later be known for the Monroe Doctrine, which shaped U.S. foreign policy in the Americas.

image.caption: Portrait of James Monroe, attributed to Samuel Finley Breese Morse.
image.credit: Samuel Finley Breese Morse — https://www.whitehousehistory.org/photos/james-monroe
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated circa 1819, about two years after the inauguration on 1817-03-04; it is contextual rather than an event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Inauguration of James Monroe

events.enhanced_description: The flag of the Pernambucan Revolt was publicly blessed by the dean of Recife Cathedral, symbolizing the local support for the uprising against Portuguese rule in Brazil. This event highlighted the growing desire for independence in the region.
events.name: Blessing of the Pernambucan Revolt Flag

events.enhanced_description: The mysterious figure known as 'Princess Caraboo' appeared in Almondsbury, claiming to be from a distant island kingdom. Her story captivated local residents until it was revealed that she was actually a servant girl from Devon, highlighting themes of identity and deception.
events.name: Appearance of Princess Caraboo

events.enhanced_description: The American School for the Deaf opened in Hartford, Connecticut, becoming the first school for the deaf in the United States. This institution played a crucial role in the education and advocacy for individuals with hearing impairments.
events.name: Opening of the American School for the Deaf

events.enhanced_description: The Rush–Bagot Treaty was signed between the United States and the British Empire, limiting the number of warships on the Great Lakes. This treaty was a significant step towards peaceful relations between the two nations following the War of 1812.
events.name: Signing of the Rush–Bagot Treaty

events.enhanced_description: The General Convention of the Episcopal Church founded the General Theological Seminary while meeting in New York City. This institution became a key center for theological education and training for clergy in the Episcopal Church.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Founding of the General Theological Seminary

events.enhanced_description: German inventor Karl Drais drove his dandy horse, known as the Draisine or Laufmaschine, in Mannheim. This early form of bicycle marked a significant innovation in personal transportation and laid the groundwork for future developments in cycling.
events.name: Karl Drais Drives the Dandy Horse

events.enhanced_description: King Ferdinand VII of Spain issued a royal decree legalizing the production and sale of tobacco in Cuba, which led to the establishment of the Cuban cigar industry. This decision had lasting economic implications for Cuba and its agricultural practices.
events.name: Legalization of Tobacco Production in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: A large riot broke out in Copenhagen Prison, prompting the Danish army to intervene and restore order. This incident highlighted the tensions within the penal system and societal unrest in early 19th-century Denmark.
events.name: Copenhagen Prison Riot

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1817, construction of the Erie Canal commenced in Rome, New York. This ambitious project aimed to connect the Hudson River with Lake Erie, facilitating trade and transportation between the Atlantic Ocean and the Great Lakes.
events.name: Construction of the Erie Canal Begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1817, the U.S. Congress established the Alabama Territory by partitioning the Mississippi Territory. This act was significant as it laid the groundwork for Alabama's eventual statehood.
events.name: Creation of the Alabama Territory

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1817, the town of Araraquara was founded in the state of São Paulo, Brazil. This establishment marked the growth of settlements in the region during the early 19th century.
events.name: Founding of Araraquara

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1817, an earthquake struck near the ancient site of Helike in Achaea, Greece, resulting in the deaths of 65 people. This event highlighted the seismic activity in the region, which has a history of earthquakes.
events.name: Earthquake near Helike

events.enhanced_description: The University of Michigan was founded on August 26, 1817, initially located in Detroit. It later moved to Ann Arbor in 1837, becoming one of the leading public universities in the United States.
events.name: Founding of the University of Michigan

events.enhanced_description: The Great Rebellion of 1817-18 began on September 11, 1817, in Sri Lanka, against British colonial rule. This uprising was a significant event in the struggle for independence in the region.
events.name: The Great Rebellion of 1817-18

events.enhanced_description: The University of Ghent was officially opened on October 9, 1817, in Ghent, Belgium. It became a significant center for higher education and research in the region.

image.caption: Mattheus Ignatius van Bree’s preparatory study depicting the inauguration of Ghent University in Ghent’s town hall.
image.credit: Mattheus Ignatius van Bree — http://www.rijksmuseum.nl/collectie/SK-A-4088
image.date_qualification: The scene is identified as the 9 October 1817 inauguration; the artwork itself is dated between 1817 and 1830.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Opening of the University of Ghent

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1817, the frigate HMS Trincomalee was launched in Bombay (now Mumbai), India, for the British Royal Navy. This ship remains notable for being one of the oldest warships still afloat.
events.name: Launch of HMS Trincomalee

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1817, Simón Bolívar established the independent government of Venezuela, marking a crucial step in the country's struggle for independence from Spanish colonial rule.
events.name: Establishment of the independent government of Venezuela

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Ninkō acceded to the throne of Japan on October 31, 1817. His reign marked a period of significant political and social change in Japan.
events.name: Accession of Emperor Ninkō

events.enhanced_description: The Bank of Montreal was established on November 3, 1817, in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. It is recognized as the oldest bank in Canada and played a crucial role in the country's financial development.

image.caption: 1844 halfpenny token depicting the Bank of Montreal facade on its obverse.
image.credit: Петров Эдуард — Own work
image.date_qualification: Token dated 1844; image date 2023-03-15 is the depicted image’s creation date, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Opening of the Bank of Montreal

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Khadki occurred on November 5, 1817, marking the beginning of the Third Anglo-Maratha War. British East India Company forces achieved a decisive victory over the Maratha Empire.
events.name: Battle of Khadki

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1817, Princess Charlotte of Wales died shortly after giving birth to a stillborn son. Her death caused widespread mourning in Britain and raised concerns about the royal succession.
events.name: Death of Princess Charlotte of Wales

events.enhanced_description: The First Seminole War commenced on November 20, 1817, in Florida. This conflict arose from tensions between the United States and the Seminole tribe, leading to significant military engagements.
events.name: First Seminole War begins

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1817, explorer Frédéric Cailliaud discovered the ancient Roman emerald mines at Sikait, Egypt. This discovery shed light on the historical significance of the region's mining activities.
events.name: Discovery of Roman emerald mines

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1817, Mississippi was admitted as the 20th U.S. state, transitioning from its previous status as the Mississippi Territory. This event marked a significant expansion of the United States.
events.name: Mississippi becomes a U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: The episodes of Mikhail Lermontov's life in Chechnya during the early 19th century reflect his experiences as a soldier and poet. These moments contributed to his literary works and shaped his views on the Caucasus, influencing Russian literature.
events.name: Mikhail Lermontov in Chechnya

events.enhanced_description: The Minnamurra River massacre in October 1818 was a tragic event in New South Wales, Australia, where colonial settlers violently clashed with Indigenous Australians. This incident is emblematic of the broader conflicts and tensions arising from European colonization.
events.name: Minnamurra River massacre, South Coast

events.enhanced_description: In January 1818, during the Third Anglo-Maratha War, the British East India Company achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Koregaon against the Maratha Empire. This battle was significant in consolidating British control over India.
events.name: Battle of Koregaon

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, Mary Shelley published her groundbreaking novel 'Frankenstein', which explored themes of creation, responsibility, and the consequences of scientific advancement. This work is considered one of the earliest examples of science fiction.

image.caption: Illustration of Frankenstein and his creature from an abridged version of Mary Shelley’s novel.
image.credit: The Cincinnati Enquirer — The Cincinnati Enquirer, January 16, 1910
image.date_qualification: Published 1910; retrospective illustration, not an image from the novel’s 1818 publication.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Frankenstein

events.enhanced_description: In June 1818, the Battle of Kafir Qala took place, where Afghan forces successfully defeated a Persian invasion. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region during this period.
events.name: Battle of Kafir Qala

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, the Old Vic Theatre was founded in London, originally known as the Royal Coburg Hall. This venue would become a significant cultural institution in British theatre history.
events.name: The Old Vic Theatre is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, the Westmorland Gazette was first published in Kendal, Cumbria. This newspaper would play an important role in local journalism and community news.
events.name: The Westmorland Gazette is first published

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, a clash occurred between Catholic and Orthodox communities in Aleppo, Syria. This conflict highlighted the ongoing tensions between different Christian denominations in the region.
events.name: Catholic-Orthodox clash in Aleppo

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, the first edition of the Farmers' Almanac was published in the United States. This publication has since become a staple for agricultural advice and weather predictions.
events.name: First edition of Farmers' Almanac published

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, Vuk Karadžić published the first Serbian dictionary, which played a crucial role in the standardization of the Serbian language and the promotion of Serbian culture.
events.name: First Serbian dictionary published

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, the Besses o' th' Barn Brass Band was formed in Whitefield, near Manchester, England. This band has since become one of the most famous brass bands in the UK.
events.name: Besses o' th' Barn Brass Band formed

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, the Barakzai brothers expelled Mahmud Shah and the Sadozais from Afghanistan, subsequently dividing the provinces among themselves. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within the region.
events.name: Barakzai brothers expel Mahmud Shah

events.enhanced_description: In 1818, the Akure-Benin War occurred, characterized by the invasion of Akure by forces from Benin. This conflict was part of the broader struggles for power and territory in the region.
events.name: Akure-Benin War

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1818, Jeremiah Chubb was granted a British patent for the Chubb detector lock, a significant advancement in security technology. This lock was designed to prevent unauthorized access and became a standard in safes and secure doors.
events.name: Jeremiah Chubb is granted a British patent for the Chubb detector lock

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1818, Sir Walter Scott discovered the Honours of Scotland, the Scottish crown jewels, hidden in Edinburgh Castle. This significant find rekindled interest in Scotland's royal history and heritage.
events.name: Sir Walter Scott finds the Honours of Scotland in Edinburgh Castle

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1818, King Charles XIII of Sweden passed away, leading to the succession of his adoptive son, Charles XIV John. This event marked the beginning of the Royal House of Bernadotte, which continues to this day.
events.name: Death of King Charles XIII of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1818, Marie André Cantillon attempted to assassinate the Duke of Wellington in Paris. This incident highlighted the political tensions of the time and the Duke's prominence as a military leader.
events.name: Assassination attempt on the Duke of Wellington

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1818, Chile proclaimed its independence from Spanish rule, marking a pivotal moment in the Chilean War of Independence. This declaration was a significant step towards establishing Chile as a sovereign nation.
events.name: Chilean Declaration of Independence from Spain

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1818, during the First Seminole War, General Andrew Jackson led American forces into Florida. This military action was part of a broader conflict involving Native American tribes and Spanish colonial interests.
events.name: First Seminole War: General Andrew Jackson invades Florida

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1818, Easter Sunday fell on its earliest possible date in the Western Christian calendar. This occurrence will not happen again until 2285, making it a notable event in the liturgical calendar.
events.name: Easter Sunday in Western Christianity

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1818, during the First Seminole War, General Andrew Jackson's forces defeated Chief Kinhagee at the Battle of Miccosukee in Florida. This victory further established American military presence in the region.
events.name: Battle of Miccosukee

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1818, the United States Congress adopted a new flag design featuring thirteen red and white stripes and one star for each of the twenty states. This design allowed for additional stars to be added as new states joined the Union.
events.name: Adoption of the United States flag

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1818, during the Chilean War of Independence, patriot rebels led by José de San Martín achieved a decisive victory over Spanish Royalists at the Battle of Maipú. This battle was crucial in securing Chilean independence.
events.name: Battle of Maipú

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1818, Brooks Brothers, the oldest men's clothier in the United States, opened its first store at the northeast corner of Catherine and Cherry Streets in New York City. This establishment would become a significant part of American fashion history.
events.name: Brooks Brothers opens its first store

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1818, operations of the United States Survey of the Coast were suspended. This survey was crucial for mapping and understanding the coastal geography of the United States.
events.name: Suspension of the United States Survey of the Coast operations

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1818, explorer John Ross set sail on his ship, the Isabella, in search of the elusive Northwest Passage. This expedition was part of the broader age of exploration and aimed to find a navigable route through the Arctic.
events.name: John Ross sets sail in search of the Northwest Passage

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1818, Charles XIV John was crowned king of Sweden, marking the beginning of his reign and the establishment of the Bernadotte dynasty. His rule would significantly influence Swedish politics and society.
events.name: Charles XIV of Sweden crowned king

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1818, Baji Rao II, the Peshwa of the Maratha Confederacy, surrendered to Sir John Malcolm of the British East India Company, effectively ending the Third Anglo-Maratha War. This surrender marked a significant consolidation of British power in India.
events.name: Surrender of Baji Rao II

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1818, Prime Minister Jenkinson dissolved the British Parliament, leading to new elections scheduled for August 4. This political maneuver was part of the ongoing shifts in British governance during the period.
events.name: Dissolution of the British Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1818, Prince William, Duke of Clarence and St Andrews, married Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. This union would eventually lead to William becoming King William IV of the United Kingdom.
events.name: Marriage of Prince William and Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1818, a catastrophic event occurred in Switzerland when the melting of a glacier released the natural dam of Lac de Mauvoisin, flooding the valley of Bagnes and resulting in at least 34 fatalities. This disaster underscored the dangers of glacial melt.
events.name: Glacier disaster in Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1818, following a series of conflicts, Baji Rao II surrendered to the British East India Company, effectively ending the Third Anglo-Maratha War. This surrender marked the consolidation of British control over much of India.
events.name: End of the Third Anglo-Maratha War

events.enhanced_description: In July 1818, English poet Lord Byron, residing in Ravenna, Italy, commenced work on his satirical epic 'Don Juan.' Although he completed the first canto by September 19, he would pass away in 1824, leaving the poem unfinished after 16 cantos.

image.caption: Cover of the first edition of Lord Byron’s Don Juan.
image.credit: Lord Byron — https://archive.org/stream/donjuan21byro#page/n5/mode/2up
image.date_qualification: 1819 publication; later than the reported 1818 start of composition.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Lord Byron begins work on Don Juan

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1818, the Bank of the United States reversed its policy of expanding credit, issuing notices to borrowers nationwide demanding immediate repayment. This decision led to widespread defaults over the following months, triggering the Panic of 1819, the first major peacetime financial crisis in the U.S.
events.name: Bank of the United States demands repayment

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1818, U.S. President James Monroe convened a cabinet meeting to discuss General Andrew Jackson's unauthorized invasion of Spanish Florida. Secretary of State John Quincy Adams successfully argued that Jackson's actions were justifiable in response to threats from the Seminole tribes.
events.name: Cabinet meeting on Andrew Jackson's actions

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1818, French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel submitted his groundbreaking work 'Memoir on the Diffraction of Light' to the French Academy of Sciences. This work provided a precise explanation of how light spreads into shadows, effectively countering longstanding objections to the wave theory of light.
events.name: Fresnel submits memoir on diffraction

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1818, the first newspaper in Cleveland, Ohio, was published by Andrew Logan. Named 'The Cleaveland Gazette & Commercial Register,' it served the small settlement with a population of 172 at the time.
events.name: First newspaper in Cleveland issued

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1818, a separate Topographical Bureau was established within the United States Department of War. This bureau was tasked with overseeing the mapping and surveying of U.S. territories.
events.name: Topographical Bureau established

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1818, the United Kingdom held a general election for the House of Commons. The Tory Party, led by Prime Minister Robert Jenkinson, retained control of the government but lost some parliamentary seats.
events.name: 1818 United Kingdom general election

events.enhanced_description: In September 1818, Sir Stamford Raffles set out to meet Lord Hastings, the Governor-General of India, to seek approval for establishing a trading station at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, which is modern-day Singapore.
events.name: Stamford Raffles visits Lord Hastings

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1818, Carl III of Sweden-Norway was crowned king of Norway in Trondheim. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the union between Sweden and Norway.
events.name: Carl III crowned king of Norway

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1818, border markers were formally installed for the European territory of Moresnet. This action established clear territorial boundaries in the region.
events.name: Border markers installed for Moresnet

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1818, Claudine Thévenet, known as Mary of St. Ignatius, founded the Roman Catholic order Religieuses de Jésus-Marie in Lyon, France. This order focused on education and the care of the poor.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Claudine Thévenet, foundress of the Religious of Jesus and Mary.
image.credit: Robinsonraju — Own work
image.date_qualification: Portrait painting of Claudine Thévenet, not a depiction of the religious order founding. The original painting or reproduction date is not established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Claudine Thévenet founds religious order

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1818, a treaty between the United States and the United Kingdom established the boundary between the U.S. and British North America along the 49th parallel, from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains, creating the Northwest Angle.
events.name: U.S.-UK treaty establishes boundary

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1818, Robert Morrison founded the Anglo-Chinese College in Malacca, which would later be renamed Ying Wa College. This institution played a significant role in the education of Chinese students in the region.
events.name: Anglo-Chinese College founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1818, Reverend Louis William Valentine Dubourg founded the Saint Louis Academy, which would later evolve into Saint Louis University. This institution became a significant center for education in the region.
events.name: Saint Louis Academy founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1818, Illinois was admitted as the 21st state of the United States. This marked a significant expansion of the U.S. territory and governance.
events.name: Illinois admitted as U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1818, Cyril VI of Constantinople resigned from his position as Ecumenical Patriarch. His resignation marked a notable event in the history of the Eastern Orthodox Church.
events.name: Cyril VI resigns as Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1818, the Christmas carol 'Silent Night' (Stille Nacht), with lyrics by priest Josef Mohr and music by organist Franz Xaver Gruber, was first performed at St. Nikolaus Parish Church in Oberndorf bei Salzburg, Austria. This carol has since become one of the most beloved Christmas songs worldwide.

image.caption: Franz Xaver Gruber’s autograph manuscript of “Stille Nacht.”
image.credit: Franz Xaver Gruber (1787–1863) — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Autograph manuscript dated circa 1860, decades after the carol’s first performance in 1818; it is not a contemporary record of that performance.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Silent Night first performed

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1819, the Panic of 1819 began, marking the first major peacetime financial crisis in the United States. This economic downturn had widespread effects on the banking system and the economy at large.
events.name: Panic of 1819 begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1819, Thomas Jefferson founded the University of Virginia in Charlottesville. This institution was designed to promote higher education and democratic ideals in the United States.
events.name: Thomas Jefferson founds University of Virginia

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1819, Sir Stamford Raffles landed on the island of Singapore, marking the beginning of British colonial influence in the region. His arrival led to the establishment of Singapore as a key trading post for the British Empire in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Sir Stamford Raffles lands on the island of Singapore

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1819, the U.S. Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice John Marshall, ruled in favor of Dartmouth College in the case against Woodward, affirming the college's right to maintain its charter and remain a private institution. This landmark decision reinforced the sanctity of contracts and limited state interference in private corporations.
events.name: Dartmouth College v. Woodward

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1819, the Treaty of Singapore was signed between Hussein Shah of Johor and Sir Stamford Raffles, establishing Singapore as a British trading settlement. This treaty laid the foundation for Singapore's development as a major port and commercial hub in Southeast Asia.
events.name: The Treaty of Singapore

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1819, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Tallmadge Amendment, which sought to prohibit slavery in the new state of Missouri. This amendment sparked significant debate and controversy, ultimately leading to the Missouri Compromise.

image.caption: Portrait of James Tallmadge.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — NLPL Digital Collections [1]
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1850; the Tallmadge Amendment was submitted in 1819.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Tallmadge Amendment

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1819, Captain William Smith, aboard the British merchant brig Williams, sighted Williams Point, the northeastern extremity of Livingston Island in the South Shetland Islands. This marked the first land discovered south of latitude 60° S, contributing to the exploration of Antarctica.
events.name: Captain William Smith sights Williams Point

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1819, the Adams–Onís Treaty was signed, in which Spain ceded Florida to the United States in exchange for the U.S. renouncing any claims on Texas and paying $5 million. This treaty significantly expanded U.S. territory and influence in North America.
events.name: Adams–Onís Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1819, the U.S. naval vessel USS Columbus was launched on the Potomac River in Washington, D.C. This ship would serve in the United States Navy, contributing to naval operations in the years to come.
events.name: Launch of USS Columbus

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1819, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in McCulloch v. Maryland that the Bank of the United States was constitutional. This decision, delivered by Chief Justice John Marshall, reinforced federal authority over state laws.
events.name: McCulloch v. Maryland

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1819, the Burlington Arcade opened in London, becoming one of the first shopping arcades in the world. It was designed to provide a covered shopping experience and has since become a notable landmark.
events.name: Burlington Arcade opens

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1819, German dramatist August von Kotzebue was assassinated by Karl Ludwig Sand in Mannheim, Baden-Württemberg. This politically motivated act was part of a larger wave of nationalist sentiment and unrest in Germany.
events.name: Assassination of August von Kotzebue

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1819, the French slave ship Le Rodeur sailed from Bonny in West Africa to Guadeloupe in the West Indies. During the voyage, many onboard suffered from blindness, and tragically, 30 slaves were thrown overboard.
events.name: Le Rodeur sails from Bonny

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1819, the Governorate of Livonia, part of the Russian Empire, emancipated its peasants from serfdom. This significant reform marked a step towards modernizing the social structure within the empire.
events.name: Emancipation of Peasants in Livonia

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1819, the SS Savannah departed from Savannah, Georgia, on a historic voyage to become the first steamship to cross the Atlantic Ocean. Although only a portion of the journey was made under steam, this marked a significant milestone in maritime history.

image.caption: Painting of the SS Savannah by Hunter Wood.
image.credit: Hunter Wood — http://www.sip.armstrong.edu/Transportation/FullView/Trans_Img14.html
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the depicted subject to 1819; no date for the painting is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: SS Savannah leaves port

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1819, the city of Memphis, Tennessee, was founded. It would grow to become a significant cultural and economic center in the American South, known for its music and historical significance.

image.caption: Woodcut depicting the waterfront of Memphis, Tennessee.
image.credit: engraved by John Filmer, based on a work by another artist (A. R. W.) — The American Cyclopædia , v. 11, 1879, p. 380
image.date_qualification: Published 1879, sixty years after the founding; not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of Memphis

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1819, the Rann of Kutch earthquake struck Gujarat, India, with an estimated magnitude of at least 7.7 Mw. The disaster resulted in the deaths of at least 1,543 people and caused significant geological changes, including the formation of the Allahbund dam.
events.name: Rann of Kutch earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1819, German astronomer Johann Georg Tralles discovered what would later be known as the Great Comet of 1819. This discovery contributed to the field of astronomy and the understanding of comets.
events.name: Discovery of the Great Comet of 1819

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1819, explorer William Parry guided the ships HMS Hecla and HMS Griper through an iceberg-laden passage in the Arctic, which would later be named the Parry Channel. This expedition was part of the ongoing quest for the Northwest Passage.
events.name: William Parry's Arctic Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1819, British Prime Minister Lord Liverpool convened a cabinet meeting to discuss an investigative report regarding an alleged adulterous affair involving Princess Caroline, the wife of George, Prince of Wales. The cabinet ultimately decided that a trial would be too embarrassing for the nation.
events.name: Cabinet meeting on Princess Caroline

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1819, the United States concluded a treaty with the Kickapoo tribe at Edwardsville, Illinois, which involved the acquisition of their lands in exchange for their relocation to Missouri. This treaty was part of the broader policy of Indian removal during this period.
events.name: Treaty with the Kickapoo tribe

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1819, the first Hep-Hep riots began in Würzburg, Bavaria, targeting Ashkenazi Jews. These communal pogroms resulted in numerous deaths and highlighted the rising anti-Semitic sentiments in the German Federation.
events.name: First Hep-Hep riots

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1819, Captain Alden Partridge founded Norwich University in Northfield, Vermont, as the first private military school in the United States. This institution played a significant role in the development of military education in the country.
events.name: Founding of Norwich University

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1819, Simón Bolívar achieved a decisive victory over the Royalist Army at the Battle of Boyacá in Colombia. This battle was pivotal in securing Colombia's independence from Spanish rule and is celebrated as a key moment in the South American independence movements.
events.name: Battle of Boyacá

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1819, the Peterloo Massacre occurred when a yeomanry unit charged into a crowd of radical protesters in Manchester, England, resulting in 15 deaths and over 600 injuries. This tragic event highlighted the growing tensions over political reform and workers' rights in Britain.
events.name: Peterloo Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1819, the Salon of 1819 opened in Paris, showcasing various artworks, including the notable painting 'The Raft of the Medusa.' This event was significant in the art world, reflecting the cultural movements of the time.
events.name: Salon of 1819 opens

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1819, the Balloon Riot occurred at Vauxhall Garden in Philadelphia when guards beat a boy who attempted to avoid buying a ticket. The incident escalated, leading to crowds breaking down fences and destroying the hot air balloon, reflecting the tensions of the time.
events.name: Balloon Riot in Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: The Carlsbad Decrees were a series of measures enacted by the German Confederation to suppress liberal and nationalist movements following the assassination of playwright August von Kotzebue. These decrees included censorship of the press and the establishment of a system of surveillance over universities.
events.name: The Carlsbad Decrees

events.enhanced_description: In October 1819, the ʻAi Noa Movement, which sought to abolish the kapu system and promote a more open society, took power in Hawaii. This marked a significant cultural and political shift in the Hawaiian Islands.
events.name: The ʻAi Noa Movement takes power in Hawaii

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political maneuver, the Raja of Cutch, Deshalji II, entered into a treaty with the East India Company, effectively placing the Cutch State under British control. This marked a pivotal moment in the expansion of British influence in India.
events.name: Treaty between Raja of Cutch and East India Company

events.enhanced_description: Captain William Smith discovered Desolation Island, part of the South Shetland Islands, during his expedition in the Antarctic region. This discovery contributed to the understanding of the geography of Antarctica and the surrounding waters.
events.name: Discovery of Desolation Island

events.enhanced_description: Bagyidaw was crowned as the Emperor of Burma at the imperial capital of Inwa, marking the beginning of his reign. His rule would see significant developments in Burmese culture and politics.
events.name: Crowning of Bagyidaw as Emperor of Burma

events.enhanced_description: The USS Congress, under the command of Captain John D. Henley, became the first American warship to visit China, landing at Lintin Island off the coast of Canton. This visit marked an important moment in U.S.-China relations.
events.name: USS Congress visits China

events.enhanced_description: The Museo del Prado, one of the world's premier art galleries, opened its doors in Madrid, initially showcasing 311 significant paintings. It has since become a cornerstone of European art and culture.
events.name: Opening of the Museo del Prado

events.enhanced_description: A British expeditionary force reached Ras Al Khaimah in the Persian Gulf, preparing for the bombardment and invasion of the town. This action was part of a broader strategy that led to the signing of the General Maritime Treaty of 1820.
events.name: British expeditionary force reaches Ras Al Khaimah

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1819, Alabama was admitted as the 22nd state of the United States. This event marked a significant expansion of the Union and reflected the growing influence of the southern states.
events.name: Alabama admitted as the 22nd U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: The Republic of Gran Colombia was formally established on December 17, 1819, with Simón Bolívar as its first president. This republic aimed to unify several South American territories that had gained independence from Spanish rule.
events.name: Establishment of the Republic of Gran Colombia

events.enhanced_description: In early 1820, Lord Cochrane occupied Valdivia in the name of the Republic of Chile, marking a significant military action during the Chilean War of Independence. This occupation was part of a broader campaign to liberate Chile from Spanish rule.
events.name: Capture of Valdivia

events.enhanced_description: In 1820, a group of 86 free African American colonists sailed from New York City to Freetown, Sierra Leone, with the intention of establishing a settlement for freed American slaves, which would later be known as Liberia. This movement was part of the broader colonization efforts during this period.
events.name: African American Colonists to Sierra Leone

events.enhanced_description: In 1820, Robert Owen delivered a report to the County of Lanark outlining a plan to alleviate public distress and discontent, marking the beginning of his advocacy for social reform and the development of the labor voucher system.
events.name: Robert Owen's Report

events.enhanced_description: In 1820, delegates in St. Louis, Missouri Territory, approved a proposed state constitution, declaring their intention to form an independent republic named 'The State of Missouri'. This event was a significant step towards Missouri's eventual statehood.
events.name: Delegates in St. Louis Approve Constitution

events.enhanced_description: The Argentine Confederation formally claimed the Falkland Islands, which at the time had no permanent population. This claim would later become a point of contention between Argentina and the United Kingdom.
events.name: Argentine Confederation claims the Falkland Islands

events.enhanced_description: Mount Rainier erupted, affecting the surrounding areas, including modern-day Seattle. This event is part of the geological history of the Cascade Range and highlights the volcanic activity in the region.
events.name: Mount Rainier erupts

events.enhanced_description: A significant number of 18,957 black slaves left Luanda, Angola, during this period. This event reflects the ongoing transatlantic slave trade and its impact on African societies.
events.name: Black slaves leave Luanda

events.enhanced_description: The construction of Citadelle Laferrière, the largest fortification in the Americas, was completed in Haiti. Built under the orders of Henri Christophe, it was designed to defend against potential French reoccupation.
events.name: Construction of Citadelle Laferrière completed

events.enhanced_description: Anchor coinage was first struck in silver in London, denominated in fractions of the Mauritian dollar for use in British colonies. This development reflects the evolving monetary systems of the British Empire.
events.name: Anchor coinage first struck in silver

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1820, a devastating fire swept through Guangzhou, destroying approximately 15,000 houses and resulting in a significant loss of life, although the exact number of casualties remains unknown. This catastrophic event highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban areas in China during this period.
events.name: Guangzhou Fire

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1820, the Missouri Compromise was enacted, allowing Missouri to enter the Union as a slave state and Maine as a free state. This legislative agreement was crucial in maintaining the balance of power between slave and free states in the U.S.
events.name: Missouri Compromise

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1820, King Ferdinand VII of Spain accepted a new constitution, marking the beginning of the Trienio Liberal, a period characterized by liberal reforms and political turmoil in Spain. This acceptance was a significant step towards constitutional monarchy in the country.
events.name: Trienio Liberal Begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1820, the Astronomical Society of London was founded, aiming to promote the study of astronomy and facilitate communication among astronomers. This organization played a pivotal role in the advancement of astronomical research in the 19th century.
events.name: Astronomical Society of London Founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1820, Maine was admitted as the 23rd state of the United States, following the Missouri Compromise. This admission was significant as it maintained the balance between slave and free states in the Union.
events.name: Maine Admitted as State

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1820, Joseph Smith, the founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, reported receiving his First Vision in Palmyra, New York. This vision is considered a foundational event in the history of the Latter Day Saint movement.
events.name: Joseph Smith's First Vision

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1820, an attempted coup d'état against the Paraguayan dictator José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia was foiled. The plot was orchestrated by Fulgencio Yegros and Pedro Juan Caballero, reflecting the political unrest in Paraguay during this period.
events.name: Failed Coup in Paraguay

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1820, a proclamation signed by the Committee of Organisation for forming a Provisional Government marked the beginning of the Radical War in Scotland. This conflict arose from demands for political reform and greater representation.
events.name: Radical War Begins

events.enhanced_description: In April 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted discovered the relationship between electricity and magnetism, a groundbreaking finding that laid the foundation for the field of electromagnetism. This discovery had profound implications for physics and engineering.
events.name: Ørsted Discovers Electricity and Magnetism

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1820, the famous statue of the Venus de Milo was discovered on the Greek island of Milos by a peasant named Yorgos Kentrotas. This ancient statue, dating back to around 150-125 BC, is now one of the most celebrated works of ancient Greek art.
events.name: Discovery of Venus de Milo

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1820, Alexander Ypsilantis became the leader of Filiki Eteria, a secret society aimed at liberating Greece from Ottoman rule. This organization played a crucial role in the Greek War of Independence.
events.name: Alexander Ypsilantis and Filiki Eteria

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1820, King William I of Württemberg married his cousin, Pauline Therese, in Stuttgart. This marriage was significant in the context of European royal alliances during the early 19th century.
events.name: Marriage of King William I of Württemberg

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1820, the last judicial decapitation in the United Kingdom was carried out following the public hanging of the Cato Street conspirators for treason. This event marked the end of an era of brutal punishments in British law.
events.name: Last Judicial Decapitation in the UK

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1820, HMS Beagle was launched at Woolwich Dockyard. This ship would later become famous for carrying Charles Darwin on his voyage that contributed to the development of his theory of evolution.
events.name: Launch of HMS Beagle

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1820, at the age of 14, John Stuart Mill embarked on a formative trip to the south of France, where he stayed with his mentor Samuel Bentham. This journey significantly influenced Mill's philosophical development.
events.name: John Stuart Mill's Trip to France

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1820, Caroline of Brunswick, the estranged wife of King George IV of the United Kingdom, returned to England after six years in Italy. Her return was marked by political tension as the King sought a divorce.
figures: George IV of the United Kingdom
events.name: Caroline of Brunswick Returns to England

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1820, Élie Decazes, the leader of the opposition in France's Chamber of Deputies, introduced the 'Law of the Double Vote'. This proposal aimed to create additional legislative seats selected by the wealthiest voters, reflecting the political dynamics of post-Napoleonic France.

image.caption: Portrait of Élie Decazes, painted by François Gérard.
image.credit: François Gérard — https://www.sudouest.fr/culture/expositions/la-destinee-romanesque-d-elie-decazes-est-a-decouvrir-a-la-chapelle-du-carmel-de-libourne-21816911.php
image.date_qualification: Portrait predating the June 1820 law proposal; the saved image date is approximate, circa 1815.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Law of the Double Vote Introduced

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1820, the events leading to the U.S. Supreme Court case known as The Antelope unfolded when a U.S. Treasury cutter captured a ship named Antelope, which was illegally transporting 281 Africans captured as slaves. This case highlighted the ongoing issues surrounding the slave trade in the United States.
events.name: The Antelope Case

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1820, a revolt led by Guglielmo Pepe forced Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies to sign a constitution modeled after the Spanish Constitution of 1812. This event was part of the broader wave of liberal revolutions across Europe.
figures: Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies
events.name: Revolt in the Two Sicilies

events.enhanced_description: Saint Cronan's Boys' National School, originally titled Bray Male School, opened in Bray, County Wicklow, Ireland. It would later be notable for having Cearbhall Ó Dálaigh, who would become President of Ireland, among its pupils.
events.name: Saint Cronan's Boys' National School opens in Bray

events.enhanced_description: The Union Chain Bridge opened across the River Tweed, connecting England and Scotland. At the time, it boasted the world's longest span for a vehicular bridge at 449 feet (137 meters).
events.name: Union Chain Bridge opens

events.enhanced_description: The Regent's Canal was officially opened, providing a vital waterway connection to the London Docks. This development significantly enhanced trade and transportation in the region.
events.name: The Regent's Canal through to the London Docks is opened

events.enhanced_description: A Constitutionalist insurrection erupted in Oporto, Portugal, marking a significant moment in the struggle for constitutional governance in the country. This uprising was part of a broader movement against absolutism.
events.name: Constitutionalist insurrection breaks out at Oporto

events.enhanced_description: The Daoguang Emperor ascended to the throne of the Qing dynasty in China, succeeding his father, the Jiaqing Emperor. His reign would witness significant challenges, including internal strife and foreign pressures.
events.name: Daoguang Emperor succeeds to the throne

events.enhanced_description: José Gervasio Artigas, a prominent leader in the struggle for Uruguayan independence, fled to Paraguay amid political turmoil. His influence on the independence movement would resonate long after his departure.

image.caption: Photograph of the Mausoleum of General José Gervasio Artigas in Uruguay.
image.credit: Sergio Zolessi. — Own work
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of a monument associated with Artigas, not a depiction of his flight to Paraguay. The image date is recorded as “Taken on 8 September 2013, 20:44:42”; no display date is supported.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: José Gervasio Artigas flees to Paraguay

events.enhanced_description: A revolution erupted in Lisbon, targeting King John VI of Portugal. This uprising was part of the broader Liberal Revolution, which sought to establish constitutional governance in Portugal.
events.name: Revolution breaks out in Lisbon against John VI of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: Guayaquil declared its independence from Spanish colonial rule, marking a pivotal moment in the Ecuadorian struggle for sovereignty. This declaration was part of a larger wave of independence movements across Latin America.
events.name: Guayaquil declares independence from Spain

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Troppau convened, bringing together the rulers of Russia, Austria, and Prussia to discuss pressing international issues, particularly the revolutions occurring in Europe. This congress was part of the Concert of Europe aimed at maintaining stability.
events.name: The Congress of Troppau is convened

events.enhanced_description: American seal hunter Captain Nathaniel Palmer became the third known explorer to sight Antarctica, contributing to the early exploration of the continent. The Palmer Peninsula was later named in his honor.
events.name: Captain Nathaniel Palmer sights Antarctica

events.enhanced_description: The American whaleship Essex sank in the Southern Pacific Ocean after being attacked by a sperm whale. The survivors faced dire circumstances, leading them to resort to cannibalism for survival.
events.name: Sinking of the whaleship Essex

events.enhanced_description: James Monroe was re-elected virtually unopposed in the 1820 United States presidential election. Notably, one elector cast a vote for John Quincy Adams to uphold the tradition of George Washington being the only president elected without opposition.
events.name: James Monroe is re-elected

events.enhanced_description: In 1821, the first edition of the Manchester Guardian newspaper was published in Manchester, England. This publication would later become known simply as The Guardian and is recognized for its significant role in journalism and media.
events.name: The first edition of the Manchester Guardian newspaper is published

events.enhanced_description: In 1821, the town of Al-Ubayyid was established in North Kordofan, Sudan. This town became an important administrative center in the region.

image.caption: Market in El Obeid, Sudan.
image.credit: محسن الفكي — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph date: 2006-07-18; not contemporary with the 1821 establishment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of Al-Ubayyid

events.enhanced_description: In 1821, Widener University was founded in Wilmington, Delaware, originally as The Bullock School for Boys. It has since evolved into a comprehensive university offering a range of undergraduate and graduate programs.
events.name: Founding of Widener University

events.enhanced_description: Peter I Island in Antarctica was first sighted by Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen, contributing to the early exploration of the Antarctic region. This discovery added to the knowledge of the uncharted territories of the time.
events.name: Peter I Island first sighted

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Laibach convened to address outstanding international issues, particularly the revolutionary movements in southern Italy. This congress was part of the efforts of the Concert of Europe to maintain order.
events.name: Congress of Laibach convenes

events.enhanced_description: Alexander Island, the largest island in Antarctica, was first discovered by Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen. This discovery added to the growing body of knowledge about the Antarctic region.
events.name: Alexander Island discovered

events.enhanced_description: Columbian College was chartered by President James Monroe in Washington, D.C. This institution would later evolve into George Washington University, becoming a significant educational establishment.
events.name: Columbian College chartered

events.enhanced_description: The Embrace of Acatempan took place in Mexico between Agustín de Iturbide and Vicente Guerrero, symbolizing the peace between the viceroyalty troops and the insurgents. This moment was crucial in the path toward Mexican independence.
events.name: Embrace of Acatempan

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Laibach formally concluded, although the leading participants remained as fresh uprisings broke out in Northern Italy and Greece. This congress was part of the ongoing diplomatic efforts to manage revolutionary movements in Europe.
events.name: Congress of Laibach formally ends

events.enhanced_description: James Monroe officially began his second term as President of the United States, continuing his leadership during a period marked by national expansion and the consolidation of the Monroe Doctrine.
events.name: James Monroe begins second term

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Rieti was fought in Italy between Austrian forces and Neapolitan rebels. This conflict was part of the broader revolutionary movements occurring in Europe during this period.
events.name: Battle of Rieti

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1821, Austrian forces led by General Johann Frimont entered Naples, effectively restoring the authority of King Ferdinand I after a brief revolutionary period. This intervention was part of the broader context of the Italian unification and the reactionary measures taken by the Austrian Empire against revolutionary movements in Europe.
events.name: Austrian forces under Johann Frimont enter Naples and restore the authority of Ferdinand I

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1821, Metropolitan bishop Germanos of Patras raised the revolutionary flag at the Monastery of Agia Lavra, symbolically marking the beginning of the Greek War of Independence against Ottoman rule. This act is celebrated annually as Greece's Independence Day.
events.name: Metropolitan bishop Germanos of Patras raises the revolutionary flag of Greece

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1821, Ecumenical Patriarch Gregory V of Constantinople was executed by hanging outside the Patriarchal Cathedral, blamed by the Ottoman authorities for the Greek independence movement. His martyrdom became a symbol of the struggle for Greek freedom.

image.caption: Nikiforos Lytras’s depiction of the hanging of Patriarch Gregory V of Constantinople.
image.credit: Nikiforos Lytras — http://www.mlahanas.de/Greece/Religion/PatriarchGregoryVOfConstantinople.html
image.date_qualification: 19th-century artwork; the supplied image date gives an approximate date of 1850, not the date of the execution.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ecumenical Patriarch Gregory V is hanged by the Ottoman government

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1821, Napoleon Bonaparte died in exile on the remote island of Saint Helena, where he had been imprisoned since 1815. His death marked the end of an era in European history, concluding the life of one of the most significant military leaders of the time.
events.name: Emperor Napoleon dies in exile on Saint Helena

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1821, during the Greek War of Independence, a small Greek force of 120 men led by Odysseas Androutsos successfully repulsed an Ottoman army of 8,000 at the Battle of Gravia Inn. This victory was significant in boosting Greek morale and resistance against Ottoman rule.
events.name: Battle of Gravia Inn

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1821, the Congress of Laibach concluded, having overseen the successful Austrian intervention in Italy. The congress set the stage for future discussions, including a planned Congress of Verona in 1822.
events.name: Congress of Laibach ends

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1821, the Filiki Eteria, a secret society aiming for Greek independence, faced a decisive defeat at the Battle of Drăgășani against Ottoman forces. This battle highlighted the challenges faced by the Greek revolutionaries in their struggle for independence.
events.name: Battle of Drăgășani

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1821, King Badi VII of Sennar surrendered without a fight to Ismail Pasha, a general of the Ottoman Empire, marking the end of the Funj Sultanate and the beginning of Egyptian control over Sudan. This event was part of the broader Egyptian expansion into the region.
events.name: Egyptian conquest of Sudan

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1821, Simón Bolívar achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Carabobo, which was crucial for Venezuela's independence from Spanish colonial rule. This battle solidified Bolívar's reputation as a key leader in the Latin American independence movements.
events.name: Battle of Carabobo

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1821, King John VI returned from Brazil to Portugal, where he approved the Bases da Constituição, a significant step towards constitutional monarchy in Portugal. His return marked a pivotal moment in the political landscape of the country.
events.name: Return of John VI from Brazil to Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1821, George IV was crowned king of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. His estranged wife, Caroline of Brunswick, was notably turned away from the ceremony, highlighting the personal and political controversies surrounding his reign.

locations.name: Westminster Abbey, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: George IV is crowned king of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1821, Argentine general José de San Martín declared the independence of Peru from the Spanish Empire, a crucial step in the broader struggle for independence across South America. This declaration marked the establishment of Peru as a sovereign nation.

image.caption: Portrait of José de San Martín.
image.credit: The exact author is disputed. Some sources attribute it to Jean Baptiste Madou, others to the art teacher of San Martin's daughter, and others suspect it to be the work of many different people. — Museo Histórico Nacional
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated 1827 or 1829; the exact date is disputed. It is not a depiction of the 1821 declaration.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: José de San Martín declares the independence of Peru

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1821, during the Greek War of Independence, Greek rebels massacred approximately 3,000 inhabitants of the city of Navarino. This brutal event underscored the violent nature of the conflict and the deep-seated animosities between the Greek revolutionaries and Ottoman forces.
events.name: Navarino massacre

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1821, Missouri was admitted as the 24th state of the United States. This event was significant in the context of westward expansion and the ongoing debates over slavery in new states.
events.name: Missouri is admitted as the 24th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1821, the crew of the Eliza Frances discovered Jarvis Island in the Pacific Ocean. This uninhabited island would later become a site of interest for various expeditions and claims.

locations.name: Jarvis Island, United States Minor Outlying Islands

events.name: Jarvis Island is discovered

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1821, the Treaty of Córdoba was signed in Córdoba, Veracruz, ratifying the Plan of Iguala and effectively concluding the Mexican War of Independence. Although not recognized by Spain, this treaty marked a significant step towards Mexican sovereignty.
events.name: Treaty of Córdoba is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1821, the Congress of Cúcuta established the Republic of Gran Colombia, a federation that included present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Panama, and Ecuador. Simón Bolívar was named the founding President, with Francisco de Paula Santander as vice president, marking a significant moment in the history of South America.
events.name: Congress of Cúcuta establishes Gran Colombia

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1821, Chilean general José Miguel Carrera was executed by an Argentinian military tribunal in Mendoza. His execution marked a significant moment in the turbulent political landscape of early 19th-century South America.
events.name: José Miguel Carrera is executed

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1821, the Ukase of 1821 was issued by Russia, proclaiming territorial sovereignty over Northwestern North America, which includes modern-day Alaska. This declaration reflected Russia's imperial ambitions in the region.
events.name: Ukase of 1821

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1821, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica declared their independence from Spain through the Act of Independence of Central America. This event was pivotal in the region's transition to sovereignty.
events.name: Central American countries gain independence

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1821, Amherst College was founded in Massachusetts, becoming one of the prominent liberal arts colleges in the United States. The college has since played a significant role in American higher education.
events.name: Amherst College is founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1821, the Siege of Tripolitsa ended when Greek rebels captured the city after months of besiegement. The aftermath saw the massacre of approximately 8,000 civilians, highlighting the brutal nature of the Greek War of Independence.
events.name: Siege of Tripolitsa ends

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1821, the Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City, leading to the proclamation of the Declaration of Independence of the Mexican Empire from Spain. This event marked the culmination of the Mexican War of Independence.
events.name: Declaration of Independence of the Mexican Empire

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1821, Tsar Alexander I of Russia issued an imperial ukase that guaranteed freedom of commerce for Persian merchants in Russia. This decree was part of Alexander's broader efforts to strengthen trade relations and modernize the Russian economy.
events.name: Tsar Alexander I issues an imperial ukase

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1821, William Becknell became the first to successfully navigate the Santa Fe Trail, establishing a vital trade route between Missouri and Santa Fe, New Mexico. This route would later facilitate commerce and migration in the American West.

locations.name: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States

events.name: First use of the Santa Fe Trail

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1821, Panama declared its independence from Spain and subsequently joined Gran Colombia. This event marked a significant step in the region's struggle for independence from colonial rule.
events.name: Panama declares independence from Spain

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1821, General José Núñez de Cáceres proclaimed the Republic of Spanish Haiti, effectively ending the España Boba era of Spanish rule in the Captaincy General of Santo Domingo. This republic would last only three months before being invaded by Haitian forces.

locations.name: Santo Domingo, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic

events.name: Establishment of the Republic of Spanish Haiti

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1821, seal hunters George Powell and Nathaniel Palmer discovered the South Orkney Islands. This discovery contributed to the exploration and mapping of the Antarctic region.
events.name: Discovery of the South Orkney Islands

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1821, the world's first geographical society, the Société de géographie, was established in Paris. This organization played a crucial role in the advancement of geographical knowledge and exploration.
events.name: Establishment of the Société de géographie

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1821, the Eyjafjallajökull volcano in Iceland began to erupt. This volcanic activity would have significant geological and climatic impacts in the region.
events.name: Eruption of Eyjafjallajökull volcano

events.enhanced_description: King George IV's visit to Scotland in 1822 was a significant royal tour that aimed to strengthen the connection between the monarchy and Scotland. This visit was marked by elaborate celebrations and ceremonies, reflecting the growing sense of Scottish identity.
events.name: Visit of King George IV to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In 1822, the First National Assembly at Epidaurus adopted the Greek Constitution of 1822, marking a significant step in the establishment of a modern Greek state during the Greek War of Independence.
events.name: Adoption of the Greek Constitution of 1822

events.enhanced_description: In 1822, Boston, Massachusetts, was incorporated as a city following a vote. This marked a significant development in the city's governance and urban development.
events.name: Incorporation of Boston as a city

events.enhanced_description: George Canning was appointed as the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, a position he held until his death in 1827. His tenure was marked by significant diplomatic efforts, including the recognition of the independence of several Latin American countries.
events.name: George Canning is appointed British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs

events.enhanced_description: The Constituent Congress of Peru convened in Lima to draft a new constitution following the country's independence from Spanish rule. This congress played a crucial role in establishing Peru's political framework and governance.
events.name: The Constituent Congress of Peru begins its first session

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1822, the French explorer Aimé Bonpland was imprisoned in Paraguay on charges of espionage. His work in South America contributed significantly to the fields of botany and geography.
events.name: Imprisonment of Aimé Bonpland

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1822, the first freed slaves from the United States arrived on the west coast of Africa, founding Monrovia. This settlement became the capital of Liberia, established by the American Colonization Society as a refuge for freed African Americans.
events.name: Founding of Monrovia

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1822, Prince Pedro I of Brazil decided to remain in Brazil against the orders of King João VI of Portugal, a pivotal moment that initiated the Brazilian independence process. This decision ultimately led to Brazil's independence in 1822.
events.name: Pedro I of Brazil's decision

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1822, the First National Assembly at Epidaurus adopted the design of the modern-day flag of Greece for their naval flag. This symbol became a representation of Greek independence and national identity.

image.caption: Painting by Antoine Roux depicting the brigs Agios Nikolaos and Poseidon.
image.credit: Antoine Roux — Μουσείο Μπουμπουλίνας
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1820 in the supplied source evidence, two years before the flag’s adoption on 13 January 1822.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Adoption of the modern Greek flag

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1822, during the Greek War of Independence, Acrocorinth was captured by Greek leaders Theodoros Kolokotronis and Demetrios Ypsilantis. This victory was significant in the struggle for Greek independence from Ottoman rule.
events.name: Capture of Acrocorinth

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1822, the Chinese junk Tek Sing sank in the South China Sea, resulting in the drowning of more than 1,800 people on board. This tragic event highlights the dangers of maritime travel during this period.
events.name: Sinking of the Tek Sing

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1822, Haitian forces led by Jean-Pierre Boyer invaded Santo Domingo to overthrow the newly established Dominican Republic. This marked the beginning of a prolonged period of Haitian control over the territory.

locations.name: Santo Domingo, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic

events.name: Haitian invasion of Santo Domingo

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1822, the first Swaminarayan temple, Kalupur Swaminarayan Mandir, was inaugurated in Ahmedabad, India. This temple became a significant center for the Swaminarayan faith and community.
events.name: Inauguration of the Kalupur Swaminarayan Mandir

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1822, the Holy Alliance issued a final ultimatum to the Ottoman Empire following the repression of Austrian subjects in Bucharest during the Wallachian uprising. This ultimatum threatened war with Austria if the situation was not addressed.
events.name: Holy Alliance ultimatum to the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1822, during the Greek War of Independence, the Chios massacre occurred, where Ottoman troops slaughtered approximately 20,000 Greeks and exiled another 23,000. This brutal event highlighted the severe consequences of the conflict.
events.name: Chios massacre during the Greek War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1822, the American Colonization Society landed at Cape Mesurado on the West African coast after purchasing 60 miles of coastline. This settlement would soon become Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, established to provide a home for freed American slaves.
events.name: American Colonization Society lands at Cape Mesurado

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1822, George Canning, President of the Board of Control in the House of Commons, moved to repeal a law that prohibited Roman Catholic peers from sitting or voting in the House of Lords. Although the motion passed in the Commons, it was ultimately rejected by the Lords.
events.name: George Canning's motion to repeal law against Catholic peers
