events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1822, Nairs, the upper caste in the British Raj, attacked Sandar women for covering their upper bodies and breasts. This incident reflects the social tensions and caste dynamics present in colonial India.
events.name: Nairs attack Sandar women

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Pichincha, fought on May 24, 1822, was a decisive engagement in the struggle for independence from Spanish rule in Ecuador. Led by Simón Bolívar, the patriot forces achieved a significant victory, securing Quito and paving the way for the liberation of the rest of Ecuador.
events.name: Battle of Pichincha: Simón Bolívar secures the independence of Quito

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1822, during the Greek War of Independence, Christos Palaskas and Alexis Noutsos were executed by forces loyal to Odysseas Androutsos. This event highlighted the internal conflicts within the Greek revolutionary movement as it sought to liberate itself from Ottoman rule.
events.name: Execution of Christos Palaskas and Alexis Noutsos

events.enhanced_description: The Grue Church fire on May 26, 1822, stands as Norway's most catastrophic fire disaster, claiming the lives of 116 individuals. The tragedy underscored the need for improved fire safety measures in public buildings.
events.name: Grue Church fire: The biggest fire disaster in Norway's history kills 116 people

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1822, Alexis St. Martin was accidentally shot in the stomach at Fort Mackinac, leading to a unique opportunity for Dr. William Beaumont to study human digestion. This incident became foundational in the field of physiology, allowing Beaumont to conduct groundbreaking experiments.
events.name: Accidental shooting of Alexis St. Martin

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1822, during the Greek War of Independence, Konstantinos Kanaris executed a daring attack by blowing up the Ottoman flagship at Chios, resulting in the death of Kapudan Pasha Ali Pasha. This act of bravery significantly boosted Greek morale in their fight against Ottoman rule.
events.name: Konstantinos Kanaris blows up the Ottoman navy's flagship at Chios

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1822, Charles Babbage published a proposal for a difference engine, which was a pioneering concept in computing aimed at calculating logarithms and trigonometric functions. Although the project faced numerous challenges and was never completed, it laid the groundwork for future developments in computer science.
events.name: Charles Babbage publishes a proposal for a difference engine

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1822, an attempted coup d'état by supporters of Ferdinand VII to overthrow the Liberal government in Spain failed. This event was part of the broader political turmoil in Spain during the early 19th century, reflecting the struggle between conservative and liberal factions.
events.name: July 1822 Spanish coup d'état fails

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1822, the Chippewa people ceded a significant tract of land in Ontario to British control. This event marked a critical moment in the colonial expansion in North America and the ongoing displacement of Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Chippewa people cede land in Ontario

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1822, Greek soldiers achieved a significant victory against Ottoman forces at Thermopylae during the Greek War of Independence. This battle was emblematic of the Greek struggle for freedom and resistance against Ottoman rule.
events.name: Greek soldiers defeat Ottoman forces at Thermopylae

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1822, José de San Martín arrived in Guayaquil, Ecuador, to meet with Simón Bolívar. This conference was pivotal in the coordination of independence efforts across South America, although it ultimately led to differing visions for the future of the liberated territories.
events.name: Guayaquil Conference: José de San Martín arrives

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1822, Simón Bolívar and General José de San Martín met in Guayaquil, Ecuador, to discuss the future of South America following independence from Spanish rule. Their meeting was significant but ultimately revealed deep ideological differences between the two leaders.

image.caption: Detail of the Hemiciclo de la Rotonda monument in Guayaquil, Ecuador.
image.credit: Padaguan — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2013 photograph of a monument in Guayaquil, not a contemporary photograph of the 1822 conference.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Guayaquil Conference: Bolívar and San Martín meet

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1822, the last public whipping was carried out in Edinburgh, marking the end of a controversial practice in Scotland. This event reflected changing attitudes towards punishment and justice in the early 19th century.
events.name: Last public whipping in Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1822, a series of devastating earthquakes struck the northern part of the Ottoman Empire, causing widespread destruction from Gaziantep to Antakya in modern Turkey and from Aleppo to Khan Sheikhun in modern Syria. The disaster resulted in the loss of at least 20,000 lives, highlighting the region's vulnerability to natural disasters.
events.name: Earthquakes in the northern Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1822, Lord Castlereagh, the British Foreign Secretary, committed suicide at his residence in Kent. His death was attributed to mental health issues, reflecting the pressures of his political career during a tumultuous period in British history.
events.name: Lord Castlereagh commits suicide

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on August 15, 1822, King George IV's visit to Scotland marked a significant royal engagement, lasting until August 29. This visit was notable for its impact on Scottish identity and the relationship between Scotland and the British monarchy.
events.name: King George IV's visit to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1822, the body of British poet Percy Bysshe Shelley was cremated at Viareggio, Italy, ten days after his death in a boating accident. His heart, which resisted burning, was preserved separately, symbolizing the enduring legacy of his literary contributions.
events.name: Cremation of Percy Bysshe Shelley

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1822, the English ship Orion, commanded by William A. Richardson, landed at Yerba Buena on the North American west coast of Mexico. This location would later become San Francisco, marking a significant moment in the exploration and eventual settlement of California.
events.name: Orion lands at Yerba Buena

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1822, Brazil declared its independence from Portugal, a pivotal moment in the history of Latin America. Dom Pedro I, the son of the King of Portugal, played a crucial role in this declaration, leading to the establishment of Brazil as an independent empire.
events.name: Brazil declares independence from Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1822, the Battle of Nauplia saw the Greek Fleet, commanded by Admiral Andreas Vokos Miaoulis, successfully repel the Ottoman Fleet in a series of naval engagements. This victory was significant in maintaining Greek control over key maritime routes during the ongoing War of Independence.
events.name: Battle of Nauplia: Ottoman Fleet fails against Greek Fleet

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1822, the Roman Catholic Church permitted the publication of Galileo Galilei's 1632 treatise, 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems.' This marked a significant shift in the Church's stance towards scientific inquiry and the legacy of Galileo.
events.name: Publication of Galileo's treatise permitted by the Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1822, George Canning was appointed as the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. His tenure was marked by significant diplomatic challenges and efforts to navigate the complexities of European politics in the post-Napoleonic era.
events.name: George Canning appointed British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1822, Portugal approved its first Constitution, marking a significant step towards constitutional monarchy and democratic governance in the country. This event was part of the broader liberal movements sweeping across Europe during this period.
events.name: Portugal approves its first Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1822, Jean-François Champollion announced his success in deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone in a letter to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in Paris. This breakthrough opened the door to understanding ancient Egyptian civilization and its written language.

image.caption: Portrait of Jean-François Champollion, painted by Léon Cogniet.
image.credit: Léon Cogniet — Musée du Louvre
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1831, after the 1822 decipherment announcement; it depicts Champollion, not the announcement itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Champollion announces deciphering of Egyptian hieroglyphs

events.enhanced_description: The Galunggung volcano erupted violently, resulting in the deaths of over 4,000 people and the destruction of 114 villages. This catastrophic event highlighted the dangers of volcanic activity in Indonesia, a region known for its seismic instability.

image.caption: Lahar at Galunggung volcano in Indonesia.
image.credit: Robin Holcomb, U.S. Geological Survey — Archived source link
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: 1983, as stated in the image metadata; this is not the 1822 event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Galunggung volcano erupts on West Java

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1822, Pedro, the Crown Prince of Portugal, was declared the constitutional Emperor of Brazil, marking the establishment of the Empire of Brazil. This declaration was a pivotal moment in Brazil's struggle for independence from Portugal.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Pedro, Crown Prince of Portugal, is declared the constitutional Emperor of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Verona convened in the Austrian province of Lombardy-Venetia, gathering major European powers to discuss the political situation in Spain and the potential for intervention. This congress was significant in shaping European diplomacy following the Congress of Vienna.
events.name: The Congress of Verona opens

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Agustín de Iturbide of the First Mexican Empire dissolved the Congress of the Union, replacing it with a military junta. This act marked a significant shift towards authoritarian rule in Mexico, undermining the democratic processes established after independence.

image.caption: Oil portrait of Agustín de Iturbide.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Museo Soumaya Foundación Carlos Slim
image.date_qualification: Image date supplied as 1822; the event is dated 31 October 1822. The date does not establish that the portrait was made during or depicts the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Emperor Agustín de Iturbide dissolves the Congress of the Union

events.enhanced_description: The USS Alligator engaged three pirate schooners off the coast of Cuba as part of the United States' anti-piracy operations in the West Indies. This action was part of a broader effort to combat piracy that threatened maritime trade.

locations.name: Off the coast of Cuba, Cuba

events.name: Action of 9 November 1822: USS Alligator engages pirate schooners

events.enhanced_description: During the Greek War of Independence, the strategic city of Nafplio fell to Greek rebels, marking a significant victory in their struggle against Ottoman rule. This event was pivotal in the establishment of an independent Greek state.
events.name: Greek War of Independence: Nafplio falls to the Greek rebels

events.enhanced_description: A devastating earthquake struck near Valparaíso, Chile, resulting in approximately 200 fatalities and triggering a tsunami that further impacted the coastal region. The earthquake raised the coastal area, altering the landscape significantly.
events.name: An earthquake near Valparaíso in Chile

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic fire in Guangzhou (then known as Canton) resulted in the deaths of 500 people and the destruction of over 13,000 homes, along with several European-owned businesses. This disaster highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban centers during this period.
events.name: A fire in Guangzhou (Canton)

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1822, Pedro I was officially crowned as the first Emperor of Brazil, solidifying his role in the newly independent nation. His reign would be marked by efforts to establish a constitutional monarchy and navigate the challenges of nation-building.

image.caption: Portrait of Dom Pedro I, then Prince Pedro, in São Paulo.
image.credit: Simplício Rodrigues de Sá — This file was derived from: Emperor Dom Pedro I 1822.jpg : , derivative work: GianniG46 , 2012-06-23 08:51 (UTC)
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated August–September 1822, before the coronation; upload metadata date is not used as the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Pedro I is crowned as the first Emperor of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Verona concluded on December 14, 1822, having endorsed French intervention in Spain to restore King Ferdinand VII. This decision reflected the ongoing tensions in Europe regarding revolutionary movements and the balance of power.
events.name: The Congress of Verona ends

events.enhanced_description: The Jackson Male Academy, which later evolved into Union University, was established in Jackson, Tennessee, marking an important development in higher education in the region.
events.name: Jackson Male Academy opens

events.enhanced_description: Gioachino Rossini's opera 'Semiramide' premiered at the renowned Teatro La Fenice in Venice, showcasing Rossini's mastery in opera composition and solidifying his reputation in the music world.
events.name: Semiramide first performed

events.enhanced_description: The Catholic Association, a campaign for religious emancipation, began in Ireland in early 1823 during a meeting of 13 people at a bookseller's house on Capel Street in Dublin, marking a significant moment in Irish history.
events.name: Catholic Association begins in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: The first Anglo-Ashanti War commenced in 1823, marking the beginning of a series of conflicts between the British Empire and the Ashanti Empire in what is now Ghana. The war was driven by British expansionist policies and the Ashanti's resistance to colonial rule.
events.name: The first Anglo-Ashanti War begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1823, a British expedition was conducted up the St. Clair River, surveying the area as a potential site for the capital of Upper Canada. This exploration was part of broader efforts to establish British governance in North America.
events.name: British expedition up the St. Clair River

events.enhanced_description: In 1823, German astronomer Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers described what is now known as Olbers' paradox, which questions why the night sky is dark if the universe is infinite and filled with stars. This paradox has implications for cosmology and the understanding of the universe.
events.name: Olbers' paradox is described by Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers

events.enhanced_description: In 1823, construction began on two significant cultural institutions: the British Museum in London, designed by Robert Smirke, and the Altes Museum in Berlin, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel. These museums would become central to the preservation and display of art and history.
events.name: Work begins on the British Museum and the Altes Museum

events.enhanced_description: In 1823, the Oxford Union was founded as a debating society for students at the University of Oxford. It has since become a prestigious platform for public speaking and debate, hosting numerous influential figures throughout its history.
events.name: The Oxford Union is founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1823, the French forces, known as the 'Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis', crossed the Bidasoa River into Spain, marking the beginning of their military intervention in the Spanish civil conflict.
events.name: French forces cross Bidasoa River

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Pamplona commenced on April 10, 1823, as French troops besieged the city's garrison, a critical event in the context of the French intervention in Spain.
events.name: Siege of Pamplona begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1823, an 11-year-old Franz Liszt performed a concert in Vienna, where he received personal congratulations from the legendary composer Ludwig van Beethoven, marking a significant moment in Liszt's early career.
events.name: Franz Liszt concert in Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1823, Emperor Pedro I of Brazil inaugurated the country's first Assembleia Geral, which included 50 Senators and 102 Deputies, laying the groundwork for Brazil's legislative framework.
events.name: Brazil's first Assembleia Geral inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1823, Mikhail Semyonovich Vorontsov was appointed as the Governor-General of Novorossiya, overseeing the southern regions of the Russian Empire bordering the Black Sea.
events.name: Mikhail Vorontsov appointed Governor-General

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1823, Russian author Alexander Pushkin began work on his verse novel 'Eugene Onegin', which would become one of the most significant works in Russian literature.
events.name: Pushkin begins Eugene Onegin

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1823, the rebel Spanish government retreated from Madrid to Seville in response to the advancing French forces, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of Spain.
events.name: Spanish government withdraws to Seville

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1823, the Duke of Angoulême, commander of the invading French forces, established a regency in Madrid on behalf of the captive Ferdinand VII, solidifying French influence in Spanish politics.
events.name: Duke of Angoulême establishes regency

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1823, Sir Stamford Raffles established the Raffles Institution in Singapore, which would become a cornerstone of education in the region and a legacy of Raffles' vision for Singapore.
events.name: Raffles Institution established

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1823, the Congress of Central America declared absolute independence from Spain and Mexico, establishing a republican system of government, a pivotal moment in Central American history.
events.name: Congress of Central America declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1823, several significant Acts of Parliament received royal assent in the United Kingdom, including the Judgment of Death Act and the Transportation Act, marking a turning point in legal reform.
events.name: Royal assent to significant Acts of Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1823, the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls in Rome was almost completely destroyed by fire, leading to significant restoration efforts in the following years.

locations.historical_name: Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls
locations.name: Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, Rome, Italy

events.name: Basilica of Saint Paul destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1823, the first theatrical adaptation of Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein', titled 'Presumption; or, the Fate of Frankenstein', opened at the Royal Opera House in London, marking a significant cultural moment.

locations.name: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, London, United Kingdom

events.name: First theatrical adaptation of Frankenstein opens

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1823, William Pitt Amherst arrived in Calcutta with Lady Amherst to take up the position of Governor-General of India, a role that would shape British colonial policy in the region.
events.name: William Pitt Amherst arrives in Calcutta

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1823, Felipe Enrique Neri, Baron de Bastrop, permitted Stephen F. Austin to form an 11-man police force in Coahuila y Tejas, which would later evolve into the Texas Ranger Division.
figures: Felipe Enrique Neri, Baron de Bastrop
events.name: Stephen F. Austin allowed to form police force

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1823, the Royal Hibernian Academy was founded in Dublin, aimed at promoting the visual arts in Ireland and providing a platform for artists.
events.name: Royal Hibernian Academy founded

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1823, Tsar Alexander I of Russia drafted a secret manifesto designating his younger brother Nikolai as his successor, bypassing his older brother Grand Duke Konstantin, a decision that would have significant implications for the Russian monarchy.
events.name: Tsar Alexander I's secret manifesto

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1823, the Demerara rebellion erupted in the British colony of Demerara-Essequibo, where approximately 10,000 enslaved individuals revolted against their oppressors; the insurrection was suppressed within three days, leading to severe reprisals.
events.name: Demerara rebellion of 1823

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1823, Pope Pius VII passed away after a reign of over 23 years, during which he notably crowned Napoleon Bonaparte as Emperor of France, leaving a significant legacy in the Catholic Church.
events.name: Pope Pius VII dies

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1823, fur trapper Hugh Glass was mauled by a grizzly bear while exploring the Missouri Territory; he famously crawled over 200 miles to seek help, becoming a legendary figure in American frontier history.

image.caption: A Milwaukee Journal newspaper article recounting Hugh Glass’s exploits.
image.credit: The Milwaukee Journal — Yahoo News
image.date_qualification: Retrospective newspaper coverage published nearly a century after the reported events; this is not a contemporary image of the mauling.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Hugh Glass mauled by grizzly

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1823, during the Battle of Trocadero, French infantry captured the fort and turned its guns on Cádiz, a decisive moment in the French intervention in the Spanish civil conflict.
events.name: Battle of Trocadero

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1823, Simón Bolívar was appointed as the President of Peru during a tumultuous period following the country's independence from Spanish rule. His leadership aimed to stabilize the nation and promote republican ideals amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Simón Bolívar is named President of Peru

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1823, after a prolonged siege lasting five months, the city of Pamplona capitulated to French forces. This event marked a significant moment in the context of the French intervention in Spain during the early 19th century.
events.name: Pamplona surrenders to French forces after a five-month siege

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1823, Joseph Smith, the founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, claimed to have been directed by an angel to the location of the golden plates, which he believed contained the record of ancient American peoples. This event was pivotal in the establishment of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Joseph Smith, attributed to an unknown painter.
image.credit: Likely William Warner Major see https://web.archive.org/web/20230122022915/http://silverepicent.com/photofound/photofound/Photograph_Found/Appendix_C.html — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Joseph Smith, painted circa 1842, roughly two decades after the reported 1823 event; it is contextual, not a depiction of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Joseph Smith first goes to the place near Manchester, New York, where the golden plates are stored

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1823, the First Anglo-Burmese War escalated as Burmese forces launched an attack on British troops stationed on Shapura, an island near Chittagong. This conflict marked the beginning of a protracted war between the British Empire and the Kingdom of Burma.
events.name: First Anglo-Burmese War: Burmese forces attack the British on Shapura

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1823, Cardinal Annibale della Genga was elected as Pope Leo XII. His papacy was marked by a conservative approach to governance and a focus on restoring the authority of the papacy in the wake of the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Cardinal Annibale della Genga is elected Pope Leo XII

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1823, Cádiz surrendered to French forces, leading to the restoration of Ferdinand VII to the Spanish throne. This event marked the beginning of a repressive regime known as the Ominous Decade, during which liberal reforms were rolled back.
events.name: Cádiz surrenders to the French and Ferdinand VII of Spain is restored to his throne

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1823, Thomas Wakley founded The Lancet, a prominent medical journal in London. The journal has since become a leading source of medical research and commentary, influencing the field of medicine significantly.
events.name: The Lancet medical journal is founded by Thomas Wakley in London

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1823, Simón Bolívar sent a letter to Paraguayan dictator José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, urging him to release his friend Aimé Bonpland. Bolívar threatened invasion if his request was not met, highlighting the tense political climate in South America.
events.name: Simón Bolívar writes to José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia

events.enhanced_description: In November 1823, according to tradition, William Webb Ellis is credited with inventing the sport of rugby football at Rugby School in England. This event is often celebrated as the origin of one of the world's most popular sports.
events.name: William Webb Ellis invents the sport of rugby football

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1823, a tragic explosion occurred at the Rainton Colliery Company's Plain Pit mine in Chilton Moor, resulting in the deaths of at least 57 coal miners. This disaster highlighted the dangers of coal mining during the Industrial Revolution.

locations.name: Chilton Moor, County Durham, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Explosion at the Rainton Colliery Company's Plain Pit mine

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1823, General Rafael del Riego was executed in Madrid for high treason. His execution marked a significant moment in the struggle between liberal and conservative forces in Spain during the early 19th century.
events.name: General Rafael del Riego is executed in Madrid for high treason

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1823, President James Monroe introduced the Monroe Doctrine during his State of the Union address. This doctrine asserted that any European attempts to recolonize the Americas would be viewed as acts of aggression against the United States, shaping U.S. foreign policy for decades.
events.name: James Monroe introduces the Monroe Doctrine

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1824, Michael Faraday was elected as a member of the Royal Society in London, overcoming significant controversy. His contributions to electromagnetism and electrochemistry would later earn him a prominent place in the history of science.
events.name: Michael Faraday is elected as a member of the Royal Society

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1824, during the First Anglo-Ashanti War, British forces faced a crushing defeat at the Battle of Nsamankow, resulting in the death of Governor Sir Charles MacCarthy. This battle underscored the fierce resistance of the Ashanti Empire against British colonial expansion.
events.name: First Anglo-Ashanti War: Battle of Nsamankow

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1824, the first issue of The Westminster Review was published in London, founded by Jeremy Bentham. This radical quarterly became a significant platform for liberal thought and social reform in the 19th century.
events.name: The first issue of The Westminster Review is published

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1824, Simón Bolívar was proclaimed dictator of Peru, a position he assumed in an effort to stabilize the country amidst political turmoil and external threats. His rule was characterized by attempts to implement reforms and consolidate power.
events.name: Simón Bolívar is proclaimed dictator of Peru

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1824, William Buckland formally announced the name Megalosaurus, marking it as the first scientifically validly named non-avian dinosaur species. This announcement laid the groundwork for the field of paleontology.
events.name: William Buckland announces the name Megalosaurus

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1824, the Chumash Revolt began against Spanish colonial rule in Alta California, specifically at Mission Santa Inés. The uprising was a response to oppressive conditions and lasted until a peace agreement was reached in June.

locations.name: Santa Barbara County, California, United States

events.name: The Chumash Revolt of 1824 begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1824, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution was founded in the British Isles to promote the saving of lives at sea. This organization has played a crucial role in maritime safety and rescue operations.
events.name: The Royal National Lifeboat Institution is founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1824, the First Anglo-Burmese War officially began, marking a significant conflict between the British Empire and the Kingdom of Burma. The war would last nearly two years and result in substantial territorial changes.
events.name: The First Anglo-Burmese War begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1824, it was announced in St. Augustine, Florida, that the capital of the Florida Territory would be moved to Tallahassee. This decision was significant as Tallahassee was chosen for its central location between the existing major cities of Pensacola and St. Augustine.
events.name: Capital Move Announcement

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1824, the Netherlands Trading Society, known as the Netherlandsche Handel-Maatschappij, was founded in Amsterdam. This institution would later evolve into the Dutch bank ABN AMRO, playing a crucial role in the financial landscape of the Netherlands.

image.caption: Photograph of De Bazel, Vijzelstraat 32, Amsterdam, home to the Amsterdam Archives.
image.credit: Jane023 ( talk ) 09:51, 20 February 2011 (UTC) — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph date: 2007-08-16; this is a later site image, not a photograph of the society’s 1824 foundation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of the Netherlands Trading Society

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1824, the United States War Department established the Bureau of Indian Affairs in Washington, D.C. This agency was created to manage relations with Native American tribes and oversee their affairs, marking a significant step in U.S. policy towards indigenous peoples.
events.name: Creation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 was signed on March 17, 1824, in London to resolve territorial disputes between the British Empire and the Netherlands over the Malay Peninsula and the Dutch East Indies. This treaty significantly shaped colonial boundaries and control in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1824, American explorer Benjamin Morrell departed Antarctica after a controversial voyage that would later be marred by accusations of fraud. His expeditions contributed to the early exploration of the Antarctic region.
events.name: Benjamin Morrell's Departure from Antarctica

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1824, the Mechanics' Institution was established at the Bridgewater Arms hotel in Manchester, England. This institution was part of a national movement aimed at providing education to working men and laid the groundwork for future universities in the city.
events.name: Establishment of the Mechanics' Institution

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1824, the first permanent settlers arrived in Tallahassee, Florida, which had been selected as the capital of the Florida Territory. The location was chosen for its strategic position, being roughly equidistant from the main cities of Pensacola and St. Augustine.
events.name: First Permanent Settlers in Tallahassee

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1824, the British poet Lord Byron died in Missolonghi, Greece, at the age of 36. He had traveled there to support the Greek War of Independence but succumbed to fever, exacerbated by the medical practices of the time.
events.name: Death of Lord Byron

events.enhanced_description: The April Revolt (La Abrilada) began on April 30, 1824, in Portugal when Prince Miguel acted against his Liberal opponents, defying his father, King John VI. This conflict marked a significant moment in the struggle between conservative and liberal factions in Portugal.
events.name: April Revolt in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1824, Ludwig van Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, also known as the 'Choral', premiered at the Theater am Kärntnertor in Vienna. Despite his deafness, Beethoven was turned around on stage to witness the audience's enthusiastic response.
events.name: Premiere of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1824, during the First Anglo-Burmese War, British forces captured Rangoon, the capital of the Kingdom of Burma, in a surprise attack. This event marked a significant escalation in the conflict between the British Empire and Burma.
events.name: British Capture of Rangoon

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1824, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) was established in London, England. This organization was created to promote animal welfare and prevent cruelty to animals, marking a significant development in social reform.
events.name: Establishment of the RSPCA

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1824, the Confederation of the Equator began in Pernambuco, Brazil, as wealthy landowners initiated a secessionist movement against the government of Emperor Pedro I. This revolt was part of a broader struggle for regional autonomy in Brazil.
events.name: Confederation of the Equator in Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1824, Queen Kamāmalu of Hawaii died of measles while visiting the United Kingdom. Her death was a significant loss for the Hawaiian monarchy and highlighted the vulnerabilities of indigenous leaders during overseas travels.
events.name: Death of Queen Kamāmalu

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1824, King Kamehameha II of Hawaii died of measles during a visit to the United Kingdom. His death, which occurred before he could meet King George IV, had significant implications for the Hawaiian monarchy and its relations with foreign powers.
events.name: Death of King Kamehameha II

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1824, Agustín de Iturbide, the former Emperor of Mexico, was executed by firing squad in Padilla, Tamaulipas, shortly after returning from exile in England. His execution marked the end of a tumultuous period in Mexican history following independence.
events.name: Execution of Agustín de Iturbide

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1824, the Montparnasse Cemetery opened in Paris, France. This cemetery would become the final resting place for many notable figures and a significant site in the cultural landscape of the city.
events.name: Opening of Montparnasse Cemetery

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1824, during the Peruvian War of Independence, pro-independence forces achieved a decisive victory against Spanish troops in the Battle of Junín. This battle was a pivotal moment in the struggle for Peru's independence.
events.name: Battle of Junín

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1824, the First Anglo-Ashanti War concluded when the forces of the Ashanti Empire retreated from the battlefield. This conflict marked the beginning of British colonial influence in the region.
events.name: End of the First Anglo-Ashanti War

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1824, the Marquis de Lafayette began his visit to the United States, arriving at Staten Island. This visit was celebrated as a triumphant return for the hero of the American Revolution, and he would remain in the U.S. for over a year.
figures: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette

locations.name: Staten Island, New York, United States

events.name: Visit of Marquis de Lafayette to the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1824, John Oxley and his crew established the Moreton Bay Penal Settlement at what is now Brisbane, Queensland, Australia. This settlement was part of the British penal colony system and played a significant role in the region's development.
events.name: Founding of Moreton Bay Penal Settlement

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1824, Charles X succeeded his brother Louis XVIII as King of France. His reign would be marked by increasing tensions between royalists and republicans, ultimately leading to his abdication in 1830.
events.name: Charles X Becomes King of France

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1824, Admiral Sir Gordon Bremer made the earliest reference by the British government to the renaming of its South Pacific territory as 'Australia' in a dispatch regarding the Melville and Bathurst Islands. This marked a significant step in the recognition of the continent's identity.

locations.name: Melville and Bathurst Islands, Northern Territory, Australia

events.name: First Reference to Australia

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1824, the First Constitution of Mexico was ratified, establishing the country as a federal republic known as the United Mexican States. This constitution laid the foundation for Mexico's political structure and governance.
events.name: Ratification of the First Constitution of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1824, the Edinburgh Town Council established the Edinburgh Municipal Fire Brigade, marking it as the first organized fire brigade in Britain. Under the leadership of James Braidwood, this initiative set a precedent for fire safety and emergency response in urban areas.
events.name: Founding of the Edinburgh Municipal Fire Brigade

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1824, Joseph Aspdin patented Portland cement, a significant advancement in construction materials. This invention revolutionized the building industry, enabling the creation of stronger and more durable structures.
events.name: Patent of Portland Cement

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1824, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute was founded in Troy, New York, becoming the first technological university in the English-speaking world. It has since played a pivotal role in engineering and technological education.
events.name: Founding of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1824, the St. Petersburg flood occurred, marking the worst flood in the city's history up to that point. Water levels rose 421 centimeters above normal, resulting in the deaths of at least 200 people and significant damage to the city.
events.name: 1824 St. Petersburg Flood

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1824, the first sod was turned in Ontario for the construction of the Welland Canal, a crucial infrastructure project aimed at connecting Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. The canal would facilitate trade and transportation in the region.
events.name: First Sodding of the Welland Canal

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1824, the United States presidential election concluded without any candidate securing a majority of the electoral votes. Andrew Jackson received a plurality of the popular vote, but the election was ultimately decided by the House of Representatives, leading to John Quincy Adams' election as President.
events.name: 1824 United States Presidential Election

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1824, the Battle of Ayacucho took place, where Colombian and Peruvian forces led by Antonio José de Sucre decisively defeated the Spanish troops. This victory marked the end of Spanish colonial rule in South America.
events.name: Battle of Ayacucho

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1824, Chi Phi, the first American social fraternity, was founded at Princeton University. This establishment laid the groundwork for the fraternity and sorority system in American higher education.
events.name: Founding of Chi Phi Fraternity

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1824, the Bathurst War concluded in New South Wales, Australia, with the defeat of the Wiradjuri indigenous nation. Chief Windradyne peacefully surrendered at a feast in Parramatta, marking a significant moment in the conflict between indigenous Australians and European settlers.
events.name: End of the Bathurst War

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified treaties with the Mandan, Belantae, Eloa, and Minnetaree tribes, marking a significant step in U.S. relations with Native American nations during a period of westward expansion.
events.name: U.S. Senate Ratifies Treaties with Native Tribes

events.enhanced_description: From October to December 1825, tensions between the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and the Empire of Brazil over the Banda Oriental region escalated, leading to the outbreak of the Cisplatine War.

image.caption: Imperial Brazilian decree formalizing the declaration of war against the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata.
image.credit: Governo do Império do Brasil — Biblioteca Brasiliana Guita e José Mindlin : [1]
image.date_qualification: Dated 10 December 1825; the decree documents Brazil’s declaration of war, rather than depicting a battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Cisplatine War Begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, Bishkek, now the capital of Kyrgyzstan, was established as a mud fort along the Silk Road, serving as a strategic point for trade and cultural exchange.
events.name: Founding of Bishkek

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, the Hudson's Bay Company established Fort Vancouver on the lower Columbia River, which became a vital trading post and a key location in the fur trade in the Pacific Northwest.
events.name: Establishment of Fort Vancouver

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, Danish chemist Hans Christian Ørsted successfully reduced aluminium chloride to produce metallic aluminium, marking a significant advancement in the field of chemistry.
events.name: Hans Christian Ørsted Produces Metallic Aluminium

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, Emperor Minh Mạng of Vietnam enacted laws outlawing the teaching of Christianity, reflecting the tensions between traditional Vietnamese culture and foreign influences.
events.name: Minh Mạng Outlaws Christianity in Vietnam

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, London saw the establishment of the first horse-drawn omnibuses, revolutionizing public transportation and paving the way for modern bus systems.
events.name: First Horse-Drawn Omnibuses Established

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, the United States Postal Service established a dead letter office to manage undeliverable mail, improving postal operations and customer service.
events.name: United States Postal Service Starts Dead Letter Office

events.enhanced_description: In 1825, London surpassed Beijing to become the largest city in the world, a reflection of the city's rapid industrial growth and urbanization during the early 19th century.
events.name: London Becomes Largest City in the World

events.enhanced_description: In May 1825, the city of Brisbane was founded as a penal colony in Queensland, Australia. It was named after Sir Thomas Brisbane, the Governor of New South Wales, and has since developed into a major urban center.
events.name: Foundation of Brisbane

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1825, Charles X was crowned at Reims Cathedral, marking the last coronation of a French monarch. This event symbolized the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy following the tumultuous years of the French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: The Coronation of Charles X

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1825, the United States Senate ratified treaties with the Great Osage and Little Osage tribes. This event was part of the broader U.S. policy of treaty-making with Native American tribes during the westward expansion.
events.name: Ratification of Treaties with the Great Osage and Little Osage Tribes

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified a treaty with the Kansas tribe, furthering the government's engagement with Native American nations during a period of significant territorial expansion.
events.name: Ratification of Treaty with the Kansas Tribe

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified a treaty with the Poncas tribe, continuing the trend of treaty negotiations with Native American tribes as the U.S. expanded westward.
events.name: Ratification of Treaty with the Poncas Tribe

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1825, a rebellion was initiated by approximately 200 enslaved individuals in the Guamacaro region of Cuba. The uprising was suppressed within 12 hours, leading to severe repercussions for the participants in the following months.
events.name: Guamacaro Slave Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1825, the Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Beck acquired Glücksburg and adopted the title of Friedrich Wilhelm, Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg. This lineage would later produce royal houses in Greece, Denmark, and Norway.
events.name: Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Beck Gains Possession of Glücksburg

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified a treaty with the Hunkpapa tribe, part of the ongoing negotiations with Native American tribes during the expansionist policies of the United States.
events.name: Ratification of Treaty with the Hunkpapa Tribe

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified treaties with the Ricara tribes, continuing the U.S. government's engagement with Native American tribes.
events.name: Ratification of Treaty with the Ricara Tribes

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1825, Malden Island, an uninhabited island in the central Pacific Ocean, was discovered by George Byron, 7th Baron Byron. This discovery contributed to the European exploration and mapping of the Pacific region.
events.name: Discovery of Malden Island

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1825, Bolivia declared its independence from Spain, becoming a republic at the instigation of Simón Bolívar, a key figure in Latin American independence movements.
events.name: Bolivia Gains Independence from Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified a treaty with the Crow tribe, part of the ongoing negotiations with Native American tribes.
events.name: Ratification of Treaty with the Crow Tribe

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1825, Scottish adventurer Gregor MacGregor issued a £300,000 loan for the fictitious Central American republic of Poyais, leading to the Panic of 1825, the first modern stock market crash in England.
events.name: Gregor MacGregor and the Poyais Scheme

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1825, the National Mexican Rite was established in Mexico City, reflecting the cultural and religious developments in post-independence Mexico.
events.name: Creation of the National Mexican Rite

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1825, Uruguay was declared independent from the Empire of Brazil by the Thirty-Three Orientals, a revolutionary group led by Juan Antonio Lavalleja, marking a significant step in the region's struggle for independence.
events.name: Uruguay Declares Independence from Brazil

events.enhanced_description: In September 1825, the Lady Margaret Boat Club was founded by 12 members of St John's College, Cambridge. This club is notable for its contributions to rowing and the development of collegiate sports in the UK.
events.name: Foundation of the Lady Margaret Boat Club

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1825, General Hendrik Merkus de Kock lifted the siege of Jogjakarta, marking the first major action of the Java War, a conflict between Dutch colonial forces and Javanese princes.
events.name: Lifting of the Siege of Jogjakarta

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified treaties with the Missouri and Ottoe tribes, continuing the U.S. government's policy of treaty-making with Native American nations.
events.name: Ratification of Treaties with the Missouri and Ottoe Tribes

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1825, the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in England, marking the world's first modern railway. This event revolutionized transportation and laid the groundwork for the railway systems that would follow.
events.name: Opening of the Stockton and Darlington Railway

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified a treaty with the Pawnee tribe, part of the ongoing treaty negotiations with Native American tribes.
events.name: Ratification of Treaty with the Pawnee Tribe

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1825, the Miramichi Fire erupted in New Brunswick, Canada, devastating vast areas of forest and leading to significant loss of property and life, marking one of the largest forest fires in North American history.
events.name: The Miramichi Fire

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1825, the PS Comet II sank off the coast of Gourock, Scotland, resulting in the tragic loss of 62 lives, highlighting the dangers of early steamship travel.
events.name: Sinking of PS Comet II

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1825, the Erie Canal was officially opened, providing a crucial transportation route from Albany to Buffalo, significantly enhancing trade and commerce in New York and the broader United States.
events.name: Opening of the Erie Canal

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1825, the U.S. Senate ratified a treaty with the Shawnee tribe, reflecting ongoing negotiations and treaties between the U.S. government and Native American tribes during this period of expansion.
events.name: U.S. Senate Ratifies Treaty with Shawnee Tribe

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1825, King Joao VI of Portugal promulgated a law recognizing his son, Dom Pedro, as the Emperor of Brazil, solidifying the monarchy's support for Brazil's independence.

image.caption: Lithograph portrait of Emperor Dom Pedro I.
image.credit: Henri Grevedon (1776—1860) — Lacombe, Lourenço Luis. Museu Imperial . Petrópolis: Colorama, 1987
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1830, five years after the event date supplied; it does not depict the event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: King Joao VI Recognizes Dom Pedro as Emperor of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1825, Nicholas I ascended to the Russian throne following the death of his brother, Alexander I, marking the beginning of a reign characterized by autocracy and repression.
events.name: Nicholas I of Russia Succeeds Alexander I

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1825, British forces commenced the Siege of Bharatpur, aiming to subdue the princely state of Bharatpur in India, which was a significant conflict during the British colonial expansion.
events.name: Siege of Bharatpur Begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1825, the Decembrist revolt occurred in Saint Petersburg, where a group of army officers attempted to challenge Nicholas I's accession to the throne, but the uprising was swiftly suppressed.

image.caption: Depiction of Decembrists in Chita.
image.credit: George Kennan — Siberia and the Exile System
image.date_qualification: Depicts or dates to 1885, decades after the revolt; the supplied image date is 1885-01-01.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Decembrist Revolt

events.enhanced_description: In 1826, Swaminarayan composed the Shikshapatri, a significant scripture in Swaminarayan Hinduism that outlines moral and ethical guidelines for followers. This text remains central to the teachings and practices of the Swaminarayan faith.
events.name: Swaminarayan writes the Shikshapatri

events.enhanced_description: In July 1826, Ludwig van Beethoven completed his String Quartet No. 14 in C♯ minor, Op. 131, which is considered one of his masterpieces. This work exemplifies Beethoven's innovative approach to form and harmony, solidifying his legacy in classical music.
events.name: Completion of Beethoven's String Quartet No. 14

events.enhanced_description: In 1826, Major Edmund Lockyer arrived at King George Sound, establishing a settlement near Albany, Western Australia. This marked a significant step in the British colonization of the western part of Australia, aimed at expanding British influence and settlement in the region.

image.caption: Pencil-and-wash drawing by William Westall of King George’s Sound, viewed from the north-west.
image.credit: William Westall — The image was found amongst the National Library of Australia 's extensive and high quality collection of digital scans. This source was this address , where it is displayed with a black bar, displaying the name of the library and a catalogue number (given in the preceding address). No claim of ownership can be inferred from this detail and it was removed from the image. The great age makes it the property of us all. It is public domain.
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: December 1801 (inscription); the associated arrival is dated 1826 in the article excerpt.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Major Edmund Lockyer arrives at King George Sound

events.enhanced_description: The Straits Settlements were established by the British East India Company in 1826, with Singapore as a key trading post. This colony played a crucial role in British trade and military strategy in Southeast Asia, facilitating commerce between Europe and the East.
events.name: The British East India Company colony of the Straits Settlements is established

events.enhanced_description: In 1826, Otto Unverdorben first isolated aniline from the destructive distillation of indigo, marking a significant advancement in organic chemistry. Aniline would later become a fundamental compound in the production of dyes and pharmaceuticals.
events.name: Aniline is first isolated by Otto Unverdorben

events.enhanced_description: In 1826, Sultan Mahmud II's council ordered the janissaries to adopt European-style military drills, a significant reform aimed at modernizing the Ottoman military. This decision was part of broader efforts to strengthen the empire in the face of internal and external challenges.
events.name: Mahmud II's council orders the janissaries to drill in the European manner

events.enhanced_description: In 1826, Nicéphore Niépce created the first permanent photograph, titled 'View from the Window at Le Gras', using a process called heliography. This groundbreaking achievement laid the foundation for the field of photography and revolutionized visual representation.
events.name: Nicéphore Niépce makes the first photograph

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1826, the French newspaper Le Figaro began publication in Paris, initially as a satirical weekly, and has since become one of France's leading newspapers.

image.caption: Image of the first issue of Le Figaro.
image.credit: Le Figaro — Bibliothèque Nationale de France
image.date_qualification: 1826 (as stated in the image metadata; the specific day is not established by this image evidence).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Le Figaro

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1826, the Ballantyne printing business in Edinburgh crashed, leading to significant financial losses for novelist Sir Walter Scott, who was a principal investor.
events.name: Ballantyne Printing Business Crash

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1826, the Siege of Bharatpur concluded with a British victory, marking a significant event in the context of British colonial expansion in India.
events.name: Siege of Bharatpur Ends

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1826, the Menai Suspension Bridge, designed by engineer Thomas Telford, was opened, becoming the first major suspension bridge in world history and a marvel of engineering.
events.name: Opening of Menai Suspension Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1826, James Fenimore Cooper's novel The Last of the Mohicans was first printed in Philadelphia, becoming a classic of American literature and a significant work in the historical novel genre.
events.name: Publication of The Last of the Mohicans

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1826, Bernardino Rivadavia was inaugurated as the first President of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, now Argentina, marking a significant moment in the country's political history.

locations.historical_name: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata
locations.name: Buenos Aires, Argentina

events.name: Bernardino Rivadavia Becomes First President

events.enhanced_description: University College London was founded in 1826 as the first university in England to admit students regardless of their religion. It played a pivotal role in the development of higher education in the UK and remains one of the leading universities in the world.
events.name: Founding of University College London

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1826, the American Temperance Society was founded in Boston, Massachusetts, advocating for the reduction or prohibition of alcohol consumption, which became a significant movement in American social reform.
events.name: Founding of the American Temperance Society

events.enhanced_description: Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky, a Russian mathematician, independently developed the principles of non-Euclidean geometry, challenging the long-held beliefs of Euclidean geometry. His work laid the foundation for modern geometry and influenced various fields, including physics and philosophy.

locations.name: Nizhny Novgorod, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Russia

events.name: Development of Non-Euclidean Geometry

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Yandabo was signed on February 24, 1826, marking the end of the First Anglo-Burmese War. The treaty resulted in significant territorial concessions from Burma to the British Empire, including Assam and Manipur, and established British influence in the region.
events.name: Treaty of Yandabo

events.enhanced_description: Chunee, a male Indian elephant brought to London in 1811, was killed on March 1, 1826, after causing chaos in a menagerie and injuring a keeper. The animal's death, following failed attempts to subdue him with arsenic and shooting, highlighted the challenges of keeping exotic animals in captivity.
events.name: Death of Chunee the Elephant

events.enhanced_description: In March 1826, Ludwig van Beethoven's String Quartet No. 13 in B♭ major, Op. 130, premiered, performed by the Schuppanzigh Quartet. This work is notable for its innovative structure and emotional depth, showcasing Beethoven's late style.
events.name: Premiere of Beethoven's String Quartet No. 13

events.enhanced_description: Ellen Turner, a wealthy heiress from Cheshire, was kidnapped on March 7, 1826, by Edward Gibbon Wakefield, who sought to marry her for her fortune. The incident drew public attention and led to Wakefield's imprisonment, after which he became involved in the colonization of New Zealand.

image.caption: Portrait of Ellen Turner by Henry Wyatt.
image.credit: various — https://www.naomiclifford.com/the-shrigley-abduction/
image.date_qualification: 1829; a post-event portrait, not a depiction of the 1826 abduction.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Kidnapping of Ellen Turner

events.enhanced_description: Dom João VI, King of Portugal and former Emperor of Brazil, died on March 10, 1826, shortly after dining at the Jerónimos Monastery. His death led to a succession crisis, with his son Pedro I briefly ruling as King Pedro IV of Portugal before abdicating in favor of his daughter.
events.name: Death of Dom João VI

events.enhanced_description: In April 1826, Samuel Morey patented an internal combustion engine in the United States, marking a significant advancement in engine technology. This invention laid the groundwork for future developments in automotive and industrial machinery.
events.name: Samuel Morey patents internal combustion engine

events.enhanced_description: The Third Siege of Missolonghi concluded on April 10, 1826, with the Ottoman forces capturing the city and massacring thousands of Greek defenders. This event was a pivotal moment in the Greek War of Independence, highlighting the brutal conflict between Greek revolutionaries and Ottoman rule.
events.name: End of the Third Siege of Missolonghi

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway was inaugurated, marking the world's first intercity passenger railway operated solely by steam locomotives. This groundbreaking development significantly advanced the Industrial Revolution and transformed transportation.
events.name: Opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1826, Emperor Pedro I of Brazil abdicated as King of Portugal, a decision influenced by the political turmoil in both Brazil and Portugal. His abdication marked a significant moment in the history of both nations as they navigated their identities and governance.
events.name: Abdication of Emperor Pedro I of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1826, Mahmud II, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, crushed the last mutiny of the Janissaries in Istanbul, an event known as the Auspicious Incident. This decisive action marked a turning point in Ottoman history, leading to significant military and administrative reforms.
events.name: The Auspicious Incident

events.enhanced_description: The Burney Treaty was signed on June 20, 1826, in Bangkok between the United Kingdom and the Rattanakosin Kingdom of Siam. This treaty secured British influence in Southeast Asia and established trade relations, shaping the region's colonial dynamics.
events.name: Signing of the Burney Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1826, the attempted Ottoman–Egyptian invasion of Mani began during the Greek War of Independence. This invasion aimed to suppress the Greek rebellion but faced fierce resistance from local fighters, further intensifying the conflict.
events.name: Attempted Ottoman–Egyptian invasion of Mani

events.enhanced_description: The Pan-American Congress of Panama was opened on June 22, 1826, by Simón Bolívar, aiming to unify the newly independent republics of the Americas. The congress lasted 23 days but ultimately failed to reach an agreement on a common defense policy.
events.name: Pan-American Congress of Panama

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1826, former U.S. Presidents Thomas Jefferson and John Adams both died, coincidentally on the 50th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Their deaths marked the end of an era for the founding fathers of the United States.
events.name: Death of Thomas Jefferson and John Adams

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Panama adjourned on July 15, 1826, after 24 days without reaching an agreement on creating a federation of Latin American nations. This failure highlighted the challenges of unifying the diverse republics in the post-colonial period.
events.name: Adjournment of the Congress of Panama

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1826, five leaders of the Decembrist revolt were executed in Senate Square, Saint Petersburg, marking a brutal crackdown on dissent against the autocratic rule of Tsar Nicholas I. This event underscored the tensions between revolutionary ideals and imperial authority in Russia.
events.name: Execution of Decembrists

events.enhanced_description: Cayetano Ripoll was executed on July 26, 1826, becoming the last person to be executed by the Spanish Inquisition during its final auto-da-fé in Valencia. His execution marked the end of a dark chapter in Spanish history, reflecting the decline of the Inquisition's power.
events.name: Execution of Cayetano Ripoll

events.enhanced_description: The first Cowes Regatta was held on August 10, 1826, on the Isle of Wight, marking the beginning of one of the oldest and most prestigious sailing events in the world. This regatta has since become a significant event in the yachting calendar.

locations.name: Cowes, Isle of Wight, England, United Kingdom

events.name: First Cowes Regatta

events.enhanced_description: Scottish explorer Alexander Gordon Laing became the first European to reach Timbuktu on August 18, 1826. His journey was significant for European exploration of Africa, although he was tragically murdered shortly after his arrival.
events.name: Alexander Gordon Laing reaches Timbuktu

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1826, a devastating landslide occurred in Crawford Notch, New Hampshire, resulting in the tragic deaths of all seven members of the Willey Family. This event is remembered in local history and has contributed to the area's lore.

locations.name: Crawford Notch, New Hampshire, United States

events.name: Landslide in Crawford Notch

events.enhanced_description: William Morgan, an anti-Mason, mysteriously disappeared on September 13, 1826, after being released from jail in Canandaigua, New York. His disappearance sparked widespread speculation and controversy, particularly among anti-Masonic groups, leading to significant political ramifications.

image.caption: William Morgan memorial pillar at Batavia Cemetery.
image.credit: Pubdog — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed April 2011, long after the 1826 disappearance.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Niagara River, New York, United States

events.name: Disappearance of William Morgan

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Rideau Canal, a significant engineering project, began on September 21, 1826, under the direction of Lieutenant Colonel John By. This canal was crucial for military and commercial navigation between Montreal and the Great Lakes, and it remains a UNESCO World Heritage Site today.
events.name: Construction of the Rideau Canal begins in Canada

events.enhanced_description: The Monkland and Kirkintilloch Railway, which opened on October 1, 1826, was one of the first railways in Scotland, facilitating the transport of coal and iron. This railway marked a significant advancement in industrial transportation and contributed to the growth of the Scottish economy.
events.name: The Monkland and Kirkintilloch Railway opens in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1826, the first train operated over the Granite Railway in Quincy, Massachusetts, marking a pivotal moment in American transportation history. This railway was the first in the United States to be built for the purpose of transporting granite, which was used in the construction of significant buildings, including the Bunker Hill Monument.
events.name: The first train operates over the Granite Railway in Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: The Paris Stock Exchange officially opened on November 3, 1826, at the Palais de la Bourse, establishing a formal marketplace for securities trading in France. This event marked the beginning of organized stock trading in Paris, which would grow to become one of the leading financial centers in Europe.
events.name: The Paris Stock Exchange opens at the Palais de la Bourse

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1826, Benjamin W. Edwards rode into Nacogdoches, Texas, and declared himself the ruler of the Republic of Fredonia, an attempt by American settlers to secede from Mexico. This declaration was part of the broader Fredonian Rebellion, which sought greater autonomy for settlers in Mexican Texas.
events.name: Benjamin W. Edwards declares himself ruler of the Republic of Fredonia

events.enhanced_description: The Fredonian Rebellion commenced on December 21, 1826, when American settlers in Mexican Texas made their first attempt to secede from Mexico. Led by Benjamin W. Edwards, the rebellion was short-lived, lasting only six weeks before it was suppressed by Mexican forces.
events.name: American settlers begin the Fredonian Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The Eggnog Riot erupted on December 25, 1826, at the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York, when cadets celebrated the holiday with a large quantity of eggnog, leading to a drunken brawl. This incident highlighted the tensions between military discipline and youthful exuberance among the cadets.
events.name: The Eggnog Riot breaks out at West Point

events.enhanced_description: In January 1827, King Anouvong of Vientiane led the Laotian Rebellion against Siam, successfully attacking Nakhon Ratchasima. This rebellion was part of a larger struggle for independence and autonomy, although it ultimately resulted in the devastation of Vientiane by Siamese forces.
events.name: King Anouvong leads the Laotian Rebellion against Siam

events.enhanced_description: The new constitution for the Mexican state of Coahuila y Tejas was ratified, which included a significant provision phasing out slavery, declaring that no one would be born a slave in the state after its promulgation.
events.name: Constitution of Coahuila y Tejas ratified

events.enhanced_description: Under the direction of Antoine Clot, the first medical school in Egypt was established, marking a significant advancement in medical education in the region.
events.name: First Medical School in Egypt Established

events.enhanced_description: In 1827, the missionary ship Messenger of Peace was constructed on Rarotonga by English Congregationalist John Williams. This vessel was intended to spread Christianity to Samoa and the Society Islands, representing the expansion of missionary work in the Pacific.
events.name: Construction of the Messenger of Peace

events.enhanced_description: In 1827, John James Audubon began the publication of his monumental work, The Birds of America, in the United Kingdom. This collection is renowned for its detailed illustrations and is considered one of the finest ornithological works ever completed.
events.name: Publication of The Birds of America

events.enhanced_description: The first regatta in Australia took place on January 5, 1827, on the River Derwent in Hobart, Tasmania. This event marked the beginning of organized rowing competitions in Australia and reflected the growing interest in recreational activities among the settlers.
events.name: The first regatta in Australia is held

events.enhanced_description: Furman University, originally founded as the Furman Academy and Theological Institution, began its first classes on January 15, 1827, in Edgefield, South Carolina. It has since evolved into a prominent liberal arts university, reflecting the growth of higher education in the United States.
events.name: Furman University begins its first classes

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1827, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe articulated his vision of Weltliteratur (world literature) in a letter to Johann Peter Eckermann, emphasizing the universal nature of poetry and the importance of cultural exchange. This concept would influence literary thought and global literature.
events.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe elaborates on Weltliteratur

events.enhanced_description: The first public theatre in Norway, the Christiania Offentlige Theater, was inaugurated on January 30, 1827, in Christiania (modern-day Oslo). This establishment marked a significant development in Norwegian cultural life, providing a venue for theatrical performances and artistic expression.
events.name: The first public theatre in Norway is inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ituzaingó occurred on February 20, 1827, where Argentine and Uruguayan troops tactically defeated a Brazilian Imperial Army force on the border of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. This battle was a significant event in the ongoing conflicts of the Argentine War of Independence.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of Brazilian infantry resisting Argentine attacks at the Battle of Ituzaingó.
image.credit: José Washt Rodrigues — https://acervoccsp.art.br/colecao-de-arte-da-cidade/batalha-dos-farrapos/
image.date_qualification: Illustration dated 1937; depicts the battle of 20 February 1827.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Ituzaingó

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1827, the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad was incorporated, becoming the first railroad in the United States to offer commercial transportation of both people and freight. This development was pivotal in the expansion of rail transport across the nation, facilitating trade and travel.
events.name: The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad is incorporated

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1827, Brazilian marines sailed up the Rio Negro and attacked the temporary naval base of Carmen de Patagones, Argentina. The assault was met with resistance from local citizens, resulting in a defeat for the Brazilian forces, highlighting the tensions in the region during this period.
events.name: Brazilian marines attack Carmen de Patagones

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1827, the new state constitution for Coahuila y Tejas was ratified, which included a phasing-out of slavery in its Article 13. This constitution represented a significant shift in the legal framework of the region, reflecting the changing attitudes towards slavery in the early 19th century.
events.name: The new state constitution for Coahuila y Tejas is ratified

events.enhanced_description: Freedom's Journal, founded by John Russwurm, became the first African-American owned and published newspaper in the United States, serving as a platform for the African-American community to express their views and advocate for civil rights.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Freedom's Journal founded

events.enhanced_description: Thousands gathered in Vienna to pay their respects at the funeral of composer Ludwig van Beethoven on March 29, 1827. Notable contemporaries, including Franz Schubert and Carl Czerny, served as torchbearers, while Chancellor Metternich delivered a eulogy.
events.name: Beethoven's Funeral

events.enhanced_description: John Walker began selling his invention, the "Lucifer" friction match, in England, revolutionizing the way people could start fires and paving the way for modern matches.
events.name: John Walker sells the Lucifer match

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Monte Santiago, a squadron of the Brazilian Imperial Navy engaged and defeated Argentine vessels after a two-day naval battle, highlighting the naval conflicts during the early 19th century in South America.
events.name: Battle of Monte Santiago

events.enhanced_description: George Canning succeeded Lord Liverpool as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, taking office during a period marked by political strife and the need for reform.

image.caption: George Canning House.
image.credit: Sahaib3005 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2021-07-03; not contemporaneous with Canning's appointment in 1827.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: George Canning becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: Scottish-born novelist John Galt founded the town of Guelph in Upper Canada, which would grow to become an important center in the region.
events.name: Founding of Guelph

events.enhanced_description: During the Greek War of Independence, the Battle of Phaleron saw Ottoman troops defeat Greek rebels, marking a significant conflict in the struggle for Greek independence.

image.caption: Konstantinos Volanakis’s painting “Karaiskakis landing at Phaleron.”
image.credit: Konstantinos Volanakis — Gallery of Bank of Greece
image.date_qualification: Depicted date not provided; the painting is not established as a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Phaleron

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Netherlands Navy's British-built paddle steamer Curaçao embarked on the first transatlantic crossing by steam, traveling from Hellevoetsluis in the Netherlands to Paramaribo in Dutch Guiana, completing the journey in four weeks.
events.name: First Transatlantic Steam Crossing

events.enhanced_description: The Fly Whisk Incident in Ottoman Algeria occurred when Hussein Dey slapped French consul Pierre Deval, an act that escalated tensions and eventually led to the French invasion of Algiers in 1830.
events.name: The Fly Whisk Incident

events.enhanced_description: Georg Ohm published 'Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet', introducing Ohm's law for the first time, which would become fundamental in the field of electrical engineering.
events.name: Georg Ohm publishes Die galvanische Kette
