events.name: Fortsas hoax

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1840, Ottoman and British troops bombarded Beirut and landed forces on the coast to pressure Egyptian ruler Muhammad Ali to retreat from Lebanon. This military action was part of the broader conflict involving the Ottoman Empire and Egypt.
events.name: Bombardment of Beirut

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1840, Joseph Strutt handed over the deeds and papers for the Derby Arboretum, which would become England's first public park. This event marked a significant development in public green spaces and urban planning.
events.name: Derby Arboretum

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1840, the French frigate Belle-Poule arrived in Cherbourg, bringing back the remains of Napoleon Bonaparte from Saint Helena to France. This event was a significant moment in French history, symbolizing the restoration of national pride.
events.name: Return of Napoleon's remains

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1840, William II ascended to the throne as King of the Netherlands. His reign would be marked by significant political changes and challenges within the kingdom.
events.name: William II becomes King of the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1840, Sultan Abdulmejid I issued a firman replacing Bashir Shihab II as Emir of Mount Lebanon with Prince Bashir Chehab III. This political shift was significant in the context of Ottoman governance in the region.
events.name: Replacement of Bashir Shihab II

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1840, Maronite leader Bashir Shihab II surrendered to the Ottomans and subsequently went into exile in Malta. This event marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of Mount Lebanon.
events.name: Surrender of Bashir Shihab II

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1840, William Henry Harrison won the United States presidential election in a landslide victory over incumbent Martin Van Buren. This election was notable for its significant voter turnout and the use of campaign slogans.
events.name: 1840 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1840, David Livingstone departed from Britain for Africa, embarking on a journey that would lead to significant discoveries and contributions to the understanding of the continent. His explorations would later play a crucial role in the history of African exploration.

image.caption: Portrait photograph of David Livingstone by Thomas Annan.
image.credit: Thomas Annan / Adam Cuerden — National Galleries of Scotland Accession number: PGP 74.2
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1864, 24 years after the departure described; use only as a portrait of Livingstone, not as an image documenting the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: David Livingstone leaves for Africa

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1840, the body of Napoleon Bonaparte was laid to rest in Les Invalides in Paris. This event marked the culmination of a long journey for his remains and symbolized the restoration of his legacy in France.
events.name: Napoleon laid to rest

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1840, the Stockport Viaduct was completed in North West England, becoming one of the largest brick structures in Europe. This engineering feat was significant for the development of railway infrastructure in the region.
events.name: Completion of Stockport Viaduct

events.enhanced_description: In 1841, El Salvador proclaimed itself an independent republic, marking the end of the Federal Republic of Central America. This declaration was a pivotal moment in Central American history, leading to the establishment of national sovereignty.

locations.name: San Salvador, San Salvador, El Salvador

events.name: El Salvador's independence proclamation

events.enhanced_description: In 1841, a devastating fire destroyed two-thirds of the city of Mayagüez, Puerto Rico. This disaster had a significant impact on the city's development and recovery efforts in the years that followed.
events.name: Fire in Mayagüez

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Pedro II was crowned in Rio de Janeiro, marking the beginning of his reign over Brazil. His leadership would later be characterized by significant modernization and cultural development in the country.
events.name: Emperor Pedro II crowned

events.enhanced_description: The first modern educational institution on the Indian subcontinent, Dhaka College, was established by Bishop Daniel Wilson and Dr. James Taylor. This institution played a crucial role in the development of higher education in the region.
events.name: Dhaka College established

events.enhanced_description: The settlement of Dallas, Texas, was founded by John Neely Bryan, marking the beginning of what would become a major urban center in the United States. The city's growth was fueled by its strategic location and economic opportunities.
events.name: Dallas founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1841, British negotiator Charles Elliot and Qing official Qishan agreed to the Convention of Chuenpi, which aimed to resolve tensions arising from the Opium Wars. The convention was a significant step towards the eventual Treaty of Nanking, which formalized British concessions.
events.name: Convention of Chuenpi

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1841, British forces occupied Hong Kong, marking the beginning of British colonial rule over the territory. This occupation was part of the broader context of the First Opium War and led to significant changes in the region's governance and economy.
events.name: Occupation of Hong Kong

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1841, British explorer James Clark Ross discovered Mount Erebus, an active volcano located on Ross Island in Antarctica. This discovery contributed to the understanding of Antarctic geography and volcanic activity.
events.name: Discovery of Mount Erebus

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1841, James Clark Ross discovered the Victoria Barrier, which is now known as the Ross Ice Shelf. This significant discovery was part of Ross's expedition to explore the Antarctic region and contributed to the mapping of the continent.
events.name: Discovery of the Ross Ice Shelf

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1841, the first known reference to Groundhog Day was made in the diary of James Morris, marking the cultural significance of this tradition in North America. Groundhog Day has since become a popular celebration, predicting the weather based on the behavior of a groundhog.
events.name: First reference to Groundhog Day

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1841, the Act of Union, also known as the British North America Act, was proclaimed in Canada, which united Upper and Lower Canada into a single province. This act was a significant step towards the eventual confederation of Canada.
events.name: Proclamation of the Act of Union

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1841, Upper Canada and Lower Canada were merged to create the United Province of Canada, a significant political change that laid the groundwork for the future confederation of Canada. This merger aimed to address governance issues and improve political stability.
events.name: Creation of the United Province of Canada

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1841, the first ongoing filibuster in the United States Senate began, lasting until March 11. This event marked a significant moment in U.S. legislative history, showcasing the use of extended debate as a political strategy.
events.name: First ongoing filibuster in the U.S. Senate

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1841, William Henry Harrison was sworn in as the ninth president of the United States. His presidency was notably short-lived, lasting only 31 days before his untimely death.
events.name: William Henry Harrison sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1841, the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in the case of United States v. The Amistad, determining that the Africans who seized control of the ship had been taken into slavery illegally. This landmark decision was a significant moment in the abolitionist movement.
events.name: United States v. The Amistad ruling

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1841, the steamship SS President, commanded by Captain Richard Roberts, sank in rough seas, resulting in the loss of all 136 passengers and crew on board. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during the era.
events.name: SS President disaster

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1841, President William Henry Harrison died of pneumonia, becoming the first U.S. president to die in office. His death led to Vice President John Tyler assuming the presidency, marking a significant transition in U.S. leadership.

image.caption: Portrait of William Henry Harrison, painted by Albert Gallatin Hoit.
image.credit: Albert Gallatin Hoit — Current version: https://npg.si.edu/object/npg_NPG.67.5 (National Portrait Gallery, Washignton D.C.) Previous version: http://lifetussle.files.wordpress.com/2008/03/william-henry-harrison.jpg
image.date_qualification: Dated 1840 in the supplied image metadata; this is a portrait from before Harrison's death on April 4, 1841.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of William Henry Harrison

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1841, John Tyler was sworn in as the tenth president of the United States following the death of William Henry Harrison. Tyler's presidency was marked by significant political challenges and controversies.
events.name: John Tyler sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: The Sino-Sikh War began in May 1841, marking a conflict between the British Empire and the Sikh Empire in India. This war was part of the broader geopolitical struggles in the region during the 19th century.
events.name: Sino-Sikh War begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1841, New Zealand was established as a separate British colony, having previously been administered as part of the Colony of New South Wales. This change marked a significant step in New Zealand's colonial governance.
events.name: New Zealand becomes a separate British colony

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1841, the province of Guria in Georgia revolted against the Russian Empire, reflecting the growing discontent and desire for autonomy among the Georgian people. This revolt was part of the larger context of resistance against Russian imperial rule.
events.name: Guria Revolt against Russian Empire

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1841, the first United Kingdom Census was conducted, marking a significant advancement in demographic data collection. This census was the first to record names and approximate ages of every household member, providing valuable insights into the population.
events.name: First United Kingdom Census

events.enhanced_description: St. John's College, which later became Fordham University, was founded by the Society of Jesus in The Bronx, New York. This institution has since grown into a prominent university known for its commitment to academic excellence and Jesuit values.
events.name: St. John's College founded

events.enhanced_description: The ballet 'Giselle' premiered at the Salle Le Peletier in Paris, featuring music by Adolphe Adam and Italian ballerina Carlotta Grisi in the title role. This performance is considered a cornerstone of the Romantic ballet repertoire.
events.name: First presentation of Giselle

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Cook organized his first railway excursion in England, marking the beginning of organized travel and tourism. This innovative venture laid the groundwork for modern tourism and travel agencies.
events.name: Thomas Cook's first railway excursion

events.enhanced_description: The first edition of the humorous magazine 'Punch' was published in London, quickly becoming known for its satirical commentary on British society and politics. It played a significant role in shaping public opinion and humor in the Victorian era.
events.name: First edition of Punch published

events.enhanced_description: Frederick Douglass delivered a powerful speech at the Anti-Slavery Convention in Nantucket, Massachusetts, advocating for the abolition of slavery. His eloquence and personal narrative significantly influenced the abolitionist movement in the United States.
events.name: Frederick Douglass speaks at Anti-Slavery Convention

events.enhanced_description: U.S. President John Tyler vetoed a bill aimed at re-establishing the Second Bank of the United States, leading to outrage among Whig Party members. This event sparked one of the most violent demonstrations in White House history.

image.caption: Oil-on-canvas portrait of John Tyler by George Peter Alexander Healy.
image.credit: George Peter Alexander Healy — npg.si.edu
image.date_qualification: Portrait, not a depiction of the bank bill veto. The image is dated 1842, after the 1841 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: John Tyler vetoes bank re-establishment bill

events.enhanced_description: Sarawak was formally separated from Brunei, and James Brooke was appointed as its Rajah. This marked the beginning of Brooke's rule, which would significantly influence the region's history and development.
events.name: Sarawak becomes Rajah

events.enhanced_description: During the First Opium War, British forces captured a Chinese garrison at the Battle of Chinhai. This victory was part of a series of military engagements that highlighted the tensions between Britain and China over trade and opium.
events.name: Battle of Chinhai

events.enhanced_description: In the context of the First Opium War, British forces occupied Ningbo, further asserting their military presence in China. This occupation was part of the broader conflict over trade and sovereignty.
events.name: British occupy Ningbo

events.enhanced_description: The Niger expedition of 1841 commenced, aiming to explore the Niger River under the auspices of the British Society for the Extinction of the Slave Trade. Unfortunately, the expedition faced significant challenges, primarily due to diseases affecting the crew.
figures: British Society for the Extinction of the Slave Trade
events.name: Niger expedition begins

events.enhanced_description: Queen's University was founded in Kingston, Ontario, by Rev. Thomas Liddell, who brought a Royal Charter from Queen Victoria. The university has since become one of Canada's leading institutions of higher learning.
events.name: Queen's University founded

events.enhanced_description: A significant fire at the Tower of London destroyed its Grand Armoury, resulting in damages estimated at a quarter of a million pounds. This incident highlighted the vulnerabilities of historical structures to disasters.
events.name: Fire at the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: Scottish surgeon James Braid witnessed a demonstration of animal magnetism by Charles Lafontaine in Manchester, which inspired him to study the phenomenon. Braid would later coin the term 'hypnotism' and develop techniques that are foundational to modern hypnosis.
events.name: James Braid studies hypnotism

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty for the Suppression of the African Slave Trade was signed in London by representatives from Austria, Britain, France, Prussia, and Russia. This treaty marked a significant step in international efforts to combat the slave trade.
events.name: Treaty for the Suppression of the African Slave Trade signed

events.enhanced_description: During the First Anglo-Afghan War, British diplomat Sir William Hay Macnaghten was assassinated by Afghan general Akbar Khan during a meeting. This event escalated tensions and conflict in the region.
events.name: Sir William Hay Macnaghten assassinated

events.enhanced_description: Michael Alexander became the first appointee to the Anglican-German Bishopric in Jerusalem, marking a significant moment in the history of Anglicanism in the Holy Land. His appointment aimed to strengthen the Anglican presence and support the local Christian community.
events.name: Michael Alexander takes office in Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: The Massachusetts Supreme Court ruled in Commonwealth v. Hunt that labor strikes and the formation of labor unions were legal, marking a pivotal moment in labor rights in the United States. This decision laid the groundwork for future labor movements and unionization efforts.
events.name: Commonwealth v. Hunt ruling

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, the Polynesian islands of Tahiti and Tahuata were declared a protectorate of France, marking a significant expansion of French colonial influence in the Pacific.
events.name: Tahiti and Tahuata declared a protectorate of France

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, the seat of government in New Zealand was moved from Russell to Auckland, reflecting the growing importance of Auckland as a political and economic center in the region.
events.name: New Zealand seat of government moves to Auckland

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, Dzogchen Monastery in Sichuan, China, was almost completely destroyed by an earthquake, leading to significant loss of life and cultural heritage.
events.name: Dzogchen Monastery destroyed by earthquake

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, English palaeontologist Richard Owen coined the term 'Dinosauria,' which would become the standard classification for a diverse group of prehistoric reptiles, fundamentally shaping the field of paleontology.
events.name: Richard Owen coins the name Dinosauria

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, Julius von Mayer proposed the principle that work and heat are equivalent, laying the groundwork for the development of thermodynamics and energy conservation.
events.name: Julius von Mayer proposes work and heat equivalence

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, the Pickelhaube helmet was introduced in the Prussian Army, becoming a distinctive symbol of German military uniforms and influencing military headgear in various countries.
events.name: Pickelhaube helmet introduced in the Prussian Army

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, The Sons of Temperance was founded in New York City as a fraternal organization aimed at promoting temperance and social reform, reflecting the growing movement against alcohol consumption in the United States.
events.name: The Sons of Temperance is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, Thomas Beecham first marketed Beecham's Pills, a laxative, in Lancashire, England, which would later form the basis of the Beecham Group and GSK plc pharmaceutical companies.
events.name: Beecham's Pills first marketed

events.enhanced_description: In 1842, several universities were founded, including Cumberland University in Lebanon, Tennessee; Hollins University in Roanoke, Virginia; Villanova University in Pennsylvania; and the Indiana University Maurer School of Law in Bloomington, Indiana, contributing to the expansion of higher education in the United States.

locations.name: Indiana University Maurer School of Law

events.name: Founding of several universities

events.enhanced_description: Hollins University, originally established as Valley Union Seminary, was founded in Roanoke, Virginia by Charles Cocke in 1842. It became one of the first institutions of higher education for women in the United States.
events.name: Hollins University (as Valley Union Seminary in Roanoke, Virginia by Charles Cocke)

events.enhanced_description: Villanova University was founded in 1842 by the Augustinian Order in Villanova, Pennsylvania. It has since grown into a prominent Catholic university known for its academic excellence and commitment to service.
events.name: Villanova University (in Villanova, Pennsylvania by the Augustinian order)

events.enhanced_description: The Indiana University Maurer School of Law, established in 1842, is located in Bloomington, Indiana. It is one of the oldest law schools in the United States and has a rich history of legal education.

locations.name: Indiana University Maurer School of Law

events.name: Indiana University Maurer School of Law at Indiana University Bloomington

events.enhanced_description: Delft University of Technology, originally established as the Royal Academy for the education of civilian engineers, was founded by William II of the Netherlands. This institution has since evolved into one of the leading technical universities in Europe, known for its engineering and technology programs.

locations.historical_name: Royal Academy for the education of civilian engineers
locations.name: Delft University of Technology

events.name: Delft University of Technology is established

events.enhanced_description: Antarctic explorer James Clark Ross charted the eastern side of James Ross Island, reaching a record latitude of 78°09'30"S. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the exploration of Antarctica, contributing to the understanding of the continent's geography.
events.name: James Clark Ross reaches Farthest South

events.enhanced_description: The Oregon Institute, which later became Willamette University, was established in Salem, Oregon, as the oldest institution of higher learning in the western United States. It played a crucial role in the education of the region's early settlers and continues to be a prominent university today.

image.caption: Waller Hall at Willamette University in Salem, Oregon.
image.credit: M.O. Stevens — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed June 2008; the image does not depict the 1842 establishment event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Oregon Institute is established

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Debre Tabor, Ras Ali Alula, the Regent of the Emperor of Ethiopia, achieved a decisive victory over the warlord Wube Haile Maryam of Semien. This battle was significant in the context of Ethiopian power struggles during the early 19th century.
events.name: Battle of Debre Tabor

events.enhanced_description: Gaylad, ridden by jockey Tom Olliver, won the prestigious Grand National at Aintree Racecourse in England. This victory is remembered as a significant moment in horse racing history, showcasing the skill of both horse and rider.

image.caption: William Barnes Wollen’s engraving of horses jumping Becher’s Brook during the Grand National steeplechase at Aintree.
image.credit: William Barnes Wollen — Original source: The Lordprice Collection Further details on the artwork: Meisterdrucke
image.date_qualification: Dated 1890; retrospective to the event dated 1842-03-02.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Gaylad wins the Grand National

events.enhanced_description: Mexican troops led by Rafael Vázquez invaded Texas, briefly occupying San Antonio before retreating to the Rio Grande. This marked the first such invasion since the Texas Revolution, heightening tensions between Mexico and the Republic of Texas.
events.name: Mexican invasion of Texas

events.enhanced_description: Giuseppe Verdi's third opera, Nabucco, premiered at La Scala in Milan, establishing him as one of Italy's foremost operatic composers. The opera's themes of freedom and oppression resonated deeply with audiences, contributing to its lasting popularity.
events.name: Nabucco premieres

events.enhanced_description: The Female Relief Society of Nauvoo was formally organized, serving as a forerunner to the philanthropic and educational women's organization of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church). This organization played a crucial role in the community and the church's development.
events.name: Female Relief Society of Nauvoo organized

events.enhanced_description: The Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra, founded by Otto Nicolai, performed its first concert, marking the beginning of one of the world's most prestigious orchestras. The orchestra has since become synonymous with classical music excellence and cultural heritage.
events.name: Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra's first concert

events.enhanced_description: American physician Crawford Long administered an inhaled anesthetic (diethyl ether) for the first time to facilitate a surgical procedure, successfully removing a neck tumor. This pioneering use of anesthesia marked a significant advancement in surgical practices.
events.name: Crawford Long administers inhaled anesthetic

events.enhanced_description: The Middleton Junction and Oldham Branch Railway line was opened, enhancing transportation links in North West England. This development was part of the broader expansion of the railway network during the Industrial Revolution.
events.name: Middleton Junction and Oldham Branch Railway line opened

events.enhanced_description: During the Dorr Rebellion, militiamen supporting Thomas Wilson Dorr attempted to attack the arsenal in Providence, Rhode Island, but were repulsed. This conflict highlighted the struggle for voting rights and political reform in the state.
events.name: Dorr Rebellion: Attack on Providence arsenal

events.enhanced_description: In a remarkable feat, hunter Dick King rode into the British military base in Grahamstown to warn that the Boers had besieged Durban. His timely warning led to the dispatch of a relief force, showcasing the importance of communication in military strategy.
events.name: Dick King's ride to warn of Boer siege

events.enhanced_description: Queen Victoria became the first reigning British monarch to travel by train, taking a journey on the Great Western Railway between Slough and London Paddington station. This event symbolized the growing importance of rail travel in the 19th century.
events.name: Queen Victoria travels by train

events.enhanced_description: A primary school system was established in Sweden, marking a significant step towards formal education for children in the country. This development laid the foundation for modern educational practices in Sweden.
events.name: Primary school system established in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1842, a total solar eclipse was visible across parts of Asia, providing a significant opportunity for scientific observation and study of solar phenomena.
events.name: The total solar eclipse of July 8, 1842 is visible from Asia

events.enhanced_description: Founded on July 13, 1842, the Tri-Kap fraternity at Dartmouth College became the oldest local fraternity in the United States, establishing a tradition of brotherhood and community service.
events.name: The Tri-Kap fraternity is founded at Dartmouth College

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1842, the Armed Occupation Act was signed into law, facilitating the settlement and armed occupation of the unsettled regions of East Florida, reflecting the expansionist policies of the United States.
events.name: The Armed Occupation Act is signed

events.enhanced_description: The Webster–Ashburton Treaty, signed on August 9, 1842, resolved several border disputes between the United States and the United Kingdom, particularly concerning the U.S.-Canada border east of the Rocky Mountains.
events.name: The Webster–Ashburton Treaty is signed

events.enhanced_description: Enacted on August 10, 1842, the Mines and Collieries Act in the United Kingdom prohibited women and girls of any age, as well as boys under ten, from working underground, marking a significant step in labor reform.
events.name: The Mines and Collieries Act 1842 is enacted

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1842, General William J. Worth declared the Second Seminole War to be over, concluding a protracted conflict between the United States and the Seminole tribe in Florida.
events.name: Second Seminole War declared over

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Nanking, signed on August 29, 1842, marked the end of the First Opium War between the United Kingdom and the Qing dynasty, resulting in significant territorial and economic concessions, including the establishment of Hong Kong as a British colony.
events.name: The Treaty of Nanking is signed

events.enhanced_description: In September 1842, Wesleyan University was established in Middletown, Connecticut, as a significant institution of higher education with a focus on liberal arts and sciences.
events.name: Wesleyan University is established

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1842, the Treaty of Chushul was signed, effectively ending the Dogra–Tibetan War, which was part of the broader Sino-Sikh conflict over territorial disputes in the region.
events.name: The Treaty of Chushul ends the Dogra–Tibetan war

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1842, Josef Groll brewed the first pilsner light lager beer in Pilsen, Bohemia, which would go on to become one of the most popular beer styles worldwide.
events.name: Josef Groll brews the first pilsner

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1842, a category 2 hurricane struck the Iberian Peninsula, causing significant damage and impacting the lives of many residents in the region.
events.name: Hurricane strikes the Iberian Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1842, the Fleet Prison and Marshalsea debtor's prisons in London were closed, with inmates transferred to Queen's Bench Prison, marking a significant reform in the treatment of debtors.
events.name: Closure of debtor's prisons in London

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1842, Father Edward Sorin established the University of Notre Dame in Notre Dame, Indiana, which would grow to become a prominent institution of higher education in the United States.
events.name: The University of Notre Dame is established

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1842, the New York Philharmonic, founded by Ureli Corelli Hill, performed its first concert, marking the beginning of one of the oldest and most prestigious orchestras in the United States.
events.name: The New York Philharmonic performs its first concert

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1842, The Citadel, The Military College of South Carolina, was established in Charleston, South Carolina, becoming a key institution for military education in the United States.
events.name: The Citadel is established

events.enhanced_description: In January 1843, the serial publication of Charles Dickens's novel 'Martin Chuzzlewit' began in London. This novel is notable for its exploration of American society and its critique of various social issues.
events.name: Publication of Martin Chuzzlewit by Charles Dickens

events.enhanced_description: In January 1843, Edgar Allan Poe's short story 'The Tell-Tale Heart' was published in a Boston magazine. This story is considered a classic of American literature and is renowned for its exploration of guilt and psychological horror.
events.name: Publication of Edgar Allan Poe's The Tell-Tale Heart

events.enhanced_description: In January 1843, the Quaker magazine 'The Friend' was first published in London. This magazine has played a significant role in disseminating Quaker beliefs and values over the years.
events.name: First publication of The Friend magazine

events.enhanced_description: In February 1843, Shaikh Ali bin Khalifa Al-Khalifa captured the fort and town of Riffa in Bahrain after a rival faction failed to maintain control. This event was part of the internal power struggles within the ruling family.
events.name: Capture of Riffa by Shaikh Ali bin Khalifa Al-Khalifa

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, Søren Kierkegaard published his influential philosophical work 'Fear and Trembling' in Copenhagen, Denmark. The book explores the nature of faith and the ethical dilemmas faced by individuals, particularly through the biblical story of Abraham and Isaac, and has had a profound impact on existentialist thought.
events.name: Søren Kierkegaard's philosophical book Fear and Trembling is first published

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton made a groundbreaking discovery in mathematics by formulating the calculus of quaternions. This discovery revealed the non-commutative nature of quaternions and laid the foundation for advancements in vector analysis and theoretical physics.
events.name: William Rowan Hamilton discovers the calculus of quaternions

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, the House of Jamalullail was established in Perlis Darul Sunnah, Malaysia, following its separation from the state of Kedah. This establishment marked a significant moment in the political landscape of the region, contributing to the formation of a distinct royal lineage.
events.name: The House of Jamalullail is established in Perlis Darul Sunnah

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, physicist James Joule conducted experiments that led to the discovery of the mechanical equivalent of heat, establishing a foundational principle in thermodynamics. His work demonstrated the relationship between mechanical work and heat, significantly advancing the understanding of energy conservation.
events.name: James Joule experimentally finds the mechanical equivalent of heat

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, Richard March Hoe invented the steam-powered rotary printing press in New York City, revolutionizing the printing industry. This innovation allowed for faster and more efficient printing, significantly reducing the cost of producing newspapers and books.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The steam powered rotary printing press is invented by Richard March Hoe

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, Saint Louis University School of Law was established as the first law school west of the Mississippi River. This institution has played a crucial role in legal education and the development of the legal profession in the western United States.
events.name: Saint Louis University School of Law becomes the first law school west of the Mississippi River

events.enhanced_description: In 1843, Kurdish leader Bedir Khan Beg launched a military expedition against the Assyrians in the Hakkari region, resulting in significant violence and loss of life. This campaign was part of the broader conflicts between Kurdish and Assyrian communities in the region during this period.
events.name: Kurdish leader Bedir Khan Beg launched an expedition against the Assyrians in the Hakkari region

events.enhanced_description: The Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Kingdoms, compiled by Wei Yuan and others, was published in China on January 3, 1843. This work is significant as it represents one of the first comprehensive Chinese accounts of Western countries and cultures.
events.name: The Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Kingdoms published

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1843, Antarctic explorer James Clark Ross discovered Snow Hill Island during his expedition in the Antarctic region. This discovery contributed to the understanding of the geography and ecology of Antarctica.

image.caption: Photograph of Snow Hill Island, Antarctica.
image.credit: Jack Child — taken by Jack Child on trip to Antarctica
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the island, not a depiction of Ross’s 1843 discovery; the image date is recorded as 1999-01.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: James Clark Ross discovers Snow Hill Island

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1843, Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná, was appointed by Emperor Dom Pedro II as the leader of the Brazilian Council of Ministers. This appointment was significant as it laid the groundwork for the future establishment of the Prime Minister's office in Brazil.
events.name: Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão appointed leader of the Brazilian Council of Ministers

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1843, during the Uruguayan Civil War, Argentina began a siege of Montevideo in support of the Uruguayan leader Manuel Oribe. This conflict was part of a larger struggle for power within Uruguay.
events.name: Uruguayan Civil War: Argentina supports Oribe and begins siege of Montevideo

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1843, The Virginia Minstrels performed the first minstrel show at the Bowery Amphitheatre in New York City. This event marked the beginning of a popular but controversial form of entertainment in America.
events.name: First minstrel show performed by The Virginia Minstrels

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1843, the 1843 Guadeloupe Earthquake struck the Caribbean island of Guadeloupe, resulting in the deaths of approximately 1,500 to 5,000 people. This devastating event highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: 1843 Guadeloupe Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1843, Giuseppe Verdi's opera 'I Lombardi alla prima crociata' premiered at La Scala in Milan. This opera marked a significant moment in Verdi's career and in the development of Italian opera.
events.name: Premiere of Giuseppe Verdi's opera I Lombardi alla prima crociata

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1843, an event took place in England that would later inspire The Beatles' song 'Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite!'. This reflects the cultural significance of historical events in shaping modern music.
events.name: Event inspiring The Beatles' song Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite!

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1843, during the Paulet Affair, Lord George Paulet occupied the Kingdom of Hawaii in the name of Great Britain. This event highlighted the tensions between indigenous sovereignty and colonial interests.
events.name: Paulet Affair: Lord George Paulet occupies the Kingdom of Hawaii

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1843, the Danish government re-established the Althing in Iceland as an advisory body by royal decree. This marked a significant step in the revival of Icelandic self-governance.
events.name: Re-establishment of the Althing in Iceland

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1843, the star Eta Carinae flared, becoming the second-brightest star in the night sky. This astronomical event was significant for the study of variable stars.

image.caption: Hubble Space Telescope image of Eta Carinae’s bipolar gas-and-dust nebula.
image.credit: Jon Morse (University of Colorado) & NASA Hubble Space Telescope — Hubble Site [1]
image.date_qualification: Hubble observation from September 1995, released June 10, 1996; depicts nebular ejecta from the star’s earlier outburst, not the 1843 flare itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Eta Carinae flares

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1843, Catawba County, North Carolina was created, with its first court held in the home of Mathias Barringer Jr. This event marked the establishment of local governance in the region.
events.name: Creation of Catawba County, North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1843, Victoria, British Columbia was founded by the Hudson's Bay Company as a trading post and fort. This establishment played a crucial role in the fur trade and the development of British Columbia.
events.name: Founding of Victoria, British Columbia

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1843, the city of Petrópolis was founded by the government of Brazil. It became known as a summer retreat for the Brazilian imperial family and is characterized by its European-style architecture.
events.name: Founding of Petrópolis, Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1843, the world did not end as predicted by American preacher William Miller. This event led to the disillusionment of many followers and the eventual formation of the Seventh-day Adventist Church.
events.name: William Miller's prediction of the world's end

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1843, the Battle of Hyderabad took place, where the Bombay Army, led by Major General Sir Charles Napier, defeated the Talpur Mirs, securing Sindh as a province of British India. This battle was pivotal in the expansion of British control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Hyderabad

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1843, Marc Isambard Brunel's Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel under the River Thames and the world's first bored underwater tunnel, was opened in London for pedestrians. This engineering feat was a significant advancement in civil engineering.
events.name: Opening of the Thames Tunnel

events.enhanced_description: The Indian Slavery Act of 1843 abolished legal support for slavery within the territories controlled by the East India Company, marking a significant step towards the eventual end of slavery in India. This act was part of broader reforms initiated by the British government in response to growing humanitarian concerns.
events.name: The Indian Slavery Act, 1843

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1843, a group of 24 West Indian Moravians, led by Danish minister Andreas Riis, arrived in Christiansborg (Osu), Gold Coast, now Ghana, to establish schools and Presbyterian churches. This marked a significant moment in the spread of Christianity and education in West Africa.
events.name: Arrival of West Indian Moravians in Gold Coast

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1843, Natal was officially proclaimed a British colony, following the British annexation of the territory. This event laid the groundwork for increased British settlement and the eventual conflicts with the indigenous populations.
events.name: Natal Proclaimed a British Colony

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1843, the Free Church of Scotland was formed in Edinburgh as a result of a schism from the Church of Scotland, primarily over issues of patronage and church governance. This event was pivotal in the history of Scottish Presbyterianism.

image.caption: Memorial brooch commemorating the foundation of the Free Church of Scotland, with its motto and commemorative inscription.
image.credit: Paton, James, 1843-1921 — https://archive.org/details/scottishhistoryl00patouoft/page/n351
image.date_qualification: The brooch is a commemorative object associated with the 1843 foundation, not a contemporary photograph of the disruption. Saved image date: 1902-12-31.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Disruption of the Free Church of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1843, the first major wagon train, consisting of approximately 1,000 pioneers, set out from Elm Grove, Missouri, heading towards the American Northwest along the Oregon Trail. This migration was part of the larger westward expansion movement in the United States.
events.name: First Major Wagon Train on the Oregon Trail

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1843, Chile formally took possession of the Strait of Magellan, a strategic waterway, through the actions of the crew of the schooner Ancud, led by John Williams Wilson. This event was crucial for Chile's territorial claims in the region.
events.name: Chile Takes Possession of the Strait of Magellan

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1843, Samuel Jackman Prescod became the first non-white person elected to the House of Assembly in Barbados, marking a significant milestone in the political history of the island and the broader Caribbean.
events.name: Samuel Jackman Prescod Elected in Barbados

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1843, a clash occurred in New Zealand between a posse of British settlers and the Ngāti Toa tribe, led by Māori chief Te Rauparaha, resulting in 26 deaths. This confrontation highlighted the tensions between European settlers and indigenous populations.

image.caption: Watercolour portrait of Te Rauparaha wearing a cloak and feather ornaments.
image.credit: Hall, R, fl 1840s — Alexander Turnbull Library, URL [1] , Reference No.A-114-047. This version has been cropped by the uploader.
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Te Rauparaha, not a depiction of the 1843 clash. The saved image date is a range, 1843–1849.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Clash in New Zealand Involving Te Rauparaha

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1843, Edgar Allan Poe's short story "The Gold-Bug" began serialization in American newspapers, gaining popularity and contributing to Poe's reputation as a master of the mystery genre.
events.name: Serialization of "The Gold-Bug" by Edgar Allan Poe

events.enhanced_description: In July 1843, Margaret Fuller's essay "The Great Lawsuit. Man versus Men. Woman versus Women" was published in The Dial magazine, advocating for women's rights and challenging societal norms of gender roles.

image.caption: Daguerreotype portrait of Margaret Fuller by John Plumbe, Jr.
image.credit: John Plumbe, Jr. — https://npg.si.edu/object/npg_NPG.2018.3 (National Portrait Gallery)
image.date_qualification: Portrait made in 1846, three years after the essay’s publication; it is contextual, not an image of the publication event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of "The Great Lawsuit" by Margaret Fuller

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1843, Joseph Smith, the founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, reportedly received a revelation that recommended the practice of polygamy, which would later become a controversial aspect of the faith.
events.name: Joseph Smith's Revelation on Polygamy

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1843, Isambard Kingdom Brunel's SS Great Britain was launched from Bristol, becoming the first iron-hulled, propeller-driven ship to cross the Atlantic Ocean. This innovation marked a significant advancement in maritime engineering.
events.name: Launch of SS Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1843, Père Antoine Désiré Mégret, a Capuchin missionary, purchased land that would become Abbeville, Louisiana, for $900. This area was founded by descendants of Acadians from Nova Scotia, contributing to the cultural diversity of the region.
events.name: Purchase of Land for Abbeville, Louisiana

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1843, Brazil became the second country after Great Britain to issue nationally valid postage stamps with the release of its Bull's Eye series. This development was significant in the evolution of postal services in Brazil.
events.name: Brazil Issues Bull's Eye Postage Stamps

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1843, Tivoli Gardens, one of the oldest amusement parks in the world still in operation, opened in Copenhagen, Denmark. This iconic venue has since become a symbol of Danish culture and entertainment.
events.name: Opening of Tivoli Gardens

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1843, Edgar Allan Poe's short story "The Black Cat" was first published in The Saturday Evening Post, showcasing his mastery of the horror genre and contributing to his legacy as a prominent American writer.
events.name: Publication of "The Black Cat" by Edgar Allan Poe

events.enhanced_description: In September 1843, Ada Lovelace translated and expanded Menabrea's notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including what is considered the world's first computer program for calculating Bernoulli numbers. This work laid the foundation for future computing.

image.caption: Daguerreotype portrait of Ada Lovelace by Antoine Claudet.
image.credit: Antoine Claudet — shared by Paul Graham on x.com https://x.com/paulg/status/1927655441913250041
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Ada Lovelace, circa 1843; contextual portrait, not a depiction of her translation work.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ada Lovelace's Translation of Menabrea's Notes

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1843, The Economist newspaper was first published in London, providing economic and political commentary that has influenced public discourse for over a century.
events.name: First Publication of The Economist

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1843, Emperor Dom Pedro II of Brazil married Dona Teresa Cristina of the Two Sicilies in a grand state ceremony at the Rio de Janeiro Cathedral, solidifying political alliances and marking a significant event in Brazilian history.
events.name: Marriage of Emperor Dom Pedro II

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1843, a popular uprising occurred in Athens, Greece, where citizens and military captains demanded a liberal constitution from King Otto. This event was pivotal in the establishment of constitutional governance in Greece.
events.name: Popular Uprising in Athens

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1843, the crew of the schooner Ancud, including John Williams Wilson, took possession of the Strait of Magellan on behalf of the Chilean government, asserting Chilean sovereignty over this crucial maritime route.
events.name: Chilean Possession of the Strait of Magellan

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1843, Elling Eielsen was ordained as the first Norwegian Lutheran minister in the United States, marking a significant moment in the establishment of Norwegian Lutheranism in America.
events.name: Ordination of Elling Eielsen

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1843, Søren Kierkegaard's philosophical work "Fear and Trembling" was published in Denmark, exploring themes of faith, ethics, and the nature of existence, and establishing Kierkegaard as a key figure in existential philosophy.
events.name: Publication of Fear and Trembling by Søren Kierkegaard

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1843, Fuerte Bulnes, the first Chilean settlement in the Strait of Magellan, was founded, establishing a foothold for Chilean presence in the region and facilitating further exploration and settlement.
events.name: Founding of Fuerte Bulnes

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1843, Shanghai opened for trade with foreigners for the first time, welcoming a party of traders from the United Kingdom. This event marked the beginning of significant foreign influence and trade in China.
events.name: Opening of Shanghai to Foreign Trade

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1843, Mount Etna erupted, causing significant destruction and resulting in the deaths of 69 people in the village of Bronte, located on the northeastern slope of the volcano. This eruption is one of the many violent episodes in the history of this active stratovolcano, which has been a source of fascination and fear for centuries.
events.name: Mount Etna erupts in Italy, and kills 69 people in the village of Bronte

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1843, Hawaii was officially recognized as an independent nation by both the United Kingdom and France, marking a significant moment in the history of the Hawaiian Kingdom. This recognition was celebrated annually as La Ku'oko'a, or Independence Day, reflecting the kingdom's sovereignty during a time of increasing foreign interest in the Pacific.
events.name: Hawaii is recognized as an independent nation by the United Kingdom and France

events.enhanced_description: In December 1843, the world's first Christmas cards were commissioned by Sir Henry Cole and illustrated by John Callcott Horsley in London. These cards marked a new tradition in holiday greetings, combining art and commerce in a way that would become a staple of Christmas celebrations worldwide.
events.name: The world's first Christmas cards are sent

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1843, Bishop's University was established as Bishop's College in Lennoxville, Quebec, by Bishop George Jehoshaphat Mountain. The institution was founded to provide education for members of the Church of England and has since evolved into a comprehensive university serving a diverse student body.

image.caption: Aerial view of Bishop's University.
image.credit: BUwiki2 — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image date is not provided. Metadata gives an upload/creation timestamp of 2010-05-24, which is not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Bishop's University is founded as Bishop's College by Bishop George Jehoshaphat Mountain

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1843, Basutoland was declared a British protectorate, marking the beginning of British colonial influence in the region. This status was established to protect the Basotho people from external threats and to stabilize the region amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Basutoland becomes a British protectorate

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1843, Charles Dickens's iconic novella 'A Christmas Carol' was published in London, quickly becoming a beloved classic. The story, which emphasizes themes of compassion and redemption, resonated with readers and has since become a staple of Christmas literature.
events.name: Charles Dickens's novella A Christmas Carol is first published

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1843, the first total solar eclipse of Saros 139 occurred, visible across parts of southern Asia. This astronomical event captivated observers and contributed to the growing interest in the study of eclipses and celestial phenomena.
events.name: The first total solar eclipse of Saros 139 occurs over southern Asia

events.enhanced_description: The Althing, Iceland's national parliament, was reopened in 1844 after a 45-year hiatus, marking a significant moment in the country's political history. This event symbolized the revival of Icelandic self-governance and cultural identity during a period of increasing nationalism.
events.name: The Althing, the parliament of Iceland, is reopened after 45 years of closure

events.enhanced_description: In 1844, Swedish chemist Gustaf Erik Pasch was granted a privilege for his invention of the safety match, which significantly improved the safety and convenience of igniting fire. This innovation marked a pivotal moment in the development of modern matches and contributed to everyday life.
events.name: Gustaf Erik Pasch granted privilege for safety match

events.enhanced_description: In 1844, Robert Chambers anonymously published 'Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation,' a work that presented a progressive view of evolution and laid the groundwork for the acceptance of Charles Darwin's theories. This publication sparked significant debate and interest in evolutionary science.
events.name: Publication of Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation

events.enhanced_description: In 1844, Reverend Alexander Duff established the Free Church Institution in Kolkata, India, which later merged with the General Assembly's Institution to form the Scottish Church College. This institution played a crucial role in the Bengali Renaissance, promoting education and social reform.
events.name: The Free Church Institution established

events.enhanced_description: In 1844, the Feldherrnhalle was completed in Munich, Germany. This monumental structure was designed to commemorate the Bavarian army and has since become a significant historical and architectural landmark.
events.name: Completion of the Feldherrnhalle

events.enhanced_description: In 1844, the Temple of Guardians in Tibet was destroyed by fire. This event marked a significant loss to the cultural and religious heritage of the region, impacting local traditions and practices.
events.name: Temple of Guardians burns down

events.enhanced_description: In 1844, the Ottoman Empire adopted a national flag, symbolizing its identity and unity. This decision was part of broader efforts to modernize the empire and assert its presence on the global stage.
events.name: National flag adopted for the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: The Cockstock Incident, which occurred on March 4, 1844, involved a violent altercation between settlers and Native Americans in the Oregon Territory. This event exemplified the tensions and conflicts arising from westward expansion and the encroachment on indigenous lands.
events.name: Cockstock Incident

events.enhanced_description: The Hong Kong Police Force was established in 1844, becoming the first modern police force in Asia and the second in the world. This development was crucial for maintaining law and order in the rapidly growing colony following the Opium Wars.
events.name: Establishment of the Hong Kong Police Force

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1844, the Persian prophet The Báb privately announced his revelation to Mullá Husayn in Shiraz, marking the foundation of the Bábí faith. This event set the stage for the emergence of the Bahá'í Faith, as The Báb proclaimed the coming of 'He whom God shall make manifest.'
events.name: The Báb announces his revelation

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sent the first electrical telegram from the U.S. Capitol to Baltimore, delivering the message 'What hath God wrought.' This landmark event marked the beginning of the telecommunication revolution.
events.name: First electrical telegram sent by Samuel Morse

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1844, the last definitively recorded pair of great auks were killed on Eldey Island, marking the extinction of this flightless bird species. This event highlights the impact of human activity on biodiversity.
events.name: Last recorded pair of great auks killed

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1844, George Williams founded the Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) in London, which aimed to put Christian principles into practice through the development of a healthy body, mind, and spirit. This organization has since grown into a global movement.
events.name: Foundation of the YMCA

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1844, heavy rains led to the overflow of the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers, initiating the Great Flood of 1844. This catastrophic event caused widespread damage and displacement across the affected regions.
events.name: Great Flood of 1844 begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1844, Charles Goodyear was granted a U.S. patent for the process of vulcanization, which significantly improved the durability and elasticity of rubber. This innovation laid the groundwork for the modern rubber industry.
events.name: Charles Goodyear receives patent for vulcanization

events.enhanced_description: Søren Kierkegaard's influential work, The Concept of Anxiety, was published in Denmark on June 17, 1844. This philosophical treatise explored the nature of anxiety and its relation to human existence, marking a significant contribution to existential thought.
events.name: Publication of The Concept of Anxiety

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1844, the Delta Kappa Epsilon fraternity was founded at Yale College in New Haven, Connecticut. This organization has since become one of the oldest and most prestigious collegiate fraternities in the United States.
events.name: Founding of Delta Kappa Epsilon fraternity

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1844, Joseph Smith, the founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, and his brother Hyrum were murdered by an armed mob at Carthage Jail in Illinois. This event led to a significant succession crisis within the movement and had lasting implications for the church.
events.name: Killing of Joseph Smith

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1844, the United States signed the Treaty of Wanghia with the Qing Empire, establishing five treaty ports in China and granting extraterritorial rights to American citizens. This treaty marked a significant step in U.S.-China relations.
events.name: Treaty of Wanghia signed

events.enhanced_description: The Bank Charter Act of 1844 was approved on July 19, 1844, restricting the powers of British banks and limiting note-issuing powers to the Bank of England. This act was a pivotal moment in the regulation of banking in the United Kingdom.
events.name: Bank Charter Act of 1844 approved

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1844, during a meeting in Nauvoo, Illinois, the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles was chosen as the leading body of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, with Brigham Young at the helm. This decision was crucial for the church's leadership following the death of Joseph Smith.
events.name: Quorum of the Twelve chosen in Nauvoo

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1844, German astronomer Friedrich Bessel deduced the existence of dark companions to the bright stars Sirius and Procyon based on their motion. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for future studies in astronomy and the understanding of binary star systems.
events.name: Friedrich Bessel deduces dark companions of stars

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1844, Abdelkader El Djezairi was defeated at the Battle of Isly in Morocco, leading to a significant shift in power dynamics in the region. Following the battle, Sultan Abd al-Rahman of Morocco repudiated his alliance with El Djezairi.
events.name: Battle of Isly

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1844, Narciso Claveria, the Governor-General of the Philippines, issued a decree that eliminated December 31, 1844, from the calendar, making December 30 immediately followed by January 1, 1845. This change aligned the Philippine calendar with its Asian neighbors.
events.name: Philippines calendar decree

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1844, Friedrich Engels and Karl Marx met in Paris, marking the beginning of a significant intellectual partnership that would lead to the development of Marxist theory. Their collaboration would profoundly influence political thought and movements worldwide.
events.name: Engels and Marx meet

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1844, the first-ever international cricket match was played in New York City, featuring teams from the United States and Canadian provinces. This event marked a significant moment in the history of cricket, showcasing the sport's growing popularity in North America.
events.name: First international cricket match

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1844, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake struck Salta Province in Argentina, causing significant damage and loss of life. This earthquake is one of the notable seismic events in the region's history.
events.name: 1844 Salta earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1844, the Millerites experienced the Great Disappointment, a moment when their predicted Second Coming of Jesus did not occur. This event led to a crisis of faith among followers and significantly impacted the development of the Seventh-day Adventist Church.
events.name: Millerites' Great Disappointment

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1844, The Báb was publicly proclaimed as the promised one of Islam, heralding the arrival of 'He whom God shall make manifest.' This proclamation was a pivotal moment in the history of the Bábí and Bahá'í faiths.
events.name: The Báb publicly proclaimed

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1844, Giuseppe Verdi's opera I due Foscari premiered at the Teatro Argentina in Rome. This opera showcased Verdi's evolving compositional style and contributed to his growing reputation as a leading composer of the time.
events.name: Debut of Verdi's opera I due Foscari

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1844, the Dominican Republic drafted its first Constitution, establishing the framework for governance in the newly independent nation. This document was a significant step toward nation-building and democratic governance.
events.name: Drafting of the Dominican Republic's first Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1844, James K. Polk won the United States presidential election, defeating Henry Clay. Polk's victory set the stage for significant territorial expansion and the implementation of policies that would shape the nation.
events.name: 1844 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1844, the Hungarian language was officially recognized as the national language of Hungary, marking a significant step in the country's cultural and political identity. This decision was part of a broader movement to promote Hungarian nationalism and assert independence from Habsburg rule.
events.name: Hungarian becomes the official language of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1844, the Rochdale Pioneers opened their cooperative store in Rochdale, England, which became a model for the cooperative movement worldwide. This initiative aimed to provide affordable goods to the working class and laid the foundation for modern cooperative societies.

image.caption: Exterior of Toad Lane Museum, the first premises of the Rochdale Pioneers’ cooperative.
image.credit: Scarletharlot69 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2009-04-26; not contemporaneous with the 1844 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Rochdale Pioneers commence business at their cooperative

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1844, the Philippines omitted this date from its calendar to align with the rest of East Asia by effectively shifting the International Date Line. This reform, initiated by Governor-General Narciso Claveria, was part of broader efforts to modernize the Philippines and improve trade relations.
events.name: Date omitted from the calendar in the Philippines

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1845, the Philippines began a new system of reckoning dates by skipping December 31, 1844, to align its calendar with other Asian countries. This reform was part of a broader initiative led by Governor-General Narciso Claveria to modernize the Philippines.
events.name: Philippines reckoning Asian dates

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1845, Dr. Crawford Long is credited with the first use of anesthesia in childbirth, utilizing ether to relieve pain. This groundbreaking practice laid the foundation for modern anesthesiology and transformed surgical procedures.
events.name: Crawford Long's Use of Anesthesia

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, newspaper editor John L. O'Sullivan articulated the concept of 'Manifest Destiny' in The United States Magazine and Democratic Review, arguing that it was the United States' divine right to expand across the continent. This idea became a driving force behind American expansionism and imperialism in the 19th century.
events.name: Manifest Destiny Concept

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, the Republic of Yucatán declared its independence from Mexico for the second time, reflecting ongoing regional tensions and desires for autonomy. This separation was part of a broader context of political instability in Mexico during the mid-19th century.
events.name: Republic of Yucatán Separates from Mexico

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, Ephraim Bee announced that the Emperor of China had entrusted him with sacred rituals through U.S. Commissioner Caleb Cushing. This revelation highlighted the cultural exchanges and diplomatic relations between the United States and China during this period.
events.name: Ephraim Bee's Revelation

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, Friedrich Engels published his influential treatise 'The Condition of the Working Class in England' in Leipzig, which critiqued the socio-economic conditions faced by the working class during the Industrial Revolution. This work laid the groundwork for modern socialist thought.
events.name: Publication of Engels' Treatise

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, Heinrich Hoffmann published 'Lustige Geschichten und drollige Bilder', introducing the character Struwwelpeter. This children's book became famous for its moral tales and illustrations, influencing children's literature in Germany and beyond.
events.name: Heinrich Hoffmann's Struwwelpeter

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, the Ancient and Accepted Rite for England and Wales was founded, establishing a new branch within Freemasonry. This rite aimed to promote philosophical and moral teachings among its members.
events.name: Founding of the Ancient and Accepted Rite

events.enhanced_description: In 1845, Eugénie Luce founded the Luce Ben Aben School in Algiers, which aimed to provide education to Jewish children in the region. This institution played a vital role in the educational landscape of Algeria.
events.name: Luce Ben Aben School Founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1845, poet Elizabeth Barrett received a love letter from fellow poet Robert Browning, marking the beginning of their romantic relationship. They met for the first time on May 20, 1845, which inspired Barrett to write her famous collection 'Sonnets from the Portuguese.'
events.name: Elizabeth Barrett receives a love letter from Robert Browning

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1845, the United States Congress established a uniform date for federal elections, setting them for the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November. This legislation aimed to standardize the electoral process across the nation.
events.name: Uniform date for federal elections established in the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1845, Edgar Allan Poe's poem 'The Raven' was published for the first time in the New York Evening Mirror. This work would go on to become one of the most famous poems in American literature, known for its haunting themes and lyrical quality.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe published

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1845, Anson Jones, President of the Republic of Texas, signed the charter officially creating Baylor University, which is recognized as the oldest university in Texas still operating under its original name. This event marked a significant development in higher education in the region.
events.name: Baylor University charter signed

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1845, a drunken visitor smashed the Portland Vase in the British Museum, causing significant damage to this valuable artifact. The vase took months to repair, highlighting the importance of preserving cultural heritage.
events.name: Portland Vase smashed in the British Museum

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1845, the United States Congress approved the annexation of Texas, a significant political move that would lead to the incorporation of Texas as a state. This decision was part of the broader expansionist policies of the United States during this period.
events.name: U.S. Congress approves annexation of Texas

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1845, President John Tyler signed a bill authorizing the United States to annex the Republic of Texas, contingent upon approval by Texas voters. This bill encompassed a vast territory that would later become several U.S. states.
events.name: President John Tyler signs Texas annexation bill

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1845, Florida was admitted as the 27th state of the United States. This event marked a significant expansion of the U.S. territory and reflected the ongoing westward movement of the nation.
events.name: Florida admitted as the 27th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1845, James K. Polk was inaugurated as the 11th President of the United States. His presidency would be marked by significant territorial expansion and the Mexican-American War.
events.name: James K. Polk inaugurated as President

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1845, the New Zealand Wars began with the Flagstaff War, led by chiefs Kawiti and Hōne Heke. The conflict started with the burning of the British colonial settlement of Kororareka (modern-day Russell), marking the beginning of a series of conflicts between Māori and British settlers.
events.name: New Zealand Wars open with the Flagstaff War

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1845, Felix Mendelssohn's Violin Concerto premiered in Leipzig, featuring Ferdinand David as the soloist. This concerto is now considered one of the most popular and frequently performed violin concertos in the classical repertoire.
events.name: Violin Concerto by Felix Mendelssohn premieres

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1845, Stephen Perry patented the rubber band in the United Kingdom. This invention revolutionized the way items could be bundled and secured, becoming a staple in offices and homes worldwide.
events.name: Stephen Perry patents the rubber band

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1845, an earthquake struck Mexico City, causing significant destruction in the city and nearby towns of Tlalpan and Xochimilco. This disaster highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity and led to discussions about urban planning and safety.
events.name: Earthquake destroys part of Mexico City

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1845, a devastating fire swept through Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, destroying a significant portion of the city. The fire, which started in a wooden building, led to widespread destruction and prompted changes in building codes and fire safety regulations.
events.name: The Great Fire of Pittsburgh

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1845, Ramón Castilla assumed the presidency of Peru, marking a significant moment in the country's political history. His leadership was characterized by modernization efforts and attempts to stabilize the nation after years of turmoil.
events.name: Ramón Castilla becomes president of Peru

events.enhanced_description: In May 1845, Frederick Douglass's autobiographical work, 'Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave,' was published by the Boston Anti-Slavery Society. This powerful narrative became a cornerstone of American literature and abolitionist thought.
events.name: Publication of Frederick Douglass's Narrative

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1845, the Yarmouth suspension bridge in Great Yarmouth, England, tragically collapsed, resulting in the deaths of around 80 people, many of whom were children. This disaster highlighted the need for improved safety standards in bridge construction.
events.name: Yarmouth suspension bridge collapse

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1845, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror, part of Sir John Franklin's expedition to find the Northwest Passage, departed from Greenhithe, England. The expedition aimed to navigate the Arctic waters but would ultimately lead to the disappearance of the crew.
events.name: Franklin Expedition sets sail

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1845, a catastrophic theater fire in Canton (now Guangzhou), China, resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,670 people. The tragedy underscored the dangers of crowded public venues and led to discussions on fire safety regulations.
events.name: The Canton theater fire

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1845, the ship Fatel Razack arrived in the Gulf of Paria, Trinidad and Tobago, carrying 227 indentured laborers from India. This marked the beginning of a significant wave of Indian immigration to the Caribbean, shaping the region's cultural landscape.

locations.name: Gulf of Paria, Trinidad and Tobago

events.name: Fatel Razack brings indentured laborers to Trinidad

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1845, former U.S. President Andrew Jackson passed away at The Hermitage in Nashville, Tennessee. His death marked the end of an era in American politics, as he was a pivotal figure in the development of the Democratic Party.

locations.name: The Hermitage, Nashville, Tennessee, United States

events.name: Death of Andrew Jackson

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1845, Isambard Kingdom Brunel's iron steamship, the Great Britain, completed the first transatlantic crossing from Liverpool to New York City, becoming the first screw-propelled vessel to make the journey. This achievement marked a significant advancement in maritime technology.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Great Britain makes transatlantic crossing

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1845, HMS Terror and HMS Erebus of the Franklin Expedition went missing in the Davis Strait while searching for the Northwest Passage. The disappearance of the ships and their crew became one of the great mysteries of Arctic exploration.
events.name: Franklin Expedition goes missing

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1845, the British emigrant barque Cataraqui was wrecked on King Island, Tasmania, resulting in the deaths of 400 people, with only 9 survivors. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during that period.
events.name: Cataraqui wreck

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1845, the Aberdeen Act was passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, empowering the British Royal Navy to search Brazilian ships as part of efforts to abolish the slave trade from Africa. This legislation was a significant step in the fight against slavery.

locations.name: Parliament of the United Kingdom, London, England

events.name: Aberdeen Act passed

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1845, a tornado struck Montville, France, resulting in the deaths of 200 people and the destruction of two large factories. This natural disaster had a profound impact on the local community and economy.
events.name: Tornado in Montville, France

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1845, the journal Scientific American began publication in New York City. It became a significant platform for scientific discourse and innovation, influencing public understanding of science and technology.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Scientific American begins publication

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1845, potato blight broke out in Ireland, marking the beginning of the Great Famine. This agricultural disaster led to widespread starvation and emigration, profoundly affecting Irish society and history.
events.name: Potato blight outbreak in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1845, the Anglo-French blockade of the Río de la Plata was formally declared, aimed at exerting pressure on Argentina during a period of political instability. This action escalated tensions between the involved nations.
events.name: Anglo-French blockade of the Río de la Plata declared

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1845, the Phi Alpha Literary Society was founded in Jacksonville, Illinois. This organization played a significant role in promoting literary and intellectual pursuits among its members.
events.name: Phi Alpha Literary Society founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1845, John Henry Newman, a prominent Anglican theologian, was received into the Roman Catholic Church. This event marked a significant shift in his theological journey and had lasting implications for the Catholic Church in England.
