This iconic building, known for its distinctive Gothic architecture, symbolizes the British political system and has been the site of numerous historical events.
events.name: The new Palace of Westminster opens

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1852, a plebiscite confirmed the establishment of the Second French Empire, with overwhelming support of 7,824,000 votes in favor and only 253,000 against. This marked a significant shift in French governance under Napoleon III, who sought to restore imperial rule.
events.name: The New French Empire is confirmed by plebiscite

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1852, the first roadside pillar boxes were introduced in Saint Helier, Jersey, at the suggestion of Anthony Trollope, an official of the British General Post Office. This innovation revolutionized mail collection and delivery in the British Isles.
events.name: The first roadside pillar boxes in the British Isles are brought into public use

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1852, a powerful earthquake, estimated to be between 7.5 and 8.8 in magnitude, struck near the Banda Islands in the Dutch East Indies, triggering a devastating tsunami. This natural disaster caused significant destruction and loss of life in the region.
events.name: A magnitude 7.5 to 8.8 earthquake strikes near the Banda Islands

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1852, Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor Napoleon III of the French, marking the establishment of the Second French Empire. His reign would be characterized by significant political and social changes in France and its empire.
events.name: Napoleon III becomes Emperor of the French

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1852, French forces captured the city of Laghouat in Algeria, furthering their colonial ambitions in North Africa. This event was part of the larger French military campaigns aimed at consolidating control over Algeria.
events.name: The French capture Laghouat

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1852, during the Taiping Rebellion, the Taiping army successfully captured Hanyang and began the siege of Wuchang. This rebellion was one of the deadliest conflicts in history, driven by social unrest and opposition to the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion: The Taiping army takes Hanyang

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1852, the Taiping army captured Hankou, further consolidating their control during the Taiping Rebellion. This event marked a significant advance for the Taiping forces against the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion: The Taiping army takes Hankou

events.enhanced_description: In March 1853, Levi Strauss & Co. was founded in San Francisco, California. The company would become famous for its denim jeans, revolutionizing the clothing industry and becoming a staple of American fashion.
events.name: Founding of Levi Strauss & Co.

events.enhanced_description: In May 1853, the world's first public aquarium opened at the London Zoo. This innovative attraction showcased aquatic life and set the stage for the development of public aquariums worldwide.

locations.name: London Zoo, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Opening of the World's First Public Aquarium

events.enhanced_description: According to popular accounts, potato chips were first prepared by George Crum in Saratoga Springs, New York, in 1853. This culinary innovation has since become a beloved snack worldwide.

locations.name: Saratoga Springs, New York, United States

events.name: Potato chips first prepared

events.enhanced_description: In 1853, the Independent Santa Cruz Maya of Eastern Yucatán were recognized as an independent nation by the British Empire. This recognition highlighted the complex political dynamics in the region during this period.
events.name: Independent Santa Cruz Maya recognized by British Empire

events.enhanced_description: Arthur de Gobineau, a French aristocrat and writer, begins the publication of his influential work 'An Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races', which argues for the superiority of the Aryan race and lays the groundwork for later racial theories.
events.name: Arthur de Gobineau begins publication of his An Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races

events.enhanced_description: In 1853, Charles Pravaz and Alexander Wood independently develop the hypodermic syringe, a groundbreaking medical device that allows for the injection of substances directly into the bloodstream, revolutionizing medicine and anesthesia.
events.name: Charles Pravaz and Alexander Wood independently invent a practical hypodermic syringe

events.enhanced_description: Wheaton Academy, a private Christian high school, is founded in West Chicago, Illinois, providing a faith-based education and becoming a significant institution in the local community.
events.name: Wheaton Academy is founded in West Chicago, Illinois

events.enhanced_description: Incorporated in London under a Royal Charter from Queen Victoria, the Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China is established by Scotsman James Wilson, facilitating trade and finance between the British Empire's territories.

image.caption: Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China building in Hong Kong.
image.credit: Arnold Wright — Twentieth century impressions
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1908, 55 years after the bank’s incorporation in 1853.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China

events.name: The Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China is incorporated in London

events.enhanced_description: The Melbourne Cricket Ground, now the largest sports stadium in the Southern Hemisphere, officially opens, becoming a central venue for cricket and Australian rules football and a significant cultural landmark.
events.name: Melbourne Cricket Ground officially opens

events.enhanced_description: Between 1853 and 1873, over 130,000 Chinese laborers migrate to Cuba, significantly impacting the island's demographic and cultural landscape, particularly in the sugar industry.
events.name: More than 130,000 Chinese laborers come to Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1853, Florida Governor Thomas Brown signed legislation that provided public support for the East Florida Seminary, which later evolved into the University of Florida. This act was a crucial step in the establishment of higher education in the state of Florida.
events.name: Establishment of the University of Florida

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1853, Benjamin "Benny" Pierce, the only child of Franklin Pierce, the 14th President of the United States, tragically died in a train accident. This event deeply affected Pierce and his family, casting a shadow over his presidency.
events.name: Death of Benjamin Pierce

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1853, during the Taiping Rebellion, Zeng Guofan was ordered to assist the governor of Hunan in organizing a militia force to combat local bandits. This marked a significant moment in the conflict, as Guofan would later become a key figure in suppressing the Taiping forces.
events.name: Zeng Guofan's Militia Organization

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1853, the Taiping army successfully occupied Wuchang, a strategic city during the Taiping Rebellion. This occupation was part of a larger campaign to capture key cities in China and establish the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.
events.name: Occupation of Wuchang by Taiping Army

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1853, Giuseppe Verdi's opera 'Il Trovatore' premiered at the Teatro Apollo in Rome. This opera would go on to become one of Verdi's most celebrated works, known for its dramatic intensity and memorable melodies.
events.name: Premiere of Il Trovatore

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1853, Taiping forces assembled at Hanyang, Hankou, and Wuchang in preparation for their march on Nanjing. This mobilization was a critical step in their campaign to capture the city and establish their rule.
events.name: Taiping Forces Assemble for March on Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1853, the city of Puerto Montt was founded in the Reloncaví Sound region of Chile. Named after the German immigrant Vicente Pérez Rosales, the city would become a key port and gateway to the southern regions of Chile.

image.caption: View of Angelmó in Puerto Montt, Chile.
image.credit: María Luisa Garrido — Own work
image.date_qualification: Depicted date stated as 06.11.06; the metadata does not clarify date format. This is not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of Puerto Montt

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1853, Washington University in St. Louis was founded as Eliot Seminary. This institution would grow to become a prominent university known for its research and academic excellence.
events.name: Founding of Washington University in St. Louis

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1853, Franklin Pierce was inaugurated as the 14th President of the United States. His presidency would be marked by significant events, including the expansion of the nation and the growing tensions leading to the Civil War.
events.name: Inauguration of Franklin Pierce

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1853, the Saint Paul Fire and Marine Insurance Company was founded in Saint Paul, Minnesota. This company would later evolve into The Travelers Companies, a major player in the global insurance industry.
events.name: Founding of Saint Paul Fire and Marine

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1853, during the Taiping Rebellion, a rebel army of approximately 750,000 seized Nanjing, resulting in the deaths of around 30,000 Imperial troops. This marked a significant victory for the Taiping forces and a turning point in the rebellion.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion: Seizure of Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1853, Manchester was granted city status in the United Kingdom. This recognition reflected the city's growth and importance during the Industrial Revolution, solidifying its place as a major urban center.
events.name: Manchester Granted City Status

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1853, Prince Leopold, the youngest son of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, was born in London. His birth added to the royal family's legacy and would lead to significant roles in European royal affairs.
events.name: Birth of Prince Leopold

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1853, the first passenger railway in India opened, connecting Bombay (now Mumbai) to Thana, covering a distance of 22 miles (35 km). This landmark event marked the beginning of railway transport in India, revolutionizing travel and trade.
events.name: Opening of the First Passenger Railway in India

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1853, a Perpetual Maritime Truce came into force between the United Kingdom and the rulers of the Sheikhdoms of the Lower Gulf, known today as the Trucial States. This agreement aimed to ensure peace and stability in maritime trade in the region.
events.name: Perpetual Maritime Truce

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1853, the Great Industrial Exhibition was held in Dublin, showcasing advancements in industry and technology. This event highlighted Ireland's role in the industrial revolution and attracted international attention.
events.name: The Great Industrial Exhibition in Dublin

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1853, the first plat for Seattle, Washington, was laid out. This event marked the beginning of Seattle's development as a city, paving the way for its growth into a major urban center in the Pacific Northwest.
events.name: Laying Out of Seattle's First Plat

events.enhanced_description: The Gavazzi Riots on June 9, 1853, in Quebec City were sparked by a speech given by Italian priest Alessandro Gavazzi, which incited violent clashes between Protestant and Catholic communities. This event highlighted the deep-seated religious tensions in Canada during the 19th century.
events.name: Gavazzi Riots

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1853, during the Taiping Rebellion, the Northern Expeditionary Force crossed the Yellow River. This maneuver was part of their military strategy to confront the Taiping forces and regain control over the region.
events.name: Crossing of the Yellow River by Northern Expeditionary Force

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1853, Georges-Eugène Haussmann was appointed as préfet of the Seine, tasked with the re-planning of Paris. His ambitious urban renewal project transformed the city, introducing wide boulevards, parks, and modern infrastructure.
events.name: Re-planning of Paris by Haussmann

events.enhanced_description: The Swiss watch company Tissot was founded in Le Locle, Neuchâtel, Switzerland, marking the beginning of a brand that would become synonymous with quality Swiss timepieces. Tissot has since played a significant role in the evolution of watchmaking, introducing innovative designs and technology.
events.name: The Swiss watch company Tissot is founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1853, U.S. Commodore Matthew C. Perry arrived in Edo Bay, Japan, with a fleet of ships, seeking to establish a trade treaty with Japan. This event marked a significant turning point in Japanese foreign relations, leading to the end of Japan's isolationist policies.
events.name: Commodore Matthew C. Perry arrives in Edo Bay, Japan

events.enhanced_description: Joaquin Murrieta, a notorious outlaw and bandit known as the 'Robin Hood of California', was killed on July 25, 1853. His life and death became legendary, symbolizing the struggles of Mexican Americans during the California Gold Rush.
events.name: Joaquin Murrieta is killed in California

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1853, Tokugawa Iesada succeeded his father, Tokugawa Ieyoshi, as the 14th shōgun of the Tokugawa shogunate. This transition marked the beginning of a period of increasing internal strife and external pressures that would eventually lead to the Meiji Restoration.
events.name: Iesada succeeds Ieyoshi as shōgun

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1853, New Zealand was granted self-government, allowing for a greater degree of autonomy from British rule. This significant political change laid the groundwork for the development of New Zealand's parliamentary system.
events.name: New Zealand acquires self-government

events.enhanced_description: The first true International Meteorological Organization was established in Brussels, Belgium, on August 23, 1853. This organization aimed to promote international cooperation in meteorology and improve weather forecasting.
events.name: International Meteorological Organization established

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Norwegian Navy Museum was founded at Karljohansvern in Horten on August 24, 1853. It is considered one of the world's first naval museums, dedicated to preserving the maritime history of Norway.
events.name: Royal Norwegian Navy Museum founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1853, Hudson Taylor, a British missionary, embarked on his first journey to China. His work would later lead to significant missionary efforts and the establishment of the China Inland Mission.
events.name: Hudson Taylor leaves for China

events.enhanced_description: Otis Elevator, the predecessor of Otis Worldwide, was founded on September 20, 1853, in the United States. The company is renowned for its innovations in elevator safety and technology, revolutionizing vertical transportation.
events.name: Otis Elevator founded

events.enhanced_description: C. Bechstein's piano factory was founded in Berlin in October 1853, becoming one of the three notable piano manufacturers established during this 'golden year' of piano history. Bechstein pianos are known for their quality and craftsmanship.
events.name: C. Bechstein's piano factory founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1853, the Ottoman Empire declared war on Russia, marking the beginning of the Crimean War. This conflict would involve several major powers and significantly alter the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: Crimean War: Ottoman Empire begins war with Russia

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1853, Donald McKay launched the Great Republic, which was the world's largest sailing ship at the time, measuring 4,500 tons. Despite its size, the ship faced challenges that hindered its success in maritime trade.
events.name: Launch of the Great Republic

events.enhanced_description: The Neue Pinakothek, an art museum in Munich, Germany, opened its doors on October 25, 1853. It was established to showcase 19th-century art, becoming a significant cultural institution in Europe.
events.name: Neue Pinakothek opened in Munich

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1853, during the Crimean War, the Ottoman army crossed the Danube River into Vidin, Bulgaria, and Calafat, Romania. This maneuver was part of the larger conflict against Russian expansion.
events.name: Crimean War: Ottoman army crosses the Danube

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1853, during the Taiping Rebellion, the Taiping Northern Expeditionary Force came within 3 miles of Tianjin, China. This marked a significant advance in their campaign against the Qing Dynasty.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion: Northern Expeditionary Force near Tianjin

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1853, William Walker and his troops captured La Paz in Baja California Territory, declaring the short-lived Republic of Sonora. This event was part of Walker's broader ambitions in Central America.

image.caption: Portrait of William Walker by George Dury, held by the Tennessee State Museum.
image.credit: George Dury — http://tnportraits.org/walker-william.htm
image.date_qualification: Depicted date unknown; the image upload date is not the portrait’s date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: La Paz, Baja California Sur, Mexico

events.name: William Walker captures La Paz

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1853, during the Crimean War, Turkish forces defeated the Russians at the Battle of Oltenitza. This victory was significant for the Ottoman Empire in the early stages of the conflict.
events.name: Crimean War: Battle of Oltenitza

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1853, Maria II of Portugal was succeeded by her son, Pedro V. This transition marked a significant moment in Portuguese history as it ushered in a new era of leadership.

image.caption: Portrait of Queen Maria II of Portugal, painted by William Charles Ross.
image.credit: William Charles Ross — http://www.royalcollection.org.uk/collection/420385/maria-ii-da-gloria-queen-of-portugal-1819-1853
image.date_qualification: 1852 portrait; not an image of the 1853 succession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Maria II of Portugal succeeded by Pedro V

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1853, during the Crimean War, the Russian fleet destroyed the Turkish fleet at the Battle of Sinop. This decisive naval engagement showcased the strength of the Russian navy and shifted the balance of power in the Black Sea.
events.name: Crimean War: Battle of Sinop

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1853, French minister de Bourboulon arrived at the Heavenly Capital, Nanjing, aboard the Cassini during the Taiping Rebellion. His arrival was part of the broader international interest in the conflict and its implications for foreign powers.

image.caption: Map of the Taiping Rebellion from Augustus Frederick Lindley’s *Ti-ping tien-kwoh: The History of the Ti-Ping Revolution*.
image.credit: Augustus F. Lindley — Ti-Ping Tien-Kwoh The History of the Ti-Ping Revolution (1866)
image.date_qualification: 1866-01-01 is the supplied image date; it dates the historical map’s source, not the 1853 arrival.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Taiping Rebellion: French minister arrives at Heavenly Capital

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1853, Compagnie Générale des Eaux was founded in Paris, France. This company would go on to become a major player in the water and waste management sectors, evolving into the global conglomerate Vivendi.
events.name: Compagnie Générale des Eaux founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1853, the United States completed the Gadsden Purchase, acquiring approximately 77,000 square kilometers of land from Mexico. This acquisition was intended to facilitate the construction of a southern transcontinental railroad.
events.name: Gadsden Purchase

events.enhanced_description: The SS City of Glasgow, a British passenger liner of the Inman Line, set sail from Liverpool bound for the United States with 480 passengers and crew on board. Tragically, the ship was lost at sea without a trace, marking one of the maritime disasters of the era.
events.name: Loss of the SS City of Glasgow

events.enhanced_description: Friedrich Eduard Beneke, a notable German psychologist, mysteriously disappeared in 1854. His remains were discovered two years later in a canal in Charlottenburg, raising questions about his fate and the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.
events.name: Disappearance of Friedrich Eduard Beneke

events.enhanced_description: The Plan de Ayutla was a significant political manifesto in Mexico that called for liberal reforms and the removal of President Antonio López de Santa Anna. This document played a crucial role in the political upheaval that followed in Mexico.
events.name: Plan de Ayutla

events.enhanced_description: The Boston Public Library opened its doors to the public in 1854, becoming the first large free municipal library in the United States. This institution has since played a vital role in promoting literacy and access to information.
events.name: Opening of the Boston Public Library

events.enhanced_description: In 1854, the Republican Party was formed in Ripon, Wisconsin, by anti-slavery activists opposing the Kansas–Nebraska Act. This marked a significant shift in American political dynamics, leading to the emergence of a major political party focused on anti-slavery and reform.
events.name: Formation of the Republican Party

events.enhanced_description: In June 1854, the Grand Excursion took prominent citizens from Chicago to Rock Island, Illinois, by railroad, and then up the Mississippi River to Saint Paul, Minnesota, by steamboat. This event showcased the expanding transportation network and the allure of the American frontier.
events.name: The Grand Excursion

events.enhanced_description: Captain William McDonald discovers the McDonald Islands while aboard the HMS Samarang, contributing to the exploration of the remote regions of the Southern Ocean.
events.name: The McDonald Islands are discovered by Captain William McDonald

events.enhanced_description: The fictional detective Sherlock Holmes, created by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, is perhaps born in 1854, marking the beginning of a literary phenomenon that would influence detective fiction for generations.

image.caption: Interior of the Sherlock Holmes Museum’s sitting room in Baker Street, London.
image.credit: User:FA2010 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Museum interior associated with the Sherlock Holmes stories, not an image of Holmes’s fictional birth. Original image date: 2011-06.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The fictional detective Sherlock Holmes is perhaps born

events.enhanced_description: The Teutonia Männerchor, a German singing society, is founded in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, promoting German culture and community through music and social gatherings.
events.name: The Teutonia Männerchor in Pittsburgh is founded

events.enhanced_description: The North Carolina General Assembly charters the Atlantic and North Carolina Railroad, facilitating transportation and commerce from Goldsboro through New Bern to the newly established seaport of Morehead City.
events.name: The Atlantic and North Carolina Railroad is chartered

events.enhanced_description: The iron clipper RMS Tayleur runs aground off the east coast of Ireland on her maiden voyage from Liverpool to Australia, resulting in the tragic loss of at least 300 of the 650 passengers on board.
events.name: The RMS Tayleur runs aground off the east coast of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1854, major streets in San Francisco are illuminated by coal gas for the first time, marking a significant advancement in urban lighting and public safety.
events.name: Major streets are lit by coal gas for the first time in San Francisco

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1854, Mexican troops successfully force William Walker and his forces to retreat to Sonora, marking a significant setback for Walker's attempts to establish control in Mexico.
events.name: Mexican troops force William Walker to retreat

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1854, Texas is connected by telegraph to the rest of the United States with the completion of a line between New Orleans, Louisiana, and Marshall, Texas, enhancing communication across the nation.
events.name: Texas is linked by telegraph with the rest of the United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1854, the British formally recognize the independence of the Orange Free State in Southern Africa, a significant step in the region's political landscape.
events.name: The British recognize the independence of the Orange Free State

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1854, Britain sends an ultimatum to Russia demanding the withdrawal of its forces from the Romanian provinces of Moldavia and Wallachia, escalating tensions leading to the Crimean War.
events.name: Britain sends Russia an ultimatum regarding Romania

events.enhanced_description: In March 1854, the British East India Company annexes Jhansi State in India under the doctrine of lapse, further expanding British control in the region.
events.name: The British East India Company annexes Jhansi State

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1854, the British Inman Line's SS City of Glasgow departs from Liverpool bound for the United States with 480 passengers on board, but is lost without a trace during the voyage.
events.name: The SS City of Glasgow sets out from Liverpool

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1854, Australia's first telegraph line linking Melbourne and Williamstown in Victoria opens, marking a significant advancement in communication technology in the region.
events.name: Australia's first telegraph line opens

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1854, a Royal Navy fleet sails from Britain under the command of Vice Admiral Sir Charles Napier, preparing for military operations during the escalating tensions of the Crimean War.
events.name: A Royal Navy fleet sails from Britain

events.enhanced_description: In March 1854, various significant events unfold across the United States, reflecting the social and political climate of the time.
events.name: In the United States

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1854, Venezuela abolishes slavery, marking a significant step towards human rights and social reform in the country.
events.name: Slavery is abolished in Venezuela

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1854, the United Kingdom officially declares war on Russia, marking the beginning of the Crimean War, a conflict that would involve several major powers and reshape the geopolitical landscape.
events.name: Crimean War: The United Kingdom declares war on Russia

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1854, France declares war on Russia, joining the United Kingdom in the Crimean War, which would see significant battles and military engagements in the coming years.

image.caption: Map of the Crimean War.
image.credit: Flappiefh, Karel Furlan — Own work based on: Crimean war map 1853-06.svg : , Crimean war map 1854-09.svg : , Crimean war map 1853-10.svg : and Crimean war map 1853-12.svg :
image.date_qualification: The map is described as 1853; the supplied 2023-01-21 image date is not the date depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Crimean War: France declares war on Russia

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1854, United States Navy Commodore Matthew C. Perry signs the Convention of Kanagawa with the Tokugawa shogunate, opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American trade and marking the end of Japan's isolationist policy.

image.caption: First page of the Convention of Kanagawa treaty, a historical document.
image.credit: U.S. Government. — National Archives ARC#299806, Record Group 11
image.date_qualification: The image is identified as the treaty’s first page; 1854-03-31 is the supplied date for the treaty, not evidence of when this document image was made.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: United States Navy Commodore Matthew C. Perry signs the Convention of Kanagawa

events.enhanced_description: Charles Dickens began the serialization of his novel 'Hard Times' in his magazine, Household Words, in April 1854. This work critically examined the social and economic conditions of the time, reflecting Dickens' concerns about industrialization and its impact on society.
events.name: Serialization of Hard Times

events.enhanced_description: The United States packet ship Powhattan was wrecked off the coast of New Jersey on April 16, 1854, resulting in the tragic loss of more than 200 lives. This disaster highlighted the dangers of maritime travel during the period.
events.name: Wreck of the Powhattan

events.enhanced_description: The Hokkien–Teochew Riots occurred in Singapore on May 5, 1854, stemming from ethnic tensions between the Hokkien and Teochew communities. This conflict highlighted the social divisions within the growing population of Singapore during the colonial period.
events.name: Hokkien–Teochew Riots

events.enhanced_description: The Catholic University of Ireland, which later became University College Dublin, was founded on May 18, 1854. This institution aimed to provide higher education in a Catholic context, reflecting the educational needs of the Irish Catholic community.
events.name: Founding of the Catholic University of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1854, United States diplomatic minister Robert McLane arrived at the Heavenly Capital, Nanjing, aboard the USS Susquehanna during the Taiping Rebellion. His presence underscored the United States' interest in the conflict and its implications for foreign relations in China.
events.name: Arrival of Robert McLane during the Taiping Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The Kansas–Nebraska Act was enacted on May 30, 1854, creating the Kansas and Nebraska Territories and allowing residents to decide on the legality of slavery. This act effectively repealed the Missouri Compromise and intensified the national debate over slavery.
events.name: Kansas–Nebraska Act becomes law

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1854, the first class of the United States Naval Academy graduated in Annapolis, Maryland. This milestone marked the establishment of a formal education system for naval officers in the United States.
events.name: First graduation of the United States Naval Academy

events.enhanced_description: During the Battle of Bomarsund on June 21, 1854, British Royal Navy seaman's mate Charles Davis Lucas heroically threw a live Russian artillery shell overboard before it exploded, saving lives. This act of bravery earned him the first Victoria Cross awarded in 1857.
events.name: Battle of Bomarsund

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1854, James Ambrose Cutting received the first of three United States patents for improvements to the wet plate collodion process, known as Ambrotype photography. This innovation significantly advanced photographic techniques of the time.
events.name: James Ambrose Cutting's patent

events.enhanced_description: The first convention of the U.S. Republican Party was held in Jackson, Michigan, on July 6, 1854. This gathering marked a pivotal moment in American political history, as the party sought to unite anti-slavery factions.
events.name: First Republican Party convention

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1854, the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was established in Mumbai, marking the beginning of the cotton mill industry in India. Founded by Cowasjee Nanabhoy Davar and associates, this company played a crucial role in the industrialization of India.
events.name: Establishment of the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1854, Mohamed Sa'id Pasha succeeded his nephew Abbas as the Wāli of Egypt and Sudan, then part of the Ottoman Empire. His leadership marked a significant period of modernization and reform in Egypt.

image.caption: Photograph of Muhammad Sa'id Pasha, wāli of Egypt, by Nadar.
image.credit: Nadar — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1855, after he became wāli in 1854; it is not a contemporary photograph of the accession event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Mohamed Sa'id Pasha becomes Wāli of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: The Bienio progresista revolutionary coup occurred in Spain on July 17, 1854, leading to significant political changes. This coup was part of a broader struggle between progressive and conservative forces in Spanish politics during the mid-19th century.
events.name: Bienio progresista revolutionary coup in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1854, Charles Wood, 1st Viscount Halifax, sent Wood's despatch to Lord Dalhousie, proposing radical improvements to the Indian educational system. This document laid the foundation for modern education in India.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Sir Charles Wood, 1st Viscount Halifax, by Walker & Boutall.
image.credit: Engraved by Walker & Boutall from a painting (artist unknown) — Recollections 1832 to 1886 by Sir Algernon West, pub. Smith, Elder, & Co., London, 1899
image.date_qualification: The depicted image dates from before 1899; 1899 is the publication date, not necessarily the date of the underlying painting.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Wood's despatch on Indian education

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1854, Johann succeeded to the throne of Saxony following the death of his brother. His reign would see significant political and social changes in the region.
events.name: Johann succeeds to the throne of Saxony

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1854, during the Battle of Bomarsund, Russian troops on the island of Bomarsund surrendered to the combined French and British forces. This battle was part of the larger context of the Crimean War.

image.caption: Antoine Léon Morel-Fatio’s painting “Escadre franco-anglaise devant Bomarsund,” depicting the French and British fleet before Bomarsund.
image.credit: Antoine Léon Morel-Fatio — musée national de la Marine
image.date_qualification: Artwork dated 1854; it is not established as depicting the specific surrender on August 16.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Bomarsund: Russian surrender

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1854, Lieutenant John Lawrence Grattan led a contingent of 29 U.S. troops in an attack on a Lakota village over a dispute involving an emigrant cow. The attack resulted in the annihilation of Grattan's command, escalating tensions between U.S. forces and Native Americans.
events.name: Grattan's attack on Lakota village

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1854, English lawyer Alfred Wills and his party set out for the first ascent of the Wetterhorn in Switzerland. This expedition is regarded as the beginning of the 'golden age of alpinism', inspiring future generations of climbers.
events.name: First ascent of the Wetterhorn

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1854, an epidemic of cholera struck London, resulting in the deaths of over 10,000 people. Dr. John Snow traced the source of one outbreak to a contaminated water pump, validating his theory that cholera is water-borne and laying the groundwork for modern epidemiology.
events.name: Cholera epidemic in London

events.enhanced_description: The SS City of Philadelphia, a British passenger liner of the Inman Line, was wrecked off Cape Race during its maiden voyage on September 9, 1854. Fortunately, there were no casualties among the passengers or crew, marking a rare instance of survival in maritime disasters.

locations.name: Cape Race, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Wreck of SS City of Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Alma, fought on September 20, 1854, was the first major land engagement of the Crimean War, where the French and British forces achieved a decisive victory against the Russian army. This battle marked a significant turning point in the conflict, showcasing the effectiveness of the allied forces.
events.name: Battle of Alma

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1854, the American paddle steamer SS Arctic sank after colliding with the French ship SS Vesta, resulting in approximately 320 deaths. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during the era and led to changes in maritime safety regulations.

locations.name: 50 miles off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada

events.name: SS Arctic disaster

events.enhanced_description: In October 1854, the watch company founded by Aaron Lufkin Dennison in Roxbury, Massachusetts, relocated to Waltham, where it became known as the Waltham Watch Company. This company was a pioneer in the American system of watch manufacturing, revolutionizing the industry.
events.name: Relocation of Waltham Watch Company

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1854, a spectacular explosion ignited the Great Fire of Newcastle and Gateshead, causing widespread destruction across the cities. The fire highlighted the need for improved fire safety measures in urban areas.

locations.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Great Fire of Newcastle and Gateshead

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1854, United States diplomats in Europe convened in Brussels to draft the Ostend Manifesto, which articulated a rationale for the U.S. to acquire Cuba from Spain. This document reflected the expansionist sentiments of the era and stirred significant controversy.
events.name: Drafting of the Ostend Manifesto

events.enhanced_description: The Age newspaper was founded in Melbourne, Australia, on October 17, 1854. It became one of the leading newspapers in Australia, known for its commitment to quality journalism and public service.
events.name: Founding of The Age newspaper

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Balaclava, fought on October 25, 1854, during the Crimean War, saw the allies achieve an overall victory despite the infamous Charge of the Light Brigade, which resulted in heavy losses. This battle is remembered for its strategic significance and the bravery displayed by the troops.
events.name: Battle of Balaclava

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1854, Florence Nightingale and her team of 38 trained nurses arrived at Selimiye Barracks in Scutari, Ottoman Empire, to provide care for British troops wounded in the Crimean War. Nightingale's efforts would revolutionize nursing and healthcare practices.
events.name: Florence Nightingale arrives in Scutari

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1854, a devastating storm struck the Black Sea, wrecking 19 British and 2 French ships that were supporting the Crimean War, resulting in the loss of at least 287 men. This disaster underscored the perils faced by naval forces during wartime.
events.name: Great Storm of 1854

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1854, the Suez Canal Company was formed in Egypt, spearheaded by Ferdinand de Lesseps. This company would oversee the construction of the Suez Canal, a pivotal project that transformed global trade routes.
events.name: Formation of the Suez Canal Company

events.enhanced_description: The Eureka Stockade Miners' Rebellion erupted on December 3, 1854, in Ballarat, Victoria, Australia, as miners protested against oppressive licensing fees and government regulations. This event is considered a pivotal moment in Australian history, symbolizing the fight for democratic rights.
events.name: Eureka Stockade Miners' Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1854, Pope Pius IX defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception in the apostolic constitution Ineffabilis Deus, affirming that the Blessed Virgin Mary was conceived without original sin. This declaration had profound implications for Catholic doctrine.
events.name: Definition of the dogma of Immaculate Conception

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1854, Sa'id Pasha officially abolished slavery in Egypt, marking a significant step towards social reform in the region. This decision reflected broader trends in the 19th century towards the abolition of slavery worldwide.
events.name: Abolition of slavery in Egypt

events.enhanced_description: The 1855 Victorian High Treason trials involved the prosecution of gold miners in Australia who were accused of rebellion against British colonial authority. These trials reflected the tensions between colonial governance and the rights of settlers during the gold rush era.
events.name: 1855 Victorian High Treason trials

events.enhanced_description: In 1855, the Wairarapa earthquake, measuring between 8.2 and 8.3 Mw, struck near the Cook Strait area of New Zealand, resulting in significant destruction and loss of life. This earthquake is one of the most powerful recorded in New Zealand's history.
events.name: The 8.2–8.3 Mw Wairarapa earthquake

events.enhanced_description: In 1855, the Great Gold Robbery occurred when a group of thieves stole £12,000 worth of gold from a moving train between London Bridge and Folkestone. This audacious crime is considered one of the first of its kind in British history, highlighting vulnerabilities in the transport of valuable goods.
events.name: The Great Gold Robbery

events.enhanced_description: In 1855, Samuel Colt incorporated his business as Colt's Patent Firearms Manufacturing Company and opened a new factory, the Colt Armory, in Hartford, Connecticut. This establishment solidified Colt's position as a leading manufacturer of firearms in America.
events.name: Samuel Colt incorporates Colt's Patent Firearms Manufacturing Company

events.enhanced_description: In 1855, German chemist Friedrich Gaedcke first isolated the cocaine alkaloid. This significant scientific achievement contributed to the understanding of the chemical properties of coca and laid the groundwork for future research into its effects and uses.
events.name: Cocaine alkaloid first isolated

events.enhanced_description: In 1855, palm oil sales from West Africa to the United Kingdom reached a remarkable 40,000 tons. This surge in trade highlighted the growing economic importance of palm oil in the global market and its role in the industrial revolution.
events.name: Palm oil sales reach 40,000 tons

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1855, Ramón Castilla commenced his third term as President of Peru, a period marked by significant political and economic reforms aimed at modernizing the country. His leadership was pivotal in stabilizing Peru after years of turmoil and establishing a more centralized government.
events.name: Ramón Castilla begins his third term as President of Peru

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1855, the first bridge over the Mississippi River was opened in Minneapolis, serving as a crucial infrastructure development for the region. This bridge, a predecessor of the Father Louis Hennepin Bridge, facilitated transportation and commerce across the river.
events.name: The first bridge over the Mississippi River opens in modern-day Minneapolis

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1855, the Point No Point Treaty was signed in the Washington Territory, establishing boundaries and rights for Native American tribes in the region. This treaty was part of a series of agreements aimed at resolving land disputes between the U.S. government and indigenous peoples.

locations.name: Point No Point, Washington, United States

events.name: The Point No Point Treaty is signed in the Washington Territory

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1855, the Panama Railway was inaugurated, becoming the first railroad to connect the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. This monumental engineering feat significantly reduced travel time and facilitated trade between the two oceans, playing a crucial role in the economic development of Panama.
events.name: The Panama Railway becomes the first railroad to connect the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1855, Lord Aberdeen resigned as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom due to criticism over his handling of the Crimean War. His resignation marked a significant shift in British politics during a tumultuous period characterized by military challenges and public discontent.
events.name: Lord Aberdeen resigns as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In February 1855, mysterious footprints appeared in the snow around the Exe Estuary, leading to widespread speculation and folklore about their origin. This phenomenon captured the imagination of the public and has since become a part of local legend.
events.name: Devil's Footprints

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1855, Lord Palmerston assumed office as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, succeeding Lord Aberdeen. His leadership was marked by a more aggressive foreign policy and a focus on expanding British influence globally.
events.name: Lord Palmerston becomes Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1855, Kassa Hailu was crowned Tewodros II, Emperor of Ethiopia, marking the beginning of a reign characterized by efforts to modernize the country and consolidate power. His rule was significant in the context of Ethiopian history, as he sought to unify the nation and resist foreign influence.
events.name: Kassa Hailu is crowned Tewodros II, Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1855, Michigan State University was established as the first land-grant college in the United States. This institution played a pivotal role in the development of higher education and agricultural research in the country.

image.caption: Linton Hall at Michigan State University in East Lansing, Michigan.
image.credit: Paul R. Burley — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2016-12-28; not contemporaneous with the university’s founding in 1855.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Michigan State University is established

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1855, the North Carolina General Assembly incorporated the Western North Carolina Railroad, aiming to construct a rail line from Salisbury to the western part of the state. This development was crucial for improving transportation and economic growth in the region.
events.name: The North Carolina General Assembly incorporates the Western North Carolina Railroad

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1855, Pennsylvania State University was founded as the Farmers' High School of Pennsylvania, marking the establishment of one of the leading public research universities in the United States. The institution has since evolved into a major center for education and research.
events.name: Pennsylvania State University is founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1855, Alexander II ascended to the Russian throne following the death of his father, Nicholas I. His reign would be marked by significant reforms, including the emancipation of serfs and modernization efforts within the Russian Empire.
events.name: Alexander II ascends the Russian throne

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1855, the United States Congress appropriated $30,000 to establish the U.S. Camel Corps, an initiative aimed at using camels for military transport in the arid southwestern territories. This unusual project reflected the innovative approaches to logistics during the period.
events.name: The United States Congress appropriates $30,000 to create the U.S. Camel Corps

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1855, Bates College was founded in Lewiston, Maine, by abolitionists who aimed to create an inclusive educational environment. The college has since become known for its commitment to social justice and academic excellence.
events.name: Bates College is founded by abolitionists in Lewiston, Maine

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1855, a massive Taiping army of approximately 350,000 invaded Anhui, China, during the Taiping Rebellion, one of the deadliest conflicts in history. This rebellion aimed to overthrow the Qing Dynasty and establish a new Christian-based kingdom.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion: A Taiping army of 350,000 invades Anhui

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1855, elections were held for the first Kansas Territory legislature, amidst significant conflict as pro-slavery and anti-slavery factions vied for control. This event was a precursor to the violent confrontations known as 'Bleeding Kansas.'
events.name: Elections are held for the first Kansas Territory legislature

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1855, the Nepalese invasion of Tibet commenced, marking the beginning of the Nepalese–Tibetan War (1855–1856). This conflict arose from territorial disputes and the desire of Nepal to expand its influence in the region.
events.name: The Nepalese invasion of Tibet starts the Nepalese–Tibetan War

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1855, the Battle of Kaba took place in the Fiji Islands, where the Kingdom of Tonga intervened in the conflict between Cakobau, the self-proclaimed Tui Viti (King) of Fiji, and the Confederation of Rewa. This battle resulted in Rewa's defeat and strengthened Cakobau's claim to unify Fiji.
events.name: Battle of Kaba

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1855, the Bordeaux Wine Official Classification was established, categorizing the finest wines from the Bordeaux region. This classification has had a lasting impact on the wine industry and continues to influence wine production and marketing today.
events.name: The Bordeaux Wine Official Classification of 1855 is first listed

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1855, Van Diemen's Land was officially separated from New South Wales and granted self-government, becoming the colony of Tasmania. This administrative change marked a significant step towards greater autonomy for the region.
events.name: Van Diemen's Land is separated administratively from New South Wales

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1855, American adventurer William Walker and a group of armed mercenaries set sail from San Francisco to Central America with the intent to conquer Nicaragua. Walker's actions were part of a larger trend of filibustering in the region during the mid-19th century.
events.name: William Walker sails to conquer Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: The Exposition Universelle, an early World's Fair, officially opened in Paris in 1855, showcasing advancements in art, technology, and industry. This event not only celebrated French culture but also introduced the Bordeaux Wine Official Classification of 1855, which remains influential today.
events.name: The Exposition Universelle officially opens in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1855, Mount Sinai Hospital was dedicated in New York City, originally named the Jews' Hospital. This institution has since grown to become one of the leading hospitals in the United States, providing comprehensive healthcare services.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Mount Sinai Hospital is dedicated in New York City

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1855, the province of Victoria was administratively separated from New South Wales in Australia, marking a significant step in the region's governance. This change allowed for more localized administration and development in Victoria.
events.name: Victoria is separated from New South Wales in Australia

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1855, the British government abolished the stamp duty on newspapers, which had been a significant financial burden on publishers. This pivotal change led to the emergence of a free press in the United Kingdom, allowing for greater access to information and the proliferation of mass media.
events.name: Stamp duty revenue tax is removed from British newspapers

events.enhanced_description: The Daily Telegraph, one of the United Kingdom's most prominent newspapers, commenced publication on June 29, 1855. Its establishment marked a significant development in British journalism, contributing to the rise of mass media and public discourse.

image.caption: Illustration of The Daily Telegraph’s new offices and printing premises on Fleet Street, London.
image.credit: Unknown (original uploader was Honbicot at English Wikipedia) — English Wikipedia
image.date_qualification: Depicted as 1882; the supplied 21 October 2005 date is the original upload date, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Daily Telegraph newspaper begins publication

events.enhanced_description: In July 1855, the Bank of Toronto was incorporated in Canada, marking a significant development in the Canadian banking sector. This institution would later merge with The Dominion Bank in 1955 to form the Toronto-Dominion Bank, one of Canada's largest financial institutions.

image.caption: Photograph of the Bank of Toronto at the northwest corner of Church and Wellington Streets in Toronto.
image.credit: William Notman — This image is available from the McCord Stewart Museum under the access number I-34474.1 This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing for more information.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1868, after the bank’s incorporation in 1855; it documents the bank’s site, not the incorporation event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Bank of Toronto incorporated

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1855, the Quinault Treaty was signed, in which the Quinault and Quileute tribes ceded their lands to the United States. This treaty was part of a broader pattern of treaties during this period that significantly altered the landscape and rights of Native American tribes.
events.name: The Quinault Treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1855, the Kansas territorial legislature convened in Pawnee, where it began passing proslavery laws. This event was a significant moment in the lead-up to the violent conflicts known as 'Bleeding Kansas,' which were fought over the issue of slavery in the territories.
events.name: Kansas territorial legislature convenes

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1855, Walt Whitman published his groundbreaking poetry collection, Leaves of Grass, in Brooklyn. This work would go on to become a cornerstone of American literature, celebrated for its innovative style and themes of individuality and democracy.

image.caption: Steel engraving of Walt Whitman by Samuel Hollyer, based on a daguerreotype by Gabriel Harrison.
image.credit: Samuel Hollyer (1826-1919) of a daguerreotype by Gabriel Harrison (1818-1902)(original lost). — Morgan Library & Museum
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1854-07; it is not a photograph of the 1855 publication event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass published

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1855, the Australian Colonies were granted self-governing status by the United Kingdom. This significant political change allowed the colonies to manage their own affairs and laid the groundwork for the eventual federation of Australia.
events.name: Australian Colonies granted self-governing status

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1855, Monte Rosa, the second-highest mountain in the Alps, was first ascended. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the history of mountaineering and showcased the growing interest in alpine exploration during the 19th century.
events.name: Monte Rosa first ascended

events.enhanced_description: The last Bartholomew Fair was held in London on September 3, 1855. This historic fair, which had been a staple of London life for centuries, marked the end of an era in public festivities and trade in the city.
events.name: Last Bartholomew Fair held

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1855, during the Crimean War, Sevastopol fell to the combined forces of French and British troops. This pivotal moment marked a significant victory for the Allies and a turning point in the conflict against the Russian Empire.
events.name: Siege of Sevastopol falls

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1855, Alfred Tennyson read from his new book Maud and other poems at a gathering in the home of fellow poets Robert and Elizabeth Browning in London. This intimate event was captured in a sketch by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, highlighting the close-knit literary community of the time.
events.name: Alfred Tennyson reads at Browning's home

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1855, the Port of Iloilo in the Philippines was opened to international trade by Queen Isabel II of Spain. This development was part of a broader effort to enhance trade and economic growth in the region, also impacting other ports like Sual and Zamboanga City.
events.name: Port of Iloilo opened to international trade

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1855, Henry Bessemer filed his patent in the United Kingdom for the Bessemer process of steelmaking. This revolutionary method significantly lowered the cost of steel production and laid the foundation for modern steel manufacturing.

image.caption: Line-art illustration of a Bessemer converter, representing the steelmaking process.
image.credit: Pearson Scott Foresman — Archives of Pearson Scott Foresman , donated to the Wikimedia Foundation
image.date_qualification: Undated illustration; the depicted patent filing is described in the event record as 1855-10-17.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Henry Bessemer files patent for steelmaking process

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1855, Van Diemen's Land was officially renamed Tasmania. This change reflected a growing sense of identity and autonomy among the island's inhabitants and marked a significant moment in Australian history.
events.name: Van Diemen's Land renamed Tasmania

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1855, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's fictional poem The Song of Hiawatha was published in Boston. This work became one of Longfellow's most famous pieces, celebrated for its portrayal of Native American culture and its innovative use of meter.
events.name: Longfellow's The Song of Hiawatha published

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1855, the Hejaz rebellion erupted against the Ottoman Empire, triggered by an anti-slave trade decree. The ulema of Mecca condemned the decree as influenced by Westerners and contrary to Islamic law, leading to significant unrest in the region.
events.name: Hejaz rebellion against Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1855, Scottish missionary explorer David Livingstone became the first European to see Victoria Falls, located on the border between modern-day Zambia and Zimbabwe. His discovery brought global attention to this natural wonder and contributed to the exploration of Africa.
events.name: David Livingstone sees Victoria Falls

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1855, large-scale violence erupted in Kansas, marking the beginning of the 'Bleeding Kansas' conflict. This violent struggle between proslavery and antislavery factions was a precursor to the American Civil War.
events.name: Bleeding Kansas violence begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1855, Ignacio Comonfort was elected President of Mexico. His presidency was marked by significant political turmoil and reform efforts during a critical period in Mexican history.
events.name: Ignacio Comonfort becomes President of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1855, the Metropolitan Board of Works was established in London. This organization was responsible for overseeing public works and infrastructure in the rapidly growing city, playing a crucial role in urban development.
events.name: Metropolitan Board of Works established

events.enhanced_description: In March 1856, the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India officially measured 'Peak XV', later known as Mount Everest, to be 29,002 feet (8,840 meters) tall. This landmark achievement established the mountain as the highest point on Earth.
events.name: Great Trigonometrical Survey of India

events.enhanced_description: In March 1856, the Treaty of Thapathali was signed, concluding the Nepalese-Tibetan War. This treaty established the borders between Nepal and Tibet and marked a significant moment in the region's history.
events.name: Treaty of Thapathali

events.enhanced_description: In April 1856, the Xhosa cattle-killing movement began in Cape Colony, leading to widespread famine among the Xhosa people. This movement was rooted in a belief that the killing of cattle would lead to the arrival of ancestral spirits and the restoration of their land.
events.name: Xhosa cattle-killing movement

events.enhanced_description: In August 1856, pre-human remains were discovered in the Neanderthal Valley in Prussia, marking a pivotal moment in the field of archaeology and human evolution. This find led to the identification of the Neanderthal species and reshaped our understanding of human ancestry.

image.caption: Photograph of a Neanderthal cranial fossil displayed at the “Néandertal, l'expo” exhibition in Paris.
image.credit: Eunostos — Own work
image.date_qualification: The depicted photograph dates to 2018-04-14; the fossil is identified in the image description as dating to 42,000 BP. This is a later photograph of the fossil, not an 1856 event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Pre-human remains found in Neanderthal Valley

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, Gregor Mendel began his groundbreaking research on genetics at the Augustinian monastery in Brünn, now Brno, Czech Republic. His experiments with pea plants laid the foundation for the field of genetics, leading to the formulation of Mendel's laws of inheritance.
events.name: Gregor Mendel starts his research on genetics

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, Kate Warne became the first female private detective, joining the Pinkerton Detective Agency in Chicago. Her pioneering role in a male-dominated field opened doors for women in law enforcement and private investigation.
events.name: Kate Warne begins work for Pinkerton Detective Agency

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, legal protection for widow remarriage was extended in India, marking a significant step towards women's rights and social reform. This legislation aimed to improve the status of widows in Indian society.
events.name: Legal protection of widow remarriage extended in India

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, St. Paul's School was founded by the Jesuits in Belgaum, India. This institution aimed to provide quality education and has since contributed significantly to the educational landscape of the region.
events.name: St. Paul's School founded in Belgaum

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, the British Guiana 1c magenta postage stamp was issued in limited numbers, becoming one of the rarest stamps in the world. Its unique history and scarcity have made it a highly sought-after item among collectors.
events.name: British Guiana 1c magenta postage stamp issued

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, Credit Suisse was founded in Zürich, Switzerland, originally known as La Schweizerische Kreditanstalt. This financial institution has grown to become one of the world's leading global banks.
events.name: Credit Suisse founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, Charles III of Monaco granted a concession to Napoléon Langlois and Albert Aubert to establish a German-style casino at Monte Carlo. This development played a crucial role in transforming Monte Carlo into a premier gambling destination.
events.name: Casino at Monte Carlo established

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, John Veatch discovered large deposits of borax in Borax Lake, California, which would later become a significant resource for various industries, including glass and ceramics.
events.name: Borax deposits discovered

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1856, the American sidewheel steamer SS Pacific departed from Liverpool, England, on a transatlantic voyage. Tragically, the ship was lost at sea with all 186 passengers and crew aboard, marking one of the maritime disasters of the era.
events.name: SS Pacific leaves Liverpool

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1856, U.S. President Franklin Pierce declared the Free-State Topeka government in Kansas to be in rebellion. This declaration intensified the violent conflict known as 'Bleeding Kansas' as pro-slavery and anti-slavery factions clashed.
events.name: Pierce declares Topeka government in rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Seattle occurred on January 26, 1856, when U.S. Marines from the USS Decatur suppressed an indigenous uprising. This conflict was a direct response to Governor Stevens' controversial declaration of a 'war of extermination' against Native communities.
events.name: First Battle of Seattle

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1856, the 223-mile North Carolina Railroad was completed, connecting Goldsboro through Raleigh and Salisbury to Charlotte. This railroad played a crucial role in the economic development of North Carolina.
events.name: Completion of North Carolina Railroad

events.enhanced_description: In February 1856, the Tintic War erupted in Utah, a conflict primarily between Mormon settlers and Native American tribes over land and resources. This war highlighted the tensions between settlers and indigenous populations during westward expansion.
events.name: Tintic War breaks out

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1856, Auburn University was first chartered as the East Alabama Male College. It has since evolved into a major public research university in the United States.
events.name: Auburn University chartered

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1856, Dallas, Texas, was officially incorporated as a city. This marked a significant step in its development as a major urban center in the American Southwest.
events.name: Dallas incorporated as a city

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1856, Wajid Ali Shah, the Nawab of Oudh, was exiled to Metiabruz as the British East India Company annexed his state. This event marked a significant moment in the colonial history of India.
events.name: Wajid Ali Shah exiled

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1856, two American clipper ships, Driver and Ocean Queen, departed from Liverpool and London respectively, only to be lost without a trace in the Atlantic Ocean, resulting in the deaths of 497 people combined.
events.name: Clipper ships lost at sea

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1856, the American Know Nothing Party convened in Philadelphia to nominate their first presidential candidate, former President Millard Fillmore. This event was significant in the context of the nativist sentiments of the time.
events.name: Know Nothing Party convention

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1856, the Maryland Agricultural College was chartered, which would later evolve into the University of Maryland, College Park, a major institution of higher education.
events.name: Maryland Agricultural College chartered

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1856, during the Filibuster War, Costa Rican troops achieved a decisive victory over William Walker's soldiers at the Battle of Santa Rosa. This battle was crucial in thwarting Walker's attempts to establish control in Central America.
events.name: Battle of Santa Rosa

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1856, during the Taiping Rebellion, Shi Dakai began his march back to the Heavenly Capital after suspecting treachery from East King Yang Xiuqing. This internal conflict was one of the deadliest in history.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion events

events.enhanced_description: Nelson College, one of New Zealand's oldest secondary schools, was founded in 1856 in Nelson. It has played a significant role in the education of young men in the region and continues to be a prominent institution today.
events.name: Nelson College is founded

events.enhanced_description: Theta Chi, an international college fraternity, was established at Norwich University in Vermont in 1856. It has since grown into a significant organization with chapters across the United States and beyond, promoting brotherhood and leadership among its members.
events.name: Theta Chi fraternity is founded

events.enhanced_description: The Paris Declaration Respecting Maritime Law, signed in 1856, abolished privateering and established regulations for the conduct of neutral and belligerent shipping on the high seas. This agreement marked a significant step towards modern international maritime law.
events.name: Paris Declaration Respecting Maritime Law

events.enhanced_description: The Chicago Historical Society Museum, now known as the Chicago History Museum, was established in 1856. It serves as a vital institution for preserving and interpreting the history of Chicago and the surrounding region.
events.name: Chicago Historical Society Museum is established

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, building workers in Melbourne, Australia, began to agitate for an eight-hour workday, marking a significant moment in labor rights history. This movement laid the groundwork for future labor reforms in Australia and beyond.
events.name: Building workers agitate for the eight-hour day

events.enhanced_description: The RMS Persia, an iron-hulled paddle steamer, completed a westbound transatlantic crossing in 1856, regaining the Blue Riband for the Cunard Line. This achievement highlighted advancements in maritime technology and the growing importance of transatlantic travel.
events.name: RMS Persia concludes transatlantic crossing

events.enhanced_description: In 1856, the province of Isabela was created in the Philippines in honor of Queen Isabella II of Spain. This administrative division played a crucial role in the governance and development of the region.
events.name: Province of Isabela is created

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1856, Queen Victoria granted Norfolk Island to the descendants of the Pitcairn Island colony, many of whom were descendants of the Mutiny on the Bounty. This act extended women's suffrage, as practiced on Pitcairn, to Norfolk Island.
events.name: Queen Victoria gives Norfolk Island to Pitcairn descendants

events.enhanced_description: The San Francisco Committee of Vigilance was founded in 1856 as a response to rampant crime and corruption. The committee took the law into its own hands, leading to the lynching of two gangsters and the arrest of numerous officials, reflecting the tumultuous political climate of the time.

image.caption: Charles B. Huestis’s illustration of James P. Casey and Charles Cora being executed by San Francisco’s Vigilance Committee.
image.credit: Huestis, Charles B. (active ca. 1856-ca. 1859), artist Town Talk, printer — http://content.cdlib.org/ark:/13030/tf229007rh/?layout=metadata
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1856; it depicts an execution, not the founding event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: San Francisco Committee of Vigilance is founded

events.enhanced_description: In May 1856, explorer David Livingstone arrived at Quelimane on the Indian Ocean, completing a two-year transcontinental journey across Africa from Luanda. His explorations contributed significantly to the understanding of Africa's geography and cultures.
events.name: David Livingstone arrives at Quelimane

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1856, pro-slavery forces captured and burned Lawrence, Kansas, in a violent act during the Bleeding Kansas conflict. This event highlighted the intense national debate over slavery and its expansion into the territories.
events.name: Sacking of Lawrence

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1856, Congressman Preston Brooks brutally caned Senator Charles Sumner in the Senate chamber after Sumner delivered a speech denouncing pro-slavery forces. This incident underscored the escalating tensions leading up to the American Civil War.
events.name: Caning of Charles Sumner

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1856, radical abolitionist John Brown and his followers killed five pro-slavery homesteaders in Franklin County, Kansas, in a violent act of retribution. This massacre intensified the conflict known as Bleeding Kansas, which was a precursor to the Civil War.
events.name: Pottawatomie massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Black Jack occurred on June 2, 1856, when anti-slavery forces led by John Brown defeated pro-slavery forces in a significant confrontation during the Bleeding Kansas conflict. This battle was pivotal in the struggle over slavery in the territories.
events.name: Battle of Black Jack

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1856, 500 Mormon handcart pioneers departed from Iowa City, Iowa, heading west to Salt Lake City, Utah. They carried all their possessions in two-wheeled handcarts, symbolizing the determination and resilience of the Mormon migration.

image.caption: Illustration depicting Mormon handcart pioneers traveling toward Salt Lake City.
image.credit: Published in above-mentioned work, which was by Benjamin F. Gue — Image:History of Iowa From the Earliest Times to the Beginning of the Twentieth Century Volume 1.djvu
image.date_qualification: The depicted date is not specified; 1903 is the illustration’s stated date, not the date of the 1856 departure.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Mormon handcart pioneers leave for Salt Lake City

events.enhanced_description: In June 1856, Shi Dakai, a prominent leader in the Taiping Rebellion, arrived at Nanjing, which was a stronghold for the Taiping forces. His leadership was crucial in the ongoing conflict against the Qing Dynasty.
events.name: Shi Dakai arrives at Nanjing during Taiping Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: General Mills was founded in 1856 in Minneapolis, Minnesota, originally as the Minneapolis Milling Company. It has since grown into one of the largest food companies in the world, known for its diverse range of products.
events.name: General Mills is founded

events.enhanced_description: In July 1856, Natal was officially declared a British Crown colony, marking a significant moment in the colonial history of South Africa. This change in governance had lasting impacts on the region's political landscape.
events.name: Natal becomes a British Crown colony

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1856, General Leopoldo O'Donnell seized control of the Spanish government, effectively ending the bienio progresista, a period of progressive reforms. His leadership marked a return to conservative governance in Spain.
events.name: General Leopoldo O'Donnell takes control in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1856, the Great Train Wreck near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, resulted in the worst railroad calamity in the world to that date, causing numerous fatalities and injuries. This disaster highlighted the dangers of early railroad travel and led to increased safety regulations.
events.name: The Great Train Wreck occurs

events.enhanced_description: In July 1856, Christchurch was officially chartered as a city in New Zealand. This designation marked a significant step in its development as a major urban center in the country.
events.name: Christchurch is chartered as a city

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1856, the Last Island hurricane struck Last Island, Louisiana, resulting in the deaths of approximately 400 people. The storm caused significant destruction, breaking the island into several smaller islands.
events.name: Last Island hurricane destroys Last Island

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Osawatomie took place on August 30, 1856, during the Bleeding Kansas conflict, where proslavery forces defeated antislavery forces. This battle exemplified the violent struggle over slavery in the Kansas Territory.
events.name: Battle of Osawatomie

events.enhanced_description: Seton Hall University was founded in South Orange, New Jersey, in 1856 by Bishop James Roosevelt Bayley. It has since developed into a prominent Catholic university, known for its commitment to academic excellence and community service.
events.name: Seton Hall University is founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1856, during the Taiping Rebellion, Wei Changhui and Qin Rigang assassinated Yang Xiuqing, a prominent leader of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. This act of violence significantly altered the power dynamics within the rebellion, leading to further internal conflicts.
events.name: Taiping Rebellion: Wei Changhui and Qin Rigang assassinate Yang Xiuqing

events.enhanced_description: The Saimaa Canal was inaugurated on September 7, 1856, facilitating navigation between Lake Saimaa and the Gulf of Finland. This significant engineering achievement improved trade routes and economic connectivity in the region.
events.name: The Saimaa Canal was inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1856, the Second Opium War commenced following the Arrow Incident on the Pearl River, where British forces clashed with Chinese authorities.
