events.enhanced_description: A new uprising erupts in Palermo, reflecting the growing discontent among Sicilians and contributing to the broader context of Italian unification and social unrest.
events.name: Uprising in Palermo

events.enhanced_description: French typesetter Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville creates a recording of the folk song 'Au clair de la lune' using his phonautograph, producing the earliest known intelligible sound recording of the human voice.
events.name: Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville creates a recording

events.enhanced_description: A Chondrite-type meteorite falls to earth in Muskingum County, Ohio, near the town of New Concord, contributing to the study of meteorites and their significance in understanding the solar system.

locations.name: New Concord, Muskingum County, Ohio, United States

events.name: Chondrite-type meteorite falls

events.enhanced_description: Giuseppe Garibaldi and his troops depart from Quarto as part of the Expedition of the Thousand, a pivotal campaign in the Italian unification process that leads to the conquest of Sicily.
events.name: Expedition of the Thousand departs

events.enhanced_description: In New Granada (modern-day Colombia), the southern state of Cauca secedes from the central government, leading to civil unrest and conflict as other regions join the secession.
events.name: Cauca secedes in New Granada

events.enhanced_description: During the Expedition of the Thousand, troops under Giuseppe Garibaldi defeat the army of Naples in the Battle of Calatafimi, a crucial victory that advances the cause of Italian unification.
events.name: Battle of Calatafimi

events.enhanced_description: The German association football club TSV 1860 München is founded, contributing to the rich history of football in Germany and establishing a legacy in German sports.
events.name: TSV 1860 München founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi's forces captured Palermo, the capital of Sicily, marking a significant step in the unification of Italy. This victory was pivotal in Garibaldi's campaign against the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
events.name: Garibaldi's forces take Palermo

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1860, the State Bank of the Russian Empire was established in Saint Petersburg, serving as a crucial institution for managing the country's finances and facilitating economic development. This marked a significant step in modernizing Russia's financial system.
events.name: Establishment of the State Bank of the Russian Empire

events.enhanced_description: Vladivostok was founded on July 2, 1860, as a military outpost in the Russian Far East. Its establishment marked the beginning of significant Russian expansion into the Pacific region.
events.name: Founding of Vladivostok

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1860, Mutsuhito was formally appointed as Crown Prince of Japan, a position that would later lead him to become Emperor Meiji. His reign marked a period of rapid modernization and westernization in Japan.
events.name: Mutsuhito becomes Crown Prince of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1860, José Ignacio Pavón assumed the role of unconstitutional interim President of Mexico, replacing Miguel Miramón. However, Miramón quickly regained the presidency just two days later.
events.name: José Ignacio Pavón becomes interim President of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1860, assisted by the British Navy, Giuseppe Garibaldi's troops successfully crossed from Sicily to the Italian mainland, continuing their campaign for Italian unification.
events.name: Garibaldi's troops cross to the Italian mainland

events.enhanced_description: The First International Chemistry Congress was held in Karlsruhe, Germany, on September 3, 1860. This event brought together chemists from various countries to discuss advancements and standardization in the field of chemistry.
events.name: First International Chemistry Congress

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1860, the PS Lady Elgin was accidentally rammed and sunk in Lake Michigan, resulting in the drowning of hundreds of passengers. This maritime disaster remains one of the deadliest in American history.
events.name: Sinking of the PS Lady Elgin

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1860, Piedmontese forces invaded the Papal States with the aim of linking up with Garibaldi's troops in Naples. This invasion was part of the broader campaign for Italian unification.
events.name: Piedmontese forces invade the Papal States

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1860, the Battle of Castelfidardo took place, where Piedmontese forces decisively defeated the Papal army. This victory allowed the Piedmontese to continue their advance into Neapolitan territory.
events.name: Battle of Castelfidardo

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1860, Ecuadorian forces led by Juan José Flores and Gabriel García Moreno captured the port of Guayaquil from Supreme Chief Guillermo Franco, who was supported by Peruvian forces. This battle was significant in the context of Ecuador's internal conflicts.
events.name: Battle of Guayaquil

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1860, the Battle of Volturnus saw Garibaldi's forces defeat the last organized army of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. This victory was crucial in the unification of Italy.

locations.name: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, Italy

events.name: Battle of Volturnus

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1860, a commission was formed by Austria, Britain, France, Prussia, and the Ottoman Empire to investigate the causes of the massacres of Maronite Christians by Druzes in Lebanon earlier that year. This event highlighted the international concern over sectarian violence in the region.
events.name: Commission on Maronite massacres

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1860, Section 377 of the British Indian Penal Code was enacted, criminalizing homosexual acts. This law would have lasting implications for LGBTQ+ rights in India.
events.name: Enactment of Section 377 in British India

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1860, the first Open Championship, also known as the British Open, was held at Prestwick Golf Club in Ayrshire, Scotland. Willie Park Sr. won the inaugural tournament, marking the beginning of one of golf's most prestigious events.
events.name: First Open Championship

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1860, the First Convention of Peking was signed, formally ending the Second Opium War between China and the British Empire. This treaty had significant implications for China's sovereignty and foreign relations.
events.name: First Convention of Peking

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1860, British General Lord Elgin ordered the burning of Beijing's Old Summer Palace in retaliation for the mistreatment of prisoners of war during the Second Opium War. This act symbolized the violent clashes between imperial powers and China.
events.name: Burning of the Old Summer Palace

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1860, a new Māori revolt began in New Zealand, reflecting ongoing tensions between Māori tribes and European settlers. This conflict was part of the broader New Zealand Wars.
events.name: New Māori revolt in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi's forces advanced on Gaeta, the last remaining stronghold of the Neapolitan army. This maneuver was crucial in the final stages of the Italian unification process.
events.name: Garibaldi's advance on Gaeta

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1860, the combined forces of Giuseppe Garibaldi and King Victor Emmanuel II besieged King Francis II of the Two Sicilies in Gaeta, marking the final stages of the Italian unification campaign.
events.name: Siege of Gaeta

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected as the 16th President of the United States, defeating three other candidates. This election marked a pivotal moment in American history, leading to the Civil War.
events.name: 1860 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1860, Charles Dickens published the first installment of his novel 'Great Expectations' in his magazine 'All the Year Round'. This work would go on to become one of Dickens's most famous novels, exploring themes of social class and personal growth.
events.name: Charles Dickens publishes the first installment of Great Expectations

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1860, Monier Monier-Williams was elected as the Boden Professor of Sanskrit at Oxford University after a competitive campaign. His tenure significantly advanced the study of Sanskrit and Indian literature in the West.
events.name: Monier Monier-Williams elected as Boden Professor of Sanskrit

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1860, South Carolina became the first state to secede from the Union, marking a pivotal moment in the lead-up to the American Civil War. This act of secession was driven by tensions over slavery and states' rights.
events.name: South Carolina secedes from the United States

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1860, after being defeated in battle, Mexico's interim president Miguel Miramón fled the country. His departure marked a significant shift in the ongoing conflict during the Reform War in Mexico.
events.name: Miguel Miramón flees Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1860, HMS Warrior, the world's first ocean-going iron-hulled and armoured battleship, was launched in Portsmouth. This revolutionary ship represented a significant advancement in naval technology and warfare.
events.name: Launch of HMS Warrior

events.enhanced_description: In early 1861, Benito Juárez successfully captured Mexico City, marking a significant victory in his efforts to restore the republic after the turmoil of the French intervention. This event solidified his leadership and set the stage for his presidency.
events.name: Benito Juárez captures Mexico City

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the first steam-powered carousel was recorded in Bolton, England. This innovation represented a significant advancement in amusement technology, paving the way for future developments in entertainment.

locations.name: Bolton, Greater Manchester, England, United Kingdom

events.name: First steam-powered carousel recorded

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, convicts at Chatham Dockyard in England staged a riot, taking over their prison. This event highlighted the tensions and conditions within the penal system during this period.
events.name: Convicts riot at Chatham Dockyard

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, Texas was officially admitted to the Confederate States of America, aligning itself with the secessionist movement. This admission was a significant event in the context of the American Civil War.
events.name: Texas is admitted to the Confederate States of America

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1861, Abraham Lincoln was sworn in as the 16th president of the United States. His presidency would be defined by the Civil War and the struggle to preserve the Union while addressing the issue of slavery.
events.name: Abraham Lincoln is sworn in as the 16th president of the United States

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1861, the Confederate States of America adopted the "Stars and Bars" as their national flag. This flag became a symbol of the Confederacy during the American Civil War, representing their identity and cause.
events.name: American Civil War: The "Stars and Bars" is adopted as the flag of the Confederate States of America

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, a devastating earthquake struck Mendoza, Argentina, resulting in widespread destruction and loss of life. This natural disaster had significant impacts on the region's development and recovery efforts.

image.caption: Ruins around Plaza Pedro del Castillo in Mendoza after the 1861 earthquake.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Museo del Área Fundacional de Mendoza
image.date_qualification: Dated 1861; depicts the earthquake’s aftermath, not the earthquake in progress.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: An earthquake completely destroys Mendoza, Argentina

events.enhanced_description: The first issue of L'Osservatore Romano, the official newspaper of the Vatican, was published in 1861. This publication has since played a significant role in communicating the Catholic Church's positions and news to the public.
events.name: First issue of L'Osservatore Romano

events.enhanced_description: During the Taiping Rebellion, the Battle of Shanghai occurred in 1861, where French and Imperial Chinese troops successfully defeated Taiping forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict that sought to suppress the Taiping uprising against the Qing Dynasty.
events.name: Battle of Shanghai

events.enhanced_description: The Wallraf-Richartz Museum of art opened in Cologne in 1861, showcasing a vast collection of European art from the Middle Ages to the 19th century. This institution has since become a significant cultural landmark in Germany.
events.name: Opening of Wallraf-Richartz Museum

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the U.S. Army officially abolished flogging as a form of punishment, reflecting changing attitudes towards military discipline and human rights. This reform was part of broader efforts to modernize the military during the Civil War.
events.name: Abolition of flogging in the U.S. Army

events.enhanced_description: HMS Warrior, the world's first ocean-going iron-hulled armored battleship, was completed and commissioned into the British Royal Navy in 1861. This ship represented a significant advancement in naval technology and warfare.

image.caption: HMS Warrior serving as an oil jetty in Pembroke Dock, Wales.
image.credit: Verbcatcher — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed July 1977; this shows the ship in its later oil-jetty role, not its 1861 commissioning.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: HMS Warrior commissioned

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, Western Union completed the first transcontinental telegraph line across the United States, revolutionizing communication by allowing messages to be sent almost instantaneously across vast distances.
events.name: First transcontinental telegraph line completed

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the Spanish, French, and British governments signed a tripartite agreement to intervene in Mexico, primarily to recover unpaid debts. This agreement set the stage for foreign intervention in Mexican affairs during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Tripartite agreement to intervene in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the Missouri secession bill was signed by Governor Jackson, marking a significant step in the state's contentious relationship with the Union during the Civil War. This act reflected the deep divisions within Missouri regarding allegiance.
events.name: Missouri secession bill signed

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, General Winfield Scott, citing failing health, resigned as Commander of the United States Army. His departure marked a significant transition in military leadership during the early stages of the American Civil War.
events.name: General Winfield Scott resigns

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the British Empire established bases in Lagos, Nigeria, as part of their efforts to suppress the slave trade. This move was part of a broader strategy to exert control over trade routes and influence in West Africa.
events.name: British Empire establishes bases in Lagos

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the Perpetual Truce of Peace and Friendship was signed between Bahrain and the United Kingdom, establishing a formal diplomatic relationship. This agreement was significant in the context of British interests in the Persian Gulf region.
events.name: Perpetual Truce of Peace and Friendship signed

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the first industrial meat packing plant was established in Fray Bentos, Uruguay. This development marked a significant advancement in the meat processing industry and contributed to Uruguay's economy and export capabilities.
events.name: First industrial meat packing plant established in Uruguay

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, the Royal Seminary in Stockholm was established as the first public institution of higher education in Sweden that admitted women. This landmark decision marked a significant step towards gender equality in education and opened doors for women's academic pursuits in the country.
events.name: The Royal Seminary becomes the first public institution of higher academic learning open to women in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1861, Thomas Sutton captured the first permanent color photograph using the three-color method proposed by James Clerk Maxwell. This groundbreaking achievement laid the foundation for modern color photography, revolutionizing the way images were captured and perceived.
events.name: The first permanent color photograph is captured by Thomas Sutton using the three-color method proposed by James Clerk Maxwell

events.enhanced_description: Statistically, 1861 is recognized as the year marking the decline of the whale oil industry, which had been a primary source of lighting and lubrication, and the rise of the petroleum oil industry as a more efficient and sustainable alternative. This transition significantly impacted energy consumption and industrial practices.
events.name: End of the whale oil industry and beginning of the petroleum oil industry

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1861, Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia died, and was succeeded by Wilhelm I. This transition marked a significant moment in Prussian and German history, leading towards the eventual unification of Germany.
events.name: Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia dies

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1861, Delaware voted against secession from the Union during the American Civil War. This decision reflected the state's complex position regarding slavery and its ties to the Union.
events.name: Delaware votes not to secede

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1861, Mississippi became the second state to secede from the Union, following South Carolina. This act was part of the broader secession movement that led to the American Civil War.
events.name: Mississippi secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1861, Florida officially seceded from the Union, joining the ranks of Southern states that sought to establish their own government. This decision was influenced by the ongoing tensions surrounding slavery and states' rights.

image.caption: Handwritten copy of Florida’s Ordinance of Secession, passed by the Florida Convention of the People.
image.credit: Florida Convention of the People (1860-1861) — http://dl.wdl.org/3939.png Gallery: http://www.wdl.org/en/item/3939/
image.date_qualification: The document is a copy of the ordinance passed on January 10, 1861; the saved image date gives only the year 1861.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Florida secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1861, Alabama seceded from the Union, becoming one of the first states to join the Confederacy. This decision was driven by the state's commitment to preserving slavery and its agricultural economy.
events.name: Alabama secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1861, Major Robert Anderson sent urgent dispatches to Washington, D.C., regarding the situation at Fort Sumter. His communications highlighted the escalating tensions between the Union and secessionist states.

locations.name: Fort Sumter, South Carolina, United States

events.name: Major Robert Anderson sends dispatches to Washington

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1861, Georgia became the fifth state to secede from the Union, following Mississippi. This decision was part of the broader movement of Southern states seeking independence from federal authority.

image.caption: Georgia’s official ordinance of secession, a document issued by the Georgia Legislature.
image.credit: Georgia Legislature — http://www.libs.uga.edu/hargrett/selections/confed/ord.html
image.date_qualification: The document is dated approximately January 1861 and directly records Georgia’s secession; it is an artifact, not a photograph of the secession proceedings.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Georgia secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1861, Jefferson Davis resigned from the United States Senate, signaling his commitment to the Confederacy. His resignation was a key moment in the political landscape leading up to the Civil War.
events.name: Jefferson Davis resigns from the United States Senate

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1861, Louisiana officially seceded from the Union, joining the Confederacy. This decision was influenced by the state's economic reliance on slavery and cotton production.
events.name: Louisiana secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1861, Kansas was admitted to the Union as the 34th state, following a contentious period known as 'Bleeding Kansas' which revolved around the debate over slavery. This admission as a free state was a significant step in the lead-up to the American Civil War.
events.name: Kansas is admitted as the 34th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1861, Kukis conducted a violent raid in the Chhagalnaiya plains of eastern Bengal, resulting in the murder and kidnapping of hundreds of individuals, particularly targeting women. This event highlighted the ongoing ethnic tensions in the region during this period.
events.name: Kukis raid the Chhagalnaiya plains

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1861, Texas officially seceded from the United States, becoming the seventh state to do so in the lead-up to the American Civil War. This act was driven by a combination of factors, including the desire to maintain slavery and states' rights.
events.name: Texas secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1861, the Provisional Confederate States Congress convened in Montgomery, Alabama, marking a pivotal moment in the formation of the Confederate States of America. This congress was composed of representatives from the first seven states that seceded from the Union.

image.caption: Northwest side of the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Alabama Dept. of Archives and History
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1886, 25 years after the event began on February 4, 1861.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Provisional Confederate States Congress is formed

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1861, the Confederate States of America was officially formed, uniting the first seven states that had seceded from the Union. This formation was a direct response to the perceived threats to slavery and states' rights posed by the federal government.
events.name: Confederate States of America are formed

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1861, Jefferson Davis was elected as the Provisional President of the Confederate States of America during the Weed Convention held in Montgomery, Alabama. His leadership would shape the Confederacy's policies during the American Civil War.
events.name: Jefferson Davis elected Provisional President

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1861, the U.S. House of Representatives unanimously passed a resolution guaranteeing non-interference with slavery in any state. This resolution was an attempt to appease Southern states and prevent further secession.
events.name: U.S. House passes resolution on slavery

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1861, the Siege of Gaeta concluded with the Piedmontese forces capturing the stronghold of King Francis II of the Two Sicilies. This event marked a significant victory for the unification of Italy and led to the exile of Francis II.
figures: King Francis II of the Two Sicilies
events.name: Siege of Gaeta ends

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1861, Jefferson Davis was inaugurated as the provisional president of the Confederate States of America in Montgomery, Alabama. His presidency would be marked by the challenges of leading a nascent nation during the Civil War.
events.name: Jefferson Davis inaugurated as President

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1861, severe storms struck Britain, causing significant damage to the Crystal Palace in London and resulting in the collapse of the steeple of Chichester Cathedral. These events highlighted the vulnerability of even the most iconic structures to natural disasters.

locations.name: Chichester, West Sussex, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Storms damage Crystal Palace and Chichester Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1861, Mariehamn was founded as the capital of the Åland Islands. This establishment marked a significant development in the region's administrative and cultural landscape.

image.caption: Coat of arms of Mariehamn.
image.credit: Hippophaë — Own work
image.date_qualification: Image dated 2007-07-28; the date describes the image, not the founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: insignia

events.name: Mariehamn is founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1861, President-elect Abraham Lincoln arrived secretly in Washington, D.C., following an assassination attempt in Baltimore. His arrival was crucial for ensuring a smooth transition of power amidst rising tensions leading to the Civil War.
events.name: Abraham Lincoln arrives in Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1861, the Battle of Ky Hoa took place, where French and Spanish forces defeated Vietnamese troops. This battle was part of the broader context of colonial expansion in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Battle of Ky Hoa

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1861, Russian troops opened fire on a crowd in Warsaw protesting against Russian rule over Poland, resulting in the deaths of five protesters. This event underscored the tensions between the Polish population and the Russian Empire.
events.name: Russian troops fire upon protesters in Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1861, Colorado was officially organized as a United States territory. This organization was part of the westward expansion and the establishment of governance in newly acquired lands.
events.name: Colorado is organized as a United States territory

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1861, Nevada was organized as a United States territory, paving the way for its eventual statehood. This organization was part of the broader movement of westward expansion in the United States.
events.name: Nevada is organized as a United States territory

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1861, Tsar Alexander II of Russia abolished serfdom in the Russian Empire, a monumental reform that aimed to modernize the country and improve the conditions of the peasantry. This reform was a significant step towards social and economic change in Russia.
events.name: Emancipation reform of 1861

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1861, Abraham Lincoln was sworn in as the 16th president of the United States. His presidency would soon be defined by the challenges of the Civil War and the struggle for national unity.
events.name: Abraham Lincoln is sworn in as president

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1861, El Hadj Umar Tall captured the city of Ségou, effectively destroying the Bamana Empire of Mali. This conquest marked a significant expansion of his influence in West Africa.
events.name: El Hadj Umar Tall seizes Ségou

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1861, the Constitution of the Confederate States of America was adopted in Montgomery, Alabama. This document established the legal framework for the Confederate government and enshrined the institution of slavery as a fundamental principle of the Confederacy.
events.name: American Civil War: The Constitution of the Confederate States of America is adopted

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1861, the Russian corvette Posadnik arrived at Tsushima Island, provoking a significant reaction from the Japanese Shogunate. This incident highlighted the growing tensions between foreign powers and Japan during a period of isolation.
events.name: Tsushima incident: The Russian corvette Posadnik arrives at Tsushima Island

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1861, the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed by the new Parliament, with Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia becoming its first king. This marked a significant milestone in the unification of Italy, bringing together various states and territories under a single monarchy.
events.name: Unification of Italy: The Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed

events.enhanced_description: The First Taranaki War, a conflict between Māori and British settlers, concluded on March 19, 1861. The war was marked by disputes over land ownership and sovereignty, leading to significant tensions in New Zealand's colonial history.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the Battle of Waireka, by A.H. Messenger.
image.credit: A.H. Messenger — New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, originally reproduced in "The New Zealand Wars' by James Cowan (published 1922)
image.date_qualification: The depicted battle is dated 28 March 1860; the supplied image_date, 28 March, 2008, is a file/date metadata entry and is not the depicted event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The First Taranaki War ends in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1861, the surrender of Civitella del Tronto marked the end of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. This event was a crucial step in the unification of Italy, as it eliminated one of the last major strongholds opposing the new kingdom.
figures: King Francis II of the Two Sicilies
events.name: Unification of Italy: The surrender of Civitella del Tronto ends the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1861, Alexander H. Stephens, the Vice President of the Confederacy, delivered his infamous Cornerstone Speech in Savannah, Georgia. In this speech, he articulated the Confederacy's justification for slavery, declaring it the foundation of their new government.
events.name: Alexander Stephens gives the Cornerstone Speech

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1861, a convention in Tucson, Arizona, ratified the ordinance of secession from the Union, forming Confederate Arizona. This marked a significant moment in the expansion of the Confederacy into the southwestern territories.
events.name: Confederate Arizona: A convention in Tucson ratifies secession

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1861, British chemist William Crookes announced his discovery of thallium, a chemical element that would later play significant roles in various scientific fields. This discovery contributed to the understanding of elements and their properties.
events.name: Discovery of thallium by William Crookes

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1861, a population census was conducted in the United Kingdom, revealing significant demographic changes since the previous census in 1851. The results indicated a dramatic increase in urban populations, reflecting the ongoing industrialization of the country.
events.name: A population census is taken in the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: The American Civil War officially began on April 12, 1861, with the bombardment of Fort Sumter in Charleston, South Carolina. This conflict marked a turning point in American history, leading to a four-year struggle over issues including states' rights and slavery.
events.name: The American Civil War begins with the bombardment of Fort Sumter

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1861, Fort Sumter surrendered to Southern forces after a 34-hour bombardment. This event solidified the start of the American Civil War and marked a significant victory for the Confederacy.
events.name: American Civil War: Fort Sumter surrenders to Southern forces

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1861, President Abraham Lincoln issued a Proclamation calling for 75,000 volunteers to serve in the military to suppress the rebellion in the South. This marked a significant escalation in the conflict and mobilized the Union's military response.
events.name: American Civil War: President Abraham Lincoln issues a Proclamation

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1861, Virginia officially seceded from the Union, joining the Confederate States of America. This decision was pivotal, as Virginia would become a central battleground in the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: The state of Virginia secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1861, Robert E. Lee resigned his commission in the United States Army to command the forces of Virginia. His decision to join the Confederacy would have lasting implications for the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: Robert E. Lee resigns his commission

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1861, a peasant uprising occurred in Bezdna, Russia, leading to military intervention and the deaths of approximately 90 individuals. This unrest was part of a broader pattern of social discontent in Russia during this period.
events.name: Bezdna unrest: Peasant uprising in Russia

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1861, the Union Army arrived in Washington, D.C., to bolster defenses in response to the secession of Southern states. This military presence was crucial in maintaining control of the capital during the early stages of the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: The Union Army arrives in Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1861, Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli discovered the asteroid 69 Hesperia. This discovery contributed to the growing field of astronomy and the study of celestial bodies.
events.name: Giovanni Schiaparelli discovers the asteroid 69 Hesperia

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1861, President Abraham Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus in the United States, allowing for the arrest of individuals without trial. This controversial decision was aimed at maintaining order during the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: President Abraham Lincoln suspends the writ of habeas corpus

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1861, Arkansas officially seceded from the Union, joining the Confederate States of America. This decision further solidified the divide between North and South during the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: Arkansas secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1861, Tennessee seceded from the Union, becoming the last state to join the Confederacy. This decision had significant implications for the Civil War, as Tennessee was a key battleground state.
events.name: American Civil War: Tennessee secedes from the Union

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1861, Richmond, Virginia, was designated as the capital of the Confederate States of America. This decision underscored the city's strategic importance and became a focal point for the Confederacy during the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: Richmond, Virginia, is named the capital of the Confederate States of America

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1861, a devastating fire swept through Glarus, Switzerland, destroying a significant portion of the town. This conflagration had lasting impacts on the community and led to discussions about urban planning and fire safety.
events.name: Conflagration in Glarus

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1861, the British merchant ship North Star departed from Hong Kong bound for Nagasaki, Japan. During its journey, the vessel was attacked by Chinese pirates who killed an officer and made off with a significant amount of gold.

locations.name: Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China

events.name: North Star affair: The British merchant ship North Star leaves Hong Kong for Nagasaki, Japan

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1861, the Canellas meteorite, weighing 859 grams and classified as a chondrite type, struck Earth near Barcelona, Spain. This event contributed to the study of meteorites and their origins.
events.name: The Canellas meteorite strikes Earth

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1861, Thomas Cook organized the first-ever package holiday, taking travelers from London to Paris. This innovative approach to travel laid the groundwork for modern tourism.
events.name: Thomas Cook runs the first package holiday

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1861, the American Civil War continued to escalate as various states took sides in the conflict. This war would become one of the most significant events in American history, shaping the nation's future.
events.name: American Civil War

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1861, Russian sailors clashed with Japanese samurai and farmers on Tsushima Island. This confrontation highlighted the tensions between foreign powers and Japan during a period of isolation.
events.name: Clash at Tsushima Island

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1861, Virginia ratified its ordinance of secession from the United States in a referendum. This decision was pivotal in the American Civil War, as Virginia became a key Confederate state.
events.name: Virginia's ordinance of secession

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1861, the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce was established to promote trade and commerce in the region. This organization played a crucial role in the economic development of Hong Kong.

locations.name: Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China

events.name: Establishment of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1861, the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate was established as a semi-autonomous region under the Ottoman Empire, separate from the Sidon Eyalet. Davud Pasha was appointed as its first Mutasarrıf, marking a significant administrative change.
events.name: Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate established

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1861, Benito Juárez was formally elected President of Mexico. His administration was marked by significant reforms and the temporary suspension of foreign debt payments.
events.name: Benito Juárez elected President of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1861, a devastating fire broke out on Tooley Street in London, resulting in the death of James Braidwood, the first superintendent of the London Fire Brigade. This incident highlighted the dangers of urban fires and the need for improved fire safety measures.
events.name: Tooley Street fire

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1861, Abdülmecid I, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, died and was succeeded by Abdülaziz. His reign was marked by significant reforms and modernization efforts within the empire.
events.name: Death of Abdülmecid I

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1861, the Lambing Flat riots occurred when white miners attacked Chinese miners in the Australian goldfields. This event reflected the racial tensions and conflicts over resources during the gold rush.

locations.name: Lambing Flat, New South Wales, Australia

events.name: Lambing Flat riots

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1861, the first issue of L'Osservatore Romano, the official newspaper of the Vatican, was published. This publication aimed to communicate the Vatican's views and news to the public.
events.name: First issue of L'Osservatore Romano published

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1861, Ivan Kasatkin landed in Hakodate, Japan, where he introduced the Eastern Orthodox Church. This marked a significant moment in the spread of Christianity in Japan.
events.name: Ivan Kasatkin introduces Eastern Orthodox Church into Japan

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1861, the Confederate States signed a treaty with the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations in Indian Territory. This agreement aimed to secure alliances and support for the Confederacy during the Civil War.
events.name: Confederate States sign treaty with Choctaws and Chickasaws

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1861, the Battle of Corrick's Ford took place in western Virginia during the American Civil War. This battle was part of the early military engagements that shaped the conflict.

locations.name: Corrick's Ford, West Virginia, United States

events.name: Battle of Corrick's Ford

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1861, the First Battle of Bull Run, also known as the First Battle of Manassas, marked the first major battle of the American Civil War, ending in a Confederate victory. This battle demonstrated the war's potential for brutality and the need for better preparation.
events.name: First Battle of Bull Run

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1861, the U.S. Congress passed the Crittenden–Johnson Resolution, which stated that the war was being fought to preserve the Union and not to end slavery. This resolution reflected the political complexities of the Civil War.
events.name: Crittenden–Johnson Resolution passed

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1861, George B. McClellan assumed command of the Army of the Potomac following the Union's defeat at the First Battle of Bull Run. His leadership would significantly influence the course of the Civil War.
events.name: George B. McClellan assumes command

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1861, Admiral Robert FitzRoy successfully issued the first public weather forecast in Britain. This pioneering effort laid the foundation for modern meteorology and weather prediction.
events.name: First public weather forecast

events.enhanced_description: In response to the financial demands of the American Civil War, the United States government enacted the Revenue Act of 1861, which introduced the first federal income tax. This tax imposed a 3% levy on incomes exceeding $800, marking a significant shift in federal revenue generation.
events.name: Revenue Act of 1861

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Wilson's Creek, fought on August 10, 1861, was the first significant battle in the Western Theater of the American Civil War. The Confederate forces, led by General Sterling Price, achieved a decisive victory against Union troops commanded by General Nathaniel Lyon.
events.name: Battle of Wilson's Creek

events.enhanced_description: In August 1861, the first description of Archaeopteryx was published, based on a feather discovered in Bavaria. This pivotal moment in paleontology was followed by the discovery of a complete skeleton near Langenaltheim, providing crucial evidence of the evolutionary link between birds and reptiles.
events.name: Discovery of Archaeopteryx

events.enhanced_description: The Weisshorn, the fifth highest peak in the Alps, was first ascended on August 19, 1861. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the history of mountaineering, showcasing the growing interest in alpine exploration during the 19th century.
events.name: First ascent of Weisshorn

events.enhanced_description: The first modern Welsh National Eisteddfod took place in Aberdare on August 22, 1861, celebrating Welsh culture, literature, and music. This event marked a revival of the Eisteddfod tradition, which has since become a cornerstone of Welsh cultural identity.
events.name: First modern Welsh National Eisteddfod

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1861, Martin Doyle was executed, marking the last instance of capital punishment for attempted murder in Britain. This event highlighted the evolving attitudes towards capital punishment and criminal justice in Victorian England.
events.name: Last execution for attempted murder in Britain

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1861, Confederate General Leonidas Polk invaded neutral Kentucky, prompting the state legislature to request assistance from the Union. This incursion marked a significant escalation in the American Civil War, as Kentucky's strategic position became a focal point for both sides.
events.name: Confederate invasion of Kentucky

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1861, Union forces under General Ulysses S. Grant captured Paducah, Kentucky, without resistance. This strategic victory allowed the Union to control the mouth of the Tennessee River, enhancing their logistical capabilities in the Western Theater of the Civil War.
events.name: Capture of Paducah

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Pavón, fought on September 17, 1861, was a decisive conflict during the Argentine Civil War, resulting in a victory for Buenos Aires over the Argentine Confederation. This battle played a crucial role in the re-unification of Argentina under a central government.
events.name: Battle of Pavón

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Santa Rosa Island, fought on October 9, 1861, saw Confederate forces attempt to capture the island but ultimately face defeat. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the American Civil War, emphasizing the strategic importance of coastal defenses.

locations.name: Santa Rosa Island, Florida, United States

events.name: Battle of Santa Rosa Island

events.enhanced_description: The Cullin-la-ringo massacre occurred on October 17, 1861, when 19 white settlers were killed by indigenous Australians, leading to a brutal retaliation that resulted in the deaths of over 300 indigenous people. This tragic event exemplified the violent conflicts during the Australian frontier wars.
events.name: Cullin-la-ringo massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ball's Bluff, fought on October 21, 1861, was a significant early engagement in the American Civil War, resulting in a Union defeat under Colonel Edward Baker, who was killed in action. This battle underscored the challenges faced by Union forces in the conflict.

image.caption: Currier and Ives illustration depicting the death of Colonel Edward D. Baker at Ball’s Bluff.
image.credit: Currier and Ives — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID cph.3b50103 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: The image metadata dates the illustration circa 1861; it is not established as a photograph made during the battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Ball's Bluff

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1861, HMS Warrior was completed and commissioned into the British Royal Navy as the world's first ocean-going iron-hulled armored battleship. This revolutionary design marked a significant advancement in naval warfare technology.
events.name: Completion of HMS Warrior

events.enhanced_description: The Toronto Stock Exchange was established on October 25, 1861, providing a formal marketplace for trading securities in Canada. This development was pivotal in the growth of Canada's financial markets and economy.

image.caption: Exterior view of the Toronto Stock Exchange on Bay Street.
image.credit: nodomain.cc — Flickr
image.date_qualification: Site photograph from 2006, not a depiction of the exchange’s establishment in 1861. The original image date is not supplied; 2006 is the metadata timestamp, not a supported depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of the Toronto Stock Exchange

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1861, the Pony Express, the famous American transcontinental mail service, announced its closure due to financial difficulties and the advent of the telegraph. This marked the end of an iconic chapter in American communication history.
events.name: Closure of the Pony Express

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1861, the Missouri legislature took up a bill proposing the state's secession from the Union. This legislative action reflected the deepening divisions within the state during the American Civil War.
events.name: Missouri's secession bill

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1861, the Missouri legislature passed a bill for the state's secession from the Union, further entrenching the conflict between Union and Confederate sympathizers within the state during the Civil War.
events.name: Passage of Missouri's secession bill

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1861, the governments of Spain, France, and Britain signed a tripartite agreement to intervene in Mexico, aiming to recover unpaid debts. This agreement set the stage for foreign intervention in Mexican affairs during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Tripartite agreement for intervention in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1861, President Abraham Lincoln appointed George B. McClellan as the commander of the Union Army, replacing Winfield Scott. This decision was pivotal as McClellan would lead the Union forces through several critical battles in the Civil War.
events.name: Appointment of George B. McClellan

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1861, Union General John C. Frémont was relieved of command in the Western Department and replaced by David Hunter. This change was part of the ongoing adjustments in military leadership during the early stages of the American Civil War.

image.caption: Portrait of John C. Frémont by Mathew Brady.
image.credit: Mathew Brady — https://www.loc.gov/item/2017896011/
image.date_qualification: Portrait dating to between 1855 and 1865; it is contextual to Frémont’s relief from command in 1861, not a depiction of that event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Relief of John C. Frémont

events.enhanced_description: The University of Washington, established in 1861, is one of the oldest universities on the West Coast of the United States. It has grown to become a leading public research university, known for its diverse academic programs and significant contributions to research and innovation.
events.name: The University of Washington is founded in Seattle

events.enhanced_description: The inaugural Melbourne Cup took place on November 5, 1861, marking the beginning of Australia's most prestigious horse racing event. Known as 'the race that stops a nation,' the Melbourne Cup has become a significant cultural event in Australia, celebrated annually.
events.name: The first Melbourne Cup horse race is held in Melbourne, Australia

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1861, Jefferson Davis was elected as the first and only president of the Confederate States of America. His leadership during the American Civil War was marked by significant challenges, including military defeats and economic hardships faced by the Confederacy.
events.name: Jefferson Davis is elected president of the Confederate States of America

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Belmont, fought on November 7, 1861, was one of the early engagements of the American Civil War, where Union forces under General Ulysses S. Grant attacked a Confederate camp. Although they initially succeeded, they were ultimately forced to retreat due to Confederate reinforcements.
events.name: Battle of Belmont

events.enhanced_description: The Trent Affair occurred on November 8, 1861, when the USS San Jacinto intercepted the British mail ship Trent and captured two Confederate envoys, James Mason and John Slidell. This incident escalated tensions between the United States and the United Kingdom, threatening diplomatic relations.

locations.name: Off the coast of Cuba, Caribbean Sea

events.name: Trent Affair

events.enhanced_description: French explorer Henri Mouhot died on November 10, 1861, after which his servant began sending his diaries and specimens back to Europe. Mouhot is best known for his exploration of Southeast Asia and for bringing international attention to the ruins of Angkor Wat.
events.name: Death of Henri Mouhot

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Round Mountain occurred on November 19, 1861, in Indian Territory (modern-day Oklahoma). This engagement was part of the American Civil War, where Confederate forces attempted to assert control over the region.
events.name: Battle of Round Mountain

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1861, Confederate President Jefferson Davis appointed Judah P. Benjamin as Secretary of War. Benjamin played a crucial role in the Confederate government, overseeing military operations during a critical period of the American Civil War.
events.name: Judah P. Benjamin appointed Secretary of War

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1861, a battle in the Sundarbans of Bengal resulted in the attack on the house of Rahimullah of Baraikhali, leading to his death along with 33 others. This event highlights the ongoing conflicts in the region during this period.
events.name: Battle in the Sundarbans of Bengal

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1861, Missouri was officially admitted as the 12th state of the Confederate States of America. This decision was part of the broader conflict of the American Civil War, as states grappled with issues of secession and allegiance.
events.name: Missouri admitted as the 12th Confederate state

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1861, the British government dispatched its response to the Trent Affair, partly drafted by Albert, Prince Consort, just weeks before his death. This diplomatic incident highlighted the fragile relations between the United States and Britain during the Civil War.
events.name: Trent Affair response from British government

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1861, Kentucky was accepted into the Confederate States of America. This admission was significant as Kentucky was a border state with divided loyalties during the American Civil War.
events.name: Kentucky accepted into the Confederate States of America

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1861, U.S. President Abraham Lincoln signed Public Resolution 82 into law, which included a provision for a Navy Medal of Valor. This legislation was part of Lincoln's efforts to recognize and honor military service during the Civil War.
events.name: Public Resolution 82 signed into law

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, the United Kingdom formally annexed Lagos Island, establishing it as a colony. This annexation was part of Britain's broader imperial ambitions in West Africa and marked the beginning of significant British influence in the region.
events.name: The United Kingdom annexes Lagos Island, in modern-day Nigeria

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, Princess Alice, the second daughter of Queen Victoria, married Prince Ludwig of Hesse and by Rhine, strengthening ties between the British royal family and German nobility.
events.name: Marriage of Princess Alice

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1862, U.S. President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railroad Acts into law, which authorized the construction of the First Transcontinental Railroad. This monumental project aimed to connect the eastern U.S. with the Pacific Coast, facilitating westward expansion and commerce.
events.name: Pacific Railroad Acts signed into law

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, the Russian State Library was founded as The Library of the Moscow Public Museum, marking a significant development in the cultural landscape of Russia. It has since grown to become one of the largest libraries in the world, housing millions of items.
events.name: Foundation of the Russian State Library

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, during the American Indian Wars, more than 300 Santee Sioux were found guilty of crimes against white settlers in Minnesota, resulting in sentences of death by hanging. This event highlighted the intense conflict and tragic consequences of the war between Native Americans and settlers.
events.name: Santee Sioux trials

events.enhanced_description: Notts County F.C. was founded in 1862 in Nottingham, England, and is recognized as the world's oldest professional football club. The establishment of the club marked a significant moment in the history of association football.
events.name: Notts County F.C. founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed an act admitting West Virginia into the Union, effectively splitting Virginia during the Civil War. This act was significant as it represented a shift in the political landscape and the ongoing struggle over slavery and statehood.
events.name: West Virginia Admitted to the Union

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Stones River commenced on January 1, 1862, near Murfreesboro, Tennessee. It was marked by fierce fighting and significant casualties, ultimately leading to a Union victory that helped to secure the region.
events.name: Battle of Stones River Opens

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, Anglo-Indian teacher Anna Leonowens accepted an offer from the Siamese consul in Singapore to teach the wives and children of King Mongkut of Siam. This position would later inspire her memoirs and the musical 'The King and I'.
events.name: Anna Leonowens Accepts Teaching Position

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, Donald McIntyre established a settlement in northwest Queensland that would later become known as Julia Creek, named after his niece. This settlement played a role in the development of the region.
events.name: Settlement of Julia Creek

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, Iwai Fumisuke Shoten was founded in Osaka, marking the beginnings of what would later become the Japanese conglomerate Sojitz. This establishment played a significant role in Japan's economic development.
events.name: Iwai Fumisuke Shoten Founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1862, the Japanese construction company Satō Kōgyō was founded in Toyama as Satō-gumi. This company would grow to become a significant player in Japan's construction industry.
events.name: Satō Kōgyō Founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1862, French, Spanish, and British forces landed in Veracruz, Mexico, as part of the foreign intervention aimed at establishing a monarchy under Emperor Maximilian I. This intervention was a significant conflict during the Second French Intervention in Mexico.
events.name: French intervention in Mexico: French, Spanish and British forces arrive in Veracruz, Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1862, the Hartley Colliery disaster occurred in Northumberland, England, resulting in the tragic deaths of 204 miners when the only shaft became blocked. This disaster highlighted the dangerous conditions of coal mining during the Industrial Revolution.
events.name: Hartley Colliery disaster in north-east England

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1862, the USS Monitor was launched at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, becoming the first ironclad warship commissioned by the United States Navy. This innovative vessel played a crucial role in naval warfare during the American Civil War, particularly in the Battle of Hampton Roads.

image.caption: USS Monitor viewed from the deck on the James River, with dents in its turret armor.

events.name: American Civil War: The first U.S. ironclad warship, USS Monitor, is launched in Brooklyn

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1862, astronomer Alvan Graham Clark made the first observation of Sirius B, a white dwarf star, using an eighteen-inch telescope at Northwestern University in Illinois. This discovery was significant in the study of stellar evolution and the nature of binary star systems.
events.name: Alvan Graham Clark makes the first observation of Sirius B

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1862, Julia Ward Howe's iconic song "Battle Hymn of the Republic" was published for the first time in the Atlantic Monthly. This song became an anthem for the Union during the American Civil War and remains a significant piece of American music history.
events.name: American Civil War: Julia Ward Howe's "Battle Hymn of the Republic" is published

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1862, the Dun Mountain Railway, the first railway in New Zealand, was officially opened by the Dun Mountain Copper Mining Company. This railway played a crucial role in the transportation of goods and resources, marking a significant development in New Zealand's infrastructure.
events.name: The first railway is opened in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1862, General Ulysses S. Grant led Union forces to capture Fort Henry in Tennessee, marking the first significant victory for the Union Army in the American Civil War. This victory opened the Tennessee River to Union forces and set the stage for further advances into the South.

image.caption: Currier and Ives lithograph depicting the Battle of Fort Henry.
image.credit: Currier and Ives — http://hdl.loc.gov/loc.pnp/cph.3b49868
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration of the battle; the saved image date is 2007-11-25, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: American Civil War: General Ulysses S. Grant captures Fort Henry

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1862, General Ulysses S. Grant attacked and captured Fort Donelson in Tennessee, securing a crucial victory for the Union Army during the American Civil War. This battle was pivotal in gaining control of the Cumberland River and furthering the Union's strategic objectives.

image.caption: Alonzo Chappel’s printed battle scene, “Capture of Fort Donelson.”
image.credit: Alonzo Chappel — Missouri History Museum URL: http://images.mohistory.org/image/A68FA693-4530-9DF4-04F9-397D2EF58DA8//original.jpg Gallery: http://collections.mohistory.org/resource/157519
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration based on an original painting; the saved image date is 1861–1865 and does not establish when the print was made.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Fort Donelson

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1862, the Battle of Valverde took place near Fort Craig in New Mexico Territory, where Confederate forces defeated Union troops. This battle was part of the larger conflict for control of the Southwest during the American Civil War.

image.caption: A brass field gun from the Val Verde Battery, brought to Freestone County after the Battle of Valverde.
image.credit: Jim Evans — Own work
image.date_qualification: The depicted cannon is a later artifact, not a photograph of the 1862 battle. The image_date is 7/4/2015.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Valverde

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1862, Jefferson Davis was officially inaugurated in Richmond, Virginia, as the president of the Confederate States for a six-year term. His leadership would shape the Confederacy's strategies and policies during the American Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: Jefferson Davis inaugurated as president of the Confederate States

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1862, an explosion at an ammunition warehouse in San Andres Chalchicomula, Mexico, resulted in the deaths of between 1,400 and 2,280 people during the Second French Intervention in Mexico. This tragic event underscored the chaos and violence of the conflict.
events.name: Ammunition warehouse explosion in San Andres Chalchicomula, Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1862, the Battle of Pea Ridge occurred in Arkansas, where Union forces successfully repelled Confederate troops, effectively shutting them out of Missouri. This battle was significant in maintaining Union control over the region.
events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Pea Ridge

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1862, the ironclad CSS Virginia, formerly known as the USS Merrimack, was launched at Hampton Roads, Virginia. This event marked the beginning of the Battle of Hampton Roads, which was notable for the clash of ironclad warships.
events.name: American Civil War: CSS Virginia launched at Hampton Roads

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1862, the U.S. federal government enacted a policy forbidding Union army officers from returning fugitive slaves, effectively nullifying the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850. This decision was a pivotal moment leading towards the Emancipation Proclamation.
events.name: American Civil War: U.S. federal government forbids returning fugitive slaves

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1862, the first railway line in Finland, connecting Helsinki and Hämeenlinna, was officially opened. This development marked a significant advancement in transportation and communication within the country.
events.name: The first railway line in Finland is officially opened

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1862, the Battle of Glorieta Pass took place in New Mexico, where Union forces successfully halted the Confederate invasion of New Mexico Territory. This battle was crucial in maintaining Union control over the Southwest.
events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Glorieta Pass

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1862, Victor Hugo's epic novel Les Misérables began its publication in Brussels. This literary masterpiece has since become a cornerstone of French literature and has been adapted into numerous films, musicals, and other artistic expressions.
events.name: Victor Hugo's Les Misérables begins publication

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Shiloh, fought on April 6-7, 1862, was a significant early battle in the American Civil War where Union forces under General Ulysses S. Grant faced off against Confederate troops led by General Albert Sidney Johnston. The battle resulted in a Union victory, marking a turning point in the Western Theater of the war.
events.name: Battle of Shiloh

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1862, Union volunteers led by James J. Andrews undertook the Great Locomotive Chase, stealing a Confederate locomotive named The General in an attempt to disrupt the Southern rail network. The raid ultimately failed, but it became a symbol of Union ingenuity and bravery.
events.name: Great Locomotive Chase (Andrews' Raid)

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1862, during the French colonial expansion in Vietnam, the government of Emperor Tu Duc was forced to cede the territories of Bien Hoa, Gia Dinh, and Dinh Tuong to France. This marked a significant step in the establishment of French colonial rule in southern Vietnam.
events.name: Cession of territories to France

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1862, the financial institution that would become UBS was founded in Winterthur, Switzerland, originally as the Bank in Winterthur. Over the years, it evolved into one of the world's largest and most influential financial services companies.
events.name: Foundation of UBS

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1862, Union Admiral David Farragut led a naval force to capture New Orleans, a critical Confederate port city. This victory allowed the Union to gain control of the Mississippi River, significantly impacting the war's dynamics.
events.name: Capture of New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Fort Macon culminated on April 26, 1862, when Confederate forces surrendered to Union troops after a prolonged siege. This victory allowed Union forces to gain control of the North Carolina coast.
events.name: Siege of Fort Macon

events.enhanced_description: The 1862 International Exhibition, held on May 1, 1862, in South Kensington, London, showcased innovations and cultural artifacts from around the world, including a notable exhibit from Japan that influenced Anglo-Japanese artistic styles.
events.name: 1862 International Exhibition

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1862, the California State Normal School was established by an act of the California legislature, laying the foundation for what would later become San Jose State University, one of the oldest institutions of higher education in California.
events.name: Creation of California State Normal School

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1862, during the Second French intervention in Mexico, Mexican General Ignacio Zaragoza led his troops to a significant victory against the French Army at the Battle of Puebla. This battle is commemorated annually as Cinco de Mayo, symbolizing Mexican resistance.
events.name: Battle of Puebla

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1862, the Confederate ironclad CSS Virginia was scuttled in the James River northwest of Norfolk, Virginia, to prevent its capture by Union forces. This marked the end of the ship's brief but impactful service in naval warfare.

image.caption: Hand-colored Currier & Ives lithograph depicting the destruction of the CSS Virginia, called “Merrimac” in the image title.
image.credit: Currier and Ives — Imported on en.wiki by en:User:Brian0918 . Originally from Library of Congress . Originally from Currier & Ives : a catalogue raisonné / compiled by Gale Research.
