image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Christian IX of Denmark Succeeds Frederick VII

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1863, during the American Civil War, Confederate troops led by General James Longstreet launched an unsuccessful attack against Union forces under General Ambrose Burnside at Campbell's Station, near Knoxville, Tennessee.
events.name: Battle of Campbell's Station

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1863, Confederate forces led by General James Longstreet laid siege to Knoxville, Tennessee. The siege lasted two weeks but ultimately failed to capture the city, marking a significant Union victory.
events.name: Siege of Knoxville

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1863, King Christian IX of Denmark signed the November Constitution, declaring Schleswig to be part of Denmark. This act was seen as a violation of the London Protocol of 1852 and contributed to the tensions leading to the German-Danish War of 1864.
events.name: Signing of the November Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. This brief but powerful speech emphasized the principles of human equality and the importance of preserving the Union.

image.caption: A view of the Gettysburg National Cemetery grounds, photographed by Alexander Gardner.
image.credit: Alexander Gardner — Library of Congress
image.date_qualification: The filename identifies a view looking northeast in connection with the Gettysburg Address; it is a site photograph, not a photograph of Lincoln delivering the speech. No image date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Gettysburg Address

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1863, during the American Civil War, Union forces led by General Ulysses S. Grant reinforced troops at Chattanooga, Tennessee, and launched a counter-attack against Confederate forces. This battle was pivotal in securing Union control of the region.
events.name: Battle of Chattanooga III

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1863, Union forces under General Ulysses S. Grant captured Lookout Mountain near Chattanooga, Tennessee. This victory was a critical step in breaking the Confederate siege of the city and securing Union dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Lookout Mountain

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1863, during the American Civil War, Union forces led by General Ulysses S. Grant achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Missionary Ridge, breaking the Confederate siege of Chattanooga and routing General Braxton Bragg's troops.
events.name: Battle of Missionary Ridge

events.enhanced_description: From November 26 to December 2, 1863, during the Mine Run Campaign, Union forces under General George Meade positioned themselves against Confederate troops led by General Robert E. Lee. After five days of failed attempts to find weaknesses in the Confederate lines, Meade's forces withdrew.
events.name: Mine Run Campaign

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1863, Confederate cavalry leader John Hunt Morgan and several of his men escaped from an Ohio state prison and successfully returned to the South. This daring escape became legendary among Confederate supporters.
events.name: John Hunt Morgan's Escape

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1863, New Zealand opened its first steam-operated passenger railway in Christchurch, marking a significant advancement in transportation for the region. This development played a crucial role in the expansion of rail networks across the country.

image.caption: Map of New Zealand’s railway network from 1863 to 2019.
image.credit: Luke.xensen — Own work
image.date_qualification: The map covers 1863–2019 and was created on 2019-08-12; it is contextual, not an event-dated image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: First Steam-Operated Passenger Railway in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1863, the First Reformed student society, C.S.A.C. Fides Quadrat Intellectum, was founded at Theologische Universiteit Kampen in the Netherlands. This society played a significant role in the academic and cultural life of the university.
events.name: Foundation of C.S.A.C. Fides Quadrat Intellectum

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1863, a devastating fire at the Church of the Company in Santiago, Chile, resulted in the deaths of between 2,000 and 3,000 people. This tragedy highlighted the need for improved fire safety regulations in urban areas.
events.name: Church of the Company Fire

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1863, Romania opened its first mountain railway, connecting Anina to Oravița. This railway was a significant engineering achievement and facilitated transportation in the mountainous regions of the country.
events.name: Romania's First Mountain Railway

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1863, linoleum was patented in the United Kingdom. This innovative flooring material became popular for its durability and ease of maintenance, revolutionizing interior design and construction.
events.name: Linoleum Patented

events.enhanced_description: In January 1864, notorious Australian bushranger Ben Hall and his gang engaged in a shootout with police after attempting to rob the Bang Bang Hotel in Koorawatha, New South Wales. The gang's daring escape highlighted the ongoing conflict between law enforcement and bushrangers during this tumultuous period in Australian history.
events.name: Ben Hall's Gang Shootout

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Noonday Creek, fought in early 1864 near Kennesaw, Georgia, saw Confederate troops defeat Union forces. This engagement was part of the broader Atlanta Campaign and illustrated the ongoing struggles in the region during the Civil War.
events.name: Battle of Noonday Creek

events.enhanced_description: In 1864, the Battle of Brice's Crossroads saw Confederate troops under Nathan Bedford Forrest achieve a surprising victory over a much larger Union force led by General Samuel D. Sturgis. This battle demonstrated Forrest's tactical prowess and had significant implications for the war in Mississippi.
events.name: Battle of Brice's Crossroads

events.enhanced_description: The January Uprising, which began in January 1863, culminated in 1864 with the defeat of Polish forces against the Russian Empire. This uprising was a significant national movement aimed at regaining independence and highlighted the struggles of Poland during this period.
events.name: The January Uprising

events.enhanced_description: The St-Hilaire train disaster occurred in 1864 when a passenger train operated by the Grand Trunk Railway derailed on a swung-open bridge while traveling from Quebec City to Montreal. This tragic accident resulted in 99 fatalities and over 100 injuries, marking it as the deadliest train accident in Canadian history.
events.name: St-Hilaire train disaster

events.enhanced_description: Confederate General John Bell Hood evacuated Atlanta on January 1, 1864, after a prolonged siege by Union General William Tecumseh Sherman. This strategic withdrawal marked a significant moment in the Civil War, as it allowed Union forces to gain control of a key Southern city.
events.name: American Civil War: Evacuation of Atlanta

events.enhanced_description: The Charlottetown Conference took place in 1864, where delegates from the Canadian colonies convened to discuss the possibility of Canadian Confederation. This meeting was a pivotal step towards the unification of Canada as a nation.
events.name: Charlottetown Conference

events.enhanced_description: In 1864, the Dutch colonial forces successfully conquered southern Sumatra, solidifying their control over the region. This conquest was part of a broader strategy to expand Dutch influence in the Indonesian archipelago.
events.name: The Dutch conquer southern Sumatra

events.enhanced_description: In 1864, Asa Mercer embarked on a journey from Seattle to the East Coast to recruit women, known as the Mercer Girls, to help balance the gender ratio in the rapidly growing Western territories. This initiative was significant in shaping the social landscape of the Pacific Northwest.
events.name: Asa Mercer travels from Seattle to the U.S. East Coast

events.enhanced_description: In 1864, the first Quanjude restaurant opened on Qianmen Street in Beijing, specializing in Peking Roast Duck. This establishment became renowned for its unique cooking method and has since become a symbol of Chinese culinary tradition.
events.name: The first Quanjude Peking Roast Duck restaurant opens

events.enhanced_description: In 1864, the Yasudaya Currency Exchange Bank was established in Edo, which later evolved into the Mizuho Financial Group. This institution played a crucial role in the development of Japan's modern banking system.
events.name: Yasudaya Currency Exchange Bank founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1864, the Merchants Bank of Halifax was founded, which later became a predecessor to the Royal Bank of Canada. This establishment marked a significant development in the banking sector in Canada.
events.name: Merchants Bank of Halifax founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1864, American songwriter Stephen Foster, known for classics like 'Oh! Susanna' and 'Old Folks at Home', died at the age of 37 in New York City. His music left a lasting legacy in American culture, with many of his songs still performed today.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Stephen Foster dies

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1864, Denmark rejected an ultimatum from Austria and Prussia to repeal its constitution, which included provisions asserting that Schleswig-Holstein was part of Denmark. This refusal escalated tensions leading to the Second Schleswig War.
events.name: Denmark rejects ultimatum from Austria and Prussia

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1864, the Tauranga campaign commenced as part of the New Zealand Wars, a series of conflicts between the British colonial forces and Māori tribes. This campaign was marked by significant military engagements and territorial disputes.

locations.name: Tauranga, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand

events.name: The Tauranga campaign begins

events.enhanced_description: In February 1864, John Wisden published The Cricketer's Almanack, which would become the premier annual reference for cricket in England. This publication has continued to be a vital resource for cricket statistics and history.
events.name: John Wisden publishes The Cricketer's Almanack

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1864, the Danish-Prussian War, also known as the Second Schleswig War, began when 57,000 Austrian and Prussian troops crossed the Eider River into Denmark. This conflict was pivotal in the struggle over the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein.
events.name: Danish-Prussian War begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1864, Gerard Adriaan Heineken founded the Heineken Brewery in Amsterdam. This brewery would grow to become one of the largest and most recognized beer brands in the world.
events.name: Heineken Brewery is founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1864, during the American Civil War, the Confederate submarine H.L. Hunley successfully sank the USS Housatonic in Charleston Harbor, becoming the first submarine to sink an enemy warship. However, the Hunley and her crew were also lost in the mission.

locations.name: Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, United States

events.name: H.L. Hunley sinks USS Housatonic

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1864, the Union Army suffered one of its costliest defeats at the Battle of Olustee near Lake City, Florida, during the American Civil War. This battle highlighted the challenges faced by Union forces in the southern theater of the war.
events.name: Battle of Olustee

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1864, the first Northern prisoners arrived at the Confederate prison at Andersonville, Georgia, after being transported from Richmond, Virginia. The prison would become notorious for its harsh conditions and high mortality rate.
events.name: First Northern prisoners arrive at Andersonville

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1864, Alejandro Mon y Menéndez was appointed as Prime Minister of Spain. His tenure was marked by political instability and challenges in addressing the country's pressing issues.
events.name: Alejandro Mon y Menéndez takes office as Prime Minister of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1864, President Abraham Lincoln appointed Ulysses S. Grant as commander in chief of all Union armies during the American Civil War. This decision marked a turning point in the war, as Grant would lead the Union to victory.
events.name: Ulysses S. Grant appointed commander in chief

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1864, the Red River Campaign commenced as Union troops reached Alexandria, Louisiana. This military operation aimed to gain control of the Red River and was part of the broader strategy in the Civil War.
events.name: Red River Campaign begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1864, a reservoir near Sheffield, England, burst, resulting in the Great Sheffield Flood, which claimed the lives of approximately 250 people. This disaster highlighted the need for improved infrastructure and safety regulations.
events.name: Great Sheffield Flood

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1864, Rossini's Petite messe solennelle was first performed in a private mansion in Paris, featuring twelve singers, two pianists, and a harmonium player. This work is celebrated for its rich harmonies and has become a staple of the choral repertoire.
events.name: Rossini's Petite messe solennelle first performed

events.enhanced_description: Gallaudet University, established as the first institution of higher education for the deaf and hard of hearing, was founded by Edward Miner Gallaudet in Washington, D.C. This landmark institution has played a pivotal role in the education and empowerment of the deaf community in the United States.
events.name: Gallaudet University is founded

events.enhanced_description: During the American Civil War, the Battle of Fort Pillow occurred on April 12, 1864, where Confederate forces under General Nathan Bedford Forrest attacked Union troops, resulting in the massacre of many African American soldiers who had surrendered. This event highlighted the brutal realities of the war and raised significant moral and political questions about the treatment of Black soldiers.

image.caption: Frank Leslie’s illustration depicts Confederate soldiers massacring Union soldiers after they surrendered at Fort Pillow.
image.credit: Frank Leslie (1821-1880) — New York Public Library Digital Collections [1]
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration of the Battle of Fort Pillow. The source supplies 1894, but whether it dates creation, later publication or reproduction is not established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Fort Pillow

events.enhanced_description: Choe Je-u, the founder of the Donghak Movement, was executed by beheading on April 15, 1864, in Daegu, Korea. His movement sought to reform Korean society and promote equality, and his death marked a significant moment in the struggle against oppressive governance in Korea.
events.name: Execution of Choe Je-u

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dybbøl, fought from April 7 to April 18, 1864, during the Second Schleswig War, saw the Prussian army decisively defeat the Danish forces. This battle was pivotal in the Prussian campaign to control Schleswig and Holstein, leading to significant territorial changes in the region.

image.caption: Photograph of the battlefield of Düppel.
image.credit: Friedrich Brandt (1823-1891) — Fritz Kempe: Daguerreotypie in Deutschland , Heering-Verlag
image.date_qualification: Day after the battle; image date 1864-04-19.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Dybbøl

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1864, the United States Congress passed the Coinage Act, which prohibited the use of privately issued tokens during the Civil War. This act also marked the first appearance of the phrase 'In God We Trust' on U.S. currency, reflecting the intertwining of faith and national identity during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Coinage Act of 1864

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1864, under the Treaty of London, the United Kingdom ceded control of the Ionian Islands to Greece. This transfer marked a significant step in the unification of Greece and the decline of British influence in the region.
events.name: Cession of the Ionian Islands

events.enhanced_description: Société Générale, one of the largest financial groups in France, was founded on May 4, 1864. This institution has played a crucial role in the development of the French banking sector and continues to be a significant player in global finance.
events.name: Foundation of Société Générale

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Wilderness began on May 5, 1864, in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, as part of the Overland Campaign during the American Civil War. This brutal encounter between Union and Confederate forces resulted in heavy casualties and marked the start of a series of fierce battles in the Virginia theater.
events.name: Battle of the Wilderness

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Spotsylvania Court House, which began on May 8, 1864, was one of the bloodiest engagements of the American Civil War, resulting in approximately 4,000 casualties. This battle exemplified the brutal nature of the conflict and the determination of both sides to secure victory.
events.name: Battle of Spotsylvania Court House

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Heligoland, fought on May 9, 1864, during the Second Schleswig War, saw the Danish navy achieve a tactical victory over the combined forces of Austria and Prussia. This battle was notable for being the last significant naval engagement involving wooden ships.
events.name: Battle of Heligoland

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1864, during the American Civil War, Confederate General J.E.B. Stuart was mortally wounded at the Battle of Yellow Tavern in Virginia. This battle was significant as it marked a turning point in cavalry operations in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Yellow Tavern

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Resaca began on May 13, 1864, as Union General William Tecumseh Sherman advanced toward Atlanta during the American Civil War. This battle was part of Sherman's campaign to capture the city and was marked by fierce fighting and strategic maneuvers.
events.name: Battle of Resaca

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1864, during the American Civil War, cadets from the Virginia Military Institute fought alongside Confederate forces in the Battle of New Market, successfully driving Union General Franz Sigel out of the Shenandoah Valley. This battle is remembered for the involvement of young cadets and their significant impact on the outcome.
events.name: Battle of New Market

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1864, the New York World and the New York Journal of Commerce published a false proclamation claiming that President Abraham Lincoln had issued a draft for 400,000 additional soldiers. This hoax caused public panic and highlighted the role of media in shaping public perception during the Civil War.
events.name: Civil War gold hoax

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ware Bottom Church, fought on May 20, 1864, during the Bermuda Hundred Campaign of the American Civil War, involved approximately 10,000 troops in a Confederate victory. This battle was part of the larger struggle for control in Virginia and demonstrated the ongoing intensity of the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Ware Bottom Church

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1864, the Russian Empire initiated the Circassian genocide, forcibly displacing over 1.5 million Circassians from their homeland to the Ottoman Empire. This tragic event marked the end of the Russo-Circassian War and had lasting impacts on the region's demographics and history.
events.name: Circassian genocide begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1864, the Montana Territory was officially organized from parts of the Washington and Dakota Territories. This marked a significant step in the westward expansion of the United States and the establishment of governance in the region.
events.name: Montana Territory organized

events.enhanced_description: In June 1864, the United States Sanitary Commission hosted a Sanitary Fair in Philadelphia, aimed at raising funds and awareness for the health and welfare of Union soldiers during the American Civil War. This event was part of a broader movement to support troops and improve medical care.
events.name: Sanitary Fair in Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1864, during the American Civil War, Union forces under General David Hunter achieved a decisive victory against a Confederate army at the Battle of Piedmont in West Virginia. This battle resulted in nearly 1,000 Confederate soldiers being captured and marked a significant moment in the campaign.
events.name: Battle of Piedmont

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Petersburg took place on June 9, 1864, during the American Civil War, marking a critical engagement in the prolonged siege of Petersburg. This battle set the stage for future confrontations as Union and Confederate forces vied for control of this strategic location.
events.name: First Battle of Petersburg

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1864, during the American Civil War, General Ulysses S. Grant ordered his troops to withdraw from their positions at Cold Harbor, Virginia, marking a significant moment in the Overland Campaign. This decision came after heavy casualties and highlighted the brutal nature of the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Cold Harbor

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1864, Arlington National Cemetery was established when U.S. Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton set aside 200 acres of Robert E. Lee's estate as a military cemetery. This decision was made to honor Union soldiers who died in the Civil War and has since become a national shrine.
events.name: Establishment of Arlington National Cemetery

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1864, Sweden enacted the Decree of Extended Freedom of Trade, which introduced complete freedom of trade across the nation. This significant reform aimed to stimulate economic growth and reduce state control over commerce.
events.name: Decree of Extended Freedom of Trade in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1864, during the American Civil War, the Confederate States Navy's CSS Alabama was sunk by the USS Kearsarge in a dramatic naval engagement off the coast of Cherbourg, France. This battle underscored the global implications of the Civil War and the effectiveness of Union naval power.
events.name: Battle of Cherbourg

events.enhanced_description: The Tauranga Campaign, part of the New Zealand Wars, concluded on June 21, 1864, marking a significant moment in the conflict between British colonial forces and Māori tribes. The campaign was characterized by fierce battles and had lasting impacts on the region's demographics and land ownership.

locations.name: Tauranga, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand

events.name: End of the Tauranga Campaign

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1864, during the American Civil War, Confederate troops achieved a victory against Union forces near Kennesaw Mountain, Georgia. This battle was part of the Atlanta Campaign and demonstrated the fierce resistance of Confederate forces in the region.

image.caption: Photograph of Confederate fieldworks at Kennesaw Mountain.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — File from The Photographic History of The Civil War in Ten Volumes: Volume Three, The Decisive Battles . The Review of Reviews Co., New York. 1911. p. 103.
image.date_qualification: The source describes the photograph as dating to 1864 and says it was published in 1911; the supported display date is null.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Kennesaw Mountain

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1864, during the Second Schleswig War, Prussian forces under General Herwarth von Bittenfeld won the Battle of Als, successfully occupying the island after crossing the Alssund. This victory was significant in the context of the war, leading to the eventual defeat of Danish forces.
events.name: Battle of Als

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1864, Dimitri Atanasescu founded the first Romanian school for the Aromanians in Trnovo, then part of the Ottoman Empire. This initiative marked a significant step in the promotion of education and cultural identity among the Aromanian community in the Balkans.
events.name: Founding of the first Romanian school for Aromanians

events.enhanced_description: The University of Bucharest was founded on July 4, 1864, marking a pivotal moment in Romanian education. This institution has since become one of the leading universities in Romania, contributing significantly to the country's academic and cultural development.
events.name: Founding of the University of Bucharest

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1864, President Abraham Lincoln issued a proclamation for the conscription of 500,000 men to support the Union Army during the Civil War. This decision reflected the increasing demands of the war and the need for manpower to sustain military efforts.
events.name: Lincoln's Conscription Proclamation

events.enhanced_description: The Third Battle of Nanking culminated on July 19, 1864, when Imperial Qing forces captured the capital of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, marking the end of the Taiping Rebellion. This battle involved massive troop deployments and resulted in significant casualties, solidifying Qing control over China.
events.name: Third Battle of Nanking

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1864, during the American Civil War, Confederate forces led by General John Bell Hood launched an unsuccessful attack against Union troops commanded by General William T. Sherman near Atlanta. This battle was part of the larger Atlanta Campaign and demonstrated the fierce fighting in the region.
events.name: Battle of Peachtree Creek

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1864, the Battle of Atlanta took place, where Confederate General John Bell Hood led an attack against Union forces under General William T. Sherman. This battle was a critical engagement in the Atlanta Campaign and resulted in significant losses for the Confederacy.
events.name: Battle of Atlanta

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1864, the Second Battle of Kernstown occurred, where Confederate General Jubal Early defeated Union troops led by General George Crook. This battle was part of the ongoing struggle for control of the Shenandoah Valley during the Civil War.
events.name: Second Battle of Kernstown

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ezra Church, fought on July 28, 1864, was a significant engagement during the American Civil War where Confederate General John Bell Hood made a third unsuccessful attempt to dislodge Union forces led by General William Tecumseh Sherman from Atlanta. This battle was part of the larger Atlanta Campaign, which aimed to secure the city for the Union.
events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Ezra Church

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1864, Confederate spy Belle Boyd was arrested by Union troops and detained at the Old Capitol Prison in Washington, D.C. Boyd was known for her intelligence-gathering efforts on behalf of the Confederacy, and her arrest highlighted the ongoing espionage activities during the Civil War.
events.name: American Civil War: Arrest of Belle Boyd

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Crater, occurring on July 30, 1864, was a pivotal moment in the Siege of Petersburg during the American Civil War. Union forces attempted to break Confederate lines by detonating a massive explosive beneath their trenches, but the ensuing chaos led to a Confederate counterattack that resulted in heavy Union casualties.
events.name: American Civil War: Battle of the Crater

events.enhanced_description: The Elgin Watch Company was founded on August 1, 1864, in Elgin, Illinois, and became one of the largest and most successful watch manufacturers in the United States. The company played a significant role in the American watchmaking industry, producing high-quality timepieces that were widely distributed.
events.name: Founding of the Elgin Watch Company

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1864, the Battle of Mobile Bay took place, where Admiral David Farragut led a Union flotilla through Confederate defenses, successfully sealing one of the last major Southern ports. This victory was crucial for the Union's naval blockade strategy and significantly weakened the Confederacy's supply lines.
events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Mobile Bay

events.enhanced_description: The undeclared Uruguayan War began on August 10, 1864, when Uruguay refused an ultimatum from the Empire of Brazil. This conflict arose from political tensions and territorial disputes, leading to significant military engagements in the region.
events.name: Beginning of the Uruguayan War

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1864, the first fish and chips shop is believed to have opened in London, marking a significant moment in British culinary history. This establishment popularized the dish, which would become a staple of British cuisine.
events.name: Opening of the first fish and chips shop

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Globe Tavern, fought on August 18, 1864, was part of the Petersburg Campaign during the American Civil War. Union General Ulysses S. Grant aimed to cut off a vital Confederate supply line, leading to a strategic engagement that forced the Confederates to rely on wagons for supplies.
events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Globe Tavern

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1864, the First Geneva Convention was signed in Geneva by twelve European states, establishing guidelines for the treatment of wounded soldiers in wartime. This landmark agreement laid the foundation for modern international humanitarian law and the future work of the International Red Cross.
events.name: Signing of the First Geneva Convention

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1864, Union forces under General William Tecumseh Sherman launched a significant assault on Atlanta, Georgia. This military action was part of the larger campaign to capture the city, which was a crucial supply hub for the Confederacy.
events.name: American Civil War: Assault on Atlanta

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1864, Confederate General John Bell Hood ordered the evacuation of Atlanta after a four-month siege by Union General William Tecumseh Sherman. This marked a significant turning point in the Civil War, as the Union gained control of a vital Southern city.
events.name: Evacuation of Atlanta

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1864, Union forces led by General William Tecumseh Sherman entered Atlanta, just a day after the Confederate defenders evacuated the city. This event solidified Union control over a key strategic location in the South.
events.name: Union forces enter Atlanta

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1864, an alliance of American, British, Dutch, and French forces engaged the powerful feudal Japanese warlord Mōri Takachika in Shimonoseki, Japan. This bombardment was part of the larger conflict known as the Shimonoseki Incident, which arose from trade disputes and the enforcement of unequal treaties.
events.name: Bombardment of Shimonoseki

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1864, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman ordered the evacuation of Atlanta, following the successful capture of the city from Confederate forces. This event marked a significant victory for the Union and a critical blow to the Confederate war effort.
events.name: Evacuation of Atlanta by Union forces

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1864, Pope Pius IX established the Diocese of Gozo, enhancing the Catholic Church's organizational structure in Malta. This move was part of the broader efforts to strengthen the Church's presence and governance in the region.
events.name: Establishment of the Diocese of Gozo

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Cabin Creek was fought on September 17, 1864, in Indian Territory during the American Civil War. This engagement was part of the larger conflict over control of the region and involved significant military operations.
events.name: American Civil War: Second Battle of Cabin Creek

events.enhanced_description: The International Workingmen's Association was founded on September 28, 1864, in London, England. This organization aimed to unite various labor movements and advocate for workers' rights, laying the groundwork for future labor movements worldwide.
events.name: Founding of the International Workingmen's Association

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1864, a calamity was narrowly averted in London due to the Erith explosion, which involved a significant industrial accident. This incident highlighted the dangers of industrialization during the period.
events.name: Erith explosion

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Saltville occurred on October 2, 1864, when Union forces attempted to attack the Confederate-held town of Saltville, Virginia. The Union troops were ultimately defeated by Confederate forces, marking a setback in their campaign.
events.name: American Civil War: First Battle of Saltville

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1864, a devastating cyclone struck Calcutta (now Kolkata), India, resulting in the deaths of approximately 70,000 people. This natural disaster had a profound impact on the region and highlighted the vulnerability of coastal cities to such calamities.
events.name: Cyclone in Calcutta

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Tom's Brook, fought on October 9, 1864, was a significant cavalry engagement during the American Civil War. Union cavalrymen defeated Confederate forces in the Shenandoah Valley, contributing to the Union's overall strategy in the region.

image.caption: The national flag of the Confederate States.
image.credit: William Tappan Thompson (1812–1882) (Vector graphics by Fornax ) — SVG based on [1]
image.date_qualification: The stated image date is 1863-05-01, before the battle; it dates the flag represented, not the 1864 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: American Civil War: Battle of Tom's Brook

events.enhanced_description: The Quebec Conference began on October 10, 1864, where leaders from various Canadian colonies met to discuss plans for the creation of a Dominion of Canada. This conference was crucial in shaping the future of Canada as a unified nation.
events.name: Quebec Conference

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1864, forces of the Empire of Brazil invaded Uruguay in support of Venancio Flores' Colorado Party. This military intervention marked the escalation of the Uruguayan War, which involved complex political dynamics in the region.
events.name: Uruguayan War: Brazilian invasion of Uruguay

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Fair Oaks, part of the American Civil War, saw Union forces under General Ulysses S. Grant withdraw after failing to breach the Confederate defenses surrounding Richmond, Virginia. This battle was significant as it highlighted the challenges faced by Union forces in their campaign against the Confederacy.
events.name: Second Battle of Fair Oaks

events.enhanced_description: The Second Schleswig War concluded with Denmark renouncing all claims to Schleswig, Holstein, and Lauenburg, which came under Prussian and Austrian administration. This marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Northern Europe and set the stage for future conflicts.
events.name: Conclusion of the Second Schleswig War

events.enhanced_description: Nevada was admitted as the 36th state of the United States, a significant milestone in the westward expansion and development of the nation. This event reflected the growing importance of the western territories during the Civil War era.
events.name: Nevada's Admission as a State

events.enhanced_description: During the Battle of Johnsonville, Confederate General Nathan Bedford Forrest led troops in a bombardment of a Union supply base, resulting in the destruction of millions of dollars worth of material. This battle was part of the broader conflict of the American Civil War and showcased Forrest's tactical prowess.
events.name: Battle of Johnsonville

events.enhanced_description: The capital of the Idaho Territory was moved from Lewiston to Boise, leading to significant political tensions as North Idaho declared the move illegal and proposed secession. This event highlighted the regional divisions and governance challenges during the territorial period.
events.name: Capital Move of Idaho Territory

events.enhanced_description: In the 1864 United States presidential election, Abraham Lincoln was reelected in a decisive victory over George B. McClellan. This election was crucial as it occurred during the Civil War and reflected the public's support for Lincoln's leadership and policies.
events.name: 1864 United States Presidential Election

events.enhanced_description: The Paraguayan War commenced with the Paraguayan ship Tacuarí capturing the Brazilian vessel Marquês de Olinda in the Paraguay River. This conflict would lead to widespread devastation and significant loss of life in Paraguay.
events.name: Opening Hostilities in the Paraguayan War

events.enhanced_description: Union General William Tecumseh Sherman initiated his infamous March to the Sea by burning Atlanta and moving southward, living off the land and causing extensive destruction to Southern infrastructure. This campaign aimed to weaken the Confederacy's ability to sustain the war effort.

image.caption: Map depicting Sherman's March to the Sea.

events.name: Sherman's March to the Sea Begins

events.enhanced_description: The judicial reform initiated by Tsar Alexander II aimed to modernize the Russian legal system, introducing significant changes to the administration of justice. This reform was part of a broader series of changes known as the Great Reforms, which sought to address the inefficiencies of the Russian Empire.
events.name: Judicial Reform of Alexander II

events.enhanced_description: Confederate General John Bell Hood launched an invasion of Tennessee in an attempt to draw Union General Sherman away from Georgia during Sherman's March to the Sea. The invasion ultimately failed, resulting in significant losses for Hood's forces.
events.name: Hood's Invasion of Tennessee

events.enhanced_description: A group of Confederate operatives known as the Confederate Army of Manhattan attempted to set fires in over 20 locations across New York City in a failed effort to burn down the city. This act of sabotage was part of the broader conflict of the American Civil War.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Confederate Army of Manhattan Fires

events.enhanced_description: The Sand Creek Massacre occurred when Colorado volunteers, led by Colonel John Chivington, attacked a peaceful encampment of Cheyenne and Arapaho noncombatants, resulting in the deaths of at least 400 individuals. This brutal event highlighted the violent conflicts between Native Americans and settlers during the American Indian Wars.
events.name: Sand Creek Massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Franklin was marked by a disastrous frontal assault by the Confederate Army of Tennessee, led by General John Bell Hood, against Union positions. The attack resulted in heavy losses for Hood, including the deaths of six generals and a significant portion of his troops.
events.name: Second Battle of Franklin

events.enhanced_description: The Great Fire of Brisbane broke out, causing significant destruction in the city. This event underscored the challenges of urban fire management in the 19th century and its impact on community development.
events.name: The Great Fire of Brisbane

events.enhanced_description: At Waynesboro, Georgia, Union forces under General Judson Kilpatrick engaged Confederate troops led by General Joseph Wheeler, preventing them from interfering with Sherman's campaign. Despite suffering heavy casualties, the Union forces managed to maintain their strategic objectives.
events.name: Waynesboro Engagement

events.enhanced_description: James Clerk Maxwell presented his groundbreaking paper, 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field,' to the Royal Society in London. This work was pivotal in treating light as an electromagnetic wave, laying the foundation for modern physics.
events.name: James Clerk Maxwell's Presentation

events.enhanced_description: Paraguay formally declared war on the Empire of Brazil in support of the Uruguayan National Party, marking the beginning of a conflict that would lead to immense casualties and devastation in Paraguay. The war would last until 1870, resulting in significant loss of life.
events.name: Paraguay Declares War on Brazil

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Nashville resulted in a decisive victory for Union forces against the Confederate Army of Tennessee. This battle was crucial in weakening the Confederate hold in the region and contributed to the overall Union strategy during the Civil War.
events.name: Battle of Nashville

events.enhanced_description: The Fort Smith Council in 1865 was a series of meetings between U.S. government representatives and various Indian tribes to negotiate treaties and address issues arising from westward expansion. These discussions were crucial in shaping the future relations between the U.S. government and Native American tribes.
events.name: Fort Smith Council

events.enhanced_description: In 1865, Washington College and Jefferson College merged to form Washington & Jefferson College, a significant event in the history of higher education in Pennsylvania. This merger aimed to strengthen the educational offerings and resources available to students in the region.
events.name: Washington College and Jefferson College are merged, to form Washington & Jefferson College

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1865, the Claywater Meteorite exploded in the atmosphere just before reaching the ground in Vernon County, Wisconsin. Fragments of the meteorite, weighing a total of 1.5 kg (3.3 lb), were recovered, providing valuable insights into meteoritics.
events.name: The Claywater Meteorite explodes just before reaching ground level

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1865, during the American Civil War, Confederate forces captured Fort Stedman from Union troops in Petersburg, Virginia. The battle resulted in significant casualties for both sides, marking a critical moment in the waning days of the conflict.
events.name: American Civil War: Confederate forces capture Fort Stedman from the Union

events.enhanced_description: In 1865, Governor Reuben Fenton signed a bill formally establishing Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. This institution was founded with the intention of providing education to all, regardless of social class, and has since become a prestigious Ivy League university.
events.name: Creation of Cornell University

events.enhanced_description: In 1865, the first recorded train robbery in the United States occurred in North Bend, Ohio, a suburb of Cincinnati. This event marked the beginning of a notorious trend of train robberies that would become common in the American West.
events.name: First Train Robbery in the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: The International Telegraph Union was founded in 1865 in Paris, France, to facilitate international cooperation in telecommunication. This organization played a crucial role in the development of global communication standards.
events.name: Founding of the International Telegraph Union

events.enhanced_description: In 1865, French missionary Father Armand David first observed Père David's deer in Beijing, China. This species, now extinct in the wild, was later saved from extinction through conservation efforts.
events.name: Observation of Père David's Deer

events.enhanced_description: In July 1865, William and Catherine Booth founded The Christian Mission, which would later be renamed The Salvation Army, in Whitechapel, London. This organization aimed to provide social services and spiritual guidance to the impoverished and marginalized.
events.name: Founding of The Salvation Army

events.enhanced_description: In 1865, Britain introduced its first speed limits, setting a maximum of 2 mph (3.2 km/h) in towns and 4 mph (6.4 km/h) in the countryside. This legislation was aimed at improving road safety during the early days of motor vehicle use.
events.name: Introduction of Speed Limits in Britain

events.enhanced_description: The paddlewheel steamer SS Republic sank off the coast of Georgia, carrying a cargo valued at $400,000 in coins. This event marked one of the significant maritime disasters of the post-Civil War era.
events.name: The paddlewheel steamer SS Republic sinks

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic forest fire near Silverton, Oregon, destroyed approximately one million acres of timber. This event highlighted the vulnerability of the region's natural resources to wildfires.
events.name: Forest fire near Silverton

events.enhanced_description: The National Temperance Society and Publishing House was founded by James Black in the United States, aiming to promote temperance and reduce alcohol consumption. This organization played a crucial role in the temperance movement of the 19th century.

image.caption: Nathaniel Currier lithograph The Drunkard’s Progress: from the first glass to the grave.
image.credit: Nathaniel Currier — The Library of Congress
image.date_qualification: Temperance-movement lithograph, not a depiction of the society’s founding; dated circa 1846 in the supplied metadata, before the stated 1865 event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of the National Temperance Society and Publishing House

events.enhanced_description: Nottingham Forest Football Club was founded in West Bridgford, Nottingham, England, becoming one of the oldest and most storied football clubs in the world. The club has since achieved significant success in English football.

image.caption: The City Ground, Nottingham Forest’s home stadium, seen from a bridge.
image.credit: mattbuck ( category ) — Own work by mattbuck .
image.date_qualification: A 2008 photograph of the club’s home stadium, which the article says has been its home since 1898; it depicts the site, not the 1865 founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Nottingham Forest Football Club

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1865, the New York Stock Exchange opened its first permanent headquarters at 10-12 Broad Street, marking a pivotal moment in the history of American finance. This location became the center of trading activities and significantly influenced the global financial landscape.
events.name: New York Stock Exchange opens its first permanent headquarters

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1865, Union forces launched a major amphibious assault against Fort Fisher, the last seaport held by the Confederates during the American Civil War. This battle was crucial in cutting off supplies to the Confederate army.
events.name: Second Battle of Fort Fisher

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1865, Union forces successfully captured Fort Fisher, a key Confederate stronghold. This victory further weakened the Confederacy's ability to sustain its war efforts.
events.name: Union forces capture Fort Fisher

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, which aimed to abolish slavery and involuntary servitude, passed narrowly in the House of Representatives. This pivotal moment marked a significant step towards civil rights in America.
events.name: Thirteenth Amendment passes in the House of Representatives

events.enhanced_description: In February 1865, as Confederate forces retreated from advancing Union troops, Columbia, South Carolina, was set ablaze. This event symbolized the devastation wrought by the Civil War on Southern cities.
events.name: Columbia, South Carolina burns

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1865, the Hampton Roads Conference took place, where Union and Confederate leaders met to discuss potential peace terms. This meeting was significant as it represented one of the last attempts to negotiate an end to the Civil War.
events.name: Hampton Roads Conference

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1865, the municipal administration of Finland was established, marking a significant step in the development of local governance in the region. This development laid the groundwork for modern administrative structures in Finland.
events.name: Municipal administration of Finland established

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1865, John Deere received a patent for his innovative plough design, which significantly improved agricultural efficiency. This invention played a crucial role in the development of farming practices in the United States.
events.name: John Deere receives patent for ploughs

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1865, Tennessee adopted a new constitution that abolished slavery, making it one of the first Southern states to take such a step during the Reconstruction era. This action was a significant milestone in the fight for civil rights.
events.name: Tennessee adopts new constitution abolishing slavery

events.enhanced_description: In March 1865, Hamm's Brewery opened in St. Paul, Minnesota, marking the beginning of one of the most famous breweries in the United States. This establishment contributed to the growth of the brewing industry in the region.
events.name: Hamm's Brewery opens in St. Paul

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1865, the U.S. Congress authorized the formation of the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen and Abandoned Lands, commonly known as the Freedmen's Bureau. This agency was established to assist formerly enslaved individuals during the Reconstruction era.
events.name: U.S. Congress authorizes Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen and Abandoned Lands

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1865, Andrew Johnson delivered a notably disjointed and rambling inaugural address as Vice President of the United States, reportedly under the influence of alcohol. This event became a point of criticism and embarrassment, reflecting the tumultuous political climate of the time.
events.name: Andrew Johnson's drunken vice-presidential inaugural address

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1865, Abraham Lincoln was sworn in for a second term as President of the United States. His second inauguration took place during the Civil War and was marked by a call for reconciliation and healing.
events.name: Abraham Lincoln's second inauguration

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1865, Gregor Mendel presented his groundbreaking paper on Experiments on Plant Hybridization at the Natural History Society of Brünn. This work laid the foundation for the modern understanding of genetics and inheritance.
events.name: Gregor Mendel reads paper on plant hybridization

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1865, the Confederate States of America agreed to the use of African American troops in their military forces. This decision came late in the Civil War and reflected the desperate need for manpower.
events.name: Confederate States agree to use African American troops

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1865, the Congress of the Confederate States of America adjourned for the last time, signaling the collapse of the Confederate government as the Civil War drew to a close.
events.name: Congress of the Confederate States adjourns for the last time

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1865, during the American Civil War, Union troops compelled Confederate forces to retreat from Four Oaks, North Carolina, in the Battle of Bentonville. This battle was one of the last major engagements of the war in the Carolinas.
events.name: Battle of Bentonville

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1865, the Claywater Meteorite exploded just before reaching ground level in Vernon County, Wisconsin. Fragments of the meteorite, weighing a combined 1.5 kg, were recovered, contributing to the study of meteorites.
events.name: Claywater Meteorite explosion

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1865, Confederate General Robert E. Lee initiated his final offensive during the Battle of Five Forks, a pivotal engagement in the American Civil War. This battle was crucial in determining the fate of Petersburg and ultimately the war itself.
events.name: American Civil War – Battle of Five Forks

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1865, Confederate President Jefferson Davis and his Cabinet fled Richmond, Virginia, as Union troops advanced on the Confederate capital. This marked a significant turning point in the American Civil War, leading to the eventual surrender of Confederate forces.
events.name: Confederate President Jefferson Davis flees Richmond

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1865, the German chemicals producer Badische Anilin- und Sodafabrik (BASF) was founded in Mannheim, Germany. This company would go on to become one of the largest chemical producers in the world, significantly impacting the global chemical industry.
events.name: Badische Anilin- und Sodafabrik (BASF) is founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1865, Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, effectively bringing an end to the American Civil War. This moment marked a significant turning point in American history, leading to the reunification of the nation.
events.name: American Civil War: Robert E. Lee surrenders to Ulysses S. Grant

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1865, President Abraham Lincoln was shot by Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth while attending a performance of 'Our American Cousin' at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C. Lincoln's assassination marked a pivotal moment in American history, leading to national mourning and significant political repercussions.

image.caption: The gun used to assassinate Abraham Lincoln, displayed at Ford’s Theatre.
image.credit: Wknight94 talk — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image shows the gun on display in 2011, not the assassination in 1865.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Ford's Theatre, Washington, D.C., United States

events.name: Assassination of Abraham Lincoln

events.enhanced_description: On the night of April 14, 1865, Lewis Powell attacked Secretary of State William H. Seward in his home as part of a conspiracy to assassinate key government officials. Seward survived the attack, which was part of a larger plot that included the assassination of President Lincoln.

image.caption: Harper’s Weekly illustration and diagrams concerning the Lincoln assassination conspiracy, including the attack on William H. Seward.
image.credit: Harper's Weekly — https://archive.org/details/harpersweeklyv9bonn/page/256/mode/2up
image.date_qualification: 1865 publication date, as stated in the image metadata; not a depiction date for the attack itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Seward's Home, Washington, D.C., United States

events.name: Attack on William H. Seward

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1865, President Abraham Lincoln died from a gunshot wound inflicted by John Wilkes Booth. Vice President Andrew Johnson was sworn in as the 17th President of the United States, marking a critical transition in leadership during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Death of Abraham Lincoln

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1865, Confederate President Jefferson Davis and his Cabinet arrived in Charlotte, North Carolina, accompanied by a contingent of 1,000 soldiers. This movement reflected the desperate attempts of Confederate leadership to maintain control amidst the collapse of their government.
events.name: Jefferson Davis arrives in Charlotte

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1865, BASF moved its headquarters and factories from Mannheim to the Hemshof District of Ludwigshafen, Germany. This relocation was part of the company's expansion strategy, which would lead to its growth into a global chemical giant.
events.name: BASF moves headquarters to Ludwigshafen

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1865, Confederate General Joseph E. Johnston surrendered to Union Major General William Tecumseh Sherman at Durham Station, North Carolina. This surrender marked the end of significant Confederate resistance in the Southeast, following the collapse of the Confederacy.
events.name: Joseph E. Johnston surrenders to William Tecumseh Sherman

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1865, Confederate General Joseph E. Johnston surrendered to Union Major General William Tecumseh Sherman at Durham Station, North Carolina. This surrender effectively marked the end of the Civil War in the Carolinas.

locations.name: Durham Station, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Surrender of Joseph E. Johnston

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1865, Union cavalry cornered John Wilkes Booth in a barn in Virginia, where he was fatally shot by cavalryman Boston Corbett. Booth was the assassin of President Lincoln, and his death marked the conclusion of a nationwide manhunt.
events.name: Death of John Wilkes Booth

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1865, the steamboat Sultana, carrying 2,300 passengers, exploded and sank in the Mississippi River, resulting in the deaths of approximately 1,800 individuals, mostly Union soldiers returning home after the Civil War. This disaster remains one of the deadliest maritime incidents in American history.
events.name: Sultana disaster

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1865, the steamboat Sultana exploded and sank in the Mississippi River, resulting in the deaths of approximately 1,800 passengers, most of whom were Union soldiers returning home after the Civil War. This disaster remains one of the deadliest maritime disasters in American history.
events.name: Sultana Steamboat Disaster

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1865, the Treaty of the Triple Alliance was formally signed, establishing an alliance between Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay against Paraguay during the Paraguayan War. This treaty significantly altered the balance of power in South America.
events.name: Treaty of the Triple Alliance is signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1865, Confederate Lieutenant General Richard Taylor surrendered his forces to Union General Edward Canby at Citronelle, Alabama. This surrender effectively marked the end of all Confederate resistance east of the Mississippi River, concluding a significant chapter in the Civil War.
events.name: Richard Taylor surrenders to Edward Canby

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1865, Jefferson Davis met with his Confederate Cabinet for the last time in Washington, Georgia, where they officially dissolved the Confederate government. This marked the end of the Confederacy following the Civil War.
events.name: Dissolution of the Confederate Government

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1865, Confederate President Jefferson Davis was captured by Union forces near Irwinville, Georgia. His capture symbolized the collapse of the Confederate government and the end of the Civil War.
events.name: Jefferson Davis is captured

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1865, the electric equipment and mobile brand Nokia was founded in Tampere, Finland. Originally a pulp mill, Nokia would evolve into a major player in telecommunications and technology.
events.name: Nokia is founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1865, the Battle of Palmito Ranch occurred in far south Texas, marking the last land battle of the American Civil War with casualties. Despite the Confederate victory, the war had effectively ended with the surrender of General Lee.
events.name: Battle of Palmito Ranch

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1865, the International Telegraph Union was founded in Geneva, Switzerland. This organization aimed to promote international cooperation in telecommunication and has evolved into the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
events.name: The International Telegraph Union is founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1865, Union Army troops paraded down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., during the Grand Review of the Armies to celebrate the end of the American Civil War. This event symbolized the reunification of the nation after years of conflict.
events.name: Grand Review of the Armies

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1865, an explosion at an ordnance depot in Mobile, Alabama, resulted in the deaths of approximately 300 individuals. This tragic event highlighted the dangers associated with military supplies during the post-Civil War period.
events.name: Mobile magazine explosion

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1865, the ship Mimosa set sail from Wales, carrying emigrants bound for Patagonia. This journey was part of a larger movement of Welsh settlers seeking new opportunities in South America.
events.name: The Mimosa sets sail for Patagonia

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1865, President Andrew Johnson issued a proclamation of general amnesty for most citizens of the former Confederacy. This act was part of his efforts to promote reconciliation and healing in the post-war United States.

image.caption: Photographic portrait of President Andrew Johnson by Mathew Brady.
image.credit: Mathew Benjamin Brady — File:Andrew Johnson photo portrait head and shoulders, c1870-1880.jpg , Library of Congress.
image.date_qualification: Circa 1870; later than the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Andrew Johnson issues proclamation of general amnesty

events.enhanced_description: Between June and August 1865, English polymath Francis Galton formulated the concept of eugenics, advocating for the improvement of human populations through controlled breeding. This controversial idea would have lasting implications for social policy and ethics.

image.caption: A photograph of an exhibit presented by the Eugenics Society.
image.credit: Wellcome Library — https://wellcomelibrary.org/item/b16239210#?m=0&cv=43&c=0&s=0&z=-0.0538%2C-0.1954%2C1.1111%2C1.0617
image.date_qualification: A 1930s photograph of a later eugenics exhibit, not an image of Galton formulating the concept in 1865.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Francis Galton formulates eugenics

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1865, Confederate General Edmund Kirby Smith surrendered the last significant Confederate forces west of the Mississippi River at Galveston, Texas. This event marked the end of organized Confederate resistance in the region, following the conclusion of the American Civil War.
events.name: Surrender of Confederate forces at Galveston

events.enhanced_description: Richard Wagner's opera 'Tristan und Isolde' premiered on June 10, 1865, at the Munich Court Theatre. This opera is considered a landmark in the history of Western music, known for its innovative use of harmony and its exploration of love and longing.

locations.name: Munich Court Theatre, Munich, Bavaria, Germany

events.name: Debut of Tristan und Isolde

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1865, the Brazilian Navy achieved a decisive victory over the Paraguayan Navy in the Battle of the Riachuelo during the Paraguayan War. This battle was crucial in establishing Brazilian naval dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Riachuelo

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1865, Union Major General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston, Texas, to announce the enforcement of the Emancipation Proclamation, effectively freeing enslaved people in Texas. This event is celebrated annually as Juneteenth.
events.name: Gordon Granger's Announcement of Emancipation
